7.7.3No per-product hemp finished-product registration with NMDA/NMED found; control is via manufacturer permit + approved-lab testing + labelling + THC limitsConfirmedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfRetained. Note the rule DOES require per-product information in the operational plan (20.10.2.8(C)(2): product name, ingredients, pH, water activity, process, packaging, label, batch/lot coding, shelf-life, distribution) and notification before manufacturing a new product or changing a process (20.10.2.8(C)(3)) — that is a permit-condition filing, not a standalone product registration, and must not be misdescribed as one. Other regimes (feed, pesticide) remain out of scope / Unavailable.
7.8.1Finished-product THC limits 20.10.2.12: 0.30% total THC concentration; ≤2.0 mg/serving; ≤20 mg/package; tinctures ≤100 mg/package; broad-spectrum ≤6.0 mg/package; cosmetics/vapes 'do not have package content limits' (presentation, truncated)Correctedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfCorrected in two points: (1) cosmetics and vapes are EXEMPT from the mg caps in 20.10.2.12(A)(2)–(3) only — 20.10.2.12(D) — i.e. exempt from the 2 mg/serving and 20 mg/package limits, not from the 0.30% concentration limit in (A)(1); the original 'do not have package content [limits]' truncation is replaced with the rule text. (2) The delayed-effect provision is 20.10.2.12(G) ('requirements of this section shall be effective 60 days after the effective date of this part' = 29 Mar 2026), not subsection (F) as originally cited; subsection (F) is the NMDA-pesticide / residue-testing provision. Serving size per Table 2 of 21 CFR 101.12 is 20.10.2.12(E), confirmed.
7.8.1Cultivation test (delta-9 ≤0.3% dry weight, 21.20.2.7(K)/21.20.2.12) vs finished-product Total THC test — a crop passing at harvest can fail as a finished product if THCA is highConfirmedhttps://www.srca.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/21.020.0002.htmlRetained in substance. Precision: 21.20.2 defines THC as delta-9 THC and 21.20.2.12 uses post-decarboxylation delta-9 >0.3% as non-compliance; the finished-product rule (20.10.2.14(B)(1)(a)) calculates Total THC as (0.877 × THCA) + THC. The breeding licence's 0.3%–5.0% total THC band is a separate breeding regime (21.20.3), not a harvest-pass standard.
7.8.2Converted/synthetic cannabinoids banned at hemp facilities; narrow ≥98%-purity exception for non-intoxicating semi-synthetics (CBD, CBG, CBC, CBN) — secondary-onlyCorrectedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfCorrected and upgraded: the ban and exception are BOTH in the published rule. 20.10.2.11(K): a hemp facility 'shall not receive, possess, manufacture, offer, advertise, market, or sell' semi-synthetic/synthetic cannabinoids or products containing them, except 20.10.2.11(L), which permits receipt/use as an ingredient, at ≥98% purity demonstrated by an approved lab using a validated method, of NINE cannabinoids: THCV, CBC, CBT, CBL, CBE, CBG, CBDV, CBD, CBN. The original four-item list (CBD/CBG/CBC/CBN) was incomplete and is replaced with the full nine-item list. Definitions: 'semi-synthetic cannabinoid' (20.10.2.7(GGG)) excludes decarboxylation products.
7.8.2Scope question: does the converted-cannabinoid ban reach pure retailers / imported finished products (vs in-state facilities only)?Correctedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfRESOLVED on rule text, with enforcement practice still Verify: the ban binds a 'hemp facility' (20.10.2.7(X): extraction, manufacturing, retail manufacturer, warehouse). A pure reseller is a 'hemp retailer' (20.10.2.7(FF)) but is NOT a 'hemp facility', so 20.10.2.11(K) does not on its face bind pure retail sale — but a retail manufacturer or other facility that offers/advertises/markets/sells a converted-cannabinoid product IS bound, including for imported product it sells. Whether NMED/AG enforce against non-facility retailers under other law is Verify (enforcement practice, not rule text).
7.8.3Labelling/packaging 20.10.2.13: English labels; Total THC per serving/package (except broad-spectrum line); FDA statement or approved alternative; drug-test warning; QR codes allowed; 'No THC'/'THC-Free' claims prohibited; food-grade/GRAS packaging; FDA Food Labeling Guide recommended for 20.10.2.13(A)(1)Correctedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfCorrected and completed from the published rule: principal display panel must state the product is produced from hemp, a THC consumer notice (unless broad-spectrum), CBD mg per serving and per package/container, and Total THC mg per serving and per package/container (20.10.2.13(C)); additional labels must carry the FDA non-approval statement, pregnancy/breastfeeding consultation statement, keep-out-of-reach-of-children statement, and (unless broad-spectrum) positive-drug-test and impairment notices (20.10.2.13(D)); labels must not carry medical/health/benefit claims or child-appealing design (cartoons, candy wording, etc.) (20.10.2.13(E)); label concentration/content must not deviate >10% (20.10.2.13(G)); a STATIC QR code may provide §13(D) information only, with 'Important Safety Information' in bold above/adjacent (20.10.2.13(H)); packaging must be food-grade or FDA GRAS (20.10.2.13(I)); multi-serving packages requiring consumer dosing must contain an accurate dosing device (20.10.2.13(J)); specified labelling items took effect 60 days after the part's effective date (20.10.2.13(K)). The original 'FDA statement or approved alternative / new warning statements / placement allowances' summary is replaced with this rule text. The 'THC-free' prohibition is 20.10.2.13(E)(3) ('unless otherwise approved'), confirmed on the FAQ as well.
7.8.4Two lab regimes: NMDA Laboratory Hemp Testing Licence (21.20.3, raw hemp, fee capped $500, no public list) vs NMED-approved analytical labs (20.10.2.14–15: DOH Medical Cannabis Program approval OR ISO accreditation; finished-product testing must use approved lab; other testing need not; manifests/supplier records kept ≥2 years)Confirmedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfRetained and completed: NMED approval routes are confirmed on the FAQ and in rule; added independence rule omitted originally — 20.10.2.15(A) requires the approved lab to have NO direct ownership or financial interest in the hemp facility it tests. Testing limits are in 20.10.2.14(C) (0.30%, 2 mg/20 mg, tincture 100 mg, label-deviation, solvents, pesticide, dried-product microbiological limits) with confirming-test and COA/QR provisions (20.10.2.14(D),(G)–(H)). NMED approved-labs list updated 8 Sep 2026 and pesticide list version 27 Jan 2026 are confirmed as list dates; the labs list itself is an NMED web list (interactive page, no download file identified). Record retention for shipping/receiving records is 2 years (20.10.2.11(G)(2)).
7.8.5Pesticides: finished-product manufacturers must show hemp grown with only NMDA-registered pesticides and test residues per 20.10.2.14; NMED CHB Pesticide Testing List version 27 Jan 2026Confirmedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfRetained and confirmed: 20.10.2.12(F) (NMDA-registered pesticides only; no residues of non-registered pesticides; testing per §14) and 20.10.2.14(C)(6) (registered pesticides ≤ EPA thresholds; non-registered must not be detected). This is a permit condition, not a separate licence.

Whether retail manufacturers are listed under 'Manufacturing' or have not yet appeared is Verify. Out-of-state sources list date remains Verify (not dated in the excerpt retrieved). 7.9Counts deliberately not stated as current; secondary snapshots 19/10/1 (Jun 2026) and 10 licensed cultivators (15 Oct 2026)Correctedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/nm-approved-hemp-facilities/The NMED side is now stated as current from the official list (26 Oct 2026, counted at audit — see §5.8 row). The '10 licensed cultivators at 15 Oct 2026' secondary figure remains secondary-only and is NOT adopted; no current NMDA grower-licence count is asserted (Unavailable).
7.10No NM statute, rule or agency guidance specifically responding to federal 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 hemp dates found in NMED/NMDA/nmlegis sources to 31 Oct 2026Confirmedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/hemp-final-rule/Retained as a search result at audit date (re-checked 1 Nov 2026: no NM implementation found). Absence is a search result, not proof no response will issue — re-check after 11 Dec 2026. This is the single most important open item for operators after 11 Dec 2026.
7.10NM's pre-existing tightening (emergency Aug 2025; permanent 20.10.2 Jan 2026: converted-cannabinoid ban + 2 mg/20 mg caps) predates and is independent of PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019; NM 'comparatively well-positioned' (Drug Policy Watch, secondary)Confirmedhttps://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1_28_2026.pdfRetained. The federal container cap (0.4 mg total THC per container after 11 Dec 2026, per the given baseline) vs NM's 20 mg/package cap (50×) tension is retained: a fully NM-compliant finished product at 20 mg/package would exceed the federal container cap, and no NM rule found lowers the state cap, creates a federal-conformity trigger, or addresses state-legal/federally-redefined product after 11 Dec 2026.
7.10AG enforcement warning Nov 2025 re over-0.3% products marketed as 'legal hemp' (Vicente LLP briefing, secondary)Unverifiedhttps://vicentellp.com/insights/vicente-llp-hemp-law-and-policy-briefing-november-2025/Retained as secondary-only. It concerns over-0.3% products mislabelled as hemp, not the federal redefinition.
7.10HB 346 (2025): House Commerce substitute; would move hemp rulemaking NMED→EIB, authorise retail regulation, ban receipt/possession/advertising/marketing/sale of semi-synthetic/synthetic cannabinoids; passed House 54–7, moved to Senate; final disposition incl. pocket veto not verified; permanent rule issued by NMED indicates HB 346 did not become law in that form (inference, not verified fact)Correctedhttps://www.nmlegis.gov/(X(1)S(fwie2b5g5givumfkgas2emeu))/Legislation/Legislation?chamber=H&legtype=B&legno=346&year=25CORRECTED on nmlegis.gov: HB 346 (2025 Regular Session, 1st Session 57th Legislature, 'Hemp Products & Synthetic Cannabinoids', sponsors Romero/Lente) PASSED the House 54–7 on 13 Mar 2025 AND PASSED the Senate 37–0 on 22 Mar 2025, then its action was POSTPONED INDEFINITELY (API) — nmlegis current location: 'Died (API.)'. It did NOT die in the Senate without a vote, and it was NOT pocket-vetoed (it never reached the Governor in enacted form). It is NOT law. The EIB-transfer detail is corrected: the agency analysis states NMED would retain rulemaking until 1 Jul 2025 with EIB assuming authority on 1 Jul 2025 — a transfer that never took effect because the bill died (API).
7.10Tribal hemp plans / NMDA–NMED tribal agreements under §76-24-10; tribal 'state-licensed' Schedule III questionUnverifiedhttps://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-76/article-24/section-76-24-2/Retained as Verify. §76-24-10 acknowledges tribal hemp-plan sovereignty and authorises cooperative/joint-powers agreements (including testing/transportation) — no tribal source was retrieved for this segment, and no statement that tribal IGA operations count as 'state-licensed' under the federal Schedule III rule is made or supported here.

Part 9 §9.2.6Sacred Garden GRT case: 2014 refund sought, TRD denied; Court of Appeals held medical cannabis qualified for prescription-drug GRT treatment; TRD via AG petitioned NM Supreme Court (Feb 2020 filing; oral argument scheduled 28 Feb 2022) arguing recommendation is not prescription and Legislature never explicitly exempted medical cannabis; final Supreme Court disposition not confirmed in originalCorrectedhttps://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/nm-court-of-appeals/2044177.htmlCORRECTED — final disposition now stated: Court of Appeals, Sacred Garden Inc. v. NM Taxation & Revenue Dept, 2021-NMCA-038, reversed the denial (medical cannabis meets §7-9-73.2 criteria). The Supreme Court then quashed its writ of certiorari as improvidently granted days before the scheduled 28 Feb 2022 argument, leaving the Court of Appeals holding as the final decision; TRD then issued refunds (secondary reporting put the total at ~$15m expected, with earlier estimates $25-30m — do not quote a single refund total without the TRD record). The CRA separately added the §7-9-73.2 cannabis deduction effective 29 Jun 2021. The original's 'Verify final disposition' is therefore resolved in substance; the NM Supreme Court docket should still be cited in the final report for the quash order itself.

11.2.4"Controlling person" 10% threshold is Verify — no definition section stating a percentage was opened; 3,279-person / 10%+ figure (Aug 2024) is a tracking figure, not a capCorrectedhttps://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/Resolved: §26-2C-2 defines "controlling person" as a person that controls a financial or voting interest of ten percent or more of, or is an officer or board member of, a cannabis establishment, excluding a bank or licensed lending institution. 10% is therefore a statutory definition, not merely a reporting convention — but still not an ownership cap.
11.2.4Medical-shortage powers: §26-2C-6(N) / 16.8.8.11 — CCD may require ≥10% of monthly stock designated for patients/caregivers/reciprocal participants, incentivise production, exclude commercial activity from new licences for ≥6 months, or require producers to devote ≤25% of monthly cultivated plants to medical programme; 25% retail-sales undertaking in 16.8.8.11(A) ran until 31 Dec 2022; no shortage invocation found at 31 Oct 2026Confirmedhttps://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.htmlKeep. 16.8.8.11(C) confirms post-31 Dec 2022 measures in exactly those terms (10% stock, per-plant-fee reduction, ≥6-month new-licence commercial exclusion after exhausting production measures, ≤25% plant quota with specific tracking). "No invocation in force" remains a negative finding — re-check CCD orders/notices before advising.

11.2.6Surrender/closure: licence void and returned on discontinuance (16.8.2.8(N)(2)); product held by ceasing licensee on behalf of another returned to originating licensee; other product surrendered to law enforcement, destroyed under 16.8.2.15, or donated to patients via licensed establishment with written CCD approval and documentation; law enforcement may remove/destroy product held by a person who has ceased to be licensed; server permit immediately returned on suspension/revocation/denial of renewal (§26-2C-11(D)); no standalone surrender form/fee foundCorrectedhttps://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-8-NMACKeep disposition rules — they match 16.8.2.8(V) — but add two notice duties the original omits: licensee anticipating permanent closure must notify CCD no later than 30 days before closure and post public notice at all public-access premises at least 14 days before closure. 11.3.1"Mature" = female plant in flowering stage (16.8.8.8(B)); four growth stages (germination, seedling, vegetative, flowering); tier placement (16.8.8.9(A)) on requested level, water-right demonstration, ≥80% of authorised count harvested in preceding 6 months (if applicable), ≥75% of production sold in preceding 6 months (if applicable), and social-equity plan (race, ethnicity, gender, age, residence, underserved rural community incl. tribal, acequia, land grant-merced, opportunity zone, other rural historic communities)Confirmedhttps://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.htmlKeep, and remove original's Verify on stage names: 16.8.8.8(A) gives all four stages in full (germination = seed sprouting to seedling; seedling = shoot emerging, first leaves; vegetative = growth between germination and flowering, including clones; flowering = reproductive state with flower budding at stem nodes).
11.3.1Plant-count increases (16.8.8.10): request at renewal, supported by current mature/harvested inventory, plants harvested in preceding 3 months, medical/commercial sales in preceding 3 months; CCD may deny for incomplete information, Act/rule violations including exceeding authorised count in prior 3 months, pending/final enforcement, medical shortage in most recent 6 months, or inadequate cultivation/water plan; increase/decrease is also a producer amended-licence event (16.8.2.23(A)(3)–(4))Correctedhttps://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.htmlKeep in outline but add operative mechanics original omits: 16.8.8.9(C)–(D) — increases may be sought at renewal AND one other time per year, only in increments of 500 mature plants, up to eight increments at a time. 16.8.8.10(B) denial factors also include failure to meet required minimum monthly medical sale for last 3 months and selling <80% of cannabis/products each month for last 3 months.

12.7Adult-use user: "Prohibited: adult-use remains Schedule I; 'unlawful user' — Settled"Correctedhttps://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1234_new_6k47.pdfNo longer "Settled" as blanket prohibition. After United States v. Hemani, 608 U.S. 772 (2026), prosecution based solely on regular marijuana use, without intoxication, addiction, or dangerousness evidence, held inconsistent with Second Amendment as applied to Hemani. Statute not struck down facially. Correct to: statutory disability remains on books, but status-only prosecution of sober, non-dangerous regular user barred as applied on Hemani facts.
12.7State-licensed medical user "arguably no longer an 'unlawful user'" after 28 Apr 2026 Schedule III reschedulingCorrectedhttps://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-22/html/2026-01141.htmDo not rest this on Schedule III alone. ATF interim final rule defines "unlawful user" as regular use over extended period continuing into present "without a lawful prescription or in a manner substantially different from that prescribed by a licensed physician" (27 CFR 478.11). NM medical certification/registry enrolment is not, without ATF/DOJ statement, federal "lawful prescription." Stronger current protection is Hemani's as-applied bar, which does not turn on medical vs adult-use status. Keep any Schedule III firearms claim as Verify, not concluded exemption.
12.7Implied standalone claim: "Schedule III status by itself removes the federal firearms disability"Removedhttps://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1234_new_6k47.pdfDelete as standalone proposition. Neither rescheduling order text given in baseline, unamended §922(g)(3), nor Hemani states Schedule III medical status alone removes disability. What changed is (a) ATF "unlawful user" definition and (b) Hemani's as-applied Second Amendment limit.

Material corrections made to the corrected file (summary)

The most material corrections, in the order they appear in the corrected text, are: (1) GRT excludes CAN receipts from 1 July 2023 (TRD FYI-260, Rev. 07/2026, p. 4), resolving the original unresolved GRT-on-excise question and correcting the s.2.5 worked illustration to GRT on the $100 price only; (2) FY2027 combined GRT range 5.25%-9.4375% (TRD schedule compilation) replacing the FY2026 maximum 10.8125% as current; (3) FY2024 General Fund CAN $32.7 million confirmed on the TRD/LFC August 2025 presentation, removing the FIR Verify flag; (4) FY2025 General Fund CAN $29.9 million downgraded from adopted official figure to secondary-reported preliminary figure, with the December 2025 consensus table itself not directly opened; (5) consensus estimates replaced with the August 2026 consensus estimate (FY2026 31.8/32.5, FY2027 32.8/35.0, FY2028 34.0/37.2, $ millions, General Fund), superseding the earlier August figures 32.4 and 35.5; (6) DFA year-to-date FY2026 CAN $29,667,265.93 confirmed as General Fund receipts with the monthly range corrected to $2,222,624-$3,093,639; (7) the October 2025 missing-file data gap deleted - October business activity is filed as November-2025, so the $142.42M vs $117.72M aggregator conflict is unresolved on coverage/vintage, not on a missing month; (8) medical GRT prescription-drug phrasing reconciled with FYI-260 itself, which describes s.7-9-73.2 that way; (9) producer Level 1 confirmed at 201-2,000 mature plants and plant increases confirmed at 500-plant increments on the current SRCA 16.8.8.9 text, removing both Verify flags (401 and 1,000 were 13 January 2022 emergency-amendment figures only, superseded 22 March 2022), with the same qualifiers removed from the VICE section; (10) the 16.8.2.23 water re-documentation trigger confirmed on the full rule text (amended licence before a water-source change; change in access to the water source on initial/amended/renewal application or a 10% or more water-use increase is a material/substantial change); (11) HB 346 (2025) corrected from proposal status only, Verify, to Died (API) - passed the House 54-7 on 13 March 2025 and the Senate 37-0 as amended on 22 March 2025, then Action Postponed Indefinitely, no House concurrence recorded - and its shorthand description corrected (NMED/EIB retail hemp authority plus a semisynthetic/synthetic ban, not a CCD-licence requirement); (12) Sunland Park 200-foot school/daycare rule and special-use requirement upgraded to the city own bilingual process document; (13) Albuquerque local fees split - Retail Location Approval no fee confirmed on the city page, while the $35 business licence, $200 plus 2% zone certification and $100/$200 food permit figures are downgraded to Unverified against a current city fee schedule; (14) Albuquerque O-26-39 drafting downgraded to Unverified against the bill text and minutes while the 6-3 rejection outcome on 3 August 2026 is retained; (15) the broken DWS source URL replaced with the DWS Labour Market Review index page, with no direct PDF filename asserted.

New Mexico — Cannabis and Hemp Research

Front matter + Run 1 Parts 0–1 only (audit-corrected)  |  Research date: 31 October 2026  |  Audit corrections: 1 November 2026

Scope. This file contains the front matter (federal baseline and cross-part consistency check) and Run 1 Parts 0–1 (Headlines and Laws) only, with audit corrections applied 1 November 2026. Parts 2–12 are not included. Each section below carries its own source flags; the Parts 0–1 Verify / Unavailable register at the end is preserved in full and updated with audit resolutions — it is part of this deliverable, not an appendix to be skipped.

Audit correction (1 November 2026). Corrections applied in this file are those in the companion audit table (part0-1-audit.md). Items resolved in the audit cite the primary source; items that remain unconfirmed are still flagged Verify or Unavailable and are listed in the register at the end of this segment. Statute text quoted from mirrors (Justia / LawServer / Cornell LII) is still to be re-checked directly on NMOneSource — see the register.

Federal baseline — fixed context (given, not re-researched)

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final.
  • IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity (Treasury guidance forthcoming); adult-use remains fully subject to §280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.

New Mexico application. New Mexico has both medical and adult-use markets, and many licensees serve both. Schedule III status and the §280E change apply to medical activity only; businesses serving both markets must split their activity, and all adult-use activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to §280E. For tribal operations under intergovernmental agreements, whether any medical activity counts as “state-licensed” under the federal rule is marked Verify throughout this file — it is not answered by the sources opened in either run.

Cross-part consistency check (both runs)

  • Excise tax: 12% to 30 June 2025, 13% in FY2026, 14% from 1 July 2026, rising 1 point each 1 July to 18% on 1 July 2030 — stated consistently in Parts 0–1 and Part 2.
  • Sales: May 2026 $48,733,374.96 and July 2026 $49,814,500.78 (adult-use $39,591,627.45 + medical $10,222,873.30) agree across Parts 0–1, 2–3 and 5–6. The May cumulative $2,309,363,209.01 plus June ($46,937,513.27) plus July ($49,814,500.78) reconciles exactly to the July all-time $2,406,115,223.06. These figures are secondary reporting of CCD/CROP data, not figures verified on the live CROP dashboard, and are not adopted as official totals.
  • Licences: 3,071 approvals (400 producers, 675 micro producers, 900 manufacturers, 1,006 retailers, 56 couriers, 28 consumption areas, 6 testing, 0 research) — DATE CONFLICT, neither date adopted as official: Parts 0–1 date this breakdown to May/June 2026 (Marijuana Herald, 8 June 2026, reporting CCD data), while this cross-part note dates it to 4 December 2024. The figure remains secondary and Verify against a CCD source; agreement across parts does not confirm it. That approvals total is not the same unit as the June 2025 premises count; do not conflate them.
  • Patients: Latest official DOH figure in this dossier is August 2026: 60,501 (data as of 2 September 2026, DOH report); the July 2026 figure 60,400 (data as of 3 August 2026) is the prior month's figure, not the latest; secondary mirror figures (20,411–47,778) and the secondary January 2026 (65,215) and May 2022 peak (135,388) figures are flagged Verify in Part 6.
  • Run 2 consistency: Parts 7–12 were checked against the Run 1 anchors and no contradiction was found, except for the items listed as resolved or flagged in the research notes below. In particular: NMDA hemp fees are resolved as rule ceilings ($800 Annual / $900 Continuous per location in posted 21.20.2.10) with 2026 forms charging below them ($650 / $750), leaving only the varietal-charge difference ($10 per variety on forms vs $25 per variety in excess of one in the rule) as a residual Verify; no CBD:Total THC ratio was found in 20.10.2 as opened (20.10.2.12(A) contains paragraphs (1)–(3) only; there is no (A)(4)) — the claimed 15:1 ratio is NOT adopted and remains Unverified; Run 1's 0.30% / 2 mg / 20 mg summary stands, with the 2 mg / 20 mg caps now confirmed in 20.10.2.12(A)(2)–(3) (see §1.5); testing-lab counts are kept in their original units (6 approvals to Dec 2024, 7 premises June 2025, plus an Oct 2025 testimony figure of seven labs across eight premises) and must not be merged into one total; and the producer per-plant $5.00 commercial / $2.50 medical-only rates are confirmed in Part 11 at 16.8.11.11 NMAC (microbusinesses and integrated cannabis microbusinesses excepted).
  • Unresolved conflicts carried forward (do not publish as settled): calendar-2024 sales ($540m vs $580m vs $590m); calendar-2025 sales ($567m–$568m near-consensus vs a rejected $628m claim); the June 2026 transaction-count split; and the many items marked Verify because statute text was read on mirrors rather than NMOneSource directly — see each part's register and the combined research notes at the end of this file.

How to read the source flags

“Direct open” means the page was opened and read in this run. “Search-index excerpt” means the wording comes from a search result and has not been upgraded to confirmed. “Verify” means uncertain, conflicting or not directly opened. “Unavailable” means no source was found by the route tried. No personal phone numbers or personal emails of individuals are reproduced in this file.

Place-name discipline: Las Vegas, Santa Fe, Roswell, Clovis, Carlsbad, Socorro, Artesia and Farmington in this file are the New Mexico places unless another state is stated. Anthony, New Mexico and Anthony, Texas are kept apart, as are Sunland Park, New Mexico and El Paso, Texas / Ciudad Juárez.

No personal phone numbers or personal emails of individuals are reproduced in this file. Contradictions with the federal baseline found in this session: None in New Mexico statute or rule text opened directly. One secondary summary (CannBus Q3 2026 legal summary, accessed via search index) describes the federal order as "signed April 22, 2026 and effective April 28, 2026" — consistent with the given baseline (effective 28 April 2026); the signing date is not part of the given baseline and is not adopted here. A separate secondary item reporting a "DEA rescheduling hearing opened June 29, 2026" is not adopted: it concerns the broader proposal, which the baseline states is not final.

PART 0 — HEADLINES

0.1 At a glance

  • Both medical and adult-use cannabis are legal in New Mexico. Medical since 2007 (Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act); adult-use possession and home grow since 29 June 2021 and licensed retail sales since 1 April 2022 (Cannabis Regulation Act, HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, signed 12 April 2021).
  • Adult-use public possession/purchase at one time: 2 ounces of cannabis, 16 grams of concentrate/extract, 800 mg of edible cannabis, plus 6 immature plants. At home: no weight ceiling if the excess is stored in a private residence and not visible from a public place. Home grow: 6 mature + 6 immature plants per adult, max 12 mature per household.
  • Medical purchase limit: 425 units (≈15 ounces) in any 90-day period, excise-tax-free; after that, further purchases go through adult-use (taxed).
  • Excise tax — the step-up that matters most in 2026: 14% from 1 July 2026 (was 13% in FY2026, 12% before 1 July 2025), rising 1 point each 1 July to 18% on 1 July 2030. A 2025 bill to freeze it at 12% (SB 89) was not enacted (final nmlegis.gov action — Verify; see §1.9); a 2026 packaging bill (HB 294) was postponed indefinitely in committee (LegiScan/CannBus, secondary — final nmlegis.gov action page Verify; see §1.9). No 2026 cannabis tax freeze or cut became law in this research.
  • Market size (secondary reporting of CCD data — see caveat in 0.2): May 2026 total $48,733,374.96 (adult-use $38,651,095.94; medical $10,082,279.06); cumulative since April 2022 $2,309,363,209.01 at May 2026. July 2026 was reported as $49.8 million, with adult-use $39.6 million described as a monthly record. Calendar 2025 is reported as $567 million (MJBizDaily) / $568 million (CannBus model) — conflicting secondary figures, see §0.2.
  • Saturation — the defining market fact: 3,071 approved cannabis licences reported at May/June 2026 (the same 3,071 breakdown is dated to 4 December 2024 in the front-matter cross-part check — date conflict; neither date is adopted as official and the figure remains secondary, Verify against CCD), including 1,006 retailers, 900 manufacturers, 675 micro producers, 400 producers, 56 couriers, 28 consumption areas and 6 testing laboratories (Marijuana Herald, 8 June 2026, reporting CCD data). MJBizDaily (20 Aug 2026) reports ≈47 retail outlets per 100,000 residents, one of the highest densities in the country, and an average transaction down from ≈$50 in 2022 to ≈$38 in 2026. New Mexico imposes no statewide numerical licence cap — saturation is a structural consequence of the statute, not an accident.
  • Enforcement has hardened sharply: HB 10 (2025, ch. 85, signed 8 April 2025, eff. 1 July 2025) created a dedicated RLD Enforcement Bureau of certified peace officers with embargo / recall / seizure powers and penalties up to $10,000 per violation (plus fourth-degree felony for intentionally interfering with an embargo order, §26-2C-43). On 25 September 2026 the Bureau and the Organized Crime Commission executed a warrant near Estancia, Torrance County (102 Howell Road), seizing/destroying an estimated 6,300 mature plants (≈21,000 lb) in 21 hoop houses after a two-month investigation (RLD press release, 25 September 2026 — RLD press office archive). The case was still open at reporting; criminal charges were being pursued — no conviction is claimed.
  • Seed-to-sale changed in 2026: CCD moved from BioTrack (in use for medical since 2015) to the state-built New Mexico Seed-to-Sale System (NMS2S), built by Albuquerque-based Real Time Solutions (RTS), contract awarded 28 January 2026 (secondary — Verify against RLD procurement record). BioTrack shut for non-retailers after 5 p.m. 25 August 2026; full retail cutover at 12:01 a.m. 4 September 2026 (reported actual timeline — secondary, Verify; planned timeline per Bulletin 26-08). Couriers now get their own track-and-trace accounts, and testing must be complete before a product is marked sale-ready. An industry lawsuit to keep BioTrack running (Oasis Cannabis Co. et al., Second Judicial District Court, filed August 2026) had its injunction request continued, not granted, on 1 September 2026 (secondary reporting — Verify) — later ruling Unavailable in this session.
  • Hemp — the 2026 turning point: NMED's emergency amendment (filed/effective 1 August 2025 per NMED; the final rule's HISTORY records that filing's duration expired by operation of law 5 August 2025 and a further filing effective 5 August 2025 followed; secondary summaries giving 1 September 2025 are not supported by the rule HISTORY — see §1.5) banning manufacture/use of semi-synthetic and synthetic cannabinoids in hemp finished products was made permanent in 20.10.2 NMAC effective 28 January 2026 (hearing 2 December 2025; Final Order signed thereafter). That covers converted delta-8 THC, delta-10, THC-O, HHC and THCP at New Mexico hemp facilities. It does not by itself ban imported finished products sold at retail — that gap was expressly noted in contemporaneous legal commentary and is Verify against the final rule text (see §1.5).
  • Water rights — live enforcement risk, not settled law: The producer-licence condition (§26-2C-7(A)(3)) requires proof of a legal right to sufficient water, evidenced by Office of the State Engineer (OSE) documentation or a water-provider letter. A 2024 amendment (SB 6, ch. 38, eff. 1 July 2024) clarified the condition applies to producers/producer microbusinesses. Industry reporting in 2026 describes a CCD/OSE enforcement shift under which water-hauling via an approved provider is being treated as a 1-year "temporary bridge" requiring direct OSE approval on renewal — secondary, unverified against any CCD/OSE bulletin in this session; flagged Verify. No producer licence count lost to water enforcement was confirmed from an official source in Parts 0–1.
  • Tribal agreements: IGAs signed 25 March 2022 with the Pueblo of Picuris and the Pueblo of Pojoaque under §26-2C-41, plus separate tax cooperative agreements (May 2022) recognising tribal authority to administer their own cannabis tax on pueblo lands; the state cannabis excise tax does not apply to tribal enterprises operating on tribal lands under those agreements. Whether any other pueblo/tribe has since signed an IGA is Unavailable in this session (Part 10 must re-check).
  • Next session: The 2026 regular session was a 30-day session, 20 January – 19 February 2026 (Second Session, 57th Legislature), adjourned 19 February 2026; the Governor's signing deadline was noon 11 March 2026. No cannabis bill enacted in 2026 was confirmed in this session. The next regular session is the 60-day session in January 2027 (odd year). Do not confuse this with North Dakota's September 2026 kratom special session (2–4 September 2026) — that was North Dakota, not New Mexico, and has no New Mexico cannabis effect.

PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status — what is legal, for whom

Medical cannabis: legal since 2007. The Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act, NMSA 1978 §§26-2B-1 to -10 (SB 523, 2007, ch. 210), created a Department of Health (DOH) medical programme. It remains in force and is expressly preserved by the Cannabis Regulation Act (§26-2C-23, "Medical cannabis provisions unaffected" — full text to be quoted from the official statute in the final HTML; section title only is relied on here).

Adult-use cannabis: legal since 29 June 2021 (possession/home grow) and licensed sales since 1 April 2022. The Cannabis Regulation Act (CRA), NMSA 1978 §§26-2C-1 to -42, plus §26-2C-43 (added by HB 10, 2025) (HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, ch. 4, signed 12 April 2021; effective 29 June 2021, 90 days after adjournment, per N.M. Const. art. IV, §23 — history note on §26-2C-12). RLD states it directly [Direct open]:

"Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham signed the bill to legalize adult use, the Cannabis Regulation Act, on April 12, 2021. The Act legalized the cultivation, manufacturing, purchasing, possession, and consumption of recreational cannabis for adults 21 and older. Additionally, the Cannabis Regulation Act combined the regulation of both adult-use and medical cannabis into one commercial cannabis framework, administered by the Cannabis Control Division. The Department of Health continues to oversee the medical cannabis patient program." — RLD, "Cannabis in New Mexico", https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/ , accessed 31 Oct 2026.

"The first licensed sales of recreational cannabis began on April 1, 2022." — same page.

What an adult 21+ may lawfully do (CRA §26-2C-25, verbatim operative text as reproduced on FindLaw mirror of NMSA 1978 — [Search-index excerpt], Verify against NMOneSource before final HTML):

"A. The following conduct is lawful for a person who is twenty-one years of age or older and shall not constitute grounds for detention, search or arrest of a person or search of property, and cannabis products that relate to the conduct are not contraband or subject to seizure or forfeiture pursuant to the Controlled Substances Act [Chapter 30, Article 31 NMSA 1978] or the Forfeiture Act [Chapter 31, Article 27 NMSA 1978]:

(1) possessing, using, being under the influence of, displaying, purchasing, obtaining or transporting not more cannabis than authorized by the Cannabis Regulation Act or the medical cannabis program;

(2) possessing in excess of two ounces of cannabis, sixteen grams of cannabis extract and eight hundred milligrams of edible cannabis if the excess is stored in the person's private residence and not visible from a public place;

(3) transferring, without financial consideration, to a person who is twenty-one years of age or older not more than the amount of cannabis lawfully purchased and obtained pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act or the medical cannabis program;

(4) ingesting or otherwise consuming cannabis or cannabis products purchased and obtained pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act or the medical cannabis program;

(5) possessing, using, displaying, purchasing, obtaining or manufacturing cannabis extract using nonvolatile solvents, alcohol or carbon dioxide or no solvents;

(6) manufacturing, transporting or giving away to a person twenty-one years of age or older cannabis paraphernalia;

…

(8) smoking cannabis or cannabis products in an area authorized pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act or a local jurisdiction;

(9) possessing, planting, cultivating, harvesting, drying, manufacturing cannabis products using nonvolatile solvents, alcohol or carbon dioxide or no solvents or transporting not more than six mature cannabis plants and six immature cannabis plants per person;"

Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/nm/chapter-26-drugs-and-cosmetics/nm-st-sect-26-2c-25/ , accessed 31 Oct 2026. Subsections (7) and (10) onward, and subsection B–D (including the odour/quantity reasonable-suspicion provisions — odour alone, possession without evidence of excess quantity, and multiple containers without evidence of excess quantity are not reasonable articulable suspicion), were returned only in part in the search excerpt; the full section must be re-opened on NMOneSource for the final HTML and the ellipsis above must be filled, not carried forward as a gap.

What is NOT legal for adults (summary of §§26-2C-26, -27, -28, -30 — titles and penalty tiers below are secondary-sourced and marked Verify where the full text was not opened):

  • Public consumption outside a private residence or a licensed consumption area: a $50 civil penalty (§26-2C-26(B); the RLD "Yes and Knows" page [Search-index excerpt] states consumption is lawful only at a licensed consumption lounge or at an individual's residence, and illegal in public spaces including festivals, expos and at a licensed dispensary itself — https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/yes-and-knows/ ). The $50 figure is confirmed in §26-2C-26(B) (civil penalty of $50 for smoking in a public place except in a cannabis consumption area).
  • Possession in public above the limits (§26-2C-30(B)): more than two but not more than eight ounces of cannabis, more than sixteen grams of cannabis extract and more than eight hundred milligrams of edible cannabis: misdemeanour, sentenced under §31-19-1; more than eight ounces of cannabis, sixty-four grams of cannabis extract or three thousand two hundred milligrams of edible cannabis: fourth-degree felony, sentenced under §31-18-15. The sentence figures “up to 364 days / $1,000” (misdemeanour) and “up to 18 months / $5,000” (fourth-degree felony) are secondary summaries, not statute text as returned — Verify against §§31-19-1 / 31-18-15.
  • Sale, barter or trade of homegrown cannabis without a licence: prohibited. RLD Personal Use page [Direct open] states: "Homegrown cannabis is intended exclusively for the personal use of the resident. New Mexico law prohibits the sale of cannabis or cannabis products by anyone not licensed to sell and cannabis cannot be used to trade or barter for other goods or services. Violators of the law are subject to a penalty ranging from a $50 fine to fourth degree felony charges." — https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/adult-use/personal-use-of-cannabis/ , accessed 31 Oct 2026.
  • Use in a vehicle, and driving under the influence: prohibited. RLD Quick Reference Guide (2023) [Search-index excerpt] lists "Use in Vehicles — No — highways and streets are [public places]" for both programmes, and RLD "Yes and Knows" states "never drive high. Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal". No per se THC blood limit was found in this session; secondary summaries agree there is no fixed THC blood limit, with impairment judged under the DWI statute (§66-8-102, driving while under the influence of any drug to the degree rendering the person incapable of safe driving — secondary citation, Verify). No open-container rule specific to cannabis was confirmed; the alcohol open-container statute (§66-8-138) is not a cannabis rule and must not be presented as one.
  • Possession/use in restricted places (school bus/public vehicle, school grounds, workplace, public park/recreation/youth centre, etc.): criminal prosecution or civil penalty under the medical rules (7.34.3 NMAC, secondary summary) and the CRA — Verify full list against §§26-2C-26/-29 and 7.34.3.15 in Run 2/Part 11.
  • Taking cannabis across a state line or the Mexico border, or obtaining it from outside New Mexico: prohibited (federal law; CRA intrastate-source provisions §§26-2C-37/-38). RLD "Yes and Knows" [Search-index excerpt]: "cannabis bought in New Mexico should stay in New Mexico. It is federally illegal to travel across state lines with cannabis."
  • Under-21 possession: not lawful adult-use possession. For under-21s, possession is reported as a civil violation (4-hour drug-education programme or 4 hours' community service — secondary, Verify against §§26-2C-26/-30 text (section attribution itself Verify). Medical patients under 21 are a separate category (see §1.4).

Decriminalisation history (context, not current possession law): SB 323 (2019) provided a $50 penalty assessment for possession of up to one-half ounce (nmlegis.gov bill text — https://nmlegis.gov/Sessions/19%20Regular/bills/senate/SB0323.pdf). The “adults 18+” qualifier and “first possession” framing in secondary summaries were not in the bill text returned and are not adopted. That regime is superseded for adults 21+ by the CRA; it must not be presented as the current adult possession rule.

1.3 Possession limits, home grow, public consumption, vehicles, product types

Possession — adult-use (21+)

SettingFlower / cannabisConcentrate / extractEdibles (THC)Immature plantsSource
At one purchase / in public (outside private residence)2 oz16 g800 mg6 immature plants (per 16.8.2.40(H), cited on RLD Adult Use page)RLD Adult Use [Direct open]: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/adult-use/ ; §26-2C-25(A)(2) (quoted §1.1)
At home (private residence, not visible from public place)No weight ceiling (excess over the public limits is lawful if stored as above)Same — no ceiling on the same conditionSame—§26-2C-25(A)(2); RLD Adult Use: "Possession is unlimited at home, provided all cannabis product is stored in a place not visible from a public location" (medical wording on same page; adult-use home rule is in §26-2C-25(A)(2))
Transport (outside home)Up to the public limits (2 oz / 16 g / 800 mg) at any one time; plants may also be transported when movingAs leftAs leftPlants when moving residenceRLD Quick Reference Guide [Search-index excerpt]: https://rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/GuidetoCannabis.pdf

Important precision: The 2 oz / 16 g / 800 mg figures are simultaneously described in official material as a purchase limit ("eligible to buy up to … at one time") and in the statute as the public-possession threshold above which the home-storage proviso is needed. There is no daily, weekly or monthly adult-use purchase cap in the material returned — repeat transactions are not barred by the statute as quoted, but carrying more than the public limits outside the home is the offence. Do not rewrite this as a "daily limit".

Home grow — adult-use

  • Per adult: 6 mature (flowering) plants + 6 immature plants (seedlings). RLD Personal Use [Direct open]: "A single adult, 21 years of age or older, can grow up to 12 plants at their private residence, but no more than six (6) plants can be mature, flowering plants." — https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/adult-use/personal-use-of-cannabis/
  • Per household: max 12 mature plants total, regardless of how many adults live there (same page; §26-2C-25(A)(9) as quoted: "not more than six mature cannabis plants and six immature cannabis plants per person" — the household cap is stated in RLD guidance and in the Quick Reference Guide; the statute excerpt returned does not itself state the 12-plant household cap in the lines shown, so cite RLD guidance for the household cap, not the statute excerpt alone).
  • Conditions: Private residence; plants/cannabis not visible from a public place; precautions where children/pets live or visit (RLD Personal Use page — ingestion by children/pets "can result in serious health consequences and possibly criminal consequences for the adult homeowner"). Homegrown product is for personal use only — sale/barter/trade without a licence is prohibited (penalties $50 fine to fourth-degree felony, per RLD page).
  • Home manufacture: Non-volatile solvents, alcohol, carbon dioxide or no solvents are lawful for home extract manufacture (§26-2C-25(A)(5)); volatile-solvent / unlicensed extract manufacture is a separate offence (§26-2C-31, title only — Verify text). Do not imply home butane extraction is lawful.

Public consumption, vehicles

  • Lawful consumption places: private residence and licensed cannabis consumption areas only (RLD "Yes and Knows" [Search-index excerpt]). Consumption in public spaces (parks, sidewalks, festivals, expos, and even at a licensed dispensary that is not a consumption area) is unlawful.
  • Vehicles: consumption by driver or passengers prohibited; driving under the influence prohibited (RLD guidance; §66-8-102 DWI — Verify text). No cannabis-specific per se THC limit was found. No cannabis open-container rule was confirmed — do not import the alcohol rule (§66-8-138).
  • Restricted places: school bus/public vehicle, school grounds/property, workplace, public park, recreation centre, youth centre or other public place — prosecution/civil penalty under medical rules and CRA (full list Verify — see §1.1).
  • Odour / suspicion shield (§26-2C-25(C) as returned [Search-index excerpt]): odour of cannabis/burnt cannabis; possession or suspected possession without evidence of quantity over 2 oz / 16 g / 800 mg; and possession of multiple containers without evidence of excess quantity — individually or combined, do not constitute reasonable articulable suspicion and are not a basis to stop/detain/search. Subsection D (remainder) was not returned — open full section for final HTML.

Allowed product types

Licensed retailers may sell (subject to testing, packaging/labelling — §1.6): flower (including "deli-style" flower in NMS2S terminology), concentrates/extracts, edibles (including beverages as an edible/infused form), vapes, tinctures, topicals (secondary summaries agree; the statute's "cannabis product" / "cannabis finished product" definitions in §§26-2C-2 and 16.8.3 NMAC govern — Verify the current definitional list in the final HTML rather than relying on this summary list).

Edible limits — the one hard numeric product cap confirmed from rule text:

16.8.3.12 (Cornell [Search-index excerpt]): "(6) edible cannabis finished products packaged for commercial sale shall not exceed 10 milligrams of Total THC per serving, or 100 milligrams of Total THC per container; (7) edible cannabis finished products packaged for qualified patients, qualified caregivers and reciprocal participants … shall be identified for medical use only and shall not exceed 50 milligrams of Total THC per serving" [per-container medical cap not stated in the excerpt returned — Verify; do not state a medical per-container cap].

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.3.12 , accessed 31 Oct 2026. A secondary summary claiming a "1,000 mg per package" adult-use limit (Flourish) conflicts with the 100 mg rule text above and is rejected — the rule text prevails. Liquid finished products: "shall be single-serving only" unless otherwise specified (same section, excerpt) — beverage serving/container treatment under 16.8.3 must be checked in full before any beverage-specific claim is made (see §1.5).

Other product rules returned: Edible/topical containers must be food-grade/GRAS, child-resistant (and resealable + continually child-resistant if multi-use/multi-serving), multi-serving solids easily separable with minimal effort, each single serving in a multi-serving package marked with the division logo ≥½" × ½", packaging not appealing to a child and not using words referring to products commonly associated with minors (including "candy…" — excerpt cuts off; open full section). Child-resistant certificates must comply with 16 CFR 1700.15/1700.20.

Gifting: Transfer without financial consideration to another adult 21+ of no more than the lawfully purchased/obtained amount is lawful (§26-2C-25(A)(3)). Medical gifting: to persons 18+ enrolled in the Medical Cannabis Program only, likewise without consideration (RLD Quick Reference Guide [Search-index excerpt]).

Practitioner certification: Certification by a New Mexico-licensed practitioner licensed to prescribe/administer controlled substances, whose practice is in New Mexico (secondary summaries of LECUA/DOH rules; practitioner types MD/DO/nurse practitioner/prescribing psychologist are listed in a secondary summary — Verify the current practitioner list in 7.34.3 NMAC).
