Purchase limits: 425 units (≈15 oz) in any 90-day period for qualified patients and primary caregivers (RLD Adult Use page [Direct open]; RLD Quick Reference Guide). Once reached, additional purchases are adult-use transactions (taxed). A practitioner may ask DOH to raise an individual limit (secondary — Verify). "Unit" equivalence (≈1 gram per unit) is the conventional conversion in RLD material ("approximately 15 ounces"); the rule definition of "unit" in 7.34.3 NMAC was not opened — Verify before stating 1 unit = 1 g as a rule.

Patient home grow — Personal Production Licence (PPL): Distinct from adult-use home grow (which needs no licence). DOH issues PPLs under 7.34.4 NMAC. PPL allowance: 4 mature female plants and a combined total of 12 seedlings and male plants (7.34.4.8(A)(1), SRCA text — 7.34.4 NMAC (SRCA PDF) [Audit direct open]; an older DOH fact sheet says "up to sixteen plants, four mature (flowering) and 12 seedlings" — consistent). Cultivation may be indoors or outdoors if hidden from streets/public areas and secured against minors/unauthorised persons (7.34.4.21, secondary). The PPL plant numbers are now confirmed in 7.34.4.8(A)(1) (above); any PPL fee must still be verified against current DOH material — older material also cites a 230-unit (8 oz) 3-month limit that is superseded by the current 425-unit limit and must not be used. Whether a PPL holder's adult-use home-grow allowance (6+6, 12-household cap) stacks with the PPL allowance at the same residence is Verify — do not state a combined household total.

Reciprocity: See §1.2 (7.34.3.22). In brief: valid government-issued medical card/document from another state, DC, US territory or New Mexico tribal nation; register with a licensed dispensary for tracking; same 425-unit/90-day limit. Reciprocal participants are not issued a New Mexico resident card. Duration limits DOH may set under §26-2B-7(I) (rules by 1 Mar 2020) were not returned — Verify.

Medical tax exemption: No cannabis excise tax on medical sales to registered patients (RLD Tax page [Direct open], quoted §1.2). Medical sales are also eligible for the GRT prescription-drug deduction (§7-9-73.2) — RLD page states providers must still file GRT returns reporting the receipts, then deduct. RLD Adult Use page phrases this as "with no tax" for the 425-unit allowance — that phrasing is shorthand: it means no excise tax; GRT treatment is via deduction, not an outright exemption from filing. Part 2 must state this precisely and must not repeat "no tax" without the qualifier. (Note: a secondary news summary stating medical is "exempt from gross receipts taxes" outright conflicts with the RLD filing/deduction description and is not adopted.)

Other medical protections (flagged, full treatment in Part 12): §26-2B-4 exempts qualified patients/caregivers/practitioners/producers from criminal/civil penalties for medical use within programme limits (secondary citation — Verify text). Workers' compensation reimbursement of medical cannabis costs was upheld in Vialpando v. Ben's Automotive Services (N.M. Ct. App. 2014) (secondary — Verify citation). Organ-transplant parity: §32A-3A-15(D) treats qualified-patient cannabis use the same as any other lawfully prescribed medication for medical-care purposes including transplant (secondary citation — Verify).

1.5 Hemp and intoxicating hemp

Hemp definition and THC measurement — state law (pre-federal-change)

  • Statutory definition (§76-24-4): Cannabis sativa L. and any part thereof, including seeds and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a THC concentration of not more than 0.3% (on a dry-weight basis — the bracket in the HB 346 bill text shows the dry-weight phrase as existing law; Verify the unamended §76-24-4 text on NMOneSource).
  • Cannabis vs hemp threshold (§26-2C-2): "cannabis" means genus Cannabis containing more than 0.3% delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis (quoted §1.2). At or below 0.3% delta-9, the plant/material is hemp, not cannabis, for CRA purposes.
  • NMED measurement (20.10.2.7, final rule 28 Jan 2026): "Total THC" = delta-9 THC as measured using a post-decarboxylation method and based on percentage dry weight; THCA is separately defined (CAS 23978-85-0). Consequence: THCA counts toward Total THC after decarboxylation. A high-THCA flower that exceeds 0.30% Total THC on that method is not compliant hemp, even if its delta-9 THC alone is ≤0.3% — this is the mechanism by which the "THCA loophole" is closed at the manufacturing level in New Mexico. The NMSU hemp guidance formula (delta-9 + 0.877 × THCA for LC) is consistent with post-decarboxylation accounting (secondary/university source [Search-index excerpt] — https://arp.nmsu.edu/chapter-11/11-50.html ) The rule itself states the formula at 20.10.2.14(B)(1)(a): Total THC = (0.877 × THCA) + THC, so the NMSU formula matches the rule formula.
  • USDA-approved state plan: New Mexico runs its own USDA-approved state plan, administered by NMDA — not the USDA direct programme. NMDA Hemp Program page [Search-index excerpt]: "As of January 1, 2022, New Mexico began operating under a USDA-approved state plan administered by NMDA." USDA AMS list (updated 17 Feb 2026) confirms "New Mexico — Approved Plan". Full plan name: New Mexico Hemp Production Regulatory Plan. (Part 7 must give grower/processor licence detail; Part 1 records only the plan status.)

Intoxicating hemp — the 2025–2026 NMED rule (the central hemp fact)

Timeline (with the date conflict preserved, not smoothed over):

DateEventSource
1 Aug 2025NMED emergency amendment to 20.10.2 NMAC effective (NMED Final Rule page; NMED Order CHB 25-53)NMED Final Rule page [Direct open]; Order [Search-index excerpt]
1 Sept 2025 / 15 Sept 2025Some secondary summaries give 1 Sept 2025 as the emergency-rule effective date, with certain provisions effective 15 days later (15 Sept)Marijuana Herald Aug 2025; Harris Sliwoski analysis [Search-index excerpts] — conflict resolved in part: 1 Aug 2025 is the NMED-stated date, and the final rule's HISTORY records the 1 Aug 2025 filing's duration expiring by operation of law 5 Aug 2025 with a further filing effective 5 Aug 2025; the 1 Sept 2025 variant is not supported by the rule HISTORY
17 Sept 2025NMED Cannabis and Hemp Bureau petition for permanent amendment filed (No. CHB 25-53 (R))NMED Order [Search-index excerpt]
2 Dec 2025Public hearing (Hearing Officer Felicia Orth, Santa Fe)NMED Order [Search-index excerpt]
7 Jan 2026NMED virtual training on the final rule (Bureau Chief Johnathan Gerhardt)NMED Final Rule page [Direct open]
28 Jan 2026Permanent 20.10.2 NMAC effective — emergency rule made permanent; Total THC limit; pesticide use/testing; food-handler cards for manufacturing employees; new warning statements; QR codes allowed; retail producers (restaurants/bakeries) held to wholesale-producer requirements; new permit type; updated feesNMED Final Rule page [Direct open]: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/hemp-final-rule/

What the permanent rule does (NMED summary + Order, paraphrased — verbatim rule sections to be quoted from the final-rule PDF in the final HTML):

  • Ban (20.10.2.8(K), permanent rule): a hemp facility shall not receive, possess, manufacture, offer, advertise, market, or sell semi-synthetic or synthetic cannabinoids or products containing them. “Hemp facility” (20.10.2.7(X)) means an extraction facility, manufacturing facility, retail manufacturer, or warehouse. Named in secondary summaries of the rule: delta-8 THC (when chemically converted), delta-10 THC, THC-O, HHC, THCP and similar converted compounds.
  • Narrow exception (20.10.2.8(L), permanent rule): nine cannabinoids may be used as ingredients only if approved-laboratory analysis using a validated method shows purity ≥98%: (1) THCV, (2) CBC, (3) CBT (cannabicitran), (4) CBL, (5) CBE, (6) CBG, (7) CBDV, (8) CBD, (9) CBN. Whether the final rule fully corrects the emergency rule's duplicated semi-synthetic definition (it was noted to have accidentally duplicated the semi-synthetic definition instead of defining “synthetic cannabinoid”) remains Verify on a full read of 20.10.2.7.
  • Finished-product limits (20.10.2.12, permanent rule): ≤0.30% Total THC; ≤2.0 mg Total THC per serving; ≤20 mg Total THC per package (20.10.2.12(A)(1)–(3)); tinctures ≤100 mg per package (B); broad-spectrum ≤6.0 mg per package (C); cosmetics and vapes exempt from (A)(2)–(3) (D). §20.10.2.12(G) makes the §12 requirements effective 60 days after the part's effective date (i.e. 60 days after 28 January 2026), and §20.10.2.13(K) similarly delays certain labelling provisions 60 days. Testing formula: Total THC = (0.877 × THCA) + THC (20.10.2.14(B)(1)(a)).
  • Numeric serving/package caps — CONFIRMED in 20.10.2.12 (see previous item). The former Verify note is withdrawn: the caps are ≤2.0 mg Total THC per serving and ≤20 mg per package (20.10.2.12(A)(2)–(3)), with the same caps applying to THC drinks made as hemp finished products; tinctures ≤100 mg per package; broad-spectrum ≤6.0 mg per package.
  • Retail/import gap — narrowed, still Verify: on the rule's face the §8(K) ban binds hemp facilities (extraction, manufacturing, warehouse, retail manufacturer — 20.10.2.7(X)); “hemp retailer” is defined separately (20.10.2.7(FF)) and a mere retailer is not listed as a facility. Whether mere retail sale of imported converted-cannabinoid finished products is banned therefore remains Verify against the full rule text and any NMED guidance, and must not be stated either way. Harris Sliwoski's analysis of the emergency rule noted it did nothing against imported finished product or retailers selling it; NMED's summary saying the amendment “applies to extraction, manufacturing, warehouse, and retail facilities operating in NM” does not by itself settle the retail-sale question, because the operative text, not the summary, decides.

Delta-8 / delta-9 / THCA / other hemp-derived THC — status table (31 Oct 2026, New Mexico law as found):

ProductStatus in New MexicoBasis / caveat
Naturally occurring hemp (≤0.30% Total THC), incl. CBD, CBG, CBC, CBNLawful hemp under Hemp Manufacturing Act; NMED-permitted manufacture; NMDA-licensed growing§§76-24-1 et seq.; 20.10.2 NMAC; 21.20.3 NMAC / USDA plan
Hemp-derived delta-9 THC within 0.30% Total THCLawful as hemp (finished-product caps apply — 20.10.2.12(A))Same; delta-9 above the threshold is cannabis under §26-2C-2, not hemp
Chemically converted delta-8 THC, delta-10, THC-O, HHC, THCP manufactured/used at a New Mexico hemp facilityProhibited under permanent 20.10.2 NMAC (28 Jan 2026)NMED Final Rule page [Direct open] + Order. Older secondary pages stating "delta-8 is legal in New Mexico" (ATLRx, LegalClarity, pre-2025) are superseded for in-state manufacture and must not be cited as current law without the 2026 rule qualification.
Converted delta-8 etc. sold at retail in New Mexico but manufactured/imported from outsideVerify — see retail/import gap above. No ban was confirmed from an official source in this session.Do not state either "banned" or "legal" without the final-rule text.
High-THCA flower marketed as "hemp"Not compliant hemp if Total THC (post-decarboxylation) exceeds 0.30%20.10.2.7 Total THC definition. Enforcement against high-THCA retail is Verify (no case/rule cited in this session).
Naturally occurring delta-8 in trace amounts (not chemically converted)Verify — the rule targets synthesised/semi-synthetic cannabinoids; whether trace naturally occurring delta-8 is distinguished in the final rule text was not confirmedDo not collapse "delta-8" into a single banned category without that distinction.
Cannabis-derived delta-9 (adult-use/medical)Lawful only via CCD-licensed supply chain, 21+ / patient rules (§§1.3–1.4)CRA; 16.8 NMAC

No rule limiting intoxicating hemp products to CCD licensees was found. The reverse is documented: CCD licensees may conduct Hemp Manufacturing Act activities (16.8.2.8(F)). Hemp manufacturing is NMED-permitted, hemp growing is NMDA-licensed, and cannabis retail is CCD-licensed — three separate licences. A hemp finished product sold through a CCD retailer does not thereby become a "cannabis product" unless it meets the §26-2C-2 cannabis definition; conversely, a CCD licensee using hemp-derived ingredients in cannabis products is covered by the NMED emergency-rule summary's note that the rule "also covers cannabis manufacturers that use hemp-derived ingredients" (Marijuana Herald [Search-index excerpt] — Verify against final rule).

NMED hemp manufacturing licensing (summary — full detail in Part 7): Permits under §76-24-8 and 20.10.2 NMAC for extraction, manufacturing, warehouse and retail-manufacturer facilities. Fees confirmed in 20.10.2.8(D) (permanent rule): extraction $1,000, manufacturing $1,000, warehouse $1,000, retail manufacturer $500 (initial/renewal); late renewal fee $200; re-inspection fee $500; variance application fee $300; permits non-transferable and expiring on the last day of the anniversary month of original issue.

Minimum age — hemp: Not confirmed from an official source in this session. Secondary sources variously state 21+ for delta-8/hemp-derived purchases and cite a June 2025 Albuquerque city ordinance restricting unregulated synthetic hemp sales with age-21 controls (Drug Policy Watch [Search-index excerpt] — Verify ordinance). Do not state a statewide 21+ hemp-purchase age as law. (21+ is confirmed for cannabis purchase/consumption and for CCD licensee employment — §1.3/§1.2.)

Testing and labelling — hemp: NMED rule requires laboratory testing (potency/Total THC, contaminants, solvents, microbial impurities; pesticide testing added in the 2026 rule per NMED page), labelling with THC/CBD content and new warning statements, QR codes permitted (NMED page [Direct open]). Testing formula confirmed: Total THC = (0.877 × THCA) + THC (20.10.2.14(B)(1)(a)). Finished-product caps confirmed in 20.10.2.12 (see above). Full label contents (including any “lab-made from hemp” delta-8 warning that appears in a DOH label guide for cannabis products — NMDOH guide, Aug 2025 [Search-index excerpt]) must still be taken from 20.10.2.12–.13 in full, not from summaries — remaining label detail Verify.

THC beverages: No New Mexico THC-beverage-specific statute was found. Beverages fall under (a) cannabis edibles/infused products when made by CCD licensees (16.8.3 edible limits — 10 mg/serving, 100 mg/container for commercial sale; single-serving rule for liquids — Verify beverage application), and (b) hemp finished products when made by NMED facilities (0.30% Total THC + 20.10.2.12 serving/package caps confirmed above). Any claim of a separate New Mexico THC-beverage tax, potency cap or on-premise rule is Unavailable in this session.

State response to the new federal hemp definition (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026): No New Mexico statute, rule, NMED/NMDA bulletin or governor's statement responding to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 was found in this session. The correct statement for 31 Oct 2026 is: New Mexico has not (as of this research date) published a conforming response; its operative state standard remains 0.30% Total THC under 20.10.2 NMAC, and the federal 0.4 mg/container cap does not appear in any New Mexico rule found here. After 11 Dec 2026, NMED/NMDA guidance and any emergency rulemaking must be re-checked — this is a priority follow-up for Run 2 / the final HTML if publication slips past 11 Dec 2026. Do not present the federal dates as New Mexico effective dates.

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery/couriers, zoning/buffers

Packaging and labelling — cannabis (16.8.3 NMAC; §§26-2C-16/-17/-17.1)

Core rule text (Cornell mirror of 16.8.3.12 [Search-index excerpt], to be re-opened on SRCA):

  • Edible/topical finished products: food-grade/GRAS containers; child-resistant; multi-use/multi-serving also resealable + continually child-resistant; multi-serving solids easily separable; each serving in a multi-serving package marked with the division logo ≥½" × ½"; packaging not designed to appeal to a child, not using words referring to products commonly associated with minors (including "candy…" — full list to be completed from the rule).
  • Edible caps: 10 mg Total THC/serving, 100 mg Total THC/container (commercial); 50 mg Total THC/serving (medical, identified "medical use only") — see §1.3. A conflicting secondary "1,000 mg/package" claim is rejected (see §1.3).
  • Liquid finished products: single-serving only unless otherwise specified.
  • Child-resistant certificates must show compliance with 16 CFR 1700.15 and 1700.20.
  • General finished-product labelling (secondary summary of 16.8.3, Verify full list): product name/type, cannabinoid strength (THC/CBD, per-serving and per-unit), net weight/quantity/volume, THC symbol, ingredients, manufacturer/distributor, manufacture/expiry dates, testing laboratory name + licence number, test date, retail licensee number, poison-control number, pictorial minor warning, FDA-not-approved disclaimer ("This product is not approved by the FDA to treat, cure, or prevent any disease. FDA has not evaluated this product for safety, effectiveness, and quality" — wording from DOH label guide [Search-index excerpt], Verify against 16.8.3.10).
  • Exit package: every product leaving a retailer goes in an opaque exit package (secondary summary — Verify in 16.8.3).
  • Misbranded / adulterated: §§26-2C-17.1 (misbranded) and -18.1 (adulterated) — titles only in this session; Verify operative text. HB 294 (2026, dead — §1.9) would have added artificial-colour-additive adulteration and packaging-colour rules; none of it is law.
  • Consumption-area labelling exemption: 16.8.3.11 provides packaging/labelling exemptions + minimum requirements for consumption areas, including a measurement device for multi-serving edibles in ≤10 mg Total THC increments (SRCA 16.8.3 excerpt [Search-index excerpt]).

Advertising and marketing (§26-2C-20; 16.8.3.8)

Verbatim operative text (§26-2C-20, LawServer mirror [Search-index excerpt], https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/new-mexico/nm-statutes/newmexicostatutes_26-2c-20 , accessed 31 Oct 2026):

"B. The division shall promulgate rules consistent with industry standards that: (1) prohibit the advertisement and marketing of cannabis products: (a) on radio, television or other broadcast media, internet pop-ups and mass transit vehicles; provided that the division shall not prohibit advertising and marketing to: 1) subscribers of subscription-based radio, television or other broadcast media who are twenty-one years of age or older; or 2) persons twenty-one years of age or older who have solicited the advertising or marketing; (b) that are false, deceptive or misleading, including making unproven health benefit claims; (c) that are on billboards, posters, handbills or other visual media that are located or can be viewed within three hundred feet of a school, daycare center or church; (d) that depict consumption by children or other persons who appear to be younger than twenty-one years of age; (e) that use predatory marketing and advertising practices targeting minors; or (f) that are designed using cartoon characters or to mimic any other product brand; and (2) require: (a) all advertisements and marketing to accurately and legibly identify all persons responsible for its content; and (b) advertisements in print and digital communications to be placed only where the audience is reasonably expected to be twenty-one years of age or older as determined by reliable, current audience composition data."

"Advertising" excludes (same section): a sign/outdoor display permanently affixed to licensed premises inducing sale of products produced/manufactured/sold there; a label on the product/container; and unpaid editorial material not intended to promote a particular brand/company. Note the 300-foot advertising buffer (school/daycare/church) is distinct from the local zoning buffer cap in §26-2C-12 (schools/daycares only, max 300 feet — below). Do not conflate them.

Delivery / couriers (§26-2C-15; 16.8.2.40–.41; 16.8.2.13 transport)

  • Licence required: a person shall not transport cannabis products directly to qualified patients, primary caregivers, reciprocal participants or consumers unless licensed under the CRA/rules (16.8.2.41(B), Cornell [Search-index excerpt]).
  • Consumer delivery: from a licensed retail establishment to a qualified patient 18+, primary caregiver, reciprocal participant, or consumer 21+; only to the intended authorised recipient identified by the retailer; only products for sale at that retail establishment (16.8.2.41(C)).
  • Operational rules (Cornell 16.8.2.41 [Search-index excerpt]): products must be individually packaged and labelled before transport; courier shall not possess a delivery package >24 hours (undelivered product returned to the originating retailer within that period); delivery vehicle shall not display signage/logos/symbols indicating cannabis transport; only shelf-stable products (perishable / time-and-temperature-controlled products may not be delivered); maximum retail value in a courier vehicle $10,000 in the rule text as returned — but the September 2025 proposed amendments would reduce this to $5,000 (CCD rule-hearing notice [Search-index excerpt]). Adoption of the $5,000 cap is Verify — do not state $5,000 as current law until the adopted rule is opened. Payments: proposed amendments would allow any legal payment method including gift-card pre-payments but exclude EBT cards (same notice — also Verify adoption).
  • Delivery address: proposed amendments "clarif[y] delivery … exclusively to residential addresses" (CCD notice) — Verify whether residential-only delivery is already in the current rule or only proposed. Secondary courier summaries state residential-only as current law; the rule text returned (16.8.2.41) does not itself state "residential only" in the excerpt — flag the conflict.
  • Inter-licensee transport (16.8.2.13, Justia/Cornell [Search-index excerpts], current through NM Register Vol. 36 No. 12, 24 June 2025): only by a licensee or its designated employees/contractors; completed transfer/sales invoice + chain-of-custody form, unalterable once transport begins; no human-powered or unmanned vehicles; product inside a motor vehicle/trailer in reasonable operating condition, not visible/identifiable from outside, locked in a box/container/cage secured inside (including in the trunk); vehicle alarm; MVD registration; driver must show employee badge, driver's licence, registration, proof of insurance, shipping manifest/chain of custody; no alcohol in the same vehicle; vehicles subject to division inspection during transport; travel only between shipping/receiving licensees and own premises (necessary rest/fuel/repair stops excepted); foot/hand-truck/forklift only where premises are in the same building/premises and vehicle transport is not operationally feasible.
  • Courier fee (secondary, Part 4 detail): $250/yr + $100/additional premises (Flourish summary of 16.8.11 — Verify against SRCA 16.8.11).

Zoning and buffer distances — state baseline (§26-2C-12)

Verbatim (§26-2C-12, Justia 2021 [Search-index excerpt], https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/2021/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-12/ , accessed 31 Oct 2026; History: Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §12):

"A. A local jurisdiction may: (1) adopt time, place and manner rules that do not conflict with the Cannabis Regulation Act or the Dee Johnson Clean Indoor Air Act [Chapter 24, Article 16 NMSA 1978], including rules that reasonably limit density of licenses and operating times consistent with neighborhood uses; and (2) allow for the smoking, vaporizing and ingesting of cannabis products within an indoor or outdoor cannabis consumption area if: (a) unless licensed pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act [Chapter 26, Article 2B NMSA 1978], access to the cannabis consumption area is restricted to persons twenty-one years of age and older; and (b) the cannabis establishment or integrated cannabis microbusiness is located at a minimum distance from a school or daycare center as determined by the local jurisdiction, but which minimum distance shall not be set at any more than three hundred feet from a school or daycare center that was in existence at the time the establishment or microbusiness was licensed.

B. A local jurisdiction shall not: (1) prevent transportation of cannabis products on public roads by a licensee that transports cannabis products in compliance with the Cannabis Regulation Act; (2) completely prohibit the operation of a licensee; (3) prohibit or limit signage attached to or located on licensed premises that identifies the premises as a cannabis establishment; (4) require a licensed premises or a cannabis consumption area to be any more than three hundred feet from a school or daycare center that was in existence at the time the cannabis establishment or integrated cannabis microbusiness was licensed; (5) require an existing licensee at a licensed premises to relocate; or (6) prohibit a person from producing homegrown cannabis as provided for in the Cannabis Regulation Act."

Reading notes (do not over-read): (1) Localities cannot ban licensees outright, cannot impose a >300-foot school/daycare buffer, cannot ban licensee-identifying signage, cannot force relocation of an existing licensee, and cannot ban homegrow. (2) They can adopt time/place/manner rules, reasonably limit density and operating times, and set a school/daycare buffer up to 300 feet. (3) There is no statewide 600-foot retailer-to-retailer spacing rule in §26-2C-12 — a secondary page claiming "600 feet from another cannabis retail establishment" as a state rule is not supported by the statute text above and must be treated as a local rule (if anywhere) or an error, Verify in Part 3. (4) Measurement method (door-to-door vs lot-line vs shortest direct line) is set locally; Estancia's ordinance (Dec 2025, secondary) uses "shortest direct line" — local variation is expected and Part 3 must not impose one method statewide. (5) CCD's standing policy, per Vicente LLP analysis [Search-index excerpt], is to defer to localities on proximity questions and CCD has not promulgated administrative rules on local zoning — Verify against CCD guidance in Part 3. Consumption-area smoking must also satisfy the Clean Indoor Air Act (smoke must not infiltrate other indoor workplaces/public places; Estancia ordinance requires a standalone building for smoking consumption areas — local rule, not state rule).

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking

Current system (from 4 September 2026): New Mexico Seed-to-Sale System (NMS2S), built by Real Time Solutions (RTS), Albuquerque-based, free for all licensees. Prior system: BioTrack (DOH medical track-and-trace from 2015; CCD-accessed after 2021; DOH contract extended through 31 Oct 2024; RLD emergency procurement with BT Government Inc. expiring 15 Sept 2026; RFP opened Oct 2025; RTS awarded 28 Jan 2026 under RFP 26-420-42000-00001 — secondary sourcing, Verify against RLD procurement record).

CCD Industry Bulletin 26-08 (10 Aug 2026) [Direct open] — https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/26-08-Upcoming-Transition-to-New-State-Mandated-Track-and-Trace-System.pdf — key passages:

"the Cannabis Control Division (CCD) is preparing to transition from BioTrack to the New Mexico Seed-to-Sale System (NMS2S), the state's successor state-mandated seed to sale track-and-trace system."

"Migration is expected to begin at the end of the day on August 25, 2026, with launch currently anticipated during the first week of September 2026."

"Couriers will be provided with track-and-trace accounts, allowing cannabis deliveries involving couriers to be tracked directly within the state-mandated track-and-trace system. Deliveries made using licensed couriers or a licensee's internal couriers will be required to be tracked through the system."

"Sale-ready products will be identified as either 'Packaged Products' or 'Deli Style Flower.' Before a product can be converted to one of these sale-ready product types, the applicable testing requirements must be completed. A finished product test that meets the compliance requirements set forth in 16.8.7.15 NMAC will be required before a package may be transferred to a retail location."

"Existing BioTrack user accounts will not be migrated… New user accounts will need to be created within the successor system. At launch, the primary controlling person identified in the licensee's NM-PLUS account will be established as the initial system administrator."

Timeline as planned vs as reported (keep distinct): Planned (Bulletin 26-08): migration from end of day 25 Aug 2026; launch first week of Sept 2026. Reported actual (secondary: CCD Bulletin 26-09 / Leafnet / GrowFlow summaries [Search-index excerpts]): BioTrack unavailable for non-retailers from 25 Aug 2026 5 p.m.; non-retailer inventory in NMS2S ~31 Aug; retailer migration 1–2 Sept; full cutover 4 Sept 2026 12:01 a.m.; third-party POS integrations supported at launch, fuller API shortly after. Verify actual cutover completion and any post-cutover CCD bulletin in Part 5 — the 4 Sept date is secondary in this session, even though the August bulletin makes it highly likely.

Requirements (from Bulletin 26-08 + rule references): All licensee inventory, transfers, testing-gated sale-ready conversion, and courier deliveries tracked in NMS2S; BioTrack inventory was the migration source of truth (only BioTrack-reflected data migrated); producer inventory types post-transition limited to Deli Style Cannabis, Bulk Flower, Bulk Trim, Clones, Seedlings, Seeds; system functionality does not authorise activity the rules prohibit ("availability of a function within BioTrack did not, by itself, authorize activity that was otherwise inconsistent with applicable statutes or rules" — Bulletin 26-08). The governing track-and-trace rule section(s) in 16.8.2 NMAC were not opened in full in this session — cite the bulletin for the system, and Verify the rule citation(s) for the final HTML. New Mexico is not a Metrc state (secondary — consistent with BioTrack/NMS2S history; do not state Metrc requirements for New Mexico).

Medical tracking note: DOH previously operated a separate medical tracking portal (mcp-tracking.nmhealth.org, cited in a secondary wiki [Search-index excerpt]). Whether medical tracking is now fully unified in NMS2S, and how medical vs adult-use product is distinguished in NMS2S (relevant to the federal Schedule III split in the baseline), is Verify in Part 5/11 — secondary NMS2S summaries state NMS2S "tracks medical and adult-use product separately and more clearly than BioTrack did", but that is secondary.

1.8 Employment and drug-testing protections

Medical patients — current law (§26-2B-9)

Verbatim current text (Justia 2025 [Search-index excerpt], quoted in full in §1.2):

"A. Unless a failure to do so would cause the employer to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or federal regulations, it is unlawful to take an adverse employment action against an applicant or an employee based on conduct allowed under the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act. B. Nothing in this section shall: (1) restrict an employer's ability to prohibit or take adverse employment action against an employee for use of, or being impaired by, medical cannabis on the premises of the place of employment or during the hours of employment; or (2) apply to an employee whose employer deems that the employee works in a safety-sensitive position."

History: Laws 2019, ch. 247, §11 (SB 406), eff. 14 June 2019.

What this does and does not do (read carefully — secondary summaries overstate it):

  • It bars adverse action "based on conduct allowed under" LECUA, subject to the federal-benefit carve-out. It does not in its current text: bar random drug testing for cannabis; provide that metabolites alone ≠ impairment; require a medical review officer; or define impairment. Those provisions were in the failed 2025 bills HB 230 / SB 269 (see §1.9) and in the pending-not-enacted 2026 bill SB 129 (see §1.9) — none of them is law.
  • Safety-sensitive carve-out: the employer deems the position safety-sensitive (statutory wording) — no statutory definition of safety-sensitive was returned; Verify whether any rule or case law defines it.
  • On-premises / during-hours use or impairment: employer may prohibit and act.
  • Case-law tension (must be disclosed, not smoothed over): Garcia v. Tractor Supply Co., 154 F. Supp. 3d 1225 (D.N.M. 2016), held LECUA + the Human Rights Act do not require an employer to accommodate medical cannabis use / do not provide a cause of action on those facts (Justia annotation [Search-index excerpt]; Baker Donelson guide, Nov 2025 [Search-index excerpt], notes courts "have not yet reconciled these inconsistencies"). Garcia predates the 2019 §26-2B-9 employment-protection amendment; whether §26-2B-9 as amended in 2019 changes the Garcia result has not been resolved in any authority opened in this session — Verify (no post-2019 appellate decision was found here). Do not present §26-2B-9 as a settled private right of action.
  • No general New Mexico drug-testing statute regulates employer drug testing of employees/applicants generally (Baker Donelson [Search-index excerpt]); sector rules exist (motor carriers; health-care providers in state facilities, §9-7-18 — secondary citation, Verify). State Personnel Office rules authorise random testing (including cannabis) of state employees in safety-sensitive positions (1.7.8.7(M) NMAC, cited in HB 230 fiscal analysis [Search-index excerpt] — Verify).
  • Adult-use employees: no employment protection in the CRA. §26-2C-34 is titled "Employer protections; exemptions" (LawServer index) — i.e. it protects employers, not adult-use employees. Secondary summaries agree: employers may take adverse action based on a positive THC/metabolite test tied to recreational use. Verify §26-2C-34 text in the final HTML; do not invert its direction.
  • Other medical workplace-adjacent protections (secondary, Verify): workers' compensation reimbursement (Vialpando, 2014); probation/parole medical use permitted per RLD Quick Reference Guide ("Yes – may use for medicinal" — Verify against current supervision rules); organ-transplant parity (§32A-3A-15(D) — Verify).

What the failed/pending bills would have changed (for contrast only — NOT law)

  • HB 230 (2025) / SB 269 (2025): metabolites alone ≠ impairment; no random cannabis testing; testing only on reasonable suspicion of impairment at work, after an accident involving another person, or after significant property damage with reasonable suspicion; medical-review-officer review; DOH + Workforce Solutions impairment guidelines. HB 230 passed the House 12 Mar 2025 (secondary reporting — verify the vote on nmlegis.gov) and was not enacted (final Senate disposition Verify); SB 269 was postponed indefinitely 10 Mar 2025 (secondary tracker — verify on nmlegis.gov). Neither is law.
  • SB 129 (2026): would have kept §26-2B-9(A)–(B) and added subsection C barring a state/political-subdivision employer from controlling an employee's off-hours medical cannabis use while a qualified patient (nmlegis text [Direct open of bill text page] — https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/26%20Regular/bills/senate/SB0129.HTML ). Not enacted in the 2026 session as far as this research found — Verify final action on nmlegis.gov (see §1.9). Its narrower scope (public employers only, off-hours control) must not be confused with the broader HB 230/SB 269 (2025) proposals.

1.9 Pending legislation — confirmed status on nmlegis.gov / session record

Session framework (confirmed): New Mexico alternates 60-day sessions in odd years (full scope) and 30-day sessions in even years (budget/appropriations + governor-messaged bills). 2026 regular session: Second Session, 57th Legislature, 20 January – 19 February 2026 (adjourned noon 19 Feb 2026); bill-signing / pocket-veto deadline noon 11 March 2026 (UNM Government Relations final report, 29 Apr 2026 [Search-index excerpt]; Stateside wrap [Search-index excerpt]). 686 bills introduced (NMML Bulletin Vol. 2026-5, 20 February 2026); 126 resolutions introduced (Stateside, secondary); 74 bills passed the Legislature (NMML Bulletin Vol. 2026-5); the Governor signed 71 of 74 bills (2026 recap, secondary). The “127 bills/resolutions passed” figure (Stateside) appears to count bills + resolutions combined and is not adopted as bills passed. Pocket-veto rule applied: any 2026 bill not signed by noon 11 Mar 2026 did not become law. Federal baseline — fixed context, not re-researched. State-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law. **No contradiction to that baseline was found in the tax or local-rule sources read for this file.** Where a secondary source gave a different federal effective date (e.g. “~22 April 2026” for the Schedule III order), the fixed baseline date of 28 April 2026 governs and the secondary date is not adopted.

2.2 Cannabis excise tax — statute, schedule, taxpayer

Citation. §7-42-3 NMSA 1978, “Cannabis excise tax.” History. Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §45 (HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, signed 12 April 2021, effective 29 June 2021 under N.M. Const. art. IV, §23, 90 days after adjournment). No amendment to the rate schedule in §7-42-3 itself was found in current text; the distribution section (§7-1-6.68) was amended in 2023 and 2025 — see §2.6. Official link for the schedule as published by the administrator: TRD, Cannabis Excise Tax — https://www.tax.newmexico.gov/businesses/cannabis-excise-tax/ (accessed 31 Oct 2026). NMOneSource re-check required before publication (see honesty note above).

Verbatim operative text — §7-42-3(A)–(C):

“A. An excise tax is imposed on a cannabis retailer that sells cannabis products in this

state. The tax imposed by this section may be referred to as the ‘cannabis excise tax’.

B. The rate of the cannabis excise tax shall be at the following rates and shall be applied

to the price paid for a cannabis product:

(1) prior to July 1, 2025, twelve percent;

(2) beginning July 1, 2025 and prior to July 1, 2026, thirteen percent;

(3) beginning July 1, 2026 and prior to July 1, 2027, fourteen percent;

(4) beginning July 1, 2027 and prior to July 1, 2028, fifteen percent;

(5) beginning July 1, 2028 and prior to July 1, 2029, sixteen percent;

(6) beginning July 1, 2029 and prior to July 1, 2030, seventeen percent; and

(7) beginning July 1, 2030, eighteen percent.

C. The cannabis excise tax shall not apply to retail sales of medical cannabis products

sold to a qualified patient or a primary caregiver who presents a registry identification

card issued pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act [Chapter 26, Article 2B

NMSA 1978] or a reciprocal participant who presents similar proof from another state, the

District of Columbia or a territory or commonwealth of the United States at the time of

the sale.”

TRD reproduces the identical schedule on its Cannabis Excise Tax page (accessed 31 Oct 2026), confirming the schedule above.

Who is the taxpayer. TRD (accessed 31 Oct 2026): “Cannabis excise tax is paid by a cannabis retailer that sells products in New Mexico,” defined by reference to its CCD licence to sell to a person who purchases for a purpose other than resale. “Wholesalers, manufacturers, and producers are not required to register for the CAN if they do not fit the definition of a cannabis retailer.” RLD CCD Tax Reporting page (accessed 31 Oct 2026) adds: “Taxpayers must be licensed with the Cannabis Control Division … before they can establish a Cannabis Excise Tax account with Tax & Rev,” and businesses already registered for GRT “must also have a Cannabis Excise Tax account” for adult-use retail sales. Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/compliance/tax-reporting/

Uniform statewide rate. TRD FAQ, verbatim in substance (accessed 31 Oct 2026): “No, the rate is the same throughout the state, but businesses must report by location so that localities can receive their share of the tax.” Example given by TRD: a retailer in the City of Albuquerque reports using the City of Albuquerque location code so TRD distributes the local share to that city. Location is determined by where the product is given to the customer — at the retail location, or, if delivered, at the delivery location (TRD, “Determining Location Code and Rate,” accessed 31 Oct 2026; TRD Gross Receipts Location Code and Tax Rate Map is the tool TRD points to).

Filing and payment (official, TRD/RLD, accessed 31 Oct 2026).

  • Filed and paid monthly by the 25th of the month following the sale (e.g. April sales by

    • 25 May). Late returns/payments are subject to penalty and interest.

  • Returns filed electronically through the Taxpayer Access Point (TAP) portal:

    • https://tap.state.nm.us/Tap/

  • Payment electronically by ACH debit (e-check) or credit card (credit-card payments subject

    • to a 2.4% convenience fee). Fedwire and ACH Credit payments cannot be accepted for CAN or for GRT on cannabis retail sales. Paper check or cash requires an approved waiver / exception from the e-pay mandate (waiver forms in the “E-File and E-Pay Exceptions” folder on TRD Forms & Publications).

Failed freeze bills — NOT current law.

  • SB 99, 56th Legislature, Second Session (2024), Sen. Duhigg — “Removing Incremental

    • Increases to the Cannabis Excise Tax,” would have fixed the rate at 12%. Text on nmlegis.gov: https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/24%20Regular/bills/senate/SB0099.pdf — **did not become law; the §7-42-3 schedule above remains in force.**

  • SB 89, 57th Legislature, First Session (2025), Sen. Duhigg — same title/purpose, fixed 12%

    • from 1 Jul 2025. Referred to Senate Tax, Business and Transportation Committee (STBTC/SFC); secondary tracking (LegiScan, accessed via search 31 Oct 2026) records it as “Introduced — Dead,” last action 23 Jan 2025, and CannBus Q3 2026 market report records it as died in committee. It did not become law. Its Fiscal Impact Report figures are cited in §2.7 ONLY as a forecast source, not as law. Final nmlegis.gov disposition should be re-confirmed on the bill page before publication — listed as Verify (low risk: the operative proof is that TRD still publishes the 13%/14% steps and the current statute still contains them).

  • No pocket-veto question arises for these bills because they were never enacted; the

    • step-ups therefore took effect on schedule on 1 Jul 2025 (13%) and 1 Jul 2026 (14%).

2.3 What the excise tax is charged on — and what it is not

  • Base: “the price paid for a cannabis product.” (§7-42-3(B).)
  • “Cannabis product” in TRD FYI-260 (TRD guidance, file https://realfile.tax.newmexico.gov/FYI-260.pdf)

    • is summarised as a product that is or contains cannabis or cannabis extract, including edible or topical products that may also contain other ingredients. TRD FYI-260, Rev. 07/2026, was opened in the audit (file: https://realfile.tax.newmexico.gov/FYI-260.pdf); p. 4 confirms the GRT rule in §2.5. The definition summary above is retained as originally sourced.

  • The excise tax is an adult-use-only tax in effect: medical sales are carved out by

    • §7-42-3(C) (see §2.4). Wholesale / producer / manufacturer sales that are not retail sales to a non-resale purchaser are not CAN-taxable sales, but those businesses must still register for GRT and other applicable business taxes (TRD, accessed 31 Oct 2026).

  • Whether GRT is charged on the CAN amount is resolved: TRD FYI-260, Rev. 07/2026, p. 4, states that the gross receipts tax “excludes receipts from the cannabis excise tax beginning on July 1, 2023” (see §2.5).

2.4 Medical exemption — excise and GRT are different mechanisms

Excise: full exemption, at the point of sale, on presentation of proof. §7-42-3(C) (verbatim in §2.2): the CAN “shall not apply to retail sales of medical cannabis products sold to a qualified patient or a primary caregiver who presents a registry identification card issued pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act … or a reciprocal participant who presents similar proof from another state, the District of Columbia or a territory or commonwealth of the United States at the time of the sale.” TRD confirms (accessed 31 Oct 2026): “Medical cannabis sales are not subject to the CAN.”

GRT: deduction, not exemption — receipts are still reported. TRD Cannabis Excise Tax page (accessed 31 Oct 2026) lists, under GRT deductions that may apply to the cannabis industry:

  • §7-9-47 NMSA 1978 — deduction for sales of cannabis products for resale; and
  • **§7-9-73.2 NMSA 1978 — deduction for medical cannabis. “This deduction is required to be

    • separately reported starting July 1, 2025.”**

RLD CCD Tax Reporting page (accessed 31 Oct 2026) phrases the same treatment as: “Medical cannabis sales are eligible for the GRT deduction for prescription drugs. Medical cannabis providers still must file GRT returns with the receipts from medical cannabis sales reported in gross receipts, but they can deduct their medical cannabis sales to reduce their GRT liability.” Reconciliation: TRD’s current, section-specific citation (§7-9-73.2, separately reported from 1 Jul 2025) is adopted as authoritative. RLD’s “prescription drugs” phrasing matches TRD FYI-260, Rev. 07/2026, which itself describes §7-9-73.2 as a prescription-drug deduction; it describes the same filing mechanics (report, then deduct) and is not a separate exemption. Secondary guides that say medical sales are simply “exempt from GRT” oversimplify: the correct statement is **exempt from CAN; deductible from GRT on a filed return, separately reported from 1 Jul 2025.** Verify: the full text of §7-9-73.2 (scope, caps, and whether any quantity limit applies) was not opened in this run; the patient purchase-limit question belongs to Part 1 and is not decided here.

2.5 Gross receipts tax (GRT)

Nature. New Mexico has no conventional sales tax. GRT is imposed on the seller under the Gross Receipts and Compensating Tax Act; sellers commonly pass it to buyers as a line item. TRD (accessed 31 Oct 2026): “all sales in New Mexico are subject to the GRT, unless a deduction or exemption exists.”

State component. 4.875%. History corroborated by secondary guides citing TRD: 5.125% before 1 Jul 2022, reduced in steps, 4.875% from 1 Jul 2023 to present. One secondary summary (CannBus Legal Summary Q3 2026) still shows “5.125% statewide base rate” — that is stale and rejected; the 4.875% figure is adopted. **Verify against the current TRD GRT rate schedule before publication**, because the TRD GRT schedule page itself was not opened in this run.

Combined rate. There is no single combined rate. The combined state + local rate is set by the destination-based location code (where the product is given to the customer). The TRD schedule effective 1 July 2026 – 30 June 2027, as compiled by Gila EDA from TRD, runs 5.25% to 9.4375%. That range is a TRD-schedule compilation, not a directly opened TRD schedule page — Verify against the TRD schedule page itself before publication. The FY2026 maximum of 10.8125% reported in secondary guides is superseded for FY2027 and must not be quoted as current. Do not quote a single “New Mexico cannabis tax rate” that adds CAN + GRT without naming the location.

Worked illustration — with its limits stated. At the current 14% CAN, a $100 adult-use price paid bears $14.00 CAN. GRT then applies at the location rate on the $100 price only — the $14.00 CAN is excluded from the GRT base from 1 July 2023 (TRD FYI-260, Rev. 07/2026, p. 4: “The gross receipts tax is on the gross receipts of a seller but excludes receipts from the cannabis excise tax beginning on July 1, 2023”). At the state component alone (4.875%), the state-component GRT illustration is $4.88 on the $100 price — that is NOT the total GRT the customer bears, because local increments are additional.

GRT-on-excise — resolved.

TRD FYI-260, Rev. 07/2026, p. 4, states the rule: “The gross receipts tax is on the gross receipts of a seller but excludes receipts from the cannabis excise tax beginning on July 1, 2023.” The GRT base therefore excludes the CAN amount from 1 July 2023. The contrary statement in a secondary tax guide (CannabisCPA.tax, New Mexico Cannabis Tax Guide 2025: “GRT is charged on the total sales price, including the excise tax amount”) and in TRD’s own 5 May 2022 release predate that change and are not adopted. The CannBus Q3 2026 “not confirmed” position is superseded by FYI-260. Source: https://realfile.tax.newmexico.gov/FYI-260.pdf.

Other GRT points.

  • Resale deduction: §7-9-47 (TRD, accessed 31 Oct 2026) — sales of cannabis products for

    • resale are deductible; wholesalers register for GRT even though they do not register for CAN.

  • Destination sourcing for CAN (and, by the same 2023 reform, the reporting that drives the

    • local CAN share) is covered in §2.6. GRT itself has long been destination-based; the 2023 change aligned CAN reporting to business-location sourcing (see §2.6).

  • No cannabis-specific local GRT rate was found. Local GRT increments are general local-option

    • increments that happen to apply to cannabis retail like any other retail sale in that location. That is why Part 3 reports local GRT only as “via the general local GRT,” not as a cannabis levy.

2.6 Distribution of cannabis excise revenue — the local share

Citation. §7-1-6.68 NMSA 1978, “Distribution — cannabis excise tax — municipalities and counties.” History. Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §50; amended 2023, ch. 85, §2 (SB 147, 56th Legislature, First Session, 2023 — destination-based sourcing; “cannabis retailers” replaced by “business locations”); amended 2025, ch. 130, §24, effective 1 Jul 2025 (each occurrence of “within” replaced by “sourced to”). Current text as reproduced by Justia (2025), opened 31 Oct 2026: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-7/article-1/section-7-1-6-68/ — NMOneSource re-check required.

Verbatim operative text — §7-1-6.68(A)–(D):

“A. A distribution pursuant to Section 7-1-6.1 NMSA 1978 shall be made to each

municipality, subject to any increase or decrease made pursuant to Section 7-1-6.15 NMSA

1978, in an amount equal to thirty-three and thirty-three hundredths percent of the net

receipts attributable to the cannabis excise tax from business locations sourced to the

municipality as reported pursuant to Section 7-42-4 NMSA 1978.

B. A distribution pursuant to Section 7-1-6.1 NMSA 1978 shall be made to each county in

an amount equal to thirty-three and thirty-three hundredths percent of the net receipts

attributable to the cannabis excise tax from business locations sourced to the county area

of the county as reported pursuant to Section 7-42-4 NMSA 1978.

C. The department may deduct an amount not to exceed three percent of the distributions

made pursuant to this section for the reasonable costs for administering the distributions.

D. As used in this section, ‘county area’ means that portion of a county located outside

the boundaries of any municipality.”

How the arithmetic works — reconciliation of the “two-thirds / one-third” shorthand. For any single sale, only ONE local recipient is paid under §7-1-6.68: the municipality if the sale is sourced to a municipality, otherwise the county for the county area. That recipient receives 33.33% of net CAN receipts attributable to that sale. The remaining ≈66.67% is not distributed under this section and remains with the state General Fund. Summaries that say “66.67% to the state General Fund, 33.33% to the local government where the sale occurred” are therefore correct per sale, and are adopted here. Summaries that imply municipalities AND counties each receive 33.33% on the same sale (totalling 66.66% to locals) are wrong and are rejected. TRD may deduct up to 3% of the distributions for administration (§7-1-6.68(C)) — so the local amount actually distributed can be up to 3% less than the gross 33.33% share. Whether TRD in practice deducts the full 3% in any given month is Verify from the distribution files.

Timing. TRD Monthly Local Government Distribution Reports page (accessed 31 Oct 2026): “Tax collections are distributed the 2nd month after the accrual (business activity) month. For example, the file ‘Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) Mar-2022’ reflects business activity in March 2022; the collection month was April (tax returns were due by April 25th), and these collections were distributed in May.” The index page lists monthly CAN Distribution Detail files and CAN ACH Distribution Reports from March 2022 business activity through August 2026 business activity (distributed October 2026) at the time of access. Source: https://www.tax.newmexico.gov/monthly-local-government-distribution-reports-can-distribution-detail-by-location/ Individual monthly files were not opened and summed in this run — totals below are therefore taken from the official aggregate sources cited, not recomputed from the monthly files.

No dedicated fund in current distribution law. The current §7-1-6.68 text distributes only to municipalities, counties (county area), and — by remainder — the General Fund. It contains NO distribution to a community reinvestment grant fund, substance-use-disorder fund, equity fund, or behavioural-health fund. Proposals to add such distributions were NOT enacted in current law:

  • HB 315, 56th Legislature, First Session (2023) would have added 16.5% each to a community

    • reinvestment grant fund and a substance-use-disorder prevention and treatment fund. It is not in the current §7-1-6.68 text and is therefore not current law (bill text: https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/23%20Regular/bills/house/HB0315.html).

  • SB 432, 57th Legislature, First Session (2025) would have distributed 5% of net CAN

    • receipts to a proposed behavioural-health grant program fund (Fiscal Impact Report, 11 Mar 2025). It is not in the current §7-1-6.68 text and is therefore not current law — final disposition Verify on nmlegis.gov, but the operative proof is the current statute.

  • Secondary summaries that describe CAN revenue as funding “public health and safety

    • programs” or “the Department of Health” in general terms are not supported by the current distribution statute and are not adopted. If General Fund money is later appropriated to such purposes through the ordinary budget, that is a separate appropriation, not a CAN distribution.

Local share ≠ local tax power. A municipality or county cannot set its own CAN rate, cannot levy an additional cannabis excise, and cannot opt out of receiving (or being the source of) the share. Its only cannabis-specific revenue lever in statute is the 33.33% distribution driven by sales sourced to it, plus its ordinary local GRT increments. See Part 3, §3.2.

2.8 Hemp product tax

  • No New Mexico hemp-specific excise tax was found. No statute, TRD page, or NMED/NMDA

    • page located in this run imposes a per-product, per-milligram, or ad valorem excise on hemp or hemp-derived products comparable to the CAN.

  • Hemp businesses are ordinary businesses for GRT purposes unless a specific deduction

    • applies; no hemp-specific GRT deduction statute was located in this run — Verify.

  • NMDA hemp grower/processor licence fees and NMED hemp manufacturing licence fees (Part 7)

    • are licence fees, not taxes, and are not included in any tax total in this Part.

  • The federal hemp redefinition dates (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026) create no New Mexico tax by

    • themselves. Whether New Mexico enacts a hemp-product tax, or routes intoxicating hemp products into the CAN-taxed CCD channel, is a legislative question for Part 1 / Part 7; as of 31 Oct 2026 no such tax is in force in the sources read. The September 2025 NMED emergency rule on synthetic/converted cannabinoids is a product rule, not a tax rule, and is not treated as a tax here.

  • Follow-up: search TRD for “hemp” in FYI publications and check whether hemp-derived

    • THC beverages sold by CCD retailers are CAN-taxed as cannabis products when sold as adult-use cannabis products (that turns on product classification, Part 1, not on a separate hemp tax).

2.9 IRS §280E and New Mexico decoupling — statute cited, limits stated

Federal position (fixed baseline, applied to New Mexico).

  • Before 28 Apr 2026, marijuana in Schedules I/II was subject to IRC §280E, which disallows

    • deductions for ordinary and necessary business expenses (rent, payroll, marketing, etc.) for a trade or business trafficking in Schedule I/II substances, while cost of goods sold (COGS) remained subtractable. That is the general §280E rule; the Ultra Health Tax Court litigation (New Mexico medical business, reported Law360 17 Oct 2025) challenged the conventional reading for the 2017–2020 period and the IRS defended the conventional reading — that litigation does not change the baseline and is noted only because it is a New Mexico taxpayer case.

  • From 28 Apr 2026, state-licensed medical marijuana (and FDA-approved products) in

    • Schedule III is generally outside §280E, which by its terms reaches only Schedule I/II substances. Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I and fully subject to §280E.

  • Consequence for New Mexico dual-market operators (many licensees serve both markets):

    • they must split their activity for federal tax purposes — medical-designated activity may deduct ordinary expenses federally; adult-use activity may not. How expenses, COGS, and inventory are allocated between the two channels for a single licensee, single premises, or vertically integrated business is Verify — no TRD or IRS allocation guidance specific to New Mexico dual licensees was located in this run. Do not advise a single allocation method in this dossier.

New Mexico decoupling — YES, since 2021, for state income tax.

  • Enactment: HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, ch. 4, amended the definition of “base

    • income” in §7-2-2 NMSA 1978 (personal income tax) and §7-2A-2 NMSA 1978 (corporate income tax) “to explicitly exclude ‘an amount equal to any expenditure that is eligible to be claimed as a federal income tax deduction but is disallowed pursuant to Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code.’” That description is taken from a New Mexico Administrative Hearings Office Tax Administration Act decision (Sandia Botanicals, AHO Case No. 19.04-043A, D&O 22-09), which quotes the 2021 amendments at length, and is corroborated by Wolters Kluwer’s state survey (“New Mexico for corporate and personal income taxpayers beginning June 29, 2021”) and by multiple secondary decoupling lists (2021) naming New Mexico.

  • Subsection numbering — Verify. The AHO decision cites §7-2-2(B)(5) (2021) and

    • §7-2A-2(C)(4) (2021). Current numbering may have shifted with later amendments. The existence of decoupling is treated as established; the current subsection cite must be re-checked on NMOneSource before publication. Do not cite (B)(5)/(C)(4) as current without that check.

  • Scope of state decoupling. Because New Mexico starts from federal taxable income /

    • federal adjusted gross income and then excludes the §280E-disallowed amount from state base income, a cannabis business may deduct ordinary expenses for New Mexico income tax even for adult-use activity that remains federally disallowed. That is why secondary summaries correctly say New Mexico is “decoupled” while also correctly saying adult-use remains federally subject to §280E — the two statements describe different tax systems. The combined position on 31 Oct 2026 is therefore: **state deductibility for all cannabis business expenses (via decoupling) + federal deductibility for the medical share only (via Schedule III) + federal non-deductibility for the adult-use share.**

  • What decoupling does NOT do. It does not change CAN or GRT. It does not make a business

    • federally deductible. It does not exempt any sale from tax. Tribal operations: whether any medical activity under an intergovernmental agreement counts as “state-licensed” for the federal Schedule III rule is Verify (per the commission’s tribal note) and is not decided in this Part; the state decoupling question for tribal operators is likewise Verify and belongs to Part 10.

  • No New Mexico guidance on post-Schedule-III state conformity was found. Because New

    • Mexico already decouples, the federal Schedule III move does not require a new state decoupling bill to preserve state deductibility, but whether TRD has issued post-April-2026 guidance on how dual licensees report the federal medical/adult-use split on state returns is Verify (search TRD bulletins / FYI-260 update after April 2026).

2.10 Other taxes and charges that touch cannabis/hemp businesses (brief)

  • State personal and corporate income tax generally: progressive personal rates and the

    • corporate rate are outside this Part’s scope; the only income-tax point decided here is §280E decoupling (§2.9). Do not import a rate table from secondary sources into this Part without an official TRD source.

  • Withholding, compensating tax, and other business taxes: TRD notes wholesalers,

    • manufacturers, and producers “must register for Gross Receipts Tax and other business taxes that apply to them” even when they do not register for CAN. No cannabis-specific withholding or compensating-tax rule was located — Verify if the parent dossier needs it.

  • Local lodgers’ / occupancy taxes, property taxes, and municipal gross-receipts increments

    • apply under general law and are not cannabis-specific; they are not quantified here.

  • No federal cannabis banking law exists (fixed baseline); bank/credit-union questions

    • belong to Part 6 and are not decided here.

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 The state rule that frames everything: §26-2C-12

Citation. §26-2C-12 NMSA 1978, “Local control.” History. Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §12 (HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, effective 29 June 2021). No amendment to §26-2C-12 was found in the current text reproduced by Justia (2025), opened 31 Oct 2026: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-12/ — NMOneSource re-check required. A 2023 bill (HB 313) that would have amended §26-2C-12 among other sections was a proposal; it is not reflected in the current text quoted below and is not current law.

“Local jurisdiction” means a municipality, home-rule municipality, or county (definition in §26-2C-2, as summarised in HB 313 bill text; exact subsection letter Verify on NMOneSource).

Verbatim operative text — §26-2C-12(A)–(B):

“A. A local jurisdiction may:

(1) adopt time, place and manner rules that do not conflict with the Cannabis Regulation

Act or the Dee Johnson Clean Indoor Air Act [Chapter 24, Article 16 NMSA 1978], including

rules that reasonably limit density of licenses and operating times consistent with

neighborhood uses; and

(2) allow for the smoking, vaporizing and ingesting of cannabis products within an indoor

or outdoor cannabis consumption area if:

(a) unless licensed pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act [Chapter 26,

Article 2B NMSA 1978], access to the cannabis consumption area is restricted to persons

twenty-one years of age and older; and

(b) the cannabis establishment or integrated cannabis microbusiness is located at a

minimum distance from a school or daycare center as determined by the local jurisdiction,

but which minimum distance shall not be set at any more than three hundred feet from a

school or daycare center that was in existence at the time the establishment or

microbusiness was licensed.

B. A local jurisdiction shall not:

(1) prevent transportation of cannabis products on public roads by a licensee that

transports cannabis products in compliance with the Cannabis Regulation Act;

(2) completely prohibit the operation of a licensee;

(3) prohibit or limit signage attached to or located on licensed premises that identifies

the premises as a cannabis establishment;

(4) require a licensed premises or a cannabis consumption area to be any more than three

hundred feet from a school or daycare center that was in existence at the time the cannabis

establishment or integrated cannabis microbusiness was licensed;

(5) require an existing licensee at a licensed premises to relocate; or

(6) prohibit a person from producing homegrown cannabis as provided for in the Cannabis

Regulation Act.”

Plain-English reading (the statute controls; this paragraph does not replace it).

  • May: set time, place, and manner rules that do not conflict with the Cannabis Regulation

    • Act or the Dee Johnson Clean Indoor Air Act, including rules that **reasonably limit density of licences and operating times consistent with neighbourhood uses; and allow** (i.e. permit, by local choice) indoor or outdoor consumption areas on the age and distance conditions in (A)(2).

  • Shall not: ban a licensee outright; block compliant transport on public roads; ban or

    • limit identifying signage on licensed premises; impose a school/daycare buffer **over 300 feet** (the 300-foot figure is a ceiling, not a floor — a jurisdiction may set a smaller buffer or none, but may not exceed 300 feet for a school/daycare in existence when the establishment was licensed); force an existing licensee to relocate; or prohibit homegrown cannabis as provided in the Act.

  • The consumption-area exception is the only opt-out in the scheme. RLD CCD FAQs

    • (accessed 31 Oct 2026) state it directly: “No. Per the Cannabis Regulation Act, section 12(A) and (B) NMSA 1978, local communities can place reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions … However, a local community cannot outright ban operations by cannabis licensees. **The only exception to this is consumption areas. Local jurisdictions can opt out of allowing consumption areas** if that is the right decision for them.” Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/licensing/faqs/

  • **What “reasonably limit density” does and does not authorise is untested in the sources

    • read.** It plainly authorises spacing / separation rules between retailers and zoning-district limits (every jurisdiction below uses them). Whether a de facto density cap that leaves almost no viable site in a jurisdiction would be treated as a “complete prohibition” under (B)(2) has no court ruling located in this run — Verify. No New Mexico appellate decision striking down or upholding a specific local cannabis zoning ordinance was located in this run; do not cite one.

  • CCD defers proximity questions to locals. A Taos proceeding presentation (secondary,

    • BoardDocs) records a 22 June 2022 letter from CCD Deputy Director of Policy Robert Sachs “explicitly leaving proximity issues to local jurisdictions,” citing §26-2C-12. That is consistent with the statute’s structure (the locality “determines” the school/daycare distance, capped at 300 feet), but the letter itself was not opened — Verify if the parent dossier needs the letter as a source.

  • State licence ≠ local permission. A CCD licence does not substitute for local zoning,

    • business registration, or (where required) a local cannabis permit/approval. Conversely, local approval does not substitute for a CCD licence. Both are required where the locality requires its own approval. Albuquerque’s page (accessed 31 Oct 2026) states this in terms: all cannabis businesses must first obtain a state licence; retail locations must also obtain a City Cannabis Retail Location Approval; and every business must obtain a City business licence.

Prohibit homegrown cannabis as provided in the ActNO§26-2C-12(B)(6)

Impose a moratorium that is in substance a complete prohibitionNO in substance under (B)(2); a time-limited, district-specific moratorium / overlay (e.g. a historic-district pause pending a zoning update) is a different question and is flagged Verify where it occurs — see §3.5§26-2C-12(B)(2); no court ruling located — Verify

3.3 Is there an official statewide list of local rules?

No. No official statewide list, index, or database of county/municipal cannabis rules was found in this run. RLD/CCD publishes no consolidated local-rules list (its FAQ answers only the ban question). TRD publishes tax distribution files by location, not zoning rules. The New Mexico Municipal League was not found to publish a consolidated cannabis ordinance list in the sources searched.

Consequence for this dossier: Part 3 therefore reports jurisdiction by jurisdiction from each locality’s own code, council, or planning page (or, where that text was not opened, from a secondary summary explicitly labelled as such), and records Verify / Not located where no rule was found. The absence of a rule in the table below means **not located in this run**, not “the jurisdiction has no rule.” Every jurisdiction in the commission’s minimum checklist is listed in §3.4, including those where nothing was located.

Jurisdictions checked (minimum checklist + counties): Albuquerque / Bernalillo County; Las Cruces / Doña Ana County; Rio Rancho / Sandoval County; Santa Fe (city) / Santa Fe County; Roswell / Chaves County; Farmington / San Juan County; Hobbs / Lea County; Clovis / Curry County; Alamogordo / Otero County; Carlsbad / Eddy County; Gallup / McKinley County; Sunland Park (Doña Ana County); Taos (town, Taos County); Las Vegas / San Miguel County; Los Alamos County; Raton (Colfax County); Torrance County. Additional jurisdictions mentioned in sources (Corrales, Valencia County) are noted only where they illuminate the state rule; they are not substitutes for the checklist.
