3.5 Attempted bans, moratoriums, and denials — and why most are NOT bans

No jurisdiction in this file enacted a citywide or countywide ban on CCD licensees. That is the expected result under §26-2C-12(B)(2), and no contrary ordinance was found. What did occur falls into four distinct buckets. Conflating them would be an error.

(a) Time-limited, district-specific moratorium — Albuquerque Old Town (2021–2022, then a permanent district prohibition)

  • 21 Jun 2021: Albuquerque City Council voted 9–0 to temporarily ban cannabis shops

    • from operating in Old Town — a moratorium on cannabis sales, cultivation, and manufacturing in Old Town until July 2022 or until the city’s zoning-code updates were released, to allow consultation with Old Town merchants and stakeholders. (Secondary: Pete Dinelli report, 24 Jun 2021, on the 17 Jun 2021 special council meeting and 21 Jun vote; 21 amendments debated, one withdrawn; medical-only retailers grandfathered.)

  • Later permanent position (official, accessed 31 Oct 2026): Albuquerque’s cannabis page

    • states cannabis retail, cultivation, and manufacturing are **prohibited in the Old Town Historic Protection Overlay Zone** (Council Bill R-21-165) and in Main Streets Corridors per the IDO effective 20 Apr 2026.

  • Legal character — Verify, no ruling found. A district-specific prohibition is not a

    • jurisdiction-wide “complete prohibition” under §26-2C-12(B)(2) on its face, because licensees may operate elsewhere in the city. Whether the Old Town overlay, alone or combined with Main Streets Corridor prohibitions and the 660-foot spacing rule, leaves a reasonable range of sites — and therefore survives a (B)(2) challenge — has **no court ruling located in this run**. Record it as an open legal question, not as a decided ban or a decided lawful zoning rule. No state enforcement action against Albuquerque for the Old Town rule was found.

(b) Failed tightening — Albuquerque Ordinance O-26-39 (2026)

  • Proposal (Councillor Renée Grout, at Mayor Tim Keller’s administration’s request):

    • update the IDO on cannabis/nicotine-retailer spacing (660 feet between cannabis dispensaries and nicotine retailers, as reported by City Desk, 6 Aug 2026) and related smoke-shop location rules. The exact bill drafting — including the scope of a reported 330-foot school/daycare figure (a cannabis school buffer, which would exceed the state 300-foot ceiling, or a nicotine-retail rule) and a reported 1,320-foot smoke-shop spacing figure — is Unverified against the council bill text and minutes and is not stated here as the bill’s text; secondary reports disagree on the 330-foot figure’s scope.

  • Outcome: rejected 6–3 on 3 Aug 2026 (City Council; had already failed in the Land Use,

    • Planning and Zoning Committee). Grout, Baca, and Bassan voted for it. (Secondary: City Desk, 6 Aug 2026; ABQ News, 8 Jun 2026.) O-26-39 is not law. The pre-existing Albuquerque rules (300-foot school/daycare, 660-foot retailer spacing) remain as stated in §3.4.

  • This episode is the clearest recent example of a locality testing the boundary of

    • §26-2C-12(A)(1) density regulation — and of the council declining to extend it to a new business class (nicotine retail) by analogy to cannabis.

(c) Quasi-judicial denials of individual applications — NOT ordinance bans

  • Sunland Park — Station X and Cronica (2025, reheard 2026).
  • Station X: proposed two-storey dispensary with indoor consumption lounge at **420 Emory

    • Drive, Sunland Park**, near the Texas line (Upper Valley, by Walmart / State Line Restaurant), adjacent to Texas residences across the state line.

  • Cronica: proposed dispensary + lounge at 3801 Emory Lane, Sunland Park, as part of an

    • entertainment complex (Independent Nation / Bucks Cabaret branding in secondary reports).

  • 21 May 2025: Sunland Park City Council unanimously denied the zoning changes /

    • special-use permits for Cronica (and, in related reporting, Station X), after public opposition and Texas-side safety concerns about customer access routes into Texas. Planning staff had recommended approval, noting compliance with New Mexico zoning requirements.

  • May 2026 (MJBizDaily, 14 May 2026): the Council again rejected special-use permits

    • for Station X Cannabis and Cronica Cannabis in a quasi-judicial hearing that followed a judge’s ruling that an earlier denial “failed to satisfy due process requirements.” Texas-side officials (including El Paso City Rep. Alejandra Chavez, per KVIA reporting cited by MJBizDaily) raised safety concerns about access from a Texas parking lot. Existing Sunland Park dispensary owners also opposed the new entrants.

  • Litigation (secondary, Verify docket): developers (Chadcor Holdings NM, LLC d/b/a

    • Top Crop Cannabis; Sunland Parking, LLC) sued the city and a coalition of local dispensaries on 21 Nov 2025 in the **3rd Judicial District Court, Case No. D-307-CV-2025-03136**, alleging an anti-competitive conspiracy / closed market and seeking treble damages under NMSA §57-1-3. The complaint alleges the city denied applications despite compliance with zoning rules. **Outcome pending / not located — Verify docket before citing as decided law.** The lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding.

  • Why this is not a “ban”: Sunland Park continues to host dozens of operating

    • dispensaries (see §3.8). The denials are site-specific special-use decisions, reviewable for due process and for compliance with the city’s own criteria — which is exactly why the matter went back for a rehearing and then to court. They do not show a jurisdiction exercising a power to prohibit licensees outright, which §26-2C-12(B)(2) forbids.

  • Farmington — zone-change denial (2026 reporting). Council unanimously denied a zone

    • change for a retailer at 511 E. 20th Street (Local Neighborhood Commercial; retail cannabis permitted only in CB/GC/I districts). The applicant had pursued the site for two years. Staff noted nearby schools and residences within 300 feet. This is a zoning-district decision, not a ban.

  • Taos — Hype Boyz Genetics (CEP2022-14, June 2022). Town denial of a business-licence

    • petition for review, on proximity grounds, with a presentation recording CCD’s deferral to locals on proximity (§3.1). The underlying ordinance and the final disposition on appeal (if any) were not opened — Verify. It illustrates local proximity discretion, not a ban.

  • Roswell — variance granted over staff/commission recommendation (Aug 2025). The

    • Greenhouse Roswell, 3107 N. Main St: Planning & Zoning recommended denial (4–1) on residential proximity; Council approved variance + CUP (5–2, one recusal). This cuts the other way: local discretion can also allow a site that staff would have denied. It also shows repeated variances becoming a policy concern (councillors debated a ch. 27 code review).

(d) Consumption-area opt-outs and prohibitions (lawful, distinct from bans)

  • Farmington: consumption areas not permitted in the city (§2.4.42, 2022 UDC).
  • Santa Fe (city): consumption areas not allowed at the time of the 2021 approval.
  • Las Cruces: on-site consumption indoors only, prohibited entirely in C-1.
  • Albuquerque: outdoor smoking/vaping consumption areas not allowed; indoor

    • consumption areas allowed in some circumstances with Retail Location Approval.

  • Hobbs: consumption area defined as indoor only (June 2024).
  • Taos: outdoor consumption permitted and regulated under Ord. 25-04 draft (contrast).
  • These are exercises of the §26-2C-12(A)(2) “allow for … if …” power and the RLD FAQ

    • opt-out. They are not violations of (B)(2), because (B)(2) prohibits completely prohibiting “the operation of a licensee” — and a consumption area is a distinct licensed activity / premises feature, not the licensee’s retail operation itself. No court ruling testing that distinction was located — Verify if the parent dossier needs it.

(e) State-level proposals to restore local power — NOT law

  • Secondary reporting (Cannabis Risk Manager, 2025, on a Taos interim Courts and Criminal

    • Justice Committee hearing) records lawmakers calling for a pause on new licences, increased enforcement, and restoring some regulatory authority to local governments, citing Sunland Park saturation and the absence of local power to limit dispensary numbers.

  • SB 152 (2025), which would have let counties petition for a licence pause, is recorded by

    • CannBus Q3 2026 as died in committee (with SB 89). Neither proposal is current law. Local governments still may not cap licence numbers outright; they may only “reasonably limit density” via spacing/zoning under §26-2C-12(A)(1). Any 2026–2027 session proposal on this point must be checked on nmlegis.gov at the time of publication — the 2027 session (60-day session, convening January 2027 per secondary note) had not occurred at the dossier date.

3.6 Local business licences — general rule

  • A state CCD licence is necessary but not sufficient where a locality requires its own

    • licence, registration, permit, or approval. Examples opened or reliably summarised: Albuquerque (Retail Location Approval + business licence), Santa Fe (city permit), Las Cruces (city permit), Rio Rancho (city approvals/permits under ch. 122 before any business is conducted), Taos (business registration before state licence application, plus town cannabis-establishment permit), Las Vegas, NM (business registration + cannabis permit / zoning permit + code inspections).

  • Local licences do not create a local cannabis tax. Fees are in §3.7.
  • A local licence/permit that is revoked or expires can have state consequences in Taos

    • (town permit null and void if the state licence is revoked/expires, Ord. 25-04 §6.K) — the converse (state licence consequences of a local revocation) is Verify and belongs to Part 4 / Part 11.

  • No locality in this file was found to impose a local cannabis licence cap (a numerical

    • cap on how many local licences it will issue). Density is controlled by spacing and zoning, not by a cap number, in every ordinance excerpt read. If a cap exists in an unopened code (e.g. Clovis, Alamogordo, Carlsbad, Raton, Torrance), it is Verify, and its compatibility with §26-2C-12(B)(2) would need legal review.

3.7 Local fees and buffer rules — consolidated

Buffer ceiling reminder: no locality may require more than 300 feet from a school/daycare in existence when the establishment was licensed (§26-2C-12(B)(4)). Every buffer in the table below at or below 300 feet for schools/daycares complies on its face. Buffers from other uses (churches, residences, other retailers, tobacco retailers) are NOT subject to the 300-foot ceiling in the statute’s terms — the ceiling in (B)(4) names only schools/daycares — which is why Rio Rancho (300 feet from churches/residences), Farmington (300 feet from religious institutions/other dispensaries), and Santa Fe city (300 feet from places of worship) can lawfully use 300-foot figures for those uses, and why Sandoval County’s 500-foot retailer/tobacco spacing is not on its face a (B)(4) violation. Whether a non-school buffer is “reasonable” under (A)(1) is a separate, untested question — Verify.

3.8 Business concentration — ONLY what official sources say

Instruction applied strictly: this section summarises only what official sources say, as reported through the sources below. It does not estimate, rank, or cluster licensees itself, beyond reproducing rankings that the cited official/secondary sources themselves state.

(a) Official source: New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions (DWS), Labour Market Review, February 2025, “New Mexico’s Flowering Cannabis Industry” (QCEW data)

  • Source: DWS Labour Market Review index page (February 2025 issue; the direct PDF URL printed in the earlier draft was broken — a spaced/line-broken URL — and no direct PDF filename is asserted here; confirm the February 2025 PDF via the index page)

    • (official DWS publication; QCEW = Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages).

  • Q2 2024: 406 establishments reported being in the New Mexico cannabis industry

    • (up from 265 in Q2 2023). **75.1% were in retail trade, operating dispensaries (305 locations). The industry employed 5,090 people in Q2 2024, of whom 81.3% (4,140) worked in dispensaries**; wholesale trade 372 (7.3%), manufacturing 297 (5.8%). Establishments paid $44.4 million in wages in the quarter (figure as extracted; full table Verify against the PDF).

  • By county (DWS, Q2 2024, qualitative ranking only): “The majority of cannabis

    • establishments were located in New Mexico’s most populous counties. **Bernalillo County had the highest number of establishments; roughly one in three were located in that county alone. The counties with the next highest number of establishments were Doña Ana, Santa Fe, and San Juan**.” Establishments reporting in more than one county are excluded; some counties are shown as ND (nondisclosed / unable to report).

  • What DWS does NOT give: the county map in the PDF as extracted by search is garbled

    • (numbers do not align reliably to counties in the text extraction). **No county-by-county establishment count is quoted in this dossier from that map**, and no retailers-per-capita figure by county is derived from DWS. Any parent-agent table that needs exact county counts must read the DWS PDF map/table directly.

  • What this proves and does not prove: concentration follows population (Bernalillo first,

    • then Doña Ana, Santa Fe, San Juan) in Q2 2024 QCEW data. It does not prove a border-town effect by itself, because QCEW counts establishments, not sales, and Sunland Park / Doña Ana sales strength (§3.8(b)) is a sales phenomenon, not an establishment-count phenomenon.

(b) Official sales data as reported by secondary press (RLD CROP data, not directly opened)

  • MJBizDaily, 20 Aug 2026 (“New Mexico cannabis sales steady as border towns drive

    • growth”), reporting RLD data:

  • First half 2026: ≈$284.9M combined sales; July 2026: $49.8M; seven months 2026: ≈$332M.
  • Leading towns by monthly sales in Q2 2026 (as reported by MJBizDaily from state data):

    • Albuquerque ≈$14.5M in each of April and May, $13.7M in June; **Sunland Park second statewide, $5.3M–$5.8M per month in Q2**; Las Cruces $2.6M–$2.7M per month.

  • Chaparral (Doña Ana County, near the Texas line): ≈$3.2M in Q2 2026, up >$200,000

    • from Q1. Santa Teresa (Doña Ana County, near El Paso): >$508,000 in Q2, up from $445,000 in Q1 (per El Paso Times reporting cited by MJBizDaily).

  • Retail density (secondary, not an official per-capita table): “The state now counts

    • 47 retail outlets per 100,000 residents, one of the highest cannabis retail densities in the country” (MJBizDaily, Aug 2026). No denominator, licence-type definition, or county breakdown is given in the snippet. **Do not present 47/100,000 as an official CCD figure, and do not derive county per-capita rates from it.**

  • MJBizDaily’s older analysis (2023, reporting RLD data Aug 2022–Feb 2023) found the same

    • pattern earlier: Albuquerque ≈31% of adult-use sales (≈36% with nearby Bernalillo/Rio Rancho metro), Santa Fe ≈7% and second at that time, and **border communities Clovis, Hobbs, and Sunland Park outpacing what population alone would predict**, with Sunland Park ZIP 88063 per-person recreational spend $1,044 (highest ZIP in the state in that period), Clovis ZIP 88135 $499, Hobbs ZIP 88240 $258, Taos $598 and Ruidoso $546 (tourism). Those per-person figures are **2022–2023 secondary calculations from RLD sales ÷ population**, not a current official table, and are included only to show the border/tourism pattern is long-standing, not to state a 2026 per-capita ranking.

  • Sunland Park — dispensary count and cumulative sales (secondary, citing CROP):

    • El Chuqueño (May 2025, “Sunland Park-Santa Teresa Chronicles”) reports, citing the Cannabis Reporting Online Portal (CROP): **37 dispensaries operating in Sunland Park as of April 2025; recreational + medicinal sales in Sunland Park $129,496,405.92 between April 2022 and April 2025; Santa Teresa $2,204,358.97** in the same period, with 4 dispensaries in April 2025. A separate secondary report (Cannabis Risk Manager, 2025, citing RLD) gives Sunland Park as “between 36 and 40 dispensaries” with population “fewer than 20,000.” The 36–40 range and the 37 point figure are consistent; the exact current count on 31 Oct 2026 is Verify against CCD/CROP. Sunland Park’s second-place sales rank (behind Albuquerque, a city >30× its population per El Chuqueño) is the secondary sources’ ranking, reproduced here, not a ranking computed in this dossier.

  • Governor’s press-release figure (secondary, 2024 vintage): “Sunland Park … $57 million

    • in adult-use sales” and “Las Vegas, Silver City, and Deming have each surpassed $5 million in adult-use sales since April 2022” (Governor’s release as reported by Beard Bros Pharms, on the $1B cumulative-sales milestone, ~2 years after launch). **Do not use the $57M figure as a 2026 figure**; it is a cumulative-to-early-2024 figure. Note also that “Las Vegas” there is Las Vegas, New Mexico, not Nevada.

(c) What is Unavailable — stated plainly

  • No official retailers-per-capita table by county was found in this run. Neither CCD,

    • TRD, nor DWS publishes (in the sources opened) a table of “retailers per 10,000 / 100,000 residents by county.” The 47/100,000 statewide figure above is the only density figure located, and it is secondary.

  • No official county-by-county licence-count table was extracted in this run. Part 5

    • (licence data sources) is the place to build one from CCD licence lists / CROP; it is not built here.

  • No official “border town” sales table (Sunland Park vs Anthony vs Clovis vs Hobbs vs

    • Farmington) was opened. The town sales figures above are press reports of RLD data, not RLD tables.

  • No ranking of clusters by this dossier. The only rankings reproduced are those stated

    • by DWS (Bernalillo > Doña Ana, Santa Fe, San Juan by establishment count, Q2 2024) and by MJBizDaily/El Chuqueño (Albuquerque > Sunland Park > Las Cruces by monthly sales, Q2 2026 / April 2025). If those two rankings appear to conflict, they do not: one counts establishments, the other counts sales dollars, in different periods.

Run 1 — Part 4 — Licence Types

Dossier date: 31 October 2026. Date accessed for all sources: 31 October 2026.

Federal baseline (fixed context, not re-researched; flag contradictions only): State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use activity remains fully subject to §280E. Consequence for this Part: every CCD licence below must carry a clear designation for medical activity, commercial (adult-use) activity, or both (NMSA §26-2C-6(C), quoted below). A dual-market licensee therefore does not get §280E relief on its adult-use activity; it must split medical from adult-use activity, and only the medical portion is within the Schedule III / §280E-relief frame. For tribal operations under intergovernmental agreements, whether any medical activity counts as "state-licensed" under the federal rule is marked Verify in §12 — no official source opened for this Part resolves it.

How to read this Part. "Licence" is used for CCD business licences. Two items listed in §26-2C-6(B) are not ordinary business licences in current law and are treated separately in §4.11–§4.12: cannabis servers (individual permits) and cannabis training and education programmes (registration only since 1 July 2024). Where a statute sets a fee as "up to" a figure and the rule sets a lower actual figure, the rule figure is the operative charged fee and both are shown. Where official sources conflict, the conflict is stated in the text and carried to §12 rather than silently resolved. No proposed bill or rule is presented as current law. No personal phone numbers or personal email addresses are reproduced.

Regulator and governing law. Licensing is by the Cannabis Control Division (CCD) of the New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department (RLD), under the Cannabis Regulation Act, NMSA 1978, Chapter 26, Article 2C (HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, signed 12 April 2021, effective 29 June 2021), and Title 16, Chapter 8 NMAC — principally Part 2 (16.8.2, licensing and operations), Part 8 (16.8.8, plant limits), Part 10 (16.8.10, server permits) and Part 11 (16.8.11, fees). Hemp cultivation is licensed by the New Mexico Department of Agriculture (NMDA) and post-harvest hemp processing by the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) — see §9. Statute text below was read on Justia's mirror of the 2025 NMSA and corroborated against nmlegis.gov bill texts; NMAC text was read on the official State Records Center (SRCA) publisher. Verify: re-check §§26-2C-2, 26-2C-6, 26-2C-7, 26-2C-9, 26-2C-10 and 26-2C-11 on NMOneSource itself before publication (see §12).

Official info pages (all accessed 31 October 2026):

  • RLD/CCD, Apply for a License (NM-PLUS route and user guides for all 10 business licence types): https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/licensing/new-applications/apply-for-license/
  • 16.8.2 NMAC (licensing and operations): https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html
  • 16.8.8 NMAC (plant limits): https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.html
  • 16.8.11 NMAC (fees): https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html (and PDF: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.pdf)
  • 16.8.10 NMAC (server permits): https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0010.pdf
  • NMSA §26-2C-2 (definitions): https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/
  • NMSA §26-2C-6 (licensing; limitations; legacy licensing): https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/

4.0 Universal rules for CCD licences

4.0.1 The licence list

NMSA §26-2C-6(B) (history as shown on the mirror: Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §6; 2023, ch. 85, §24; 2024, ch. 38, §3; accessed 31 October 2026):

"B. The division may issue, renew, deny, suspend or revoke licenses or discipline licensees for the following: (1) cannabis consumption areas; (2) cannabis couriers; (3) cannabis manufacturers; (4) cannabis producer microbusinesses; (5) cannabis producers; (6) cannabis research laboratories; (7) cannabis retailers; (8) cannabis servers; (9) cannabis testing laboratories; (10) cannabis training and education programs; (11) integrated cannabis microbusinesses; and (12) vertically integrated cannabis establishments."

The 10 CCD business licence types are therefore: producer, producer microbusiness, manufacturer, retailer, courier, testing laboratory, consumption area, research laboratory, integrated cannabis microbusiness (ICMB), and vertically integrated cannabis establishment (VICE). This matches the RLD "Apply for License" page, which lists user guides for exactly those 10 types (accessed 31 October 2026).

4.0.2 Validity, designation, non-transferability, decision clock, renewal window, tax gate

  • Validity — §26-2C-6(E): "A license is valid for twelve months from the date the license is issued and may be renewed annually." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The same 12-month period is in 16.8.2.14(A) NMAC (N, 08/24/2021): "The licensure period of a license shall be from the date of approval of the license application for a period of 12 months." Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026).
  • Medical/commercial designation — §26-2C-6(C): "The division shall include a clear designation on all licenses that indicates whether the license is for medical cannabis activity, commercial cannabis activity or both." Source as above. This designation is the administrative mechanism by which a dual-market licensee's medical activity is separated from its adult-use activity for the federal Schedule III / §280E analysis in the headnote.
  • Non-transferability — §26-2C-6(G): "A license shall not be transferable or assignable from a licensee to another person." Source as above. Rule version, 16.8.2.8(N) NMAC: a licence shall not be transferred by assignment or otherwise to other persons or locations; unless the licensee applies for and receives an amended licence, the licence is void and must be returned to the division when the location changes, operation at a licensed premises is discontinued, or the licence is suspended or revoked. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026). A change of controlling person is therefore handled as an amendment, not as a transfer (see §4.0.4).
  • Decision clock — §26-2C-7(B): "Once the division deems an application complete, the division has ninety days to issue or deny a license application." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-7/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The same 90-day rule is in 16.8.2.8(G) NMAC: "A license shall be granted or denied within 90 days upon acceptance of a completed application." Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026).
  • Renewal window — 16.8.2.14(C) NMAC: to timely renew, a completed renewal application and the annual licence fee in 16.8.11 NMAC must be received by the division no earlier than 60 calendar days before expiration and no later than 30 days before expiration, through the division's electronic licensing portal. If a renewal application is not submitted and approved before the expiration date, "the licensee must not sell, transfer, transport, manufacture, test, or distribute any medical or commercial cannabis or cannabis products until the license is renewed." Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026). Failure to receive a renewal notice does not relieve the licensee of the duty to renew.
  • Expiry — 16.8.2.14(B) NMAC: unless otherwise renewed, suspended or revoked, a licence expires at 11:59 p.m. on the day indicated on the licence as the expiration date. Source as above.
  • Tax gate on renewal — §26-2C-6(F): "The director shall not renew a license until the director receives notification from the secretary of taxation and revenue… that on a certain date: (1) the licensee is not a delinquent taxpayer pursuant to Section 7-1-16 NMSA 1978 only with respect to the cannabis excise tax or the gross receipts tax; and (2) there are no unfiled tax returns due with respect to the cannabis excise tax or the gross receipts tax." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  • Fees: payment and refunds — 16.8.2.8(P) NMAC: licence and additional-premises application or renewal fees must be paid at the time of application submission; annual plant fees must be paid upon the division's approval of the initial or renewal application and approval of the number of plants. 16.8.2.8(Q) NMAC: "All licensing or renewal fees are non-refundable and must be paid for each new application." 16.8.11.15 NMAC: the division shall collect all renewal fees, including annual per-plant fees, at the time of renewal. 16.8.11.14 NMAC: accepted payment is credit/debit cards, electronic checks, electronic bank transfers, ACH and cashier's checks; cash is not accepted. Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html and https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html (accessed 31 October 2026).
  • General application contents (all types, in substance): proof each controlling person is at least 21; proof of compliance with local laws (local business licence, which may include zoning approval and a fire inspection report); proof of registration with the New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department for gross receipts tax; Secretary of State good standing where applicable; criminal-history screening documents under 16.8.2.9 NMAC; and the applicant's social and economic equity plan (see §4.7). Example: 16.8.2.22 NMAC (producer) and 16.8.2.57 NMAC (research laboratory). Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.22 and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.57 (accessed 31 October 2026).

4.0.3 Caps — licences vs. plants

No total-number cap on CCD licences was found in §26-2C-6, 16.8.2 NMAC, or on the RLD application page opened for this Part. §26-2C-6(J) provides, in relevant part: "Except as otherwise provided in the Cannabis Regulation Act, the division shall not limit the number of licensed premises a licensee may occupy or operate under a license." That is a bar on limiting a licensee's premises count, not by itself a statement that total licence numbers are uncapped, and the RLD social-equity page (not directly opened — see §12) is reported to state that New Mexico does not place caps on the number of licences issued and has no lottery system. Therefore: "uncapped licence numbers" is stated here as "no cap found in the law/rules opened," not as a CCD statement — Verify against a CCD statement or live CCD confirmation before asserting it unqualifiedly. Plant counts, by contrast, are capped (§4.1, §4.10): the binding caps in New Mexico are plant-count caps, not licence-count caps. New Mexico regulates cultivation by mature-plant count, not by canopy (square footage). A cultivation plan must still measure mature-plant cultivation area in square feet (16.8.2.27(B)(2) NMAC), but that is a plan/diagram requirement, not a canopy cap.

4.0.4 Amended licences, ownership changes, additional premises

  • An amended-licence application, fee and CCD approval are required before implementing, among other things, an increase or decrease in plant count, a change in the licensee's access to the water source or a 10% or more increase in water usage, or a material/substantial modification of the premises. Example: 16.8.2.23 NMAC (producer). Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-23-NMAC (accessed 31 October 2026). For consumption areas, 16.8.2.51 NMAC requires an amended application, fee and approval before a change of legal/business name, addition/elimination of a controlling person, or material/substantial premises modification; CCD must approve or deny within 90 days of a completed amended application.
  • Amendment fee: $75 per amendment; designation of a non-controlling person as agent: $75 per designation (16.8.11.10 NMAC, as replaced 7 May 2024). Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html (accessed 31 October 2026).
  • A full cross-type amended-licence schedule was not opened — Verify the amended-licence section for each licence type before publishing a general transfer/amendment procedure (see §12).
  • For VICE/ICMB, applicants must request authority to add or remove an activity by amended application and any required additional fees, and must not conduct an activity requiring additional authority until written division approval is received (16.8.2.8(Y)(3), (5) NMAC). Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026).

4.0.5 Whether applications are open as of October 2026

Yes, on the evidence available, with a live-check caveat. The official RLD application page (accessed 31 October 2026) states: "The New Mexico Cannabis Control Division (CCD) has implemented a new automated licensing system called NM-PLUS, which is designed to streamline and simplify your licensing experience with the CCD, making it easier for applicants and licensees to apply for, amend and renew licenses in New Mexico…" and "To apply for, amend or renew a license, you MUST submit your application online using NM-PLUS. Paper applications for initial licensure, amendments and renewals will no longer be accepted." It lists user guides for all 10 business licence types and states no closed window, moratorium or suspension of new applications. Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/licensing/new-applications/apply-for-license/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Caveat: this establishes NM-PLUS as the live application route; it does not prove that every individual licence type accepted a submission on a given day in October 2026. A live NM-PLUS login check would be needed for absolute confirmation (see §12). A third-party page found in search claiming research-laboratory applications were "currently not open" is not on an official page opened for this Part and is not adopted.

4.1 Cannabis Producer

What it allows. NMSA §26-2C-2, "cannabis producer": "a person that: (1) cultivates cannabis plants; (2) has unprocessed cannabis products tested by a cannabis testing laboratory; (3) transports unprocessed cannabis products only to other cannabis establishments; or (4) sells cannabis products wholesale." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Rule scope, 16.8.2.21(A), (C), (D) NMAC [N, 08/22/2021; A/E, 12/06/2021; A, 03/22/2022]: "(A) License types: The division may license two classes of producers: (1) A cannabis producer; and (2) A cannabis producer microbusiness"; "(C) License required: Unless licensed pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act or division rules, a person shall not cultivate cannabis, including planting, growing, and harvesting cannabis, except for personal use as provided by the Cannabis Regulation Act and the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act"; "(D) Other activities prohibited: Except as provided in Subsection BB of 16.8.2.8 NMAC, no cannabis producer establishment licensee may manufacture cannabis products, courier cannabis or cannabis products, or engage in the retail sale of cannabis or cannabis products unless the licensee has properly applied for, and the division has approved, the applicable license type required for those activities." Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026).

Plant / canopy limits — plant count only, no canopy cap. 16.8.8.9 NMAC [N, 08/24/2021; A/E, 01/13/2022; A, 03/22/2022]: "(B) Designated mature cannabis plant levels: (1) Level 1: 201 – 2,000 mature cannabis plants; (2) Level 2: 2,001 – 6,000 mature cannabis plants; (3) Level 3: 6,001 – 12,000 mature cannabis plants; or (4) Level 4: 12,001 – 16,000 mature cannabis plants"; "(F) Maximum cannabis plant count: In no event shall a licensee be permitted to grow more than 20,000 mature cannabis plants at one time"; "(E) Immature Plants: For purposes of calculating the maximum number of authorized mature cannabis plants, the germination, seedling, and vegetative stages are classified as immature cannabis plants and are excluded from a licensees approved cannabis plant level." Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.html (accessed 31 October 2026). "Mature cannabis plant" — 16.8.8.8(B) NMAC: "a female cannabis plant in the flowering stage." Source as above. History: the 401 lower bound was the 13 January 2022 emergency amendment only (NM Register Vol. XXXIII, Issue 2); the 22 March 2022 amendment (Vol. XXXIII, Issue 6) restored 201, and the current SRCA 16.8.8.9 text (opened in the audit, 1 November 2026) states Level 1 as 201–2,000. The 401 figure must not be used as current law. The older 8,000-plant figure in the June 2023 CCD fee PDF, and earlier/proposed tiers of 4,500 and 10,000, are superseded — do not use them as current law.

Increases. 16.8.8.9(C)–(D) NMAC and 16.8.8.10(A) NMAC: a licensee may increase the number of mature plants at renewal and one other time per year, in increments of 500 mature plants (statute, §26-2C-9(C), same: "in increments of five hundred mature plants. Fees may be prorated for the remainder of the licensing year"), up to eight increments at a time upon application and approval. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.html and https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-9/ (accessed 31 October 2026). History: a 1,000-plant increment was reported for the 13 January 2022 emergency amendment only; the current SRCA 16.8.8.9(C) text (opened in the audit, 1 November 2026) states increases in 500-plant increments, consistent with §26-2C-9(C). The flat $5.00/$2.50 per-plant rates are unaffected by this question.

Fees. Annual licence fee $2,500 + $1,000 per additional licensed premises, plus per-mature-plant fee $5.00 per commercial plant / $2.50 per medical-only plant (16.8.11.9(D) and 16.8.11.11 NMAC). Worked example (arithmetic from the rule rates, not a quoted total): a producer at 2,000 commercial plants = $2,500 base + (2,000 × $5.00) = $12,500, before any additional-premises fees; at 2,000 medical-only plants the plant fees are 2,000 × $2.50 = $5,000, plus the medical-only base fee (one-half — see §4.5). Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html and https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-9/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Any source quoting $10 commercial / $5 medical per plant or an 8,000-plant cap is pre-2022 and must not be used.

Capped? Yes, by plant count (20,000 mature maximum; level designated by the division). No total-number-of-producer-licences cap found (§4.0.3).

Requirements (in addition to §4.0.2). Application contents at 16.8.2.22 NMAC, including: proof of compliance with local laws; TRD gross-receipts registration; plant numbers proposed and monthly water use for a 12-month period; cultivation plan and waste procedures; NMDA pesticide compliance certification; social and economic equity plan (§4.7); and proof of water rights (§4.6). Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.22 (accessed 31 October 2026).

Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate (§4.0.2). Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

4.2 Cannabis Producer Microbusiness

What it allows. A producer, but only at a single licensed premises and only up to the plant cap below. It does not by itself authorise manufacturing, retail or courier activity — those require separate approval (16.8.2.21(D) NMAC, quoted in §4.1).

Definition — NMSA §26-2C-2: "‘cannabis producer microbusiness’ means a cannabis producer at a single licensed premises that possesses no more than two hundred total mature cannabis plants at any one time." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026).

Plant / canopy limits: 200 total mature cannabis plants at any one time, at a single licensed premises. No canopy limit stated. Immature plants are excluded from the mature count under the 16.8.8 framework, but the statutory microbusiness cap is expressly framed as mature plants.

Capped? Yes — by the 200-mature-plant cap and single-premises condition. No total-number cap found.

Fees. $1,000 annually, flat (16.8.11.9(H) NMAC, as amended 7 May 2024, NM Register Vol. XXXV, Issue 9). No per-plant fee (16.8.11.11 NMAC expressly excepts producer microbusinesses). The old $500 (≤100 plants) / $1,000 (101–200 plants) tier in the CCD fee PDF dated 12 June 2023 is superseded; a ≤100-plant microbusiness therefore pays more than under the old schedule. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html (accessed 31 October 2026); superseded PDF for identification only: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/2023-06-12-CCD-Licensing-Description-and-Fees-.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026).

Anti-evasion. §26-2C-9(E) and 16.8.11.13 NMAC: a producer microbusiness (or ICMB) entering a business arrangement with another licensee with the purpose or effect of evading its licence limitations loses the lower fee and must pay the per-plant fee (and, under the rule, the applicable producer or VICE fee). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-9/ (accessed 31 October 2026).

Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Plant-count increases/decreases require an amended licence application (16.8.2.23(A)(3)–(4) NMAC). Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5). Water: the water condition applies to producer microbusinesses as well as producers (§4.6).

4.3 Cannabis Manufacturer — Classes I–IV

What it allows. NMSA §26-2C-2, "cannabis manufacturer": "a person that: (1) manufactures cannabis products; (2) packages cannabis products; (3) has cannabis products tested by a cannabis testing laboratory; or (4) purchases, acquires, sells or transports wholesale cannabis products to other cannabis establishments." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026).

Classes — 16.8.2.29(A) NMAC [N/E, 09/08/2021; N, 12/28/2021; A, 03/22/2022]: "A. License Types: The division may license four classes of manufacture: (1) Class I: A licensee that only packages or repackages cannabis products, or labels or relabels the cannabis product container; (2) Class II: A licensee that conducts Class I activities, and manufactures edible products or topical products using infusion processes, or other types of cannabis products other than extracts or concentrates, and does not conduct extractions; (3) Class III: A licensee that conducts Class I and Class II activities, and extracts using mechanical methods or nonvolatile solvents; and (4) Class IV: A licensee that conducts Class I, Class II, and Class III activities, and extracts using volatile solvents or supercritical CO2." Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-29-NMAC (accessed 31 October 2026). Class I manufacturers are exempt from the 16.8.6 NMAC health-and-safety facility requirements that Classes II–IV must follow for edible/topical finished products (CCD guidance, 23 March 2022, summarising 16.8.6.7(A)(2) NMAC). The class distinction is not a fee tier — the manufacturer fee is flat (below).

Other activities prohibited — 16.8.2.29(D) NMAC: except as provided in 16.8.2.8(BB) NMAC, no manufacturer licensee may produce cannabis, courier cannabis or cannabis products, or engage in retail sale unless it has applied for and the division has approved the applicable licence type. Source as above.

Plant / canopy limits: None — a manufacturer licence carries no plant count or canopy limit. (A manufacturer that also holds producer authority is limited under its producer/VICE/ICMB plant count, not under the manufacturer licence itself.)

Capped? No numerical licence cap and no plant cap found for this licence type alone.

Fees: $2,500 annually + $1,000 per additional licensed premises (16.8.11.9(C) NMAC; §26-2C-9(A)(3)). Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html (accessed 31 October 2026).

Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Application/renewal contents at 16.8.2.30 NMAC, including class sought (I–IV) and, for Classes II–IV, Environment Department authority for edibles/topicals. Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

4.4 Cannabis Retailer

What it allows. 16.8.2.35(B) NMAC [N, 12/28/2021; A, 03/22/2022]: "B. License required: Unless licensed pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act and division rules, a person shall not sell cannabis products to qualified patients, primary caregivers or reciprocal participants, or directly to consumers." Statutory definition, NMSA §26-2C-2: "‘cannabis retailer’ means a person that sells cannabis products to consumers." Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html and https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026).

Plant / canopy limits: None.

Capped? No numerical licence cap found.

Fees: $2,500 annually + $1,000 per additional licensed premises (16.8.11.9(E) NMAC; §26-2C-9(A)(5)), subject to the consignment discount below. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html (accessed 31 October 2026).

Retailer consignment discount — §26-2C-6(D): "The division shall issue a license to a cannabis retailer applicant at a discount if the applicant provides documentation of an agreement to accept cannabis products on consignment from a cannabis producer microbusiness or an integrated cannabis microbusiness." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The discount amount/percentage is not stated in the section — Verify; do not quote a figure.

Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Application/renewal contents at 16.8.2.36 NMAC. Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

4.5 Medical-only fee rule, VICE cap, and server-permit fee cap (cross-cutting fee rules)

  • Medical-only licences cost one-half. §26-2C-9(D): "The initial application fee and the annual renewal fee for a license or renewal of a license that authorizes only medical cannabis activity shall be one-half the fee applicable to a license authorizing both medical cannabis activity and commercial cannabis activity." Repeated in 16.8.11.12 NMAC. So a medical-only retailer/producer/manufacturer/testing/research base fee is $1,250, not $2,500. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-9/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  • VICE total cap. 16.8.11.12 NMAC and §26-2C-9(D): application, licence, premises and plant fees, and renewal equivalents, shall not exceed $125,000 for a VICE licence for both medical and commercial activity. Source as above.
  • Per-plant statutory ceiling vs. charged rate. §26-2C-9(B): except for producer microbusinesses and ICMBs, a cultivating licensee "shall be assessed an additional annual fee no greater than fifty dollars ($50.00) per mature cannabis plant at the time of licensing or renewal." The charged rates are the flat $5.00 commercial / $2.50 medical-only rates in 16.8.11.11 NMAC — the $50 figure is a ceiling, not the fee. Source as above.
  • Server-permit fee cap. §26-2C-9(G) caps a cannabis server permit fee at not more than $35. The actual charged issuance fee was not confirmed from the statute/rule text opened — Verify; a $10 replacement-permit figure appears only in secondary sources and is not adopted (see §4.11).

4.6 Proof of water rights — exact requirement, accepted proof, enforcement

Statute — §26-2C-7(A)(3) (2025 text, as amended effective 1 July 2024 by Laws 2024, ch. 38):

"if a cannabis producer or cannabis producer microbusiness, require as a condition of licensing that the applicant demonstrate that the applicant has a legal right to a commercial water supply, water rights or other source of water sufficient to meet the water needs as determined by the division related to the license as evidenced by documentation from the office of the state engineer of a valid water right or from a water provider that the use of water for cannabis production is compliant with that water provider's rules"

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-7/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The 2024 amendment annotation expressly states it clarified that the water condition applies only to cannabis producers and cannabis producer microbusinesses. Do not apply the water condition to manufacturers/retailers as a licensing condition on the basis of this section. Note for VICE/ICMB: a VICE or ICMB applicant must meet all qualifications for each establishment type authorised (16.8.2.8(Y)(1) NMAC), so the production limb of a VICE/ICMB application carries the same water demonstration in practice — Verify the VICE/ICMB application forms for the water item before stating it as a separate VICE/ICMB condition. Producers must additionally submit an energy/water-reduction plan (§26-2C-7(A)(4): drip irrigation and water collection, natural lighting/energy efficiency, renewable energy).

Rule — 16.8.2.22(A)(5) NMAC (producer application): "demonstration of a legal right to use the quantity of water that the division determines is needed for cannabis production, as evidenced by either: (a) documentation from a water provider that the applicant has the right to use water from the provider and that the use of water from cannabis production is compliant with provider's rules, or (b) documentation from the office of the state engineer showing that the applicant has a valid and existing water right, or a permit to develop a water right, for irrigation purposes for outdoor cultivation, or a commercial purpose for indoor cultivation at the proposed place of use of the cannabis establishment." Acceptable OSE documentation includes: (i) a state engineer permit or licence in good standing, excluding a permit under §§72-12-1, -1.1, -1.2 or -1.3 NMSA 1978 (domestic-well provisions); (ii) a subfile order or decree from a water-rights adjudication court; (iii) findings of an OSE hydrographic survey; or (iv) other documentation OSE has deemed in writing acceptable under the rule. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.22 (accessed 31 October 2026). The application must also state the initial mature/immature plant numbers and "the amount of water the applicant plans to use on a monthly basis for a 12 month period" (16.8.2.22(A)(11) NMAC). A CCD producer application checklist repeats the same OSE documentation list and requires an OSE Accession Form as part of the water-rights review process. Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/CCD-Producer-Application-Checklist1.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026).

OSE practice (official OSE page and FAQ v.10, valid 10 July 2025). Source: https://www.ose.nm.gov/WR/cannabis.php and https://api.realfile.rtsclients.com/PublicFiles/5f809ddfc9864dad89f9d03375144a14/f9872ec4-f50d-46fd-adf0-6a34392be86a/OSE Cannabis FAQv10071025.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026):

  • Municipal water (e.g. Albuquerque, Las Cruces, Santa Fe): "you don't need to go to the OSE. RLD/CCD will review and validate this source of water."
  • Privately owned right: OSE validates the right and whether it is configured correctly for the proposed use and place of use; outdoor = irrigation/agriculture configuration, indoor = commercial configuration.
  • "Water Rights must be in the applicant's name, or they must have a lease or user agreement in place and provide copies to the OSE with their Water Rights Accession Form." A permit or change of ownership must be completed before submitting the Accession Form.
  • Short-term water hauling is treated as a 1-year "bridge" only: the hauler must provide a letter verifying a valid water right in sufficient amounts and a contract for the amount of water required, plus documentation of the hauler's own source; the hauler must itself have legal access.
  • Do not assume a property purchase, or an acequia share, carries a usable right — an OSE district-office check is required.

Enforcement. Failure to meet the Act/rules is a ground for denial: §26-2C-7(C): "The division shall deny an application for an initial license or renewal if the application does not include information required by the division or the applicant does not meet the requirements of the Cannabis Regulation Act or rules." The division may refuse, suspend or revoke under the Uniform Licensing Act for non-compliance (§26-2C-7(D)). Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-7/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Verify: 16.8.2.23 NMAC (opened in the audit, 1 November 2026) confirms the trigger: a producer must obtain division approval of an amended licence before implementing a change of water source or of its water and energy conservation plan (16.8.2.23(A)(2)), and a change in the licensee’s access to the water source submitted with an application for initial, amended, or renewal licensure, or a 10% or more increase in water usage, is a material or substantial change (16.8.2.23(D)(3)).

4.7 Social equity provisions — what officially exists, and what does not

There is an official equity framework, but there is NO standalone social-equity licence, lottery, set-aside, or fee waiver found in the statute or rules read. That negative finding is explicit, per the instruction not to invent a programme.

What officially exists:

  1. Statutory duty — §26-2C-3(B)(7)–(10). CCD must promulgate rules with "procedures that promote and encourage full participation in the cannabis industry … by representatives of communities that have been disproportionately harmed by rates of arrest through the enforcement of cannabis prohibitions in law and policy, rural communities likely to be impacted by cannabis production and agricultural producers from economically disadvantaged communities" and "procedures that promote and encourage racial, ethnic, gender and geographic diversity and New Mexico residency among license applicants, licensees and cannabis industry employees," plus a certification process for products from ICMBs/producer microbusinesses or businesses owned by representatives of those communities and underserved communities (tribal, acequia, land grant-merced, other rural historic communities), and a technical-assistance resource guide for rural residents. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-3/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  2. Required equity plan in every application. Example, 16.8.2.22(A)(19) NMAC (producer): "applicant's social and economic equity plan to encourage economic and social diversity in employment, including race, ethnicity, gender, age, and residential status of licensee, controlling persons and employees of applicant and whether the applicant, controlling persons, employees or the locations where the cannabis products are produced are located in an underserved rural community, including tribal, acequia, land grantmerced, federally designated opportunity zone, or other rural historic communities." The same item appears in the research-laboratory application rule (16.8.2.57 NMAC) and in CCD checklists. Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.22 and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.57 (accessed 31 October 2026). A CCD producer checklist states: "The social and economic equity plan should describe the applicant's plan to encourage economic and social diversity in employment" with the same race/ethnicity/gender/age/residential-status and underserved-rural-community contents. Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/CCD-Producer-Application-Checklist1.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026).
  3. Annual demographic reporting — §26-2C-3(F). CCD "shall collect and publish annually on the division's website" demographic data on applicants, controlling persons and employees (race, ethnicity, gender, age, residential status, underserved-rural location) and present it to the legislature's interim committee. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-3/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  4. Low-barrier licence design as the equity mechanism. The RLD social-equity page (full page not directly opened — see §12) is reported to state: "In New Mexico, we do not place caps on the number of cannabis licenses issued nor is there a lottery system. Instead, the Cannabis Control Division promotes participation … by offering a variety of license types with plant fees as low as $2.50 per mature plant for those growing only for qualified medical patients, and $5.00 per mature plant for those growing for adult-use" plus discounted microbusiness licences. Those plant rates match current 16.8.11.11 NMAC, so the substance is corroborated even though the RLD page itself was not opened. The microbusiness/ICMB structure (§4.2, §4.9) and the retailer consignment discount (§4.4) are the concrete low-barrier mechanisms in the statute/rules.
  5. Rule — 16.8.1.8 NMAC (Social and Economic Equity) repeats the §26-2C-3(B)(7)–(8) mandate. A CCD goal that at least 50% of applicants/licensees/employees represent those groups, quoted in secondary summaries, was not verified in the rule text opened — Verify only.
  6. Not adopted. A $5 million New Mexico Finance Authority microbusiness loan programme and "loans up to $250,000" claims appear only in secondary sources. Neither was found in the statute/rules opened and neither is presented here as an official programme — Verify before any mention.

4.8 How Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act (LECUA, ch. 26, art. 2B) medical operators converted

This was a legacy-continuation + relicensing model, not an automatic conversion of the old licence into an adult-use licence and not a new competitive application round for incumbents:

  1. Priority processing window — §26-2C-7(A)(1). CCD was to "no later than September 1, 2021, accept and begin processing license applications for cannabis producers, cannabis producer microbusinesses and any person properly licensed and in good standing as a licensed cannabis producer pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act." All other licence types followed by 1 January 2022 (§26-2C-7(A)(2)). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-7/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  2. Continued operation until comparable licences existed — §26-2C-6(M). "A person properly licensed and in good standing pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act on the effective date of the Cannabis Regulation Act may continue to operate pursuant to that license for medical cannabis until comparable licenses for commercial cannabis activity are available. … A facility of such a licensee, upon issuance of the applicable cannabis establishment license, shall constitute licensed premises of the licensee and the licensee shall be entitled to continued and uninterrupted operations of the licensed premises." Retail commercial sales were to begin no later than 1 April 2022 (in fact 1 April 2022). For medical activity, the licensee continued under medical-programme rules until CCD promulgated medical-activity rules. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  3. Rule mechanism — 16.8.2.8(W) NMAC. "In order to be entitled to continue operating as a cannabis establishment, a person properly licensed and in good standing pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act on June 29, 2021, must submit a completed renewal application for a cannabis establishment license, along with required fees, within 30 days of the division notifying the licensee that a renewal application is available. In the event the person does not apply for such a license renewal within the required timeframe, the person shall cease all production operations immediately." On approval the licensee operates under the Cannabis Regulation Act/CCD rules, continuing under Department of Health medical rules only where they do not conflict. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026).
  4. Designation + fee consequence. Every new licence carries a clear designation for medical, commercial, or both (§26-2C-6(C)); medical-only licences cost one-half the both-activity fee (§26-2C-9(D), §4.5). Legacy producers that took a both-activity licence therefore moved onto the full fee schedule, with the $5.00/$2.50 plant rates applying by plant designation.
  5. Corporate-form conversion (separate, 2024) — §26-2C-6(Q). "A medical cannabis legacy nonprofit corporation that was required by the department of health to organize under the provisions of the Nonprofit Corporation Act [Chapter 53, Article 8 NMSA 1978] in order to qualify for a medical cannabis license may be converted into a corporation under the Business Corporation Act [Chapter 53, Articles 11 through 18 NMSA 1978], a limited liability company under the Limited Liability Company Act [Chapter 53, Article 19 NMSA 1978], a limited partnership under the Uniform Revised Limited Partnership Act [Chapter 54, Article 2A NMSA 1978] or a partnership under the Uniform Partnership Act (1994) [54-1A-101 to 54-1A-1206 NMSA 1978] upon the nonprofit corporation's filing with the secretary of state of restated articles of incorporation, articles of organization, certificate of limited partnership or statement under Section 54-1A-105 NMSA 1978." Added by Laws 2024, ch. 38, effective 1 July 2024. This is the mechanism by which legacy medical nonprofits became for-profit entities; it is distinct from licensure itself. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ (accessed 31 October 2026).
  6. Not found. No separate "conversion fee," conversion application form, or automatic adult-use entitlement for legacy licensees was found in the sections opened. Secondary claims that legacy licensees were "first" to apply are consistent with the §26-2C-7(A)(1) priority processing, but no CCD conversion guidance document was opened — Verify if the dossier needs the operational checklist.

4.9 Remaining CCD business licences

4.9.1 Cannabis Courier

What it allows — 16.8.2.41(B)–(C) NMAC [N, 12/28/2021; A, 03/22/2022]: "B. License required: Unless licensed pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act and division rules, a person shall not transport cannabis products directly to qualified patients, primary caregivers or reciprocal participants, or directly to consumers"; "(C) Consumer delivery: (1) A licensee may deliver cannabis or cannabis products from a licensed retail establishment to a qualified patient who is at least 18 years of age, a primary caregiver or a reciprocal participant, or a consumer who is at least 21 years of age." Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.41 (accessed 31 October 2026). Operating limits (same section): deliveries only from a retail licensee with which the courier is employed or has a disclosed delivery agreement (16.8.2.41(D)(1)–(2)); only shelf-stable products may be delivered — perishable / time-and-temperature-controlled products may not (16.8.2.41(D)(9)); a delivery package may not be held longer than 24 hours (16.8.2.41(D)(7)); delivery vehicles must not advertise cannabis transport (16.8.2.41(D)(8)); vehicle value cap — 16.8.2.41(F): "Maximum retail value: The maximum retail value allowed in a cannabis courier's vehicle at any one time shall be $10,000 and each product shall be associated with a specific order for delivery"; per-consumer delivery cap — 16.8.2.41(I)(3): delivery to an individual consumer of more than two ounces of cannabis, 16 grams of cannabis extract and 800 milligrams of edible cannabis is prohibited. Plant/canopy limits: None. Capped? No numerical licence cap found; capped instead by the $10,000 vehicle value limit and per-delivery quantity limits. Fees: $250 annually + $100 per additional licensed premises (16.8.11.9(A) NMAC — the statute, §26-2C-9(A)(1), allows up to $1,500 + up to $1,000 per additional premises; the rule amount is operative). Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Application/renewal contents at 16.8.2.42 NMAC (including vehicle registration/insurance and a delivery plan). Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5). Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0011.html and https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026).

4.9.2 Cannabis Testing Laboratory

What it allows — NMSA §26-2C-2: "‘cannabis testing laboratory’ means a facility that samples, collects and tests cannabis products and transports cannabis products for the purpose of testing." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Testing categories — 16.8.2.43(A) NMAC [Rp, 01/11/2022; A, 03/22/2022]: the division may license testing laboratories to perform analytical testing in one or more of: (1) visual inspection; (2) microbiological; (3) residual solvents; (4) potency and homogeneity; (5) heavy metals; (6) pesticides; and (7) such other categories as the department may identify. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026). Ownership bar — critical and distinctive. 16.8.2.43(D) NMAC: "No person with a direct or indirect interest in any cannabis establishment other than a cannabis research laboratory may hold an interest in a cannabis testing laboratory." And §26-2C-6(G): "The division shall not allow a person that is licensed as any type of cannabis establishment other than a cannabis research laboratory to hold, directly or indirectly, a cannabis testing laboratory license." Internal quality-control testing by an establishment using validated methods, without offering testing services to others, does not require a testing-lab licence (16.8.2.43(B) NMAC). Plant/canopy limits: None. Capped? No numerical licence cap found; the ownership bar is the binding restriction. Fees: $2,500 annually + $1,000 per additional licensed premises (16.8.11.9(B) NMAC; statute allows up to $2,500). Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate, plus an annual continuing demonstration of capability (CDC) for each test as part of renewal (16.8.2.44(C) NMAC: ISO/IEC 17025 scope evidence, proficiency testing, or re-performance of the initial demonstration of capability). Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

4.9.3 Cannabis Consumption Area — Type I and Type II

What it allows — two classes. 16.8.2.49(A) NMAC [Rp, 06/07/2022]: "A. License types: The division may license two classes of cannabis consumption areas: (1) Type I permit: A licensed cannabis consumption area where cannabis products may be consumed on the licensed premises, except for products consumed through the respiratory system. (2) Type II permit: A licensed cannabis consumption area where cannabis products may be consumed, including products that are consumed through the respiratory system." Note the rule's own wording calls these "permits" within the consumption-area licence; the §26-2C-6(B)(1) item is "cannabis consumption areas." Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-49-NMAC (accessed 31 October 2026). Retailer-qualification prerequisite — 16.8.2.49(E) NMAC: "Cannabis consumption area license: Applicants for a cannabis consumption area must meet all qualifications for a cannabis retailer to be approved for, and authorized to conduct, a cannabis consumption area." General consumption bar — 16.8.2.8(D) NMAC: licensees shall prohibit consumption of cannabis or cannabis products on or within the licensed premises unless a cannabis consumption area has been approved by the division. Smoking restriction: smoking in a consumption area is allowed only if it is in a designated smoking area or a standalone building from which smoke does not infiltrate other indoor workplaces/public places where smoking is otherwise prohibited under the Dee Johnson Clean Indoor Air Act (16.8.2.55 NMAC; §26-2C-6(K)). Server-permit link: all employees who directly offer, sell or serve cannabis in a consumption area must hold a current cannabis server permit (16.8.2.54(F) NMAC, citing 16.8.10 NMAC). Plant/canopy limits: None. Capped? No numerical licence cap found. Fees: $2,500 annually (16.8.11.9(J) NMAC; statute allows up to $2,500). The 2023 CCD PDF phrased this as "Up to $2,500.00/year"; the current rule states $2,500 annually with no "up to" qualifier and no additional-premises line for this type in §16.8.11.9(J) — additional-premises treatment for consumption areas is Verify. A secondary claim of a $2,500/$5,000 Type I/Type II fee split was not adopted — the official rule states a single $2,500 fee. Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Application/renewal contents at 16.8.2.50 NMAC. Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

4.9.4 Cannabis Research Laboratory — Tiers I–III

What it allows — NMSA §26-2C-2: "‘cannabis research laboratory’ means a facility that produces or possesses cannabis products and all parts of the plant genus Cannabis for the purpose of studying cannabis cultivation, characteristics or uses." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Tiers — 16.8.2.56(A) NMAC [Rp, 07/12/2022]: "(1) Tier I: A cannabis research laboratory Tier I may produce cannabis to be ingested by human or animal subjects, or produce cannabis not meant for ingestion, for division approved clinical, agricultural, or market research studies; produce federally legal cannabis products; and may conduct division approved clinical, agricultural, or market research studies; (2) Tier II: A cannabis research laboratory Tier II may produce cannabis not meant for ingestion, or purchase cannabis to be ingested by human or animal subjects, for division approved clinical, agricultural, or market research studies; and may conduct division approved clinical, agricultural, or market research studies (3) Tier III: A cannabis research laboratory Tier III may not produce cannabis and may only purchase cannabis or cannabis products from licensed cannabis research laboratories Tier I and Tier II, as appropriate for approved clinical, agricultural, or market research studies; and may conduct clinical, agricultural, or market research studies." Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/nmac/nmregister/xxxiii/16.8.2amend_xxxiii13.html (accessed 31 October 2026). General research authority — 16.8.2.56(C) NMAC: except as noted in subsection B, a research laboratory licence permits a licensee to produce, process, transport, transfer, sell and possess cannabis consistent with its licence type for research and related purposes. Tier II/III purchase from another licensed establishment requires division approval and is limited to brand-specific/cultivar-specific inquiries where research-lab product is impossible (16.8.2.56(B) NMAC). Plant/canopy limits: Verify — no plant-count limit for research laboratories was stated in 16.8.2.56 as opened. Production is tied to division-approved studies, not to the 16.8.8 producer tiers (which by their terms apply to producer and VICE licences). Do not apply the 200 / 20,000 figures to research labs. Capped? No numerical licence cap found; the binding limits are tier scope and division approval of each study. Fees: $2,500 annually + $1,000 per additional licensed premises (16.8.11.9(F) NMAC). Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Application/renewal contents at 16.8.2.57 NMAC, including tier sought (I, II or III), research plan, and any DEA licence/conditional approval or plan to seek it. Applications open Oct 2026? Yes on the RLD page evidence (§4.0.5); the conflicting third-party "not open" claim is not adopted (see §4.0.5).

4.9.5 Integrated Cannabis Microbusiness (ICMB)

What it allows — NMSA §26-2C-2, "integrated cannabis microbusiness": a person licensed to conduct one or more of: (1) production of cannabis at a single licensed premises, provided the person shall not possess more than two hundred total mature cannabis plants at any one time; (2) manufacture of cannabis products at a single licensed premises; (3) sales and transportation of cannabis products produced or manufactured by that person or another cannabis producer microbusiness or integrated cannabis microbusiness; (4) operation of only one retail establishment; and (5) couriering of cannabis products to consumers. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The older CCD fee PDF phrased the same five activities as: production at a single location, manufacturing at a single location, operation of a single cannabis retail establishment, sale and transport of cannabis products produced or manufactured by the licensee, and couriering of cannabis products. Rule application route — 16.8.2.8(Y)(1)–(2) NMAC: applicants for a VICE or ICMB must meet all qualifications for each type of cannabis establishment authorised; an initial ICMB/VICE applicant must submit an application for authorisation to conduct one or more of production, manufacturing, retail establishment, or courier; applicants/licensees shall request authority to add or remove an activity by amended application and any required additional fees; and an applicant/licensee shall not conduct any activity for which additional authority is required until it has received written approval from the division. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html (accessed 31 October 2026). Plant/canopy limits: 200 total mature cannabis plants at any one time (production limb only, single licensed premises). No canopy limit. ICMBs are exempt from the per-plant fee (16.8.11.11 NMAC). Capped? Yes — by the 200-plant cap, single-premises-per-activity condition, and single-retail-establishment condition. No total-number cap found. Fees: $2,500 annually, flat (16.8.11.9(I) NMAC, as amended 7 May 2024). The old $1,000 (2 activities) / $1,500 (3) / $2,000 (4) / $2,500 (5) tier in the 2023 CCD PDF is superseded. Statute allows an additional $500 per licensed premises (§26-2C-9(A)(9)); the rule text in 16.8.11.9(I) as read lists no additional-premises amount — Verify. Evasion rule: §4.2. Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate. Adding/removing an activity requires an amended application. Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

4.9.6 Vertically Integrated Cannabis Establishment (VICE)

What it allows — NMSA §26-2C-2: "‘vertically integrated cannabis establishment’ means a person that is authorized to act as one or more of the following: (1) a cannabis courier; (2) a cannabis manufacturer; (3) a cannabis producer; and (4) a cannabis retailer." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-2/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The application route is the same §16.8.2.8(Y) NMAC text quoted under ICMB: the applicant must meet all qualifications for each establishment type authorised, apply for authorisation for one or more of production / manufacturing / retail / courier, and obtain written approval before conducting any activity requiring additional authority. If not all activity is on a single premises, each additional premises requires an additional premises fee (16.8.2.8(Y)(4) NMAC). Plant/canopy limits: Same producer tiers as a standalone producer — 16.8.8.9(A) NMAC expressly covers all cannabis producer and VICE licences issued on or after 15 August 2021. Therefore: Level 1: 201–2,000; Level 2: 2,001–6,000; Level 3: 6,001–12,000; Level 4: 12,001–16,000; absolute maximum 20,000 mature cannabis plants at one time (16.8.8.9(F) NMAC); increases in 500-plant increments, up to eight increments at a time, at renewal and once more per year (16.8.8.9(C)–(D) NMAC). No canopy limit. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.html (accessed 31 October 2026). Capped? Yes, by plant count (20,000 mature maximum). No total-number cap found. Fees: $7,500 annually + $1,000 per additional licensed premises, plus per-plant fees ($5.00 commercial / $2.50 medical), subject to the $125,000 total cap for both-activity licences (16.8.11.9(G) and 16.8.11.12 NMAC; §26-2C-9(D)). Medical-only VICE fees are one-half (§4.5). Renewal: 12 months; 60-to-30-day window; tax gate; plant-count increases may be requested at renewal (16.8.8.10 NMAC). Applications open Oct 2026? Yes, per the RLD NM-PLUS page (§4.0.5).

All fees annual, for issuance or renewal; all licensing/renewal fees non-refundable (16.8.2.8(Q) NMAC).
