4.11 Cannabis Server Permit — NOT a business licence (included because §26-2C-6(B)(8) lists it)

What it allows. An individual to be employed as a server — directly offering, selling or serving cannabis — in a licensed cannabis consumption area. It does not authorise operating a business. Statute — §26-2C-11(B), (E): "B. The division shall issue cannabis server permits to persons twenty-one years of age or older who satisfy the requirements of this section and rules promulgated by the division. An applicant shall provide proof of satisfactory completion of a program provided by a cannabis server permit education provider approved by the division. A person shall not be employed as a cannabis server on a licensed premises unless that person obtains a cannabis server permit within thirty days of employment." "E. Cannabis server permits shall be valid for a period of three years from the date the permit is issued and may be renewed upon providing proof that the permit holder has successfully completed up to four and one-half hours of continuing education and an examination as determined by the division." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-11/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Rule detail — 16.8.10.8(A)–(B) NMAC (N, 07/12/2022): a server must complete a programme every three years; satisfactory completion requires a score of 80% or higher on an approved test; a person not previously certified must obtain a permit within 30 days of employment. Source: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0010.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026). A cannabis research laboratory or its employee is not required to obtain or possess a server permit while performing activities authorised under a research laboratory licence (§26-2C-11(A)). Plant/canopy limits: None. Capped? No. Fee: statute caps the permit fee at not more than $35 (§26-2C-9(G)); the actual charged issuance fee was not confirmed from the statute/rule text opened — Verify. A $10 replacement-permit figure appears only in secondary sources and is not adopted. Applications open Oct 2026? Server permits are issued via approved education providers, not via the NM-PLUS business-licence guides; no closure was found. Verify via CCD if a current provider list is needed.

4.12 Cannabis Training and Education Programme — REGISTRATION ONLY, not a licence (included because §26-2C-6(B)(10) lists it)

Current law — NMSA §26-2C-10 (repealed and reenacted by Laws 2024, ch. 38, §6, effective 1 July 2024): "A New Mexico public post-secondary educational institution may offer a practical or academic curriculum designed to prepare students for participation in the cannabis industry. The institution shall register its cannabis training and education program with the division, which shall include the information about the program on its website." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-10/ (accessed 31 October 2026). Consequence for the dossier: do not present "cannabis training and education" as an 11th CCD business licence type in October 2026. Pre-July-2024 material describing it as a licence is superseded. It is open only to New Mexico public post-secondary institutions, it is registration (not licensure), and the 12-month licence validity / 60-to-30-day renewal window for business licences does not apply to it on the face of §26-2C-10. No fee, plant limit, or cap applies. Registration is the mechanism; no registration window/closure was found in §26-2C-10. The CCD programme list itself was not directly opened — see §12.

4.13 Other CCD authorisations found on official sources — and items NOT found

  • No separate "cannabis nursery" CCD licence was found in §26-2C-6(B) or 16.8.2 NMAC as opened. A 2023 bill (HB 313, 56th Legislature, 1st Session) proposed creating a cannabis nursery licence and raising microbusiness plant counts to 1,000 — that bill is proposed only and is not current law; it is noted here only to prevent its adoption. Do not list a nursery licence as a CCD type. (Hemp nursery licensing is a separate NMDA matter — §4.14.3.)
  • No separate CCD "distributor," "transporter" (other than courier), or "wholesaler" licence was found; wholesale movement is within producer/manufacturer/VICE authority as defined in §4.1/§4.3/§4.9.6, and consumer delivery is courier authority (§4.9.1).
  • Personal production (home grow) is not a CCD business licence and is out of scope for this Part except to note the boundary: 16.8.2.21(C) NMAC excepts personal use as provided by the Cannabis Regulation Act and LECUA from the producer-licence requirement. Patient personal-production rules belong to Part 1/Part 11 scope, not to this licence inventory.

4.14 Hemp licences — Part 4 summary (full detail belongs to Part 7; cross-reference)

Correction to tentative citations: the Hemp Manufacturing Act is NMSA 1978, §§76-24-1 et seq. — not §§26-2C-x. NMED's rule states: "'Act' means the Hemp Manufacturing Act, Section 76-24-1, et seq., NMSA 1978." There is no Chapter 26, Article 2C hemp act in the sources opened. Do not use 26-2C for hemp.

Who does what. NMDA issues licences to businesses/individuals cultivating hemp; NMED issues permits to businesses/individuals for processing activities following harvest, including extraction, distillation, and manufacturing. Verbatim, NMDA Hemp Registration page: "As required by state law, New Mexico Department of Agriculture issues licenses to businesses/individuals cultivating hemp. The New Mexico Environment Department issues licenses to businesses/individuals for processing activities following harvest, including extraction, distillation, and manufacturing." Source: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/licensing-and-registrations/hemp-registration.html (accessed 31 October 2026). There is no NMDA "processor licence" — post-harvest processing is NMED-only. Any draft listing NMDA as the processor licensor is wrong.

USDA plan status — own approved state plan, NOT USDA-direct. USDA AMS, List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans (page stated "Updated February 17, 2026"): "New Mexico | NM Approved Plan (pdf)\" — where "\" = "Plan approved under the final rule which took effect March 22, 2021." Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review (accessed 31 October 2026). NMDA Hemp Program page, verbatim: "As of January 1, 2022, New Mexico began operating under a USDA-approved state plan administered by NMDA." Source: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/aes/hemp-program.html (accessed 31 October 2026). Growers are therefore licensed by NMDA under the state plan, not by USDA directly.

4.14.1 NMDA cultivation licences (Hemp Cultivation Rule, 21.20.2 NMAC; 2026 forms)

Annual Hemp Commercial (Research) Production Licence — field / annual crop. What it allows: planting an annual hemp crop in the field only; the 2026 form states it is "not intended for growers maintaining viable hemp plants throughout the year as part of a greenhouse or plant nursery operation." Term: "License expires 240 [days] after date of issuance, please ensure you will be harvesting within the 240 day period"; 21.20.2.7(A) NMAC: "'Annual Production License' means license issued for the production of a single crop that is destroyed within 240 days of planting." Application timing (21.20.2.8(A) NMAC): apply "no less than 25 business days prior to planting of each crop at each location"; a separate application and fee are required for each new crop at each location. Area rule (2026 form): no acreage limit for a single contiguous growing area; multiple non-contiguous areas on one licence only if within a 2.5-mile radius, total <10 acres, and all planted within a 3-week period; a landowner affidavit is required if the applicant does not own the land. Fees — current (2026 form, Updated January 2026): base registration/inspection fee $650.00 + $6.00 per acre (minimum $6.00) + $10.00 per variety (minimum $10.00). "Fees based on: $650.00 registration fee + $6.00 / acre of hemp production + $10.00 per variety. Once payment is processed, refunds are not available or transferable to another license." Form: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/media/pdf/annual-hemp-commercial-production-application.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026). Rule-vs-form variance to flag in Part 7: the still-posted 21.20.2.10 NMAC text (dated 11 December 2018) states higher caps — $800 per location for annual, $900 for continuous, and $25 per variety in excess of one. The 2026 NMDA forms charge $650/$750 and $10 per variety. Use the 2026 form figures as the current charged fees; note the 2018 rule text has not been updated on the SRCA posting. Do not present $800/$900 as the 2026 fee.

Continuous Hemp Commercial (Research) Production Licence — indoor / greenhouse / nursery, year-round. What it allows: maintaining viable hemp plants throughout the year as part of a greenhouse or plant nursery operation (including clonal production); the form states it is not intended for production of an annual crop. Term: "License is valid from February 1, 2026 through January 31, 2027"; 21.20.2.7(F) and 21.20.2.8(B) NMAC: a continuous licence expires 31 January of each year and renewal must be applied for prior to 1 February. Area rule (2026 form): no limit for a single contiguous growing area; multiple non-contiguous areas on one licence only if within a 2.5-mile radius and total <10 acres / 435,600 sq ft. Fees — current (2026 form, Updated January 2026): base registration/inspection fee $750.00 + $0.75 per 1,000 square feet (minimum $5.00) + $10.00 per variety (minimum $10.00). Form: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/media/pdf/continuous-hemp-commercial-application.pdf (accessed 31 October 2026).

Common requirements (both grower licences, 2026 forms + 21.20.2.9 NMAC). Criminal background check required; "Hemp commercial production licenses cannot be issued to individuals with felony convictions related to controlled substances within the last ten (10) years." The applicant must supply the state Department of Public Safety report/stamp ($15.00 DPS charge stated in the form). Compliance with the New Mexico Child Support Enforcement Act — failure can result in denial/revocation. Licence is non-transferable; the licensee may not reassign/transfer to another business, location, individual or entity. Harvest only with NMDA-issued documents authorising harvest of the specific varieties listed; field inspections and plant samples within 30 days of the estimated harvest date; the licensee is responsible for delivery of samples to an NMDA-approved laboratory for THC determination (post-decarboxylation) before harvest, and for destruction/disposition costs of non-compliant (>0.3% THC) varieties. Harvest Notification Document: "Submitted no less than 30 days prior to estimated harvest date. Allows department staff time to schedule for sampling." Hemp Harvest Certificate: NMDA document certifying a quantity of hemp meets the THC concentration required — NMED facilities may only accept New Mexico hemp with a "PASS" harvest certificate plus a transportation manifest (§4.14.2). Licence is proof of state registration as a hemp producer; NMDA states it "is required by law enforcement if you have viable hemp plants or a grower in possession of raw hemp." Info links: licence hub https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/licensing-and-registrations/hemp-registration.html; programme page https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/aes/hemp-program.html; rules/statutes hub https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/aes/hemp/hemp-laws-and-regulations.html; cultivation rule (SRCA) https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title21/21.020.0002.html (all accessed 31 October 2026).

4.14.2 NMED post-harvest permits (20.10.2 NMAC, effective 28 January 2026)

Rule status — do not present the old rule as current. 20.10.2 NMAC, Hemp Extraction, Production, Transportation, Warehousing, and Testing, was repealed-and-replaced, effective 28 January 2026 (20.10.2.5 NMAC: "Effective Date: January 28, 2026, unless a later date is cited at the end of a section."). It makes permanent the emergency amendment effective 1 August 2025. Statutory authority (20.10.2.3 NMAC, verbatim): "Section 76-24-8 NMSA 1978 authorizes the environment department to issue permits to extract, process, or engage in other manufacturing activities regarding hemp and directs the department to adopt permitting rules that include fees." Objective (20.10.2.6 NMAC): "To establish uniform standards for the transportation, extraction, processing, and testing of hemp products for the purpose of ensuring the safe manufacture and accurate presentation of hemp products for human consumption, absorption, and inhalation." Scope (20.10.2.2 NMAC): "All individuals, businesses, agencies, institutions, or other entities engaged in the transportation, extraction, storage, or processing of hemp products in New Mexico." Rule PDF: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/wp-content/uploads/sites/34/2025/12/20.10.2-NMAC-Final-Rule-1282026.pdf; final-rule hub: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/hemp-final-rule/ (accessed 31 October 2026). §76-24-8 NMSA 1978 itself: "The department of environment shall issue permits pursuant to rules issued under Subsection C of this section to extract, process or engage in other manufacturing activities regarding hemp, including manufacturing intermediate hemp-derived products and hemp finished products" and "A person shall not extract, process or engage in other manufacturing activities regarding hemp, including manufacturing intermediate hemp-derived products and hemp finished products without a permit issued by the department of environment or a license issued pursuant to Subsection C of Section 76-24-10 NMSA 1978"; fees "not to exceed the lesser of one thousand dollars ($1,000) or the cost of administration of a permit." History: Laws 2019, ch. 116, §6; 2020, ch. 32, §6. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-76/article-24/section-76-24-8/ (accessed 31 October 2026).

The four current permit types — verbatim definitions (20.10.2.7 NMAC) and fees (20.10.2.8(D)(1) NMAC):

Permit typeWhat it allows (verbatim definition)Initial + renewal fee
Hemp Extraction Facility"an operation that produces hemp extract" (20.10.2.7(W) NMAC) — "hemp extract" means oil and extracts derived from hemp, containing THC in any concentration, including cannabidiol, cannabidiolic acid, and other identified and non-identified compounds$1,000
Hemp Manufacturing Facility"an operation, other than a hemp extraction facility, hemp retail manufacturer, or hemp warehouse that produces or repackages hemp products, other than hemp extract, and provides hemp products for sale or distribution to other business entities" (20.10.2.7(BB) NMAC) — i.e. wholesale manufacturing$1,000
Hemp Warehouse"a location, other than a hemp extraction facility, hemp manufacturing facility, or hemp retail manufacturer where hemp extract is stored" (20.10.2.7(II) NMAC)$1,000
Hemp Retail Manufacturer (NEW in the 28 Jan 2026 rule; replaces the former "Hemp Processing Facility" type)"an operation that produces or repackages hemp finished products and provides them directly to consumers" (20.10.2.7(EE) NMAC). NMED's final-rule summary: retail producers such as restaurants and bakeries meet the same requirements as wholesale producers. Special limit: "Unless approved, a hemp retail manufacturer shall only receive and use hemp extract that is broad spectrum" (20.10.2.8(C)(6) NMAC) — broad spectrum = THC removed, ≤0.005% total THC (20.10.2.7(H) NMAC)$500

Other NMED fees (20.10.2.8(D) NMAC): late renewal fee $200 if renewal application + fee are not received on or before the permit expiration date; re-inspection fee $500 (payable before the re-inspection or before renewal approval); variance application fee $300; the regulatory authority may also charge administrative compliance costs; all fees are non-refundable.

Permit mechanics (20.10.2.8 NMAC). "A person may not operate a hemp facility without a valid permit to operate issued by the regulatory authority" (20.10.2.8(A)(1) NMAC). "when more than a single hemp facility is operated on the premises, each one shall be separately permitted" (20.10.2.8(A)(2) NMAC) — so an operation that both extracts and then formulates finished product needs two permits (extraction + manufacturing). Exception: "A hemp facility that is permitted as a hemp manufacturing facility, hemp extraction facility, or hemp retail manufacturer is not required to also be permitted as a hemp warehouse" (20.10.2.8(A)(9) NMAC). Permits are non-transferable — "from one person to another person, from one location to another location, or from one type of operation to another type of operation" (20.10.2.8(E)(5) NMAC). Permits "shall expire on the last day of the anniversary month of the date of original issue" (20.10.2.8(D)(3) NMAC). Application must be submitted at least 30 calendar days before operating, constructing, converting, remodelling/changing facility type, or opening/changing ownership (20.10.2.8(B)(1) NMAC); issuance requires a completed application, fee, approval, and a pre-operational inspection. Each facility must file a written operational plan plus per-product information (ingredients by weight, pH, water activity, full procedure including extraction method and solvent removal, packaging, label, batch/lot coding, shelf-life, distribution). Manufacturing employees must hold a valid food handler card (within 30 days of employment if not held at hire; card valid 3 years; requirement effective 60 days after the rule's effective date) (20.10.2.9(H) NMAC). Transport only to NMED-permitted facilities or persons approved by the regulatory authority, under a hemp transportation manifest (20.10.2.10 NMAC). Testing (20.10.2.14 NMAC): every batch/lot of finished product for human consumption, cosmetics or inhalation must be tested by an NMED-approved analytical laboratory before it leaves the facility — cannabinoid profile (Total THC = 0.877 × THCA + THC, Δ9-THC, THCA, CBD, CBDA), label-content verification, solvents, and pesticide profile as determined by NMED.

When is an NMED permit actually required? — NMED FAQ (opened 31 October 2026). "A permit from NMED is required when manufacturing hemp-containing products for human ingestion, absorption, or smokable products." "Yes, a hemp manufacturing permit from NMED [is] required for drying and/or processing (i.e. trimming) of hemp/hemp flower into a finished product, or product that does not need further processing to be offered as a finished product." Source: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/faqs/ (accessed 31 October 2026). The FAQ's blanket statement that a non-refundable fee of $1,000 is required with each hemp application predates the $500 retail-manufacturer distinction — use the rule's $500 retail figure, not the FAQ's blanket $1,000. The FAQ also still defines "hemp facility" as extraction/manufacturing/warehouse only (omitting retail manufacturer) — where FAQ and 20.10.2 NMAC conflict, the rule governs.

Finished-product THC limits (20.10.2.12 NMAC, effective 60 days after 28 January 2026). Unless otherwise specified, a hemp finished product shall (1) not exceed 0.30% total THC concentration, (2) contain no more than 2.0 mg total THC per serving, and (3) no more than 20 mg total THC per package. Exceptions: hemp tinctures ≤100 mg total THC per package; broad-spectrum finished products ≤6.0 mg total THC per package; cosmetics and vapes are exempt from the per-serving/per-package mg limits (but not from the 0.30% concentration limit as written in §12(A)(1) — flag this nuance rather than stating vapes/cosmetics are uncapped).

Synthetic / semi-synthetic cannabinoids (20.10.2.11(K)–(L) NMAC). As a general rule "a hemp facility shall not receive, possess, manufacture, offer, advertise, market, or sell semisynthetic cannabinoids or synthetic cannabinoids or products containing" them. Narrow exception: the nine listed cannabinoids — THCV, CBC, CBT, CBL, CBE, CBG, CBDV, CBD, CBN — may be received/used as ingredients only if approved-lab analysis by a validated method shows ≥98% purity before use. Delta-8, delta-10, THC-O and HHC are not on the nine-item exception list and therefore fall under the general prohibition as written — but Part 7 should quote 20.10.2.11(K)–(L) NMAC rather than naming a product-by-product ban list, since the rule works by exception list. This is the current (28 January 2026) position; it supersedes looser summaries of the August 2025 emergency rule.

Hemp-derived product registration / retailer rule — what exists and what does not. No separate "hemp-derived product registration" was found on any official NMDA or NMED source opened. Products are controlled through the facility permit + per-product operational-plan information + batch/lot testing + labelling (20.10.2.12–.14 NMAC), not through a standalone product-registration licence. Do not invent a product-registration fee or number. No retailer licence/permit: NMED FAQ, verbatim: "Do I need a permit to sell pre-packaged CBD or other hemp products? No, not at this time." NMED recommends verifying that pre-packaged product comes from a properly permitted/licensed manufacturer. "Hemp Retailer" is defined in 20.10.2.7(FF) NMAC ("a person that provides hemp finished products directly to consumers") but it is not a permit type — the permit type for direct-to-consumer production is Hemp Retail Manufacturer (above). A pure reseller of pre-packaged product needs no NMED permit as of 31 October 2026.

4.14.3 Other NMDA licences under 21.20.3 NMAC — "Hemp Manufacturing Rule" (name is misleading)

Despite its title, 21.20.3 NMAC does NOT license NMED post-harvest manufacturing. Its scope (21.20.3.2 NMAC) is only: (A) testing of raw hemp for regulatory purposes as identified by NMDA, and (B) plant breeding involving viable plants >0.3% and <5% THC. Rule text (SRCA): https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title21/21.020.0003.html (accessed 31 October 2026).

LicenceWhat it allows (verbatim scope)Fee in rule textTerm

Requires demonstrated analytical proficiency, department-approved SOPs, lab-director credentials, and proficiency-test participation (max 2 per 12 months if satisfactory)."shall not exceed five-hundred dollars ($500)" per year (21.20.3.9(A) NMAC); double fee if late. Citation trap to flag in Part 7: NMED's 20.10.2.7(Z) NMAC defines "hemp harvest certificate" as certifying THC "pursuant to 21.20.3 NMAC," and NMED's FAQ repeats 21.20.3. The cultivation/THC rule itself is 21.20.2 NMAC; 21.20.3 NMAC is the lab/breeding rule that defines the harvest-certificate document (21.20.3.7(E) NMAC). Part 7 should cite 21.20.2 for cultivation and 21.20.3 for lab/breeding, and note NMED's cross-reference as written.

4.14.4 Interaction with CCD — VERIFY, do not assert

No official source opened states that intoxicating hemp products require a CCD licence. The position that can be stated on official sources runs the other way. NMED Hemp Rule FAQ, Q8 (official, opened 31 October 2026), verbatim: "I make cannabis products that include hemp ingredients under my CCD license, do I need any type of permit from CHB?" — "Yes. You will need a hemp warehouse or hemp manufacturing permit. Please email us for further info." I.e. a CCD licence does not substitute for an NMED hemp permit where hemp ingredients are handled — the permits stack. Source: https://www.env.nm.gov/hemp-rule-frequently-asked-questions/ (accessed 31 October 2026). NMED FAQ, cultivation section, verbatim: "If you perform extraction, process or manufacture hemp-derived material and/or hemp finish products, or store hemp extract a permit from NMED is required" — even if you already hold an NMDA grower licence. Source: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/faqs/ (accessed 31 October 2026). What was NOT verified on an official source: (a) any statute or rule transferring intoxicating-hemp retail/manufacture to CCD; (b) 2025 HB 346, “Hemp Products & Synthetic Cannabinoids” — Died (API): passed the House 54–7 on 13 March 2025 and passed the Senate 37–0 as amended on 22 March 2025, then Action Postponed Indefinitely, with no House concurrence recorded (nmlegis.gov legislation record; bill text: https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/25%20Regular/bills/house/HB0346CES.pdf). Its committee-substitute synopsis gave NMED and the Environmental Improvement Board authority over hemp finished products at retail and banned semi-synthetic and synthetic cannabinoids; it did not make intoxicating hemp a CCD-licensed product, and it is not law; (c) any CCD hemp-THC licence category. Third-party commentary asserting that intoxicating products "must" be sold through licensed dispensaries was not adopted, because no CCD or RLD official page opened for this Part says so. For Part 4/Part 7, write: "CCD interaction: Verify — no official NMDA/NMED/CCD source opened for this dossier states that an intoxicating hemp product requires a CCD licence; the only official CCD interaction found is NMED's statement that a CCD licensee handling hemp ingredients still needs an NMED hemp warehouse or manufacturing permit. Intoxicating-hemp products that exceed the 20.10.2 NMAC finished-product limits (0.30% / 2 mg per serving / 20 mg per package) cannot lawfully be sold as hemp finished products under NMED's rule; whether they fall under CCD cannabis licensing is Verify on a CCD/RLD source before publication."

4.15 Estimated startup costs — NON-OFFICIAL ESTIMATE ONLY

No official (RLD/CCD/state) startup-cost estimate was found. Do not present any figure in this section as official.

One dated, non-official, New-Mexico-specific estimate was opened in full:

  • Source: KORONA POS, "How to Open a Dispensary in New Mexico: Licenses, Costs & Compliance," https://koronapos.com/blog/how-to-open-a-dispensary-in-new-mexico/ — NON-OFFICIAL (POS vendor blog). Publication date not shown on the page as opened; search crawl described it as updated ~131 days before 31 October 2026 — date therefore UNVERIFIED, treat as undated for citation purposes.
  • Total (vendor estimate): "Total estimated range $100,000 to $400,000+" for a dispensary.
  • Breakdown as published: licence application fee $1,000–$5,000; store buildout/fixtures $30,000–$150,000; security (cameras, alarm, vault) $10,000–$40,000; opening inventory $20,000–$60,000; POS/compliance tech $2,000–$8,000; legal/consulting $5,000–$25,000; signage/branding $3,000–$10,000; working-capital reserve $30,000–$100,000+.
  • Caveats that must travel with this estimate: (a) its licence-fee range ($1,000–$5,000) does not match the official retailer fee ($2,500 + $1,000 per additional premises) and must not be quoted as the licence cost; (b) its excise-tax statement (12%) is out of date on its face and is out of scope here; (c) it covers a retail dispensary only — no official or dated non-official total for a producer, manufacturer, testing lab or VICE startup was found in this research.
  • A second non-official figure found in search only (THD Wholesale: "up to $450,000 upfront and $42,000 per month operational") was not opened and is not adopted — listed only so the parent does not mistake it for a verified figure.

If no dated estimate is acceptable to the dossier editor, the correct entry is: Startup costs — Unavailable (no official estimate found; one undated vendor estimate exists, above).

PART 5 — LICENCE DATA SOURCES

5.0 How to use this inventory

  • "Interactive dashboard/search, no download" means the public interface is a web page/search; no bulk CSV/XLSX download was found on that page on 31 October 2026. Where a page has an export/download button, it is stated.
  • "Exact direct download link" is given only where the source page itself linked a file. File names below are as displayed on the source page (e.g. TRD "CannabisExcise-ACH-0926"). Where a link resolves through a RealFile/CDN host, that host URL is the link the source page exposes; it is not reconstructed here.
  • Licence counts in §5.12 are NOT a single consistent series: the December 2024 figures are "business licenses approved" (a cumulative approvals count, by licence type, including integrated types folded differently), while the June 2025 figures are "licensed premises" from a CCD presentation to legislators. They must not be added together or trended against each other without that caveat.
  • No personal phone numbers or emails of individuals are reproduced. Agency/business public contact details only, and only where the source page itself publishes them.

5.1 Cannabis Control Division (CCD) — Cannabis Reporting Online Portal (C.R.O.P.)

  • Holder type: All CCD-licensed cannabis establishments (sales reporters); sales, transactions and city-level sales. Not a licence-holder register by itself.
  • URL: https://crop.rld.nm.gov/ (portal home); https://crop.rld.nm.gov/sales.html (sales page). Accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Format: Interactive dashboard/search — no bulk download option found on the sales page as fetched. The portal displays charts, a date-range selector, and city tables. No CSV/XLSX export button was identified in the fetched text. Verify whether an export exists behind the interactive chart controls (the fetched text does not show one).
  • How to access: Open the URL; select date range / city. Data are described on the portal as reported by licensed cannabis entities through the state's track-and-trace system and as public information subject to the New Mexico Inspection of Public Records Act, NMSA 1978 §§ 14-2-1 to 14-2-12 (per the CROP description reproduced in secondary compilations of CROP data).
  • Update frequency as stated: Not stated on the fetched page. In practice, monthly sales are posted after the month closes; the latest month shown in indexed CROP data is July 2026 (see §6.1). August and September 2026 sales were not in the CROP headline indexed at dossier date — Unavailable / lag — Verify whether August-September 2026 have since been posted.
  • Latest data date: July 2026 (headline); all-time April 2022-July 2026 (see §6.1).
  • Fields available: Medical sales ($), medical transactions (count), adult-use sales ($), adult-use transactions (count), total sales ($), total transactions (count); by month and by city (city table shows medical sales/transactions, adult-use sales/transactions, total sales/transactions — see §6.5 for Albuquerque and Alamogordo totals as indexed).
  • Limitations:

The page states definitions/field descriptions are available for download below the table (exact definitions file name not extracted in fetched text — Verify on the live page).
  • How to access / download: Click the month's report link on the TRD page. The page warns: "If having issues downloading files - right click > open link in new tab." Files are served via realfile.tax.newmexico.gov.
  • Exact direct download links / file names (latest months, as displayed on the page):
  • Business activity August 2026 → distribution October 2026: "Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) Septembre-2026" [sic — page spelling] and "CannabisExcise-ACH-0926".
  • Business activity July 2026 → distribution September 2026: "Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) August-2026" and "CannabisExcise-ACH-0826".
  • Business activity June 2026 → distribution August 2026: "Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) July-2026" and "CannabisExcise-ACH-0726".
  • The page runs back monthly, without a break in the fetched table, to business activity March 2022 ("Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) Mar-2022" / "CannabisExcise-ACH-0422"). The full month-by-month file-name pattern is visible on the page itself; only the latest three are listed here to avoid reproducing the entire index, but the page is the authoritative index.
  • Note on the page's labelling: The page's column headings are Business Activity (sales) month / Reporting and Collection Month / Distribution Month. The file name uses the reporting/collection month, not the business-activity month (e.g. August 2026 activity is filed as "Septembre-2026"). TRD's note on the page: "Tax collections are distributed the 2nd month after the accrual (business activity) month. For example, the file 'Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) Mar-2022' reflects business activity in March 2022; the collection month was April (tax returns were due by April 25th), and these collections were distributed in May."
  • Update frequency as stated: Monthly (one distribution per month, two months after activity).
  • Latest data date: Business activity August 2026 (distribution October 2026) is the latest row on the page as fetched 31 October 2026.
  • Fields available: Per the page title, distribution detail by location (local government). Exact field list is in the definitions download on the page (Verify — not extracted here).
  • Limitations:
  • A secondary compiler claims TRD's index carries no CAN workbook for revenue period October 2025. The TRD page as fetched 31 October 2026 DOES list "Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) October-2025" (business activity September 2025, distribution November 2025) and "Cannabis Excise Tax (CAN) November-2025" (business activity October 2025, distribution December 2025) — so the compiler's "hole" claim appears to reflect its own labelling (revenue period = ?) rather than a missing month on the TRD page. Do not repeat the "missing October 2025" claim without this labelling caveat. The safe statement is: TRD's page as fetched lists a CAN file for every business-activity month from March 2022 through August 2026.
  • CAN distributions are cash distributions net of TRD retention, on an adult-use-only excise base (medical exempt), and are lagged two months — they are NOT the same as CROP monthly sales and must not be trended against CROP without the lag/base adjustment.
  • No licensee-level tax data are published in these reports.

5.13 Local (county/municipal) business licence / zoning records where published

No statewide index of local cannabis business licences exists (none found). Local records are fragmented by jurisdiction and, where they exist, are permit/registration systems, not licence-holder registers. Examples confirmed in this run (not an exhaustive local inventory — that belongs to Part 3):

  • City of Albuquerque — Business Registration / Online Business Services: https://www.cabq.gov/311/business-services (indexed 31 October 2026) — online business licence & renewals, building permits, code enforcement/zoning, including "Cannabis Cultivation, Odor Control, Retail Location Information" and "Cannabis Retail Locations — Online applications for cannabis retail locations". Format: interactive online applications/registration; no downloadable cannabis-licensee list found.
  • City of Albuquerque — Environmental Health, Cannabis Regulations / Cannabis Health Permit: https://www.cabq.gov/environmentalhealth/food-safety/cannabis-regulations (indexed 31 October 2026) — establishments manufacturing, allowing on-site consumption and/or selling prepackaged edible cannabis products (including drinks) must obtain a food-related cannabis permit from Albuquerque Environmental Health; a Cannabis Health Permit Application PDF exists (City of Albuquerque Environmental Health Department, Consumer Health Protection Division) requiring NM Business Tax ID, CABQ Business Registration, and RLD cannabis permits as attachments. Format: PDF application + permit system; no public permittee list found.
  • City of Albuquerque / Bernalillo County edible permits: NMED's Bureau page (§5.8) confirms edible manufacturers outside Albuquerque/Bernalillo County go to NMED; inside that jurisdiction they go to City of Albuquerque Environmental Health / Bernalillo County. No Bernalillo County cannabis permit list was located in this run — Verify.
  • Other jurisdictions (Las Cruces/Doña Ana, Rio Rancho/Sandoval, Santa Fe, Roswell, Farmington, Hobbs, Clovis, Alamogordo, Carlsbad, Gallup, Sunland Park, Taos, Las Vegas NM, Los Alamos, Raton, Torrance County, etc.): No published local cannabis business-licence list or searchable register was located for any of these in the Part 5 searches performed. That is a negative finding, not proof of non-existence — local business registrations, if published, are typically in city clerk / planning portals that are not indexed as "cannabis" lists. Each jurisdiction must be checked individually in Part 3; do not claim a local list exists where none was found.
  • TRD CAN distribution detail by location (§5.7) is the only official, downloadable, location-level dataset that indirectly shows where adult-use sales (and therefore retail activity) occur, by local government — it does not name licensees.

6.0 Basis and conflicts — read before using any total

  • Two different "annual total" series circulate and do NOT agree, and NO official calendar-year total is adopted for 2024 or 2025: every annual figure below is a secondary compilation citing CCD/CROP, none was verified against CROP's full monthly series or an official CCD annual publication, and the 2024 spread ($50m) cannot be explained by rounding. They are reported side by side below as labelled secondary figures; do not pick one silently and do not cite any of them as an official total.
  • Series 1 (CCD via Marijuana Herald / MJBizDaily / CannBus, rounded): 2023 $557m; 2024 $540m (CannBus calc.) vs $580m/$590m in other secondary compilations citing CCD; 2025 $567m-$568m.
  • Series 2 (secondary market compilation citing CCD): 2023 $557m (adult-use $394m + medical $163m); 2024 $590m (adult-use 76%); 2025 $567m (adult-use 77%).
  • The 2024 discrepancy ($540m vs $580m vs $590m) is unresolved in this run — it may reflect rounding, restatement, or inclusion/exclusion differences, but no source in this run explains it. Verify the 2024 calendar-year total against CROP's full monthly series before publishing any 2024 figure as definitive.
  • A third secondary figure — "$628 million in total cannabis sales during 2025" (CannaMLS newsletter, May 2026) — conflicts with the $567-568m consensus above and is not adopted; it is recorded here only as a conflicting figure. Verify / do not use.
  • Monthly 2026 figures below are CCD/CROP figures as reported by The Marijuana Herald to the cent. They are internally consistent across the Herald's monthly reports except for the June 2026 transaction-count discrepancy flagged in §6.2.
  • "Since April 2022" cumulative totals grow month by month and are therefore date-stamped; always cite the "through [month]" date with the total.
  • City totals are CROP city-table totals as reported by press/secondary sources from CROP; they include both channels unless stated as adult-use-only or medical-only. Border-city totals do NOT by themselves prove buyer residency — see §6.5.

6.3 Sales to out-of-state buyers / border towns — officially reported only

No official source in this run reports buyer residency or a Texas-buyer share. The following are the ONLY border-related figures that may be cited, and none of them proves residency:

  • CROP city totals (official source, via press reporting of CROP): See §6.5 for Sunland Park, Las Cruces, Chaparral, Santa Teresa and Albuquerque city totals. A high city total in a border city is consistent with, but does not prove, out-of-state buying — residents of Sunland Park, Anthony NM, Chaparral and Santa Teresa themselves buy cannabis, and CROP does not record buyer home state.
  • Secondary claim — NOT adopted as official: CannaMLS newsletter (May 2026) states "approximately 38% of cannabis purchases are coming from non-residents, with border counties near Texas continuing to produce some of the strongest sales volumes". No official source, methodology, or underlying dataset is cited for the 38% figure in the excerpt retrieved. Do NOT cite 38% as an official or verified share. Verify whether any CCD/RLD study states a non-resident share; if none is found, the share is Unavailable.
  • Secondary attribution — labelled as such: El Paso Times (20 August 2026) and MJBizDaily (20 August 2026) both attribute Sunland Park's sales strength "in large part" / "in part" to customers crossing from El Paso, Texas. That is press attribution, not a CCD residency measurement. It may be quoted as press attribution with date, not as an official finding.
  • What CROP/TRD do NOT publish: No buyer-residency, buyer-ZIP, or "out-of-state sales" field exists in the CROP fields listed in §5.1 or the TRD CAN fields described in §5.7. Unavailable as an official series.

6.6 Official price data, price declines, market saturation

Price — official / CCD-commissioned figure (secondary reporting of it)

  • $4.04 per gram (adult-use average retail flower price, excluding sales and excise tax) — DankReports price tracker (accessed 31 October 2026, page updated 4 days before), stating: "a weighted average compiled from over 85 million BioTrack retail records by the Cannabis Policy & Practice Center (CPPC) on behalf of the NM Cannabis Control Division shows the price collapsed 61.92% from $10.61 per gram at market open in April 2022". This is the closest to an official price figure retrieved: it is a CPPC-for-CCD analysis, reported by a price tracker, not published on a CCD page found in this run. Verify the CPPC/CCD report directly (title/date not given in the tracker excerpt) before citing $4.04 as an official CCD price.
  • Corroborating secondary statements (same direction, different bases — do not average them):
  • CannaMLS newsletter (May 2026): "Average flower pricing has reportedly fallen nearly 62% since adult-use sales launched, dropping to approximately $4 per gram by late 2025" — consistent with the CPPC 61.92% / $4.04 figure.
  • MJBizDaily (20 August 2026): "The average transaction has fallen from about $50 in 2022 to about $38 today" — transaction value, not price per gram; do not convert it to a per-gram price.
  • A 2021-era legislative handout (Carver Family Farm / NM IndCA, 26 July 2021, nmlegis.gov) states "New Mexico average gram price $10 retail $4 wholesale" — historic, pre-adult-use-sales, do not use as a current price.
  • Conflicting secondary price figures — rejected / Verify: CannBus cross-state price page lists New Mexico flower at $77.33/gram for "February 2025, infrequent special report" — this is irreconcilable with every other price figure and is almost certainly a unit/parsing error on that page (possibly a per-ounce or bulk figure mislabelled). Do NOT cite $77.33/g. Cannabis Promotions (2025) lists New Mexico at $6.90/g (basis: Cannabis Benchmarks, per that page) — different methodology/year; record as conflicting secondary only.
  • No official CCD monthly price series (price per gram by month) was found on CROP or rld.nm.gov in this run. CROP publishes sales dollars and transaction counts, from which an average transaction value can be derived (e.g. July 2026: $49,814,500.78 ÷ 1,256,210 = $39.66 per transaction; adult-use $39,591,627.45 ÷ 1,047,035 = $37.81; medical $10,222,873.30 ÷ 209,175 = $48.87) — those are arithmetic derivations by this research from official CROP dollars/counts, labelled as such, not CCD-published prices, and they mix product types/quantities so they are NOT flower prices.

Saturation — official statements only (none found as a CCD saturation finding)

  • No CCD/RLD statement using the word "saturated" or giving a saturation threshold was found in this run. Do not describe the market as "officially saturated".
  • What secondary sources state (labelled, dated):
  • MJBizDaily (20 August 2026): sales "holding steady in 2026", market "moved past an early legalization growth spurt and into a more mature phase"; H1 2026 $284.9m vs H1 2025 $286.7m (flat); retail density 47 per 100,000 (see §6.5 caveat); average transaction $50 (2022) → ~$38 (2026).
  • CannBus Q3 2026: "Sales are flat in 2026: the first half totaled $284.9 million against $286.7 million a year earlier."
  • CannaMLS (May 2026): "active cannabis licenses have now declined for seven consecutive quarters" nationally, with mature markets including New Mexico driving contraction — national, not New Mexico-specific.
  • Safe summary sentence (with attribution): "Secondary market reporting in August-September 2026 describes New Mexico sales as flat/mature in 2026 after rapid early growth, with falling average transaction values and falling flower prices; no official CCD saturation assessment was located." That is the limit of what Part 6 can say on saturation.

1. Fixed points carried from Run 1 (not re-researched)

  • NMED hemp rule: permanent 20.10.2 NMAC effective 28 January 2026; finished-product limits 0.30% total THC, 2 mg total THC per serving, 20 mg per package (with the tincture/broad-spectrum/cosmetic/vape variants in §8).

2. Who licenses what — the split that explains everything else

New Mexico splits hemp licensing by stage of the supply chain. This is the single most common source of error in secondary summaries, which often attribute all hemp licensing to one agency.

StageIssuerLegal basis
Growing / production of hemp plants, including breeding and regulatory raw-hemp testingNew Mexico Department of Agriculture (NMDA), Agricultural and Environmental Services Division — Entomology and Nursery Industries / Hemp SectionHemp Manufacturing Act, NMSA 1978 §§ 76-24-1 to 76-24-10; 21.20.2 NMAC (cultivation) and 21.20.3 NMAC (breeding/testing)
Post-harvest extraction, processing, manufacturing, warehousing of hemp extract, and retail manufacture of hemp finished productsNew Mexico Environment Department (NMED), Cannabis and Hemp BureauHemp Manufacturing Act § 76-24-8; 20.10.2 NMAC
Sale of pre-packaged finished hemp products by a pure retailer (no manufacture)No state hemp licence/permit at this time (§7)NMED FAQ (see §7)
Cannabis (marijuana) establishmentsRegulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis Control Division (CCD) — not a hemp licenceCannabis Regulation Act, NMSA 1978 ch. 26, art. 2C; 16.8 NMAC

NMDA's own programme summary states the split in one sentence:

"As required by state law, New Mexico Department of Agriculture issues licenses to businesses/individuals cultivating hemp. The New Mexico Environment Department issues licenses to businesses/individuals for processing activities following harvest, including extraction, distillation, and manufacturing."

Source: NMDA, Hemp Registration (directly opened at audit). https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/licensing-and-registrations/hemp-registration.html

2.1 State plan vs. USDA programme — verified

  • NMDA's 2026 Continuous form states: "As of January 1, 2022, New Mexico will be operating under a USDA-approved state plan administered by NMDA." Source: NMDA, Continuous Hemp Commercial Production Application, 2026, updated January 2026, opened directly. Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/media/pdf/continuous-hemp-commercial-application.pdf
  • USDA's list (updated 17 February 2026) lists New Mexico as "NM Approved Plan (pdf)*", i.e. approved under the final rule effective 22 March 2021. Source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans. Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review
  • NMDA's Hemp Program page repeats: "As of January 1, 2022, New Mexico began operating under a USDA-approved state plan administered by NMDA." Source: NMDA, Hemp Program (search-indexed text). Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/aes/hemp-program.html

Conclusion: New Mexico does NOT use the USDA producer programme for in-state growers. A New Mexico grower needs an NMDA licence, not a USDA licence. The USDA route would apply only to a producer in a jurisdiction with no approved plan, which New Mexico is not.

2.2 Statutory anchors (verbatim operative text)

Growing — § 76-24-2(B)-(C) NMSA 1978 (Laws 2017, ch. 140, § 1, as amended Laws 2019, ch. 116, § 11):

"B. Notwithstanding any other provision of law to the contrary, the board, through the New Mexico department of agriculture, shall issue licenses pursuant to rules enacted under Subsection C of this section to grow hemp for research and development, agricultural, agronomic, ecological, processing, sales and marketing purposes."

"C. The board, on behalf of the director of the New Mexico department of agriculture, shall adopt rules to establish and carry out the provisions of this section, including requirements for licensure, training of law enforcement personnel, inspection, recordkeeping, fees not to exceed program costs and compliance processes."

Source (mirror of statute text; NMOneSource direct text to be re-checked at audit): Justia, NMSA § 76-24-2 (2025). Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-76/article-24/section-76-24-2/

Manufacturing — § 76-24-8(A)-(B), (C)(5) NMSA 1978 (Laws 2019, ch. 116, § 6; amended Laws 2020, ch. 32, § 6):

"A. The department of environment shall issue permits pursuant to rules issued under Subsection C of this section to extract, process or engage in other manufacturing activities regarding hemp, including manufacturing intermediate hemp-derived products and hemp finished products."

"B. A person shall not extract, process or engage in other manufacturing activities regarding hemp, including manufacturing intermediate hemp-derived products and hemp finished products without a permit issued by the department of environment or a license issued pursuant to Subsection C of Section 76-24-10 NMSA 1978."

"C. The department of environment shall adopt rules that include: … (5) fees not to exceed the lesser of one thousand dollars ($1,000) or the cost of administration of a permit issued pursuant to this section."

Source (mirror of statute text; NMOneSource direct text to be re-checked at audit): Justia, NMSA § 76-24-8 (2025). Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-76/article-24/section-76-24-8/

Note the § 76-24-8(C)(5) $1,000 ceiling: it is the statutory cap that the NMED $1,000 permit fees sit at, not above. The $500 retail-manufacturer fee sits below it. The late ($200), reinspection ($500) and variance ($300) charges in the 2026 rule are presented by NMED as additions to the permit-fee schedule (§6); whether each ancillary charge is itself within the § 76-24-8(C)(5) "lesser of $1,000 or cost of administration" test is a Verify item (§11), because the final-rule fee paragraph was not directly read in this run.

3. NMDA grower licences — Annual vs. Continuous

Both are issued under 21.20.2 NMAC, "Hemp Cultivation Rule", Title 21, Chapter 20, Part 2. Issuing agency: New Mexico State University, New Mexico Department of Agriculture, MSC 3189, Box 30005, Las Cruces, New Mexico 88003. Effective date 11 December 2018; duration permanent; no amendment history is shown on the posted SRCA text — every section still carries the "[21.20.2.x NMAC - N, 12/11/2018]" tag. That fact is central to the fee conflict in §4.

Source: SRCA, 21.20.2 NMAC, opened directly. Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://www.srca.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/21.020.0002.html

3.1 Definitions (verbatim, 21.20.2.7)

"A. 'Annual Production License' means license issued for the production of a single crop that is destroyed within 240 days of planting."

"F. 'Continuous Production License' means license issued for the production of hemp as part of a plant nursery, greenhouse or similar operation in which viable hemp plant(s) are produced or present throughout the year in a location."

"N. 'Location' means one contiguous growing area of any size, or multiple non-contiguous growing areas, totaling no more than 10 acres, within a 2.5 mile radius. Non-contiguous growing areas must be owned or leased by a single licensee."

3.2 Annual Hemp Commercial Production Licence

ItemDetail
What it allowsField production of a single annual hemp crop at a specified location, for specified varieties. A separate application and fee are required before planting each new crop at each location.
Apply byNo less than 25 business days before planting each crop at each location (21.20.2.8(A)).
TermValid 240 days after date of issuance, or until crop destruction, whichever occurs first (21.20.2.8(A)).
Area ruleSingle contiguous growing area: no acreage limit (2026 Annual form, directly read at audit); for multiple non-contiguous areas on one licence: within a 2.5-mile radius, under 10 acres / 435,600 sq ft in total, and all planted within a 3-week period (2026 Annual form, directly read at audit).
Transferable?No. 21.20.2.9(B): a licensee shall "not reassign or transfer to another business, location, individual, or other entity a license." The 2026 Continuous form repeats: "Annual or Continuous Hemp Commercial Production License cannot be transferred to another individual, business, or entity."
Other core conditions (21.20.2.9)Submit required documents by department due dates; destroy non-compliant varieties as directed; do not sell, transport, process or use a variety without a valid department document showing compliance; pay enforcement-related fees within 20 calendar days of notice; follow all state and federal requirements.
Background check / barCriminal background check required. The 2026 Continuous form: "Hemp commercial production licenses cannot be issued to individuals with felony convictions related to controlled substances within the last ten (10) years." NMDA conducts the national check; the applicant obtains the state record from the Department of Public Safety ($15.00 DPS charge, per the form). Child Support Enforcement Act compliance is also screened; failure can result in denial or revocation.
Harvest controlHemp covered by a licence cannot be harvested without NMDA-issued documents authorising harvest of the specific varieties listed. A Harvest Notification Document must be submitted no less than 30 days before the estimated harvest date so NMDA can schedule sampling (NMDA Hemp Registration summary, search-indexed text). Field inspections and samples are collected by NMDA staff within 30 days of the estimated harvest date (2026 Continuous form, acknowledgment 7).
FeeFee: directly confirmed on the 2026 Annual form at audit: $650 base + $6.00/acre + $10/variety (minimums $6.00 / $10.00). See 4.

3.3 Continuous Hemp Commercial Production Licence

ItemDetail
What it allowsYear-round production where viable hemp plants are maintained throughout the year, as part of a greenhouse or plant-nursery operation — expressly including clonal production. The 2026 form: "The Continuous Hemp Commercial Production License is not intended for production of an annual crop."
Apply by / renewApply no less than 25 business days before planting or other propagative activities; renew before 1 February each year (21.20.2.8(B)).
Term1 February 2026 through 31 January 2027 on the 2026 form; in rule terms, "A continuous production license expires January 31 of each year" (21.20.2.8(B)).
Area rule (2026 form, directly read)"Under a single continuous hemp license, there is no acreage limit for a single contiguous growing area." Multiple non-contiguous areas may be registered on one licence only if all are within a 2.5-mile radius and total under 10 acres (435,600 sq ft). Areas outside that radius or over 10 non-contiguous acres need a separate licence. Multiple contiguous greenhouse bays count as a single growing area.
Transferable?No (same 21.20.2.9(B) rule and form acknowledgment as Annual).
Other core conditionsAs Annual, plus: clones/seed marketed must be tracked by variety, quantity, buyer and destination, with records kept 3 years (2026 form, acknowledgment 10); licensee or representative must be present for all inspections; licensee delivers samples to an NMDA-approved laboratory for pre-harvest THC determination (post-decarboxylation); licensee bears destruction/disposition costs for non-compliant (>0.3% THC) varieties and for post-harvest destruction/remediation.
FeeDirectly verified on the 2026 form — see §4.2.

Link: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/media/pdf/continuous-hemp-commercial-application.pdf — Application forms index: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/forms-and-applications.html

3.4 "Commercial" vs. "Research" in form names — a naming trap

Older forms and many secondary pages call these licences "Commercial Research Production" licences; the 2026 Continuous form opened in this run calls itself "Continuous Hemp Commercial Production Application, 2026" (no "Research"). NMDA's registration summary likewise lists "2026 Continuous Hemp Commercial Research Production License" and "2026 Annual Hemp Commercial Research Production License" in the same breath. Treat "Research" in older names as legacy wording, not as a separate research-only licence class. No separate research-only grower licence was found in the 2026 NMDA materials. The statutory authority (§ 76-24-2) still uses "research and development" language, but the operative 2026 licences are commercial production licences.

4. THE RUN 1 FEE CONFLICT — RESOLVED, WITH ONE RESIDUAL VERIFY

4.1 What the posted rule actually says (directly read)

21.20.2.10, "FEES" (SRCA text, still dated 12/11/2018 throughout):

"A. Fees associated with the application for a license shall include but not exceed the following stated amounts for each license: (1) Annual production license: $800 per location. (2) Continuous production license: $900 per location. (3) Additional $100 late fee for continuous production license renewal application received after February 1. (4) Annual inspection fees for continuous and annual licenses per location: (a) Outdoor production: $6.00 per acre; minimum $6.00. (b) Indoor production: $0.75 per 1,000 square feet; minimum $5.00. (c) Additional varietal fee: $25 per variety in excess of one variety."

Two features of that wording matter:

  1. "Shall include but not exceed" — $800 and $900 are ceilings ("not exceed"), not fixed charges. A form charging less than the ceiling does not contradict the rule.
  2. The inspection/varietal items are listed separately from the per-location licence amount, so the form's "base + area + variety" structure mirrors the rule's structure.

4.2 What the 2026 Continuous form actually charges (directly read)

From the fee box on page 4 of the 2026 Continuous form:

"Fees based on: $750.00 registration fee + $.75 / 1,000 square feet of hemp production + $10.00 per variety."

With minimums: area charge minimum $5.00; variety charge minimum $10.00. Payment by check or money order with the application.

Reconciliation for Continuous:

ComponentRule (21.20.2.10)2026 formConsistent?
Base / registrationNot to exceed $900 per location$750Yes — $150 below the ceiling
Indoor area rate$0.75 per 1,000 sq ft; min $5.00$0.75 per 1,000 sq ft; min $5.00Yes — identical
Variety charge$25 per variety in excess of one$10.00 per variety (min $10.00)Partly — see below
Late renewal$100 if received after 1 FebruaryNot stated on the fee box of the form as readVerify — rule figure stands; form silence is not a contradiction

The variety charge is the only genuine tension, and it is small: for one variety the rule implies $0 extra while the form charges $10; for two varieties the rule implies $25 while the form charges $20; for three, $50 vs. $30; the form is cheaper than the rule's varietal schedule for every case with two or more varieties, and $10 more for a single-variety grower. Because the rule's varietal line is also framed by "shall include but not exceed", the form's $10-per-variety charge can be read as NMDA exercising its discretion below the rule's varietal ceiling for multi-variety growers, but the single-variety $10 (where the rule's schedule would be $0) is not explained by the posted rule text. No amendment to 21.20.2.10 appears on the posted SRCA text. That single-variety point, and the absence of any published fee-schedule amendment, remain Verify (§11). They do not overturn the headline resolution:

rule ceilings; the 2026 forms charge $650 (Annual, directly verified on the 2026 Annual form at audit) and $750 (Continuous, directly verified) respectively

4.3 Annual form fee — what is verified and what is not

  • Verified: the $800 Annual ceiling and the $6.00/acre outdoor inspection rate, from the posted rule text directly read (§4.1).
  • Directly opened at audit (1 November 2026): the NMDA 2026 Annual form PDF states 'Fees based on: $650.00 registration fee + $6.00 / acre of hemp production + $10.00 per variety' with minimums of $6.00 (area) and $10.00 (variety), and that once payment is processed refunds are not available or transferable to another license. The fee is therefore CONFIRMED, not Verify. The secondary corroboration below is retained for the record only:
  • "Annual license: $650 base registration and inspection fee, plus $6.00 per acre, plus $10 per variety." — Sativa University, New Mexico cannabis laws summary. Link: https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/new-mexico/
  • Identical $650 + $6/acre + $10/variety formula in the 2021 Annual form as mirrored on Readkong (showing the formula predates 2026 and was stable): "Fees based on: $650.00 registration fee + $6.00 / acre of hemp production + $10.00 per variety. Once payment is processed, refunds are not available or transferable to another license." Link: https://www.readkong.com/page/annual-hemp-commercial-research-production-application-2021-9843103
  • The same $650 formula repeated in a second secondary summary (New Mexico State Cannabis overview). Link: https://newmexicostatecannabis.org/hemp
  • The Annual area rate ($6/acre) matches the rule exactly; the Annual base ($650) sits $150 below the $800 ceiling, exactly paralleling the Continuous case ($750 vs. $900). That parallel is now confirmed by the direct read of the 2026 Annual PDF itself (see above).

4.4 Worked examples (using the form formulas, for scale only)

  • Annual, 10 acres, 2 varieties: $650 + (10 x $6) + (2 x $10) = $730 (form formula; confirmed on the 2026 Annual form at audit).
  • Continuous, 50,000 sq ft indoor, 3 varieties: $750 + (50 × $0.75) + (3 × $10) = $817.50 (form formula; directly verified on the 2026 form).
  • Continuous, single variety, 10,000 sq ft: $750 + $7.50 + $10 = $767.50.

5. Other NMDA licences: Special Hemp Breeding, Laboratory Hemp Testing, Nursery Plant

All three exist, but they are not grower licences and must not be counted as such.

5.1 Special Hemp Breeding Licence — 21.20.3 NMAC

  • Source: SRCA, 21.20.3 NMAC (directly opened at audit). https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title21/21.020.0003.html
  • What it allows: For "qualified plant breeders that will be breeding new or improved varieties of hemp and may possess viable plants or plant material in excess of 0.3% and less than 5.0% total THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol + THCA)." Source: NMDA Hemp Registration summary (search-indexed text). Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/licensing-and-registrations/hemp-registration.html
  • Rule scope (21.20.3.2(B), verbatim): "Plant breeding for the purpose of developing improved or new hemp varieties in which breeding activities involve the possession of viable plants that are in excess of three-tenths percent and less than five percent THC."
  • Term: Licence year 1 February through 31 January; licences issued at any time during the year expire the following 31 January (21.20.3.8).
  • The rule also provides for double fees on late renewal of licences under BOTH subsections (21.20.3.9(D)) and for fee waiver by the director where special circumstances warrant (21.20.3.9(E)). Added rule detail omitted originally: breeding stock must be kept indoors in a secure department-approved area, not available to the public, transferable only to another breeding licensee, and for breeding only (21.20.3.12(C)).
  • Transferability: 21.20.3 contains no general non-transfer clause equivalent to 21.20.2.9(B). For breeding stock specifically, 21.20.3.12(C)(2) provides that plants/material over 0.3% and under 5.0% THC shall not be available to the public or transferred to another person that does not possess a valid Special Hemp Breeding License. A general 21.20.3 transfer rule beyond that remains Verify.
  • Info link: NMDA Hemp Registration page (above) lists a "2026 Special Hemp Breeding License Application". The direct application PDF link was not retrieved in this run — Verify.

5.2 Laboratory Hemp Testing Licence — 21.20.3 NMAC

  • What it is: A licence for persons "testing of raw hemp for regulatory purposes as identified by New Mexico Department of Agriculture" (21.20.3.2(A)). This is a raw-hemp, NMDA-identified testing licence. It is not the same thing as NMED approval for finished-product analytical laboratories (§8.4).
  • Term: Same 1 February-31 January licence year as breeding (21.20.3.8).
  • Fee: "The annual fee for a Laboratory Hemp Testing License shall not exceed five-hundred dollars ($500)" (21.20.3.9(A)); nonrefundable once issued (21.20.3.9(C)). Actual 2026 charge: Verify (no 2026 testing-licence form retrieved; the registration-page excerpt lists the breeding application and does not confirm a current testing-licence form).
  • Whether NMDA lists a 2026 Laboratory Hemp Testing application alongside the breeding application: The NMDA registration summary retrieved in this run lists the breeding application but the excerpt does not confirm a current 2026 testing-licence form. Verify.

  • What it is: Required by state law "for any business selling live plants, including hemp clones" (2026 Continuous form, directly read) and, per the NMDA registration summary, a "2026 Nursery Plant License: Required by state law for any business selling live plants, including hemp."

The boundary (own-use vs. sale) is Verify if a dossier needs it stated precisely.

6. NMED permits — extraction, manufacturing, warehouse, retail manufacturer

6.1 Legal basis and rule history

  • Statute: § 76-24-8 (quoted in §2.2). NMED must issue permits for extraction, processing and other manufacturing, including intermediate and finished products; operating without one is prohibited (subject to the § 76-24-10 tribal-licence cross-reference).
  • Rule: 20.10.2 NMAC, "Hemp Extraction, Production, Transportation, Warehousing, and Testing". Original effective 28 January 2020; permanent replacement/repromulgation effective 28 January 2026 (every section in the 2026 version carries "[20.10.2.x NMAC - Rp, 20.10.2.x NMAC, 1/28/2026]").
  • NMED's Final Rule page (opened directly) confirms: the amendments "have been finalized and will be effective January 28, 2026"; the amendment "Makes Emergency Rule, which was effective August 1, 2025, permanent"; it "Creates new permit type" and "Updates and/or adds fees associated with permit and variance applications, re-inspections, administrative-related costs"; following a hearing on 2 December 2025, the NMED Cabinet Secretary signed the Final Order and Statement of Reasons. Source: NMED, Hemp Final Rule, opened directly. Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/hemp-final-rule/
  • Note on the emergency-rule date discrepancy: secondary coverage variously gives the emergency rule as effective 1 August 2025 or 1 September 2025. NMED's own Final Rule page says "effective August 1, 2025". The permanent rule (28 January 2026) supersedes that question for current law; the emergency-rule start date is not material to licensing and is not resolved here.

6.2 The four permit types

Each facility type must be permitted separately — except that an extraction or manufacturing facility (and, under the 2026 rule, a retail manufacturer) does not need an additional warehouse permit for the same location. Source: NMED Hemp Manufacturing Facility Application, version 5.0 revised 29 September 2025 (search-indexed text); NMED Final Rule training presentation (search-indexed text; direct open rate-limited).

PermitWhat it allows (definitions / scope)Fee (initial & renewal, per application)
Hemp Extraction FacilityAn operation that produces hemp extract. A grower who extracts needs this in addition to the NMDA grower licence.$1,000
Hemp Manufacturing FacilityAn operation, other than an extraction facility, that produces hemp products other than hemp extract and provides them for sale or distribution to other business entities. Includes drying/trimming hemp flower into a finished product (NMED FAQ).$1,000
Hemp WarehouseStorage of hemp extract at a location that does not hold a current extraction or manufacturing permit. No permit is required to warehouse or sell packaged hemp finished products (application instructions).$1,000
Hemp Retail Manufacturer (new in the 2026 rule)"An operation that produces or repackages hemp finished products and provides them directly to consumers" (20.10.2.7, per NMED training presentation). This is the closest thing to a hemp retail licence, but it is a manufacturer permit: a pure reseller of pre-packaged product does not need it (§7). NMED's summary adds that retail producers such as restaurants and bakeries must meet the same requirements as wholesale producers.$500

Removed type: The 2026 rule removed the former "Hemp Processor" permit type and added "Hemp Retail Manufacturer" in its place (NMED training presentation, 7 January 2026, search-indexed text). Any source still listing a "Hemp Processor" permit as current is out of date. The pre-2026 fee schedule quoted in older rule text ($1,000 extraction / $1,000 manufacturing / $1,000 warehouse / $500 "processing facility") is the ancestor of the current schedule; the $500 line now attaches to retail manufacture, not to "processing".

CONFIRMED in the published rule: 20.10.2.8(D)(1) states verbatim: '(a) $1000.00 for a hemp extraction facility; (b) $1000.00 for a hemp manufacturing facility; (c) $1000.00 for a hemp warehouse.; and (d) $500.00 for a hemp retail manufacturer' (initial and renewal). The NMED FAQ's '$1000.00 with each hemp application submitted' is a stale pre-retail-manufacturer sentence: it corroborates the $1,000 line only and must not be cited for the $500 retail fee. The former Verify flag on the fee paragraph is removed. 20.10.2 NMAC final rule (PDF)

7. Retailers, minimum age, and "hemp-derived product registration"

7.1 No standalone hemp retailer licence

NMED FAQ, opened directly (31 October 2026):

"Do I need a permit to sell pre-packaged CBD or other hemp products? No, not at this time. IT is highly recommended that all pre-packaged product comes from a business is permitted/licensed by the proper state authority to manufacture hemp finished products."

And:

"A permit from NMED is required when manufacturing hemp-containing products for human ingestion, absorption, or smokable products."

Consequence: A shop in, say, Santa Fe, New Mexico (not Santa Fe, Texas) that only resells sealed, pre-packaged hemp products made by a permitted manufacturer needs no NMED hemp permit and no NMDA licence on the sources retrieved. The moment it produces or repackages finished products for direct sale to consumers, it becomes a Hemp Retail Manufacturer (§6.2) and needs the $500 permit. The moment it manufactures for wholesale, it needs a Manufacturing (and, if it extracts, an Extraction) permit.

7.2 Minimum age — none found for hemp

  • No minimum-age provision was found in 20.10.2 NMAC as published (the full final-rule PDF was searched at audit for age provisions and contains no purchase-age section). General law outside 20.10.2 (e.g. any local ordinance, or general restrictions on sales to minors for particular product types) was not searched in this Part and is Unavailable here.
  • Do not import the cannabis age rule. The 21+ rule (16.8.2.8(C): applicants/controlling persons and employees of commercial cannabis establishments must be 21+) and the 21+ purchase rule for cannabis apply to CCD cannabis licences, not to NMED hemp permits. A hemp retail manufacturer is not a cannabis establishment by virtue of holding a hemp permit.
  • General law outside 20.10.2 (e.g. any local ordinance, or general restrictions on sales to minors for particular product types) was not searched in this Part and is Unavailable here.

7.3 No hemp finished-product registration found

No separate "hemp-derived product registration" — i.e. a per-product filing with NMDA or NMED before sale — was found in any official source retrieved for this Part. Finished products are controlled instead by:

  • the manufacturer's permit (§6),
  • finished-product testing by an NMED-approved laboratory (§8.4),
  • labelling/packaging rules (§8.3), and
  • the THC limits (§8.1).

If a per-product registration exists under some other programme (e.g. NMDA commercial-feed or food-product registration for a specific product class), it was not found here and is Unavailable/Verify (§11). Do not present the absence as proof that no registration of any kind could ever apply to a particular product (e.g. animal feed or pesticide products have their own regimes, outside this Part's scope).

8. Testing, labelling and THC limits as they interact with licensing

These are not licences, but a licence is worthless without them: a permit holder who cannot meet them cannot lawfully sell.

8.1 Finished-product THC limits (20.10.2.12, permanent 2026 rule)

From the 2026 rule text (search-indexed snippets of the final-rule PDF):

"A. Unless specified in Subsections B or C of this section, a hemp finished product shall: (1) not have a Total THC concentration of more than three-tenths of one percent (0.30%); (2) contain no more than 2.0 milligrams of Total THC per serving; (3) contain no more than 20 milligrams of Total THC per package; "

"B. Hemp tinctures shall contain no more than 100 milligrams of Total THC per package."

"C. Broad spectrum hemp finished products shall contain no more than 6.0 milligrams of Total THC per package."

Cosmetics and vapes are exempt from the milligram caps in 20.10.2.12(A)(2)-(3) only - 20.10.2.12(D) - i.e. exempt from the 2 mg/serving and 20 mg/package limits, not from the 0.30% concentration limit in (A)(1). Serving size must comply with Table 2 of 21 CFR 101.12 (20.10.2.12(E)). The 20.10.2.12 requirements took effect 60 days after the part's effective date - 29 March 2026 - per 20.10.2.12(G), directly read at audit.

Interaction with cultivation: The cultivation THC test is delta-9 THC ≤0.3% on a dry-weight basis (21.20.2.7(K), 21.20.2.12), while the finished-product test is Total THC (delta-9 + THCA, per the breeding definition and the finished-product rule). A crop that passes at harvest can therefore still fail as a finished product if THCA is high. That distinction is why the breeding licence's 0.3%-5.0% total THC band (§5.1) exists.

8.2 Converted / synthetic cannabinoids — banned at hemp facilities

subject to a narrow exception in 20.10.2.11(L): a hemp facility may receive and use as an ingredient, at >=98% purity demonstrated by an approved analytical laboratory using a validated method, nine semi-synthetic/synthetic cannabinoids - delta-9 tetrahydrocannabivarin (THCV), cannabichromene (CBC), cannabicitran (CBT), cannabicyclol (CBL), cannabielsoin (CBE), cannabigerol (CBG), cannabidivarin (CBDV), cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabinol (CBN) - directly read in the published rule at audit.

Scope, resolved on rule text: the ban in 20.10.2.11(K) binds a 'hemp facility' (20.10.2.7(X): extraction, manufacturing, retail manufacturer, warehouse) and covers receiving, possessing, manufacturing, offering, advertising, marketing or selling semi-synthetic/synthetic cannabinoids or products containing them - so a facility that sells an imported converted-cannabinoid product IS bound. A pure reseller is a 'hemp retailer' (20.10.2.7(FF)) but is NOT a 'hemp facility', so 20.10.2.11(K) does not on its face bind pure retail sale. Whether NMED or the Attorney General enforce against non-facility retailers under other law is Verify (enforcement practice, not rule text).

8.3 Labelling and packaging (20.10.2.13)

From the final-rule text snippets and NMED's summary:

  • Labels must be in English; must state Total THC content per serving and per package (except broad-spectrum variants, which follow their own labelling line); must carry the FDA statement or an approved alternative; must carry a warning including the potential for a positive drug test; QR codes are allowed; new warning statements were added in the 2026 rule, with allowances for their placement.
  • "No THC" / "THC-Free" claims are prohibited: "The Hemp Rules prohibit statements representing or inferring a product is THC-free" (NMED FAQ, opened directly).
  • Packaging must be food-grade or Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) material (20.10.2.13, snippet truncated — Verify exact wording).
  • The FDA Food Labeling Guide is NMED's recommended tool for the 20.10.2.13(A)(1) requirements (NMED FAQ).

Exact labelling line items beyond those above were not exhaustively extracted in this run; the full 20.10.2.13 text should be read at audit (Verify).

RegimeForApproval routePublic list?

NMED-approved analytical laboratories (20.10.2.14-15)Hemp finished-product testing required by 20.10.2 NMAC(1) Approved by the NMDOH Medical Cannabis Program, or (2) ISO-accredited for hemp and/or cannabis within the scope of the hemp-rule testing requirements (NMED FAQ, opened directly). No licence fee for "approval" was found — approval is by recognition of DOH approval or ISO accreditation, not by a paid NMED licence.Yes — NMED, Approved Hemp Analytical Laboratories, updated 8 September 2026 (search-indexed text). Link: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/analytical-laboratories/

Finished-product testing must be done by an NMED-approved lab; other (e.g. customer-requested) testing need not be (NMED FAQ). Records of manifests and supplier permits/licences must be kept at least two years (NMED FAQ, §4 purchasing answers).

8.5 Pesticides

Finished-product manufacturers must demonstrate that hemp used was grown using only NMDA-registered pesticides and must test for pesticide residues as specified in 20.10.2.14 (final-rule text, §12(F) snippet). NMED publishes a CHB Pesticide Testing List (version 27 January 2026, per the analytical-laboratories page). This is a condition of the manufacturing permit, not a separate licence.
