10. Federal 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates — New Mexico's response (if any)

Finding: No New Mexico statute, rule, or agency guidance specifically responding to the federal 12 November / 11 December 2026 hemp dates was found in the official sources searched for this Part (NMED, NMDA, nmlegis.gov) as of 31 October 2026.

What does exist, and why it is not a response to those dates:

  1. Pre-existing state tightening (2025-2026). The NMED emergency rule (August 2025) and permanent 20.10.2 NMAC (28 January 2026) already banned semi-synthetic/synthetic cannabinoids at hemp facilities and imposed the 2 mg/serving / 20 mg/package finished-product caps (§8). Those measures predate and are independent of the federal dates; they were adopted for state public-health reasons, not as implementation of PL 119-37 § 781 or PL 119-103 § 2019. Secondary coverage (Drug Policy Watch, New Mexico brief, accessed 31 October 2026) reaches the same conclusion, noting New Mexico is "comparatively well-positioned because the state already moved first" on converted cannabinoids. Link: https://drugpolicywatch.info/states/new-mexico.html
  2. The federal cap would still bite. The fixed federal baseline for this dossier is a 0.4 mg total THC per container cap after 11 December 2026. New Mexico's 20 mg per package cap is fifty times that figure. Even a fully compliant New Mexico hemp finished product (20 mg/package) would therefore exceed the federal container cap. No New Mexico rule found in this Part lowers the state cap to 0.4 mg, creates a federal-conformity trigger, or addresses how NMDA/NMED will treat products that are state-legal but federally redefined after 11 December 2026. That gap is the single most important open item for any operator relying on this Part after 11 December 2026.
  3. Attorney General enforcement warning (November 2025, secondary). Vicente LLP's November 2025 briefing reports that the New Mexico Attorney General warned retailers about illegal cannabis products with THC over 0.3% marketed as "legal hemp", with civil and criminal action planned. That warning concerns over-0.3% products mislabelled as hemp, not the federal redefinition, and it is secondary-only here. Source: Vicente LLP, Hemp Law and Policy Briefing: November 2025. Accessed 31 October 2026. Link: https://vicentellp.com/insights/vicente-llp-hemp-law-and-policy-briefing-november-2025/
  4. It passed the House 54-7 on 13 March 2025 AND passed the Senate 37-0 on 22 March 2025, and was then postponed indefinitely - nmlegis.gov current location: 'Died (API.)'. It never reached the Governor in enacted form and was NOT pocket-vetoed. The permanent rule was ultimately issued by NMED under 20.10.2 NMAC, not by the Environmental Improvement Board, because HB 346 did not become law. HB 346 is therefore not presented as current law anywhere in this Part.
  5. Tribal dimension. § 76-24-10 NMSA 1978 acknowledges that federally recognised Indian nations, tribes and pueblos wholly or partly in New Mexico may develop their own hemp production plans under § 10113 of the federal Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 as a matter of inherent tribal sovereignty, and authorises NMDA/NMED cooperative or joint-powers agreements with them (including on testing and transportation). Whether any tribal hemp plan or agreement bears on the federal dates, and the fixed-baseline tribal "state-licensed" Schedule III question, both remain Verify — no tribal source was retrieved for this Part.

Bottom line for operators: As of the dossier date, New Mexico has no published implementation of the federal 12 November / 11 December 2026 hemp redefinition. State hemp licences/permits remain valid under state law on their own terms, but state compliance does not guarantee federal compliance after 11 December 2026, and no state guidance found here resolves that tension.

New Mexico Cannabis & Hemp — Run 2, Part 8: Cannabis-Zoned Properties

Dossier date: 31 October 2026. All sources accessed 31 October 2026 (in the user's Eastern Time zone; a small number of page crawls are timestamped 1 November 2026 UTC, which is still 31 October 2026 EDT).

Scope of this part only. Publicly listed properties in New Mexico that are zoned for, or marketed for, cannabis or hemp use, with address, zoning type as stated, lot/building size if stated, water-rights status if stated, price if listed, and a source link. This part does not re-research Parts 0–7. The zoning summary in §1 is carried over from the Run 1 brief, with one Albuquerque corroboration noted as search-result evidence only (see §1, note).

Counting rule — read before using the totals. A property is counted once even if it appears on several aggregators (LoopNet, Crexi, Realmo, 420Property, an MLS broker page and a broker flyer are often the same listing). Business-only sales, leased dispensary addresses inside a portfolio sale, properties whose listing says only that cannabis might be possible, and properties whose cannabis use is not stated in the excerpt retrieved are not counted in the core dedicated total; they are shown separately so the core total is not inflated. No property has been included on the basis of industrial zoning alone.

Headline result

  • 29 address-identified, dedicated cannabis/hemp properties currently presented as for sale, for lease/sub-lease, or coming soon (Table A).
  • 10 further dedicated presentations with no street address given in the material retrieved (Table B) — portfolios, a no-address extraction facility, acreage parcels and a county-level land lease. These are real listings, but a buyer cannot diligence a site from the material retrieved.
  • 3 historical / sold / no-longer-advertised address-identified properties (Table C) — included so a reader does not mistake an old listing for a live one.
  • 6 suitability-only or tenant-only properties (Table D) — explicitly not counted as cannabis-zoned. Industrial or retail space that a listing says could suit cannabis, or a centre that merely contains a cannabis tenant, is not a cannabis-zoned property.
  • CORRECTED core total: 38 marketed presentations (29 + 10 minus B10, a leased-site business sale removed from all totals), of which 0 are officially verified as cannabis-zoned. Every Table A/B zoning entry is CONDITIONAL (listing claim only) until city/county zoning verification is obtained. Of those, only a minority state a zoning code at all; most state a use ("cannabis cultivation", "turnkey dispensary") without naming the zone. That gap is itself a finding: do not treat "marketed for cannabis" as proof of zoning compliance.
  • Geography. The live, address-identified supply is heavily Albuquerque-centred (11 of the 29 are in Albuquerque, plus Bernalillo immediately north and Belen/Los Lunas to the south), with a second cluster around Estancia (Torrance County) and singletons in Alamogordo, Clovis, Las Cruces, Portales, San Cristobal (Taos County), Santa Fe, Sunland Park, Veguita and Aztec. No address-identified, dedicated, currently-presented listing was found in Farmington, Roswell or Las Vegas (NM) in the searches for this part — Farmington and Roswell appear only as leased dispensary addresses inside the Purlife portfolio (Table B, note), not as real estate for sale. That is a search result, not proof that no such property exists off the public listing sites searched.
  • Water is mentioned in some form for 6 of the 29 Table A properties (only 2 quantified) (Howell Rd, State Road 522, Highway 236 Portales, Edith Blvd, County Road 41 Alcalde — the last two as irrigation access/rights, not quantified). Every other Table A entry says "not stated" below. Given the Run 1 water-proof rule (see §1), a missing water statement is a diligence gap, not a neutral omission.
  • Prices are unusually dispersed and partly irreconcilable across aggregators (see the conflict flags on 911 N Camino del Pueblo and 1100 2nd Street NW). Treat every price below as "as listed on that source on 31 October 2026", not as a verified current asking price.

1. Zoning context carried over from Run 1 (not re-researched in depth)

From the Run 1 brief, which this part must not contradict:

  • Local jurisdictions cannot ban cannabis businesses, but may set time/place/manner rules, including a 300 ft school/daycare ceiling under §26-2C-12 (NMSA 1978). In other words, a locality may not impose a school/daycare buffer greater than 300 ft; it may impose a smaller one.
  • Producer plant tiers run to a 20,000-plant maximum; there is no statewide numerical licence cap.
  • The water-proof rule is §26-2C-7(A)(3) + 16.8.2.22(A)(5) — a producer must demonstrate a legal water supply. A listing that says nothing about water therefore leaves a statutory diligence item unanswered.
  • State-licensed adult-use public possession limits (2 oz flower / 16 g concentrate / 800 mg edibles) and the medical 425-unit / 90-day, excise-free allowance do not change what a site may be used for, and are noted here only so the reader does not confuse a possession limit with a zoning permission.

Albuquerque corroboration (search-result evidence only, not directly opened — see Verify register). The City of Albuquerque's cannabis information page states that its Integrated Development Ordinance (IDO) provides that a cannabis retail establishment shall not be located within 300 feet of a school or child daycare facility or within 660 feet of another cannabis retail establishment, with the retailer-to-retailer separation increased from 600 to 660 feet on 3 August 2024, and that every cannabis retail location requires a Cannabis Retail Location Approval from the Planning Department. A separate Albuquerque rule document retrieved by search states the 300 ft school/daycare rule and, for non-microbusiness retailers, a 600 ft retailer separation — an older figure that conflicts with the 660 ft figure on the city's information page; the 660 ft figure is CONFIRMED on the City of Albuquerque official cannabis page (600 ft superseded 3 August 2024) — audit-resolved. The 2026 history is corrected: O-26-39 proposed 1,320 ft; the 990 ft figure was a floor amendment that failed 3–6 on 3 August 2026; neither is enacted law as stated here. Source: City of Albuquerque, "City of Albuquerque Cannabis Information" / "Application for Cannabis Retail Locations in Albuquerque", https://www.cabq.gov/city-of-albuquerque-cannabis-equity-workspace/city-of-albuquerque-cannabis-information-1 — accessed 31 October 2026 (search result; direct open was rate-limited, see §6).

Sunland Park local variation (secondary source, from search). A secondary report states Sunland Park requires cannabis establishments/consumption areas to be at least 200 feet from a school or daycare (city code 3-8-4), reduced from 300 feet in mid-2022, and that the city permits drive-thru cannabis sales. That is within the state 300 ft ceiling and is consistent with it, but it is a secondary-source claim and is flagged Verify in §6; it is not used to certify any Sunland Park property below. Source: The Green Border, "Proposed Sunland Park Cannabis Dispensary Sparks Zoning Controversy", https://www.thegreenborder.com/proposed-sunland-park-cannabis-dispensary-sparks-zoning-controversy/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

Practical reading rule for every table below. "Zoning: NR-C / MX-L / AP-5 / I-3" means the listing states that code. "Zoning: not stated" means the listing states a cannabis use but no zone code in the material retrieved. Neither proves that the local authority will approve a cannabis use at that address: the reader must still check (a) the current zone, (b) the school/daycare distance measured the way that jurisdiction measures it, (c) any retailer-to-retailer spacing (660 ft in Albuquerque), (d) any consumption-area or drive-thru rule, and (e) the water proof.

Same-name safeguards applied. Every property below was checked against its state/ZIP/county: Las Cruces, Sunland Park, Clovis, Portales, Alamogordo, Farmington, Roswell, Santa Fe and Socorro addresses are all New Mexico (NM ZIPs and counties stated). No property from Las Vegas NV, Santa Fe TX, Roswell GA, Clovis CA, Carlsbad CA, Socorro TX, Artesia CA, Anthony TX or El Paso TX/Juárez has been carried over. Where a source itself gives a conflicting ZIP (Lordsburg, Table D), that conflict is flagged and the property is excluded from the core count.

Conflict notes for Table A (do not silently pick one figure):

  • A6 (214 Menaul): 3,636 SF (Crexi) vs 3,633 SF (LoopNet/Showcase) is a rounding-level difference and is immaterial; 8,100 SF (Realmo) is materially different and most plausibly describes a larger building/area than Suites B & C.   • A7 (911 Camino del Pueblo): $4,124,000 / 20,620 SF (flyer) vs $4,400,000 / 10,000 SF (LoopNet search record). These cannot both describe the same offering in the same terms; one may be a partial interest, a different phase, or a stale round. Flagged, not resolved.
  • A8 (Howell Rd): 46.88 ac (MLS/LandSearch) vs "~50 acres" (flyer) is a rounding difference; Realmo's second 4.00-ac entry for the same address is treated here as the fenced operational area, not a second parcel, because the MLS text describes a 4-ac fenced operational area on the same property.
  • A11 (Portales): 1841 vs 1864 NM Highway 236. The opened Crexi page title reads 1864; the earlier search record reads 1841. APN on the opened page is 400000000334600 (a different APN, 400000000196111, appeared in the search record). Street number and APN must both be confirmed with the broker.
  • A21 (1100 2nd St): $1,000,000 vs $1,240,000. No reconciliation was retrieved.
  • A10 (San Cristobal): Land.com carries the property under two MLS numbers (114333 and 114350) with identical text; treated as one property, not two.

Other limitations.

  • No county assessor, zoning-map or parcel search was run for any individual address in this part; zone codes are listing-stated only. Albuquerque IDO zone meanings (NR-C = Non-Residential Commercial, NR-LM = Non-Residential Light Manufacturing, MX-L / MX-M = Mixed-Use Low / Medium intensity) are the standard IDO expansions and should be confirmed against the current IDO text before use — they are not separately sourced in this part.
  • "Zoning: not stated" is common because commercial aggregators often omit the zone field even when the underlying use is lawful. It must not be read as "not zoned for cannabis".
  • Licence transferability is not established by any listing below. Several listings bundle a business/licence with real estate (A1, A4, A11) or claim a licence (A9, B2, A22); New Mexico licence transfer/ownership rules were not re-researched in this part, and a buyer must confirm with the Cannabis Control Division whether a licence can move with the property, with the business, or not at all.
  • No property in this part was checked against the 300 ft school/daycare distance or, in Albuquerque, the 660 ft retailer separation. The tables give the reader the addresses to run those checks; they do not run them.
  • Hemp-specific properties are thin in the public listings: only A10 (past industrial hemp), C3 (past hemp crop, sold) and D5 (hemp-suitable farmland, excluded) mention hemp at all. There is no evidence in the searches of a currently-listed, dedicated, hemp-only zoned property with a street address in New Mexico on the sites searched. That may reflect hemp being grown on ordinary agricultural land (where no "hemp-zoned" marketing is needed) rather than an absence of hemp land.
  • No New Mexico county or municipal "cannabis zone" map or overlay district was found in the searches for this part; New Mexico's model is use permission inside ordinary commercial/industrial/agricultural zones plus buffers, not a freestanding cannabis zone — which is why this part is organised by marketed cannabis use rather than by a single zone code.

Federal baseline — fixed context, not re-researched. State-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final. IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. Do not tell any tribal operator that it has Schedule III / §280E relief on the basis of this file.

9.1.2 RLD / CCD — what it is, and what it is not

The Cannabis Control Division sits inside the Regulation and Licensing Department. The CRA (HB 2, 2021 First Special Session, ch. 4, signed 12 April 2021) created the division and transferred licensing authority under the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act to CCD, while DOH continues to run the patient programme. That division of labour is the single most common source of confusion in secondary writing: **CCD licenses businesses; DOH enrolls patients.** CCD does not issue patient cards, and DOH does not issue producer/retailer licences.

CCD's Enforcement Bureau was created by HB 10 (2025, ch. 85, effective 1 July 2025), which added §26-2C-43 (enforcement, embargo, recall, seizure) — Run 1, Part 1. The bureau's chief was reported in secondary coverage in 2026 as Vince Mares (see §9.2; name from secondary coverage only — Verify against an RLD staff page before publishing a name). CCD's public rule-hearing and rulemaking notices, industry bulletins (e.g. Bulletin 25-05 on OSE water hauling, 27 March 2025, and Bulletin 26-08 cited in Run 1), licence verification search, and C.R.O.P. sales dashboard are the Part 5 data sources; they are not repeated here.

9.1.3 Cannabis Regulatory Advisory Committee — statute and practice

Statutory basis: §26-2C-3(G)–(H), quoted from the 14 April 2023 CRAC minutes [Search-index excerpt]:

"the Cannabis Control Advisory Committee shall advise the Division on the development

of rules pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act, including best practices and the

promotion of economic and cultural diversity in licensing and employment opportunities

and protection of public health and safety while ensuring a regulated environment for

commercial cannabis activity that does not impose unreasonable barriers that would

perpetuate, rather than reduce and eliminate, the illicit market for cannabis. The

Cannabis Regulatory Advisory Committee shall elect from among its member a chair and

such other officers as it deems necessary. The Committee shall meet at the call of the

chair, the Director or the Superintendent. A majority of members currently serving

constitutes a [quorum] for the conduct of the business. Members serve at the pleasure

of the Superintendent."

Note: the minutes excerpt reads "forum" where "quorum" is plainly meant; the bracketed correction is this file's, and the verbatim text must be re-checked on NMOneSource / the RLD minutes PDF before quotation in the final HTML. The committee is advisory only — it does not license, does not set tax rates, and its recommendations do not bind CCD. Its current membership list was not opened in this run: the RLD C-RAC page opened here carries meeting notices, not a roster, so any named 2026 membership is Verify (the April 2023 minutes name a Chair Moore and a Member Chief Christopher Williams, but that roster is stale and must not be presented as current). A 2025 rulemaking notice proposed amending 16.8.1.11 NMAC to clarify that C-RAC meetings may be held remotely at the Superintendent's discretion (hearing 3 September 2025) — whether that amendment was adopted is Verify on the NM Register; do not present it as adopted law.

9.1.4 DOH Medical Cannabis Program — scope after the CRA

DOH's programme page states that DOH "does not charge any fees to enroll and participate in the Medical Cannabis Program or to register and use the Online Patient Portal" [Search-index excerpt], https://www.nmhealth.org/about/mcpp/mcp — consistent with Run 1 (DOH state fee $0; 2-year card under SB 242, 2023, ch. 108). DOH publishes monthly programme statistics (counts only) — July 2026: 60,400 patients (Run 1, Part 6, DOH report opened in Run 1: https://www.nmhealth.org/publication/view/report/9756/). The programme now sits in a "Center for Medical Cannabis and Psilocybin" — the psilocybin half reflects the Medical Psilocybin Act (SB 219, signed April 2025, per secondary briefing; Verify bill/session details on nmlegis.gov before citing it as law in the final HTML, and it is outside the cannabis/hemp scope of this file except as the reason for the Center's renamed title). The Medical Cannabis Advisory Board hears petitions to add qualifying conditions under 7.34.2.9 NMAC [Search-index excerpt].

9.1.5 TRD, NMED, NMDA, OSE — division of hemp and tax labour

Hemp is split by design, and the split is a frequent error in secondary sources:

  • NMDA = growing/cultivation (licences, sampling, harvest) under the USDA-approved

    • state plan from 1 January 2022.

  • NMED (Cannabis and Hemp Bureau) = post-harvest extraction, manufacturing,

    • warehousing and finished products under 20.10.2 NMAC (effective 28 January 2026), plus cannabis edibles manufacturers outside Albuquerque/Bernalillo County.

  • TRD = money: cannabis excise tax and GRT, and the tribal cooperative tax

    • agreements under §9-11-12.1 / §7-9-88.1 (see §10.1.4 for the general tribal tax framework, which is distinct from the cannabis-specific Picuris/Pojoaque tax agreements).

  • OSE = water only: it does not license cannabis businesses and does not set

    • plant limits; it validates (or declines to validate) the water right behind a producer licence application.

No single "New Mexico cannabis agency" exists. Any source that attributes hemp cultivation licensing to NMED, or cannabis excise collection to CCD, is wrong on this division and must not be followed.

9.1.6 DPS and AG — what was actually found

DPS's concrete, sourced cannabis role in this run is narrow: background checks for CCD controlling persons (DPS authorisation form, $15 fee, submitted to DPS, not to CCD — CCD producer checklist [Search-index excerpt]). DPS also operates the State Central Repository for criminal history, which is the records system behind expungement, but no DPS cannabis-specific programme page, cannabis arrest series, or DPS cannabis enforcement report was opened in this run. **Do not attribute a DPS cannabis arrest total or a DPS cannabis policy to this file.**

The AG's concrete, sourced cannabis/hemp roles in this run are: (a) representing TRD in the Sacred Garden medical-cannabis GRT litigation (see §9.2), and (b) New Mexico's inclusion among the 39 state/territory attorneys general on the NAAG letter of 24 October 2025 urging Congress to clarify the federal hemp definition [Search-index excerpt], https://www.naag.org/press-releases/bipartisan-coalition-of-39-state-and-territory-attorneys-general-urges-clarify-federal-definition-of-hemp/ — a policy letter, not a New Mexico AG opinion, and not New Mexico law. **No standalone New Mexico AG opinion on cannabis or hemp was located in this run.** That is a gap, not a finding that none exists: the AG opinion index must be searched directly in the Run 2 follow-up (see register).

9.2.6 Courts — the Sacred Garden GRT case (why it belongs in history)

In 2014, medical producer Sacred Garden sought a GRT refund from TRD; TRD denied it; the Court of Appeals held medical cannabis qualified for the prescription-drug GRT treatment; TRD, via the AG's office, petitioned the New Mexico Supreme Court (February 2020 filing; oral argument scheduled 28 February 2022) arguing a recommendation is not a prescription and the Legislature never explicitly exempted medical cannabis [Search-index excerpts], https://cannabislaw.report/nm-supreme-court-tasked-with-cannabis-grt-issue/ and https://cannabislaw.report/nm-supreme-court-to-hear-oral-arguments-in-medical-cannabis-tax-case/. The CRA then dealt with the issue legislatively (medical excise exemption; GRT deduction under §7-9-73.2, separately reported from 1 July 2025 — Run 1, Part 2). **The final Supreme Court disposition was not confirmed in this run — Verify** on the Court's docket before stating an outcome; AUDIT RESOLUTION: the Court of Appeals holding (Sacred Garden Inc. v. NM Taxation & Revenue Dept, 2021-NMCA-038) IS the final decision — the Supreme Court quashed its writ of certiorari as improvidently granted days before the scheduled 28 February 2022 argument, and TRD then issued refunds. Cite the quash order from the Supreme Court docket in the final report.

9.3 Ballot history and public opinion polling

9.3.1 No statewide citizen initiative — confirmed, with the precise qualification

New Mexico has no statewide citizen initiative. Citizens cannot put a proposed statute (or constitutional amendment) on the statewide ballot by petition. What New Mexico does have is a veto referendum: citizens may petition to repeal (disapprove, suspend and annul) an enacted law, subject to broad exclusions. Sources [Search-index excerpts]:

  • Ballotpedia, "New Mexico 2026 ballot measures":

    • https://ballotpedia.org/NewMexico2026ballotmeasures — "citizens have the power to initiate veto referendums, which seek to repeal legislation, but not initiatives, which seek to enact legislation."

  • Ballotpedia, referendum-process summary: "Citizens of New Mexico may repeal

    • legislation via veto referendum. New Mexico does not feature the power of initiative." Veto-referendum petitions must be filed at least four months before the next general election following the session in which the law was approved; the Constitution (art. IV, § 1) excludes, among other things, general appropriation laws, laws "providing for the preservation of the public peace, health or safety", debt/payment laws, school/institution maintenance laws, and local or special laws.

  • Contemporary reporting (2019, on a gun-control referendum attempt): New

    • Mexico's constitution "includes one of the most restrictive referendum processes of any state and no process at all for citizen initiatives", and "issues that other states have addressed through the ballot box, such as taxes or the legalization of recreational cannabis, are left to lawmakers in New Mexico."

Consequence for cannabis: **New Mexico legalised adult-use cannabis by legislation (HB 2, 2021), not by ballot measure** — unlike Arizona, Montana, New Jersey and South Dakota in 2020. No statewide cannabis ballot measure has ever been voted on in New Mexico, and none was found certified for the 3 November 2026 ballot in the Ballotpedia 2026 list opened in search (seven measures certified as of 26 October 2026, none identified as cannabis in the excerpt — Verify the full 2026 list on Ballotpedia / SOS before stating categorically that no 2026 cannabis measure exists). A veto referendum against the CRA itself would in any event face the "public peace, health or safety" exclusion, which is why no such referendum is recorded — that application of the exclusion to the CRA is this file's legal reasoning, not a court holding, and is marked as such.

10.1.2 Legal framework — the statute, verbatim (mirror text — re-check on NMOneSource)

§26-2C-41, "Indian nations, tribes and pueblos; intergovernmental agreements" (Justia 2021 [Search-index excerpt], https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/2021/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-41/; History: Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, § 41; effective 29 June 2021 per the Justia history note):

"A. The department may enter into one or more intergovernmental agreements with

any tribal government to efficiently coordinate the cross-jurisdictional

administration of the laws of this state and the laws of tribal governments

relating to the use of cannabis products set forth in the Cannabis Regulation

Act and the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act [Chapter 26, Article 2B NMSA

1978]. The agreements may include, without limitation, provisions relating

to: (1) criminal and civil law enforcement; (2) regulatory issues relating to

the possession, delivery, production, processing or use of cannabis products;

(3) the administration of laws relating to taxation; (4) any immunity,

preemption or conflict of law relating to the possession, delivery, production,

processing or use of cannabis products; and (5) the resolution of any disputes

between a tribal government and the state, which may include, without

limitation, the use of mediation or other nonjudicial processes.

B. An agreement entered into pursuant to this section shall: (1) provide for

the preservation of public health and safety; (2) ensure the security of

cannabis establishments and the corresponding facilities on tribal land;

(3) establish provisions regulating business involving cannabis that passes

between tribal land and non-tribal land in New Mexico; and (4) be negotiated

in good faith, which shall respect and protect state and tribal sovereign

immunity.

C. As used in this section, 'tribal government' means a federally recognized

Indian nation, tribe or pueblo located wholly or partially in the state."

Three consequences follow from the text itself, without needing the (unpublished) IGA texts:

  1. An IGA is permissive ("may enter into"), not mandatory, and it is the

    2. department (RLD) that enters into it — which is why only two IGAs exist despite 23 eligible governments.

  2. Every IGA must address cross-boundary business (tribal land ↔ non-tribal

    3. land in New Mexico) — §26-2C-41(B)(3). That is the statutory hook for the "state licence needed off tribal land" rule reported in secondary coverage (§10.1.3), but the IGA-specific mechanism (recognition, testing, tracking, tax) is in the IGA text, not in the statute, and therefore remains Verify for Picuris and Pojoaque individually.

  3. The statute does not say that IGA-regulated activity is "state-licensed",

    4. does not deem tribal licensees to be CCD licensees, and does not address federal scheduling at all. That silence is precisely why the federal Schedule III / §280E "state-licensed" question cannot be answered from §26-2C-41 and remains Verify (see the federal baseline note at the top of this file).

Related provisions whose texts were not returned in this run and are therefore Verify on NMOneSource, not quoted here:

    • index [Search-index excerpt]).

  • §76-24-10, the Hemp Manufacturing Act's tribal provision (Run 1: "text not

    • returned, Verify"). No New Mexico tribal hemp plan, tribal hemp licence, or tribal hemp ordinance was found in this run, and no New Mexico tribe appears on the USDA tribal-plan list as confirmed in Run 1 — Verify against the current USDA AMS tribal-plan list before stating that no tribal hemp programme exists.

The verbatim rule text was not opened in this run — Verify on SRCA. Reciprocity is the one place where tribal-nation medical participation is expressly contemplated in the medical rules, and it is a patient provision, not a tribal-enterprise licensing provision; do not conflate the two.

General federal/tribal framework (stated at the level the sources support, no further): tribes are sovereign governments; federal controlled-substances law applies in Indian Country unless Congress has provided otherwise; the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Office of Justice Services enforces federal law on tribal lands; and the federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider (through 11 December 2026, federal baseline) bars DOJ spending to interfere with state-legal medical programmes — whether and how that rider applies to a tribal medical programme operating under an IGA is Verify and is not answered in this file. The Governor's 2022 announcement's sentence — "With cannabis still illegal under federal law, IGAs prevent federal law enforcement action on tribal lands where communities want to participate in the adult-use market in New Mexico" [Direct open] — is a political assurance in a press release, not a legal immunity: the 2018 and 2021 Picuris raids (§10.1.5) show federal enforcement on tribal land both before and after the CRA, and the 2021 raid post-dates the CRA's effective date (though it pre-dates the March 2022 IGAs).

the Pueblo's Indian country and will not be required to file any return with

responsible for the enforcement, administration, collection and remittance

and auditing of Pueblo cannabis excise tax from Pueblo enterprises."

"The agreement stipulates that the tribe shall determine what constitutes a

That quotation is secondary (a newspaper's quotation of the agreement), not a direct opening of the agreement, and the agreement's own rate, base, filing, audit-sharing and cross-boundary provisions were not returned. What can be stated on official/secondary authority combined:

It is not the cannabis-specific Picuris/Pojoaque agreement, and its 25/75 credit mechanics must not be presented as the cannabis tax terms. Fort Sill Apache and the Navajo Nation do not appear on TRD's §9-11-12.1 list as opened — Verify whether that is a list-completeness issue or a substantive exclusion before drawing any conclusion.

10.2 Interstate issues

10.2.1 The New Mexico interstate framework — a dormant permission, not an open border

§26-2C-37, "Intrastate source" (title only in this run; text Verify on NMOneSource). The medical programme's "adequate supply" definition (§26-2B-3(A), FindLaw [Search-index excerpt], https://codes.findlaw.com/nm/chapter-26-drugs-and-cosmetics/nm-st-sect-26-2b-3/) requires supply "derived solely from an intrastate source", and the CCD/DOH comparison handout states "Out of State Product — No — must be an intrastate (instate) purchase" for both medical and adult-use [Search-index excerpt]. The commercial rule is therefore: **New Mexico cannabis sold in New Mexico must come from New Mexico.**

§26-2C-38, "Imports and exports" (LawServer [Search-index excerpt], https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/new-mexico/nm-statutes/newmexicostatutes_26-2c-38), in operative substance:

"A. Notwithstanding … Section 37 … or any other provision of law, the

governor shall enter into agreements with other jurisdictions within or

outside of the United States for the purposes of cross-jurisdictional

delivery of cannabis products between this state and the other jurisdictions.

Such agreements shall: (1) ensure enforceable public health and safety

standards; (2) include a system to regulate and track the interstate or

international delivery of cannabis products; and (3) ensure that any cannabis

products delivered into this state, prior to sale to a consumer, are tested,

packaged and labeled pursuant to New Mexico laws and rules.

B. … a person licensed to: (1) courier cannabis products may deliver cannabis

products to a person located in, and authorized to receive cannabis products

by, another jurisdiction in the United States; and (2) receive cannabis

products may receive cannabis products from a person located in, and

authorized to export cannabis products by, another jurisdiction in the United

States or internationally.

C. This section shall take effect on the earlier date on which: (1) federal

law is amended to allow for the interstate or international transfer of

cannabis products between authorized cannabis-related businesses; or

(2) the United States department of justice issues an opinion or memorandum

allowing or tolerating the interstate or international transfer of cannabis

products between cannabis-related businesses as authorized by state law."

§26-2C-38 is therefore dormant: its own subsection C suspends it until a federal amendment or a DOJ opinion/memorandum. Neither trigger was found to have occurred as of 31 October 2026 in this run, and **no §26-2C-38 agreement with any state or country was found**. The practical rule today is the opposite of what §26-2C-38's title might suggest: **no lawful interstate or international commercial cannabis trade into or out of New Mexico exists under state law today**, and a courier delivering New Mexico cannabis to another state (or receiving out-of-state cannabis) outside a §26-2C-38 agreement would be acting outside the CRA's permission. The MPP summary of HB 2 states the same trigger in plain English [Search-index excerpt].

Hemp is different, and the difference must be kept exact. Hemp (as federally defined) is not marijuana and is not subject to §26-2C-38's marijuana-trade dormancy; hemp shipments move under the federal hemp framework and New Mexico's hemp rules (NMDA cultivation, NMED post-harvest permits, 20.10.2 NMAC transport scope). But hemp that exceeds the THC definition is marijuana, not hemp, and the federal definition itself changes after 11 December 2026 (federal baseline: full total-THC definition + 0.4 mg/container cap). **No New Mexico statute, rule, or agency guidance responding to the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal hemp dates was found in Run 1 or in this run** — whether New Mexico will conform its hemp definition, its 20.10.2 finished-product limits (0.30% / 2 mg / 20 mg, Run 1), or its shipment documentation to the new federal definition is Verify and is the most time-sensitive follow-up in this file, because the federal dates fall after the dossier date. Do not state that New Mexico hemp shipments after 11 December 2026 are unaffected.

The often-repeated secondary claim that a large share (e.g. "38% non-resident") of sales are to out-of-state buyers was recorded in Run 1 as not adopted (no methodology/source) and is likewise not adopted here. What is reported is city-level sales, which invite — but do not prove — a cross-border inference:

That episode is about land use and traffic, not about the legality of a Texan buying in New Mexico.

Neighbouring-state buyer notes (kept to what the sources support):

  • Texas: adult-use cannabis is not legal in Texas; Texas has only a

    • low-THC medical programme (outside this file's New Mexico scope — Verify current Texas law in the Texas dossier before stating Texas rules in the final HTML). A Texas resident may lawfully purchase in New Mexico under New Mexico law if 21+ (or as a reciprocal medical participant), but may not lawfully take that cannabis back into Texas, and Texas law enforcement / federal enforcement at checkpoints (§10.2.4) may seize it. The secondary claim that "Texans no longer fear prosecution" for crossing to buy (Veriheal, updated 12 May 2026 [Search-index excerpt]) is a journalist's characterisation of enforcement priorities, not a legal protection, and must not be presented as one.

    • Oklahoma/Utah-specific New Mexico border-market figure, was found. Oklahoma's medical market and Utah's medical programme are outside this file's scope; do not import their rules here.

    • purchase adult-use cannabis (Run 1, Part 1 context; secondary briefs agree). Residency is therefore not a barrier at the till — the barrier is at the state line on the way home.

10.2.4 Border Patrol checkpoints and federal-land rules

Checkpoints — locations (secondary, to be confirmed against CBP sources):

  • Interstate 10, approximately 22 miles west of Las Cruces; Interstate 25,

    • about 23 miles north of Las Cruces (LegalClarity summary of the El Paso Sector / Las Cruces Station [Search-index excerpt]); U.S. Highway 70 between Las Cruces and the White Sands area (same source). A secondary news item counts "five [checkpoints] on the major highways of New Mexico" [Search-index excerpt] — the count and the full list (including any Alamogordo-area and Lordsburg-area checkpoints) are Verify on CBP sources; do not publish a definitive checkpoint map from this file.

  • Legal character: fixed interior checkpoints within 100 miles of the

    • international border, where Border Patrol may stop vehicles for brief immigration questioning without individualised suspicion; secondary inspection may follow on a dog alert or observed probable cause [Search-index excerpts]. Checkpoints on the I-25 / I-10 corridors north of Las Cruces stop northbound traffic (ACLU of New Mexico [Search-index excerpt]), which is why a Las Cruces grower moving product north to Albuquerque faces checkpoint risk that an Albuquerque grower moving product south does not — the asymmetry is geographic, not a legal distinction between growers.

  • State licence does not protect product at a checkpoint. CBP's stated

    • position (via its public information officer, secondary reporting [Search-index excerpt]): "although medical and recreational marijuana may be legal in some U.S. States and Canada, the sale, possession, production and distribution of marijuana or the facilitation of the aforementioned remain illegal under U.S. federal law." Reported seizures include: at least a dozen regulated-product seizures in two weeks in early 2024 (industry reporting via secondary item **[Search-index excerpt]**); a Top Crop Cannabis vehicle seized at a checkpoint on Valentine's Day (year not given in the excerpt — Verify); a Head Space Alchemy employee arrested at the I-25 checkpoint ~25 miles north of Las Cruces while delivering samples to a Santa Fe lab (same item). A 2024 petition by licensed providers reported "more than $300,000 worth of marijuana confiscated" (KRQE via secondary news item **[Search-index excerpt]**). All counts are secondary and none was confirmed on a CBP release in this run — Verify before publishing any seizure total. The equity point made by ACLU-NM and the Drug Policy Alliance [Search-index excerpts] — that checkpoint risk falls hardest on small southern New Mexico businesses that cannot absorb a seizure — is an advocacy analysis, not a CBP or CCD finding, and should be labelled as such.

  • Medical Schedule III nuance — Verify, do not assume. The federal

    • baseline moves state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III. Whether that change alters CBP checkpoint treatment of a state-licensed medical patient's medicine, or of a medical licensee's shipment, was not addressed in any CBP, DOJ, or CCD source opened in this run. Do not state that medical product is now checkpoint-safe; equally, do not state that Schedule III is irrelevant at checkpoints. The question is open and is listed in the register.

Federal land — the rule and the New Mexico examples:

  • General rule (secondary legal guides, consistent with federal law):

    • cannabis possession/use is prohibited on federal land regardless of New Mexico law, including national parks, national forests, federal courthouses, military installations, and airports under federal jurisdiction [Search-index excerpts]. A New Mexico medical card or a New Mexico retail receipt does not authorise possession on federal land.

  • White Sands National Park (Otero County, in the Tularosa Basin,

    • surrounded by White Sands Missile Range): federal land; cannabis is off-limits there. Secondary visitor guides variously describe it as "completely off limits for cannabis" and, in one guide, misleadingly suggest a "private, low-key cannabis experience" in the park — the latter is wrong and must not be repeated: the park is federal land and the prohibition applies. Missile testing can close the park and nearby roads (secondary visitor guidance [Search-index excerpt]) — that is an access fact, not a cannabis rule.

  • Los Alamos National Laboratory (Los Alamos County): a federal

    • Department of Energy laboratory site. No LANL-specific cannabis policy (employee, visitor, or contractor) was opened in this run — the general federal-land rule applies, but any LANL-specific policy, clearance consequence, or drug-testing rule is Verify on LANL/DOE sources and must not be invented here.

  • Military bases generally: White Sands Missile Range, Holloman Air

    • Force Base (near Alamogordo), Kirtland Air Force Base (Albuquerque), and Cannon Air Force Base (near Clovis) are the major New Mexico installations commonly listed — but **no base-specific cannabis policy was opened in this run**, and the list itself is given here only to identify the follow-up, not as a sourced inventory. The general federal rule (no cannabis on a federal installation, Uniform Code of Military Justice consequences for service members) is the only statement this file supports; base orders, gate-search practice, and civilian-visitor consequences are Verify per installation.

  • Tribal land vs federal land: tribal land is not "federal land" in the

    • national-park sense, but federal criminal law (including the Controlled Substances Act) applies in Indian Country as described in §10.1.2. Do not merge the White Sands / LANL / base rule with the tribal-land rule: the enforcement authorities, the governing codes, and the IGA overlay are different.

New Mexico Cannabis and Hemp — Parts 11–12 (Corrected)

Last audited: 31 October 2026. This file is the corrected text of Parts 11–12 only (operations rules and consumer/social rules, plus the combined Parts 11–12 Verify/Unavailable register) from the original complete Parts 0–12 dossier dated 31 October 2026. Every section and all detail of the original segment are preserved; only items changed by the audit are altered, and each inline change is marked “”. Every fact in the original kept its source link; new audit findings carry their primary-source links in the audit table (part11-12-audit.md) and in the corrections box below. No personal phone numbers or personal emails of individual licence holders are reproduced.

Corrections applied in this audit — summary (see audit table for full rows and sources)

  1. Testing Table 1 is pre-amendment and obsolete. The 31 Aug 2026 amendment (NM Register Vol. XXXVII, Issue 16) replaces the product categories; former pesticide exception (E)(1) was deleted. Check current SRCA 16.8.7.15 before any compliance use. Heavy-metal/mycotoxin mandatory status remains Unverified (amendment PDF rendering garbled).
  2. General recall rule exists: 16.8.2.11 — written procedures, customer/establishment notification, 24-hour CCD notification, CCD immediate-recall orders under (E). The original “no general recall rule” sentence is deleted.
  3. 24-hour failed-product notice IS in 16.8.7.15(O) itself (distinct from the 5-business-day general wastage notice in 16.8.2.15(E)). Full remediation text in 16.8.7.15(N)(2)–(6) is now confirmed; there is NO pesticide-failure remediation route — pesticide failures go to destruction under (O).
  4. Bluebonnet Labs hold continued: Bulletin 25-19 (13 Nov 2025) + Permanent Restraining Order, Case No. D-202-CV-2025-00809 — unretested product may not enter the market under any circumstances. Bluebonnet must not be listed as currently operating/hold-free.
  5. §26-2C-40 was NOT repealed 31 Dec 2025. The scheduled repeal (Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §73) was itself repealed by Laws 2024, ch. 38, §19. 16.8.8.9 tiers (201–2,000 / 2,001–6,000 / 6,001–12,000 / 12,001–16,000; 20,000 maximum) stand under a live statute. The 11.5–11.10 checker's contrary claim was overruled on the Justia 2025 annotation. Multi-licence interaction with the 20,000 cap remains Unverified.
  6. “Controlling person” = 10%+ by statute (§26-2C-2) — not a reporting convention; still not an ownership cap. Per-plant fees confirmed: 16.8.11.11 — $5.00 commercial / $2.50 medical-only at every tier, microbusinesses/ICMBs excepted, no 8,000-plant cap. NMDA pesticide list now 30 Oct 2026 (not July 2026). Energy/water plan duty covers manufacturers too: §26-2C-7(A)(4) (“any type of cannabis producer or manufacturer license”). Water hauling: OSE case-by-case approval for one additional year exists (Bulletin 25-05, 27 Mar 2025) — “1-year only, no exceptions” overstated. No OSE enforcement action is cited in §11.6 — none invented.
  7. Security corrections: delete the 6-foot fence figure (current 16.8.2.10(N) states no height); theft/security-incident reporting is 16.8.2.8(M), not (N); closure notices omitted in the original are added by reference: 30 days' notice to CCD and 14 days' public posting before permanent closure (16.8.2.8(V)). Courier $10,000 cap remains current; the $5,000 proposal was not shown adopted.
  8. Worker/server corrections: DPS controlling-person form fee $15.00 (CCD guidance, not rule text); server ladder §26-2C-11(F) — 30 days / 1 year / permanent revocation; curriculum §26-2C-11(C)(1)–(6); 4.5 hours is renewal continuing education only; provider 120-day permanent-permit notice sits against the 90-day distribution duty (16.8.10.8(D)–(E)); §26-2C-7(D)/(G) substantially-related grounds replace the blanket “no disqualifying list” wording. Research: zero narrowed to the June 2025 official count (Research Laboratory — 0 premises); currency after June 2025 and any NMSU/UNM CCD licence remain Verify; UNM Medical Cannabis Research Fund existence is confirmed on unm.edu (est. Aug 2016) but is NOT a CCD licence. Insurance/bonding minimum: negative finding retained as Unverified, not confirmed.
  9. Guns (§12.7) — materially updated: United States v. Hemani, 608 U.S. 772, decided 18 June 2026, 9-0 in judgment, as-applied only — §922(g)(3) NOT struck down; addiction, present intoxication and individualised-danger cases reserved. “Adult-use Prohibited: Settled” and “no binding ruling” are deleted. Schedule III status alone does NOT remove the §922(g)(3) disability — that standalone claim is Removed. ATF Jan 2026 interim final rule confirmed (91 FR 2698, eff. 22 Jan 2026): “unlawful user” = regular use over an extended period continuing into the present without a lawful prescription; cessation and isolated/sporadic use expressly excluded; no bright-line abstinence period. Draft Form 4473: proposed-rule comments closed 6 Aug 2026 (Federal Register doc. 2026-09182); July was the separate information-collection window; final-form status at 31 Oct 2026 remains Verify; the Aug 2023 form governed at the counter on sources checked. NM concealed-carry: §29-19-4(A)(9) addiction bar, (B)(3) 10-year drug-misdemeanor denial, DPS application Q9 — a state licence does not override §922(g)(3). False-statement liability under §922(a)(6) is untouched by Hemani.
  10. Paraphernalia (§12.1): §30-31-25.1(D) offence exists — delivery by a person 18+ to an under-18 at least 3 years junior is a fourth-degree felony (subject to the §30-31-2(T) carve-out analysis for the item). §26-2C-25(B) is broader than (A)(6) alone. Retailer paraphernalia-sale right and paraphernalia-only-shop licence/age-gate remain Verify.
  11. Driving (§12.2): HB 55 (2024) died (API.); HB 567 (2025) died (API.) — oral-fluid testing is NOT law; HB 106 (2025) died but its substance passed as HB 8, 2025 ch. 4 (§66-8-103, eff. 20 June 2025: EMTs + certified phlebotomists). Implied Consent range corrected to §§66-8-105–112. No per se THC limit; no cannabis open-container statute found (targeted search). UJI verbatim text remains Unverified (law-firm source only).
  12. Expungement (§12.3): law confirmed (§29-3A-8 as amended 2023, ch. 74, eff. 16 June 2023). Official cumulative total remains Unavailable; ~14,000 (Apr 2023, AOC via press) and the 151,640/155,000 pool are secondary-only, must never be presented as a 2026 total or summed from district filings. Follow-up: direct AOC/DPS request.
  13. Consumption areas (§12.4): fee FOUND — 16.8.11.9(J) $2,500/yr (§26-2C-9(A)(10) up to $2,500); server-permit part is 16.8.10 NMAC, not “18.8.10”; §16.8.2.49(D) liquor bar is stale against 2024 §26-2C-6(J)/(L) (co-location ban only). Operating Type I/II count remains Unavailable. Sept 2025 proposed consumption-area changes (≤10 mg pre-packaged units, COA copy) were proposals only on sources checked.
  14. Visitors/reciprocity (§12.5): no-residency basis is §26-2C-6(I) directly (not omission or §26-2C-7). Reciprocity citation settled as 7.34.3.22 (DOH “7.34.2.22” is an error). Tribal-programme exception is in 7.34.3.22(A)(3)(b) (NM Indian nation/tribe/pueblo programme members may participate as reciprocal participants). No NM qualifying-condition test applies to reciprocal participants. “90-day registration validity” must not be used — the rule states a 425-unit purchase limit in any three-month period. Reciprocal expiry-mid-visit consequence remains Verify.
  15. Landlord/tenant (§12.6): ORRA periods resolved — §47-8-33: 7-day cure, second 7-day termination, 30-day notice-giving deadline, 3-day substantial-violation/nonpayment; §47-8-37: 30 days month-to-month / 7 days week-to-week. HUD post-rescheduling position remains Verify. Silent-lease and mid-tenancy cannabis-case questions remain Verify.
  16. Schools (§12.9): SB 204 effective 14 June 2019 (Laws 2019, ch. 247 + ch. 261; ch. 261 compiled as §22-33-5). Inhaled/aerosol forms BANNED at school (§22-33-5(E)(3)(b); 6.12.10.7(I)(3) — oral capsule/extract/concentrate only, not food/beverage/topical, not refrigerated). “School setting” is rule text (6.12.10.7(O)), not local policy; certification + treatment plan valid ≤1 year (6.12.10.9(F)). State-licensed medical marijuana + FDA-approved products are Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; 26 U.S.C. §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and fully applies to adult-use; hemp under P.L. 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026 but limited by P.L. 119-103 §2019 until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg/container cap apply; USDA DEA-laboratory hemp-testing enforcement delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal banking law. 11.1 Testing: required tests, sampling, failed tests and recalls, licensed laboratories

11.1.1 Who must test, and when — the gate rule

"A cannabis establishment shall segregate a batch of cannabis product and arrange for samples to be collected and tested by a cannabis testing laboratory if required by this section. The batch must pass all required tests prior to the sale or delivery to a qualified patient, primary caregiver or consumer." — 16.8.7.15 NMAC, introductory text.

  • Producers / producer microbusinesses / VICE / ICMB must arrange and pay for Table 1 testing of any flower and trim they harvest before (a) packaging for retail sale, (b) transfer to another establishment for retail sale, (c) retail sale, or (d) delivery to a patient or consumer — 16.8.7.15(A)(1).
  • Manufacturers / VICE / ICMB must arrange and pay for Table 1 testing of any product they manufacture, including a concentrate or extract, before the same four events — 16.8.7.15(A)(2).
  • Retailers / VICE / ICMB must not sell or deliver any product unless it has undergone all testing required by the section — 16.8.7.15(A)(3).
  • The statutory duty behind the rule is §26-2C-18 NMSA 1978 (Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §18; amended 2024, ch. 38, §8, effective 1 July 2024): testing must comply with applicable law and rules; the Cannabis Control Division (CCD), in consultation with NMED and consistent with industry standards, must promulgate rules requiring producers and manufacturers to have products tested before distribution to retailers or sale by ICMBs, specifying frequency, cost-bearer, chain-of-custody, transport/storage, laboratory-staff sample collection, and destruction of a non-compliant batch unless remediation can bring it into compliance or it can be used for research.
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-18/ — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Rule source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-7-15-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026. Part 7 (16.8.7 NMAC) was originally effective 1 March 2022 (16.8.7.5 NMAC); §15 itself carries later amendment dates, including an amendment effective 31 August 2026 (see §11.1.6, Verify note).

11.1.2 Required tests — Table 1 and the pass standards

The column alignment of the asterisk in the source rendering is ambiguous for edible / other-inhalable / other rows. Do not rely on this table alone for whether a particular edible or topical needs a pesticide panel — see the Verify note in §11.1.6 on the 31 August 2026 amendment and on secondary-panel practice. Pass standards in 16.8.7.15, in brief:

  • Visual inspection (F): pass if, under minimum 40× magnification, a 1-gram sample shows no living or dead insects, hair, eggs or faeces, and no more than 2% sand, soil, mould or rocks.
  • Microbiological (G, Table 2): E. coli 100 CFU/gram (a product may instead be tested for Shiga-toxin producing E. coli); Aspergillus flavus, fumigatus, niger or terreus — present in 1 gram fails; Salmonella spp. — present in 1 gram fails. Shiga-toxin producing E. coli, Clostridium botulinum and Pseudomonas aeruginosa testing is effective 1 July 2022 and, for the latter two plus Shiga-toxin E. coli, is required only for edible products manufactured from fresh cannabis with water activity ≥ 0.65. Results are reported as "Present", "Absent" or CFU per 1 gram. The division may add microbes on 30 days' written notice, except no notice is required when human illness is linked to contaminated product.
  • Residual solvents (H, Table 3): pass if each solvent is below its action level (µg/g / ppm), e.g. propane 5,000; n-butane and isobutane 5,000; n-pentane 5,000; n-hexane 290; benzene 2.0; toluene 890; n-heptane 5,000; ethylbenzene + xylenes 2,170 total; ethanol 5,000; methanol 3,000; isopropanol 5,000; acetone 5,000. Report to two significant digits; report below-limit-of-quantitation results as e.g. "Benzene < 2.0 µg/g".
  • Potency (I, Table 4): determine THC, THCA, CBD and CBDA per gram (solids: mg/g and % by weight; liquids: mg/ml). Total THC (solids) = (THCA % × 0.877) + THC %; total CBD (solids) = (CBDA % × 0.877) + CBD %; the same 0.877 decarboxylation factor applies on a mg/ml basis for liquids.
  • Pesticides (J, Table 5): pass if every targeted residue is below its Table 5 action level, with separate inhalable and non-inhalable levels (e.g. abamectin 0.1 inhalable / 0.15 non-inhalable; acequinocyl 2.0 / 2.0; bifenazate 0.2 / 0.2; bifenthrin 0.1 / 0.1; etoxazole 0.1 / 1.0; imazalil 0.1 / 0.1; imidacloprid 0.1 / 3.0; myclobutanil 0.1 / 0.4; paclobutrazol 0.04 / 0.04; piperonyl butoxide 3.0 / 8.0; pyrethrins 0.5 / 1.0 — full Table 5 controls; this list is illustrative, not exhaustive). The division may adopt testing for additional residues on 30 days' written notice if quality-control or inspection testing by a testing laboratory, the New Mexico Department of Agriculture (NMDA), the Department of Health (DOH) or CCD identifies their presence. Nothing in §15 waives the Pesticide Control Act, §§76-4-1 et seq. NMSA 1978; CCD alone or with NMDA may investigate suspected use of a pesticide not registered with NMDA for cannabis.

  • Pesticide action-level amendment source (New Mexico Register Vol. XXXVII, Issue 16, 25 August 2026; amendment to 16.8.7.15 effective 31 August 2026): https://prod-rf-lambda.rtssaas.com/PublicFiles/d89c47bd0d70402dba89b03a22bda6d1/569087d5-8e49-4af7-b24e-d7952291de01/16.8.7amend.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.

Heavy metals, mycotoxins, terpenes. These are testing categories a laboratory may be licensed for under 16.8.2.43(A) (see §11.1.5), but Table 1 as opened does not make them universally required for every product. Secondary summaries describe them as optional. Verify: whether CCD has, by separate notice or by the 31 August 2026 amendment, made any heavy-metal or mycotoxin panel mandatory for a particular product category — no such notice was found in the searches for this part.

Exceptions (E). (1) No separate pesticide-residue test is required for a product made from a concentrate or extract with verified pesticide-residue results, so long as the establishment can demonstrate the resulting product will not exceed the action levels for that product type. (2) No retest is required for a product acquired from another establishment if the batch, in its present form, previously passed and is accompanied by a Certificate of Analysis (COA) from a licensed testing laboratory issued within the previous 90 days. (3) If additional testing requirements take effect after a laboratory obtains a sample, the laboratory performs only the tests required when the sample was obtained.

Passing does not cure other violations (D). Passage of testing does not relieve an establishment of compliance with the Cannabis Regulation Act, the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act, the Pesticide Control Act, CCD rules, or other non-conflicting local, state and federal law. A product to which a pesticide was applied in violation of CCD rules or the Pesticide Control Act, or manufactured using an unapproved solvent, must be wasted and disposed of.

Records. An establishment must maintain all laboratory test results for products it produced or manufactured for at least two years and make them available to consumers or cannabis retailers on request — 16.8.7.15 (retention subsection, as carried in the 2022 emergency amendment and the current rule text).

11.1.3 Sampling rules — who collects, who transports, batch discipline

  • Laboratory responsibility (C). A cannabis testing laboratory is responsible for collection of samples for any required test, retest after a failing result, retest after remediation, or test for labelling purposes.
  • Who may collect: (a) laboratory employees with requisite training as specified in 16.8.2.26 NMAC; or (b) contractors who have completed the sampling-agent training offered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's domestic hemp production programme and sign an affidavit that they have no ownership interest in, and are not employed by, any cannabis establishment that produces or manufactures cannabis. The contractor must obtain necessary training to comply with the laboratory's protocols, and the laboratory may reject any sample it suspects was collected outside its protocols.
  • Who may transport samples: laboratory employees with 16.8.2.26 training, or contractors who sign an affidavit of no ownership interest in / employment by a producing or manufacturing establishment. Transporting cannabis for an establishment on a contractual basis does not preclude a person from transporting samples in secure containers for testing laboratories.
  • No duty to collect or accept. Nothing in the rule requires a laboratory to collect samples from, or transport samples on behalf of, any establishment, or to accept samples from an establishment; a laboratory may reject a sample suspected of being collected outside its protocols.
  • Distance / checkpoint delay (B, C(4)). CCD may delay implementation of sample-collection and testing requirements in whole or in part, considering whether a laboratory has validated a method and laboratory capacity to collect and transport. It may set different implementation dates for: microbusinesses/ICMBs up to 100 miles by automobile from the nearest licensed testing laboratory; producers/manufacturers/VICEs up to 200 miles; microbusinesses/ICMBs over 100 miles; producers/manufacturers/VICEs over 200 miles; and establishments for which travel to the nearest laboratory requires passing through a U.S. Border Patrol checkpoint. Where CCD has delayed the laboratory-collection requirement on distance/checkpoint grounds, any person collecting or transporting samples for required testing must receive training in sample-collection and transportation protocols.
  • Batch discipline. The establishment must segregate the batch and give the laboratory access to the entire batch. It may specify reasonable precautions against contamination (gloves/PPE, inspection of tools and containers, collection location, areas laboratory staff may not enter, refusal of entry to non-compliant laboratory staff/contractors). While awaiting results, product is held in containers for storage; the "AWAITING TEST RESULTS. DO NOT TRANSFER" labelling discipline in the rule text applies to product undergoing testing (see also §11.1.4 on storage of failed product). Routine testing is not required before the establishment segregates products into batches and places them in containers for storage while awaiting results.
  • Chain of custody and transport for testing. Sampling/testing is a track-and-trace shipping-manifest activity under 16.8.2.13(B)(1) (see §11.4). §26-2C-18(B)(5)–(7) requires chain-of-custody protocols, transport/storage preventing degradation, contamination, tampering or diversion, and laboratory-staff collection.
  • CCD quality-assurance testing (16.8.2.16). CCD or its representative may conduct quality-assurance sampling and testing, may adopt a randomised testing schedule, may prohibit sale/transfer of product found to contain prohibited contaminant levels or to have been improperly tested, or may require remediation consistent with CCD remediation standards. If CCD receives a verified complaint about mould, bacteria or another contaminant, or has reason to believe a contaminant may jeopardise public health and safety, it may inspect and require samples for CCD testing; licensees must allow access and sample collection. Division employees may possess samples solely to establish compliance. The licensee bears the cost of any testing required by CCD — 16.8.2.16(D).
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-16-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.1.4 Failed tests, retesting, remediation, destruction — and recalls

  • Retesting (M). If a sample fails any test, the establishment may request retesting by the same laboratory or another laboratory. If the repeated test is within acceptable limits, the batch may be sold, transferred or further manufactured.
  • Remediation (N) — 120-day window. "Within 120 days of a failed test, a cannabis establishment may remediate and retest the batch according to the procedures described in this subsection. A cannabis establishment shall adopt and maintain on the premises protocols regarding remediation consistent with this rule." In outline: dried cannabis or concentrates that fail microbiological testing may be remediated by extraction using an approved volatile solvent; other products that fail microbiological testing may not be remediated. A remediated product must undergo any test previously failed, and a product remediated with volatile solvents must additionally undergo residual-solvent testing. Cannabis failing visual inspection may be remediated as provided in §15(N)(6) (full sub-paragraphs (2)–(6) — including any pesticide-failure remediation limits — were not fully reproduced in the sources opened for this part; see Verify register).
  • Destruction (O). "Any cannabis product that fails a test and cannot be remediated, including any remediated cannabis product that fails any test after remediation, is subject to destruction in accordance with the wastage requirements of 16.8.2.15 NMAC." The CCD enforcement summary of the same rule adds the operational steps: notify CCD within 24 hours, confirm wastage and disposal, remove the wasted product from inventory with the removal noted in the track-and-trace system. Note the tension with the general wastage notice rule (5 business days, §11.5) — the 24-hour figure is the failed-product formulation in the enforcement summary; Verify whether 24 hours is in the current §15(O) text itself or is CCD enforcement practice, before relying on it as the rule deadline.
  • Storage of failed / awaiting-test product. Enforcement practice cited in CCD Case No. 2024-015 (WH Agriculture, LLC d/b/a Maggie's Farm, Notice of Contemplated Action, 9 September 2024) treats failure to properly label and store product undergoing testing, failure to maintain testing records, failure to destroy product that did not pass and could not be remediated, and failure to remove it from inventory so it could not be transferred, as violations of 16.8.7.15(L)(1)–(4) and (O) as then numbered. That case is an enforcement allegation/summary, not a rule text — do not cite its paragraph letters as current rule numbering without checking the current §15.

11.1.5 Testing laboratories — licensing, independence, and what can (and cannot) be confirmed

Licensing categories (16.8.2.43). CCD may license testing laboratories to perform analytical testing in one or more of: (1) visual inspection; (2) microbiological; (3) residual solvents; (4) potency and homogeneity; (5) heavy metals; (6) pesticides; and (7) such other categories as the department may identify. A cannabis establishment may conduct analytical testing using validated methods for internal quality control without a testing-laboratory licence, but may not offer testing services to another person or entity. All applications are on current CCD forms on the CCD website.

  • Independence bar (16.8.2.43(D); §26-2C-6(G)). "No person with a direct or indirect interest in any cannabis establishment other than a cannabis research laboratory may hold an interest in a cannabis testing laboratory." Statutorily: "The division shall not allow a person that is licensed as any type of cannabis establishment other than a cannabis research laboratory to hold, directly or indirectly, a cannabis testing laboratory license." This is the single most important ownership rule in Part 11: vertical integration stops at the laboratory door.
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-43-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026; statute: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Laboratory policies, training, capability (16.8.2.47; application forms). A testing laboratory must develop, implement and maintain on the licensed premises standard policies and procedures covering sample collection (tools and containers), methodology for each test (including sample preparation), employee policies, and related matters; must implement a CCD-approved training programme covering, within 30 days of start of employment, employee health and safety and related topics; must provide and document specific training before any person independently collects samples, and before any agent/employee independently performs any testing process; and must retain employee training documentation for two years (current employees; at least six months after termination is the parallel research-laboratory formulation — see §11.9 for the testing-laboratory retention wording, Verify). Renewal applications require, where applicable, proof of a Continuing Demonstration of Capability (CDC) for each test performed, and ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation within scope is the recognised way to evidence CDC. Commercial reference standards for cannabinoids and other contaminants/chemicals are required.
  • Sources: https://regulations.justia.com/states/new-mexico/title-16/chapter-8/part-2/section-16-8-2-47/ (current through Register Vol. 36, No. 12, 24 June 2025) — accessed 31 October 2026; application form: https://www.rld.state.nm.us/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Testing-Laboratory-Application.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Fee (Run 1 anchor, confirmed in statute). Testing-laboratory licence up to $2,500 per year plus up to $1,000 per year for each additional licensed premises — §26-2C-9(A)(2); 16.8.11 NMAC.
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-9/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

List of licensed testing laboratories — what is confirmed and what is not.
