CCD's own bulletin points to an "approved-testing-labs" page, but that page's live contents were not opened and verified for this part, and secondary sources state CCD does not list licensed testing laboratories on its website. No laboratory is listed below as "currently licensed" on the basis of a secondary list alone.
  • Counts (do not conflate units). Run 1 counts, retained unchanged: 6 testing approvals to 4 December 2024 (CCD approvals count; a contemporaneous CCD presentation also described "6 testing laboratories" in January 2025 reporting on Bluebonnet) and 7 testing premises in June 2025 (CCD presentation to legislators, 30 June 2025: "Testing Laboratory — 7" in the Licensed Premises table; the same presentation's narrative describes seven licensed laboratories operating across eight premises in October 2025 committee testimony — premises vs. licences vs. companies are different units, and the 7 vs. 8 discrepancy is flagged Verify, not resolved). A September 2026 secondary market report repeats "7 testing labs" citing the June 2025 CCD presentation — that is republication, not a new official count.
  • Source for June 2025 premises table: https://www.nmlegis.gov/(X(1)S(lwlkmr0y3i3lcdrg02ubogvl))/handouts/CCJ%20063025%20Item%201%20Cannabis%20Enforcement.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Individually confirmed on an official source (one laboratory, with a hold caveat). Bluebonnet Labs, LLC, licence TSTL-2024-0004-PRM-0001, is the only laboratory whose licence number is confirmed on an official CCD document opened for this part — and that document is the February 2025 administrative hold (see §11.1.4). It is not confirmed as currently operating or hold-free at 31 October 2026.
  • Hemp laboratories are a different list — do not merge them. NMED maintains a separate approved list for hemp finished-product testing under 20.10.2 NMAC. NMED's page, updated 8 September 2026, lists as New Mexico-based: PREE Laboratories NM LLC (Las Cruces), Rio Grande Analytics, and Scepter Lab (Santa Fe), plus out-of-state laboratories with scope limits (e.g. Adams Independent Testing — cannabinoid profile and water content only; Alkemist Labs — cannabinoid profile only). NMED approval routes are (1) approval by the DOH Medical Cannabis Program, or (2) ISO accreditation for hemp and/or cannabis within the scope of the hemp-rule analytical requirements. Inclusion on the NMED hemp list does not prove CCD cannabis testing licensure, and vice versa.
  • Source: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/analytical-laboratories/ — accessed 31 October 2026; NMED hemp FAQs: https://www.env.nm.gov/cannabis-hemp/faqs/ — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Names appearing only in secondary sources (Verify, not confirmed). Rio Grande Analytics, Scepter Labs / Scepter Lab, Argon Labs and PREE Laboratories NM are named by secondary sources as New Mexico cannabis testing laboratories. PREE's own site states it is a licensed and accredited cannabis and hemp testing facility in Las Cruces and describes CCD requirements, but a business's own claim is not an official licence confirmation. None of these is listed in this dossier as confirmed CCD-licensed; the route to confirmation is an Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA) request to CCD or the CCD approved-testing-labs page, which secondary sources have previously described as the only route.

11.1.6 Testing — 31 August 2026 amendment and open questions

  • CCD amended 16.8.7.15 effective 31 August 2026 (New Mexico Register Vol. XXXVII, Issue 16, 25 August 2026). A laboratory's September 2026 summary describes the amendment as changing "final product and secondary testing", including a secondary-panel concept (product made from material already carrying a passing COA; retests on acquired product past 90 days) and CCD staff confirmations that NMS2S does not currently assign pesticide testing to infused pre-rolls or infused cannabis material made from two inputs that each passed, with CCD intending to update the system. The full amended Table 1 / secondary-testing text was not verified against the current Cornell/NM Register text in this part (a browser rate-limit prevented re-opening the §15 page to its later lines), so the pre-amendment Table 1 above must be checked against the post-31-August-2026 text before it is used for a compliance decision. This is the largest single Verify item in Part 11.
  • Verify also: (a) whether heavy-metal / mycotoxin testing is now mandatory for any category; (b) the full §15(N)(2)–(6) remediation sub-paragraphs, especially for pesticide failures; (c) whether the 24-hour failed-product notice is in §15(O) itself; (d) current sample-size / batch-size rules — no batch-weight or sample-quantity table was found in the §15 text opened for this part, and none is stated here; (e) laboratory accreditation — no accreditation standard is named in the §15 text opened; ISO/IEC 17025 is the recognised CDC route on application forms, not a §15 mandate as stated here.

11.2 Licence rules: transfers/sales, ownership changes, renewal, ownership caps, relocation, surrender/revocation, insurance/bonding

11.2.1 The non-transferability rule — the starting point for every "sale"

"A license shall not be transferable or assignable from a licensee to another person." — §26-2C-6(G) NMSA 1978.

"A license shall not be subject to execution, attachment, a security transaction, liens or receivership." — §26-2C-6(H).

The rule version is identical in substance:

"A license shall not be transferred by assignment or otherwise to other persons or locations. Unless the licensee applies for and receives an amended license, the license shall be void and returned to the division when any one of the following situations occurs: (1) location of the licensed premises changes; (2) the discontinuance of operation at a licensed premises; or (3) suspension or revocation of the license by the division." — 16.8.2.8(N).

Practical consequence. There is no "licence sale" in New Mexico in the sense of assigning the licence itself. What can be sold is the business, its assets, and — subject to CCD approval — its controlling-person structure via an amended licence (see §11.2.2). A buyer who assumes it has bought a licence without an amended licence (or a new licence) is operating unlicensed. Unlicensed commercial cannabis activity is subject to a civil disciplinary fee of $10,000 for each instance under §61-1-3.2 NMSA 1978 (Uniform Licensing Act), as cited in CCD Case No. 2025-006.

  • Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-6/ and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-8-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.2.2 Ownership changes — amended licence, 90 days, prior approval for new controlling persons

Every licence type has a parallel amended-licence section. The producer version (16.8.2.23) is representative:

"A licensed producer shall submit to the division an application form for an amended license, pay the required fee, and must obtain approval from the division, prior to implementing any of the following: (1) change of licensee's legal or business name; (2) change in water source, or licensees water and energy conservation plan, including, the reuse of water and disposal of effluent; (3) increase in plant count beyond which licensee is currently licensed to produce; (4) decrease in plant count which licensee is currently licensed to produce; (5) addition or elimination of a controlling person; or (6) material or substantial modification of the premises."

  • Processing: the amended-licence application must comply with all requirements applicable to initial applications, except it must be clearly designated as an amended licence. CCD must approve or deny within 90 days of receiving a completed application. Denial is pursuant to the Uniform Licensing Act.
  • Material/substantial change (producer): increase or decrease in premises size, including sale of property used for the establishment or purchase of additional property; addition or removal of licensed activities on a single licensed premises; or a change in access to the water source submitted with an initial, amended or renewal application, or a 10% or more increase in water usage.
  • No amended licence needed for changes to standard operating policies and procedures, provided the licensee maintains at each licensed premises a copy of all current and prior operating policies and procedures.
  • The consumption-area version (16.8.2.51, adopted 7 June 2022, amended 7 May 2024) is to the same effect for (1) legal/business name change, (2) addition/elimination of a controlling person, and (3) material/substantial modification of the premises, including size change, sale/purchase of property, or a change in location; same 90-day decision rule; same SOP exception.
  • Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-23-NMAC and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.51 — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Background checks on change (16.8.2.9(B)). If there is a change in membership of any person subject to screening (see §11.8), an amended application and background-check documentation must be submitted, and each new member must be approved by CCD before assuming any duties or responsibilities for the licensee. A change of controlling persons is therefore not effective on signing — it is effective on CCD approval.

11.2.3 Renewal — 12 months, 60–30 days, no operation if not renewed, tax clearance

  • Term. "A license is valid for twelve months from the date the license is issued and may be renewed annually." — §26-2C-6(E). Rule version (16.8.2.17(A)–(B)): the licensure period runs from approval of the application for 12 months; unless otherwise renewed, suspended or revoked, a licence expires at 11:59 p.m. on the date indicated on the licence as the expiration date or other written notification by CCD.
  • Timely-renewal window (16.8.2.17(C)). "To timely renew a license, a completed license renewal application and annual license fee set forth in 16.8.11 NMAC shall be received by the division from the licensee no earlier than 60 calendar days before the expiration of the license and no later than 30 days before the expiration of the license through the division's electronic licensing portal." Failure to receive a renewal notice from CCD does not relieve the licensee of the obligation to renew. If a renewal application is not submitted and approved before the expiration date, the licensee must not sell, transfer, transport, manufacture, test or distribute any medical or commercial cannabis or cannabis products until the licence is renewed. On non-renewal, CCD may initiate disciplinary action under the Uniform Licensing Act. The NM-PLUS portal enforces the same window (it prohibits submitting a renewal more than 60 days or fewer than 30 days before expiration) and prohibits making amendments through the renewal application — amendments must be submitted before or after renewal.
  • Sources: 16.8.2.17 as summarised in CCD enforcement documents: https://api.realfile.rtsclients.com/PublicFiles/1ee897135beb4b1c82715d36398de4c5/54977dae-2c9c-44f3-b7c4-7740b9f9f20b/12.22.25Default%20OrderTHC%20dba%20The%20Weed%20Shack.pdf and https://api.realfile.rtsclients.com/PublicFiles/1ee897135beb4b1c82715d36398de4c5/0a96cb79-4fe4-4228-865e-e06644042f0f/1.29.25Final%20Pre-NCA%20Settlement%20AgreementFly%20High%20NM%20LLC.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026; NM-PLUS notice: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/4-5-2024.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Renewal conditions. All applications for initial licensure, amended licensure, additional premises and renewal must be available on the CCD website and made online (16.8.2.8(O)); a completed application and fees are required before CCD accepts an application as complete (16.8.2.8(P)); licence and additional-premises/renewal fees are paid at submission; annual plant fees are paid on CCD approval of the initial or renewal application and approval of the plant number; all licensing/renewal fees are non-refundable and must be paid for each new application. Before issuing a renewed licence, the licensee must provide proof of a business licence (16.8.2.8(BB), as amended).
  • Tax clearance — a hard gate on renewal (§26-2C-6(F)). "The director shall not renew a license until the director receives notification from the secretary of taxation and revenue or the secretary's designee that on a certain date: (1) the licensee is not a delinquent taxpayer pursuant to Section 7-1-16 NMSA 1978 only with respect to the cannabis excise tax or the gross receipts tax; and (2) there are no unfiled tax returns due with respect to the cannabis excise tax or the gross receipts tax." (2023 amendment, effective 1 July 2023.)
  • Renewal fees are the 16.8.11 NMAC annual fees in the Run 1 anchor (retailer $2,500, courier $250, testing $2,500, research $2,500, VICE $7,500 capped at $125,000, plus per-additional-premises fees and, for producers, per-plant fees). Renewal fees for all licensed premises are collected at the time of renewal (§26-2C-9(F)).
  • Applications generally — 90 days. "Once the division deems an application complete, the division has ninety days to issue or deny a license application." — §26-2C-7(B).
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-7/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.2.4 Ownership caps — what exists and what does not

  • No statewide licence-count cap and no general percentage ownership cap were found in the Cannabis Regulation Act or 16.8.2 NMAC in the searches for this part. The Act expressly provides the opposite for premises: "Except as otherwise provided in the Cannabis Regulation Act, the division shall not limit the number of licensed premises a licensee may occupy or operate under a license. Multiple licensees may occupy a single licensed premises" — §26-2C-6(I) (as carried in 2024 bill summaries of §26-2C-6). A secondary market report likewise states New Mexico does not cap the number of licences or use a lottery.
  • The caps that do exist are functional, not percentage caps:
  • Plant caps by licence type (see §11.3) — the real quantitative limit on scale.
  • Testing-laboratory independence (§11.1.5) — no direct/indirect interest in a testing laboratory for any person with an interest in another cannabis establishment (research laboratories excepted).
  • VICE fee cap ($125,000 total, §26-2C-9(D)) — a fee cap, not an ownership cap.
  • Medical-shortage quotas (§26-2C-6(N); 16.8.8.11) — CCD may, to address a medical shortage, require at least 10% of stock monthly designated for patients/caregivers/reciprocal participants, incentivise production, exclude commercial activity from new licences for at least six months, or require producers to devote no more than 25% of monthly cultivated plants to the medical programme with specific tracking. These are contingent shortage powers, not standing ownership caps. The 25% retail-sales-to-patients undertaking in 16.8.8.11(A) ran until 31 December 2022 and must not be presented as a current standing quota without checking whether CCD has invoked §26-2C-6(N) — Verify whether any shortage invocation is in force at 31 October 2026 (none was found in this part).
  • Controlling-person disclosure/tracking. CCD tracks controlling persons (a secondary report cites 3,279 people with a 10%+ ownership stake as of August 2024). Whether "controlling person" is defined by a 10% threshold in current rule/statute, or whether 10% is a reporting convention, is Verify — no definition section stating a percentage was opened for this part, and no percentage cap should be inferred from the tracking figure.
  • Former legislator bar (expired by its terms). §26-2C-6(P) barred a person who was a member of the Senate or House on the effective date of the Act from applying for or being granted a licence before 1 July 2026. That date has passed; the bar is spent, not a current cap.
  • Tribal-land limit (not an ownership cap, but a location bar). CCD must not approve licensure within the exterior boundaries of a federally recognised Indian Nation, Tribe or Pueblo wholly or partially in New Mexico unless the tribal government and the department agree as provided in 16.8.2.8(B). Cross-reference only — tribal compacts are in Run 1.

11.2.5 Relocation

Relocation is an amended-licence event, not a notification. A change in the location of the licensed premises voids the licence and requires its return unless the licensee applies for and receives an amended licence (16.8.2.8(N)(1)); the consumption-area rule expressly lists "a change in the location of the cannabis establishment" as a material/substantial change requiring an amended licence (16.8.2.51(D)); the producer rule lists premises-size and property changes the same way (16.8.2.23(D)). A relocated premises must still satisfy local-law proof (business licence / zoning / fire inspection), the 300 ft school/daycare buffer ceiling in §26-2C-12 (Run 1), and — for producers — water proof at the new place of use (see §11.6). Verify: whether CCD imposes a separate relocation fee or a new-premises fee in 16.8.11 NMAC beyond the amended-licence fee — no separate relocation fee schedule was found in this part.

11.2.6 Surrender, revocation, suspension, discipline, closure

  • Authority. CCD may issue, renew, deny, suspend or revoke licences or discipline licensees for consumption areas, couriers, manufacturers, producer microbusinesses, producers, research laboratories, retailers, servers, testing laboratories, ICMBs and VICEs — §26-2C-6(B) — in accordance with the Uniform Licensing Act, Chapter 61, Article 1 NMSA 1978, unless otherwise provided in the Cannabis Regulation Act (§26-2C-6(A)). Denial of an amended licence is likewise pursuant to the Uniform Licensing Act (16.8.2.23(C), 16.8.2.51(C)).
  • Grounds in outline (§26-2C-7, as amended 2024, effective 1 July 2024). CCD's authority to deny, suspend and revoke was clarified by the 2024 amendment; the full current grounds list in §26-2C-7 was not reproduced in the sources opened for this part. Verify the current §26-2C-7 denial/suspension/revocation grounds before advising on a specific case. What is confirmed: operating without an active licence engages §61-1-3.2 ($10,000 per instance, see §11.2.1); server-permit violations carry their own suspension ladder (§11.8.3); and CCD enforcement in 2025 proceeded by Notice of Contemplated Action, pre-NCA settlement, and default order under the Uniform Licensing Act (Cases 2025-001, 2025-006).
  • Closure / discontinuance — disposition of product (16.8.2.8, closure paragraph). Cannabis or cannabis products held by a licensee ceasing business operations on behalf of another licensee must be returned to the originating licensee. Other cannabis/products held by the licensee must, before closure, be surrendered to state or local law enforcement, destroyed by the licensee in accordance with the wastage standards (16.8.2.15), or donated to patients via a licensed cannabis establishment, provided the donation has been approved in writing by CCD and the licensee has submitted documentation of the donation to CCD. State and local law enforcement are authorised to remove and destroy any cannabis/products held by a person who has ceased to be licensed by CCD.
  • Surrender mechanics. No standalone "surrender form / surrender fee" rule was found in 16.8.2 in the searches for this part. The operative surrender consequences are: licence void and returned on discontinuance (16.8.2.8(N)(2)), product disposition as above, and — for a server permit — immediate return of the permit to CCD on suspension, revocation or denial of renewal (§26-2C-11(D)). Verify any CCD surrender procedure or form (NM-PLUS) before advising a licensee to surrender.

11.2.7 Insurance and bonding minimums — a negative finding

  • No statewide CCD insurance minimum and no statewide CCD surety-bond minimum were found in the Cannabis Regulation Act or in 16.8.2 NMAC in the searches for this part. Secondary insurance marketing states New Mexico cannabis dispensaries "aren't required to carry insurance" as a state licence condition (secondary, not official). That negative finding must be stated as Unavailable/Verify for a hidden minimum: it is possible a minimum sits in a licence-type section not opened for this part, in a local ordinance, or in a lender/landlord requirement, and none of those was confirmed here.
  • What is confirmed:
  • A transport driver must be prepared to show proof of insurance (with employee badge, driver's licence, vehicle registration, shipping manifest and chain-of-custody form) to law enforcement and CCD on request — 16.8.2.13(A)(18). That is vehicle insurance for the act of transport, not a premises liability minimum.
  • Security-alarm monitoring, vehicle alarm systems, and commercial-grade locks are security requirements (§11.4), not insurance.
  • Workers' compensation, general liability, product liability and crop insurance remain ordinary business / employer obligations under non-cannabis law and contract; no cannabis-specific minimum is stated in this part.
  • Do not invent a figure. No dollar minimum for general liability, product liability, workers' compensation (beyond general New Mexico employer law) or surety bonding is stated in this dossier for a CCD licence.

11.3 Cultivation rules: plant/canopy limits by licence type, indoor/outdoor/greenhouse, personal production and home grow

11.3.1 Commercial plant limits — plant count, not canopy

New Mexico limits commercial cultivation by mature-plant count, not by canopy square footage. The governing plant-limit rule is 16.8.8 NMAC (effective 24 August 2021; §§9–10 amended 22 March 2022). The scheduled repeal of the statutory plant-limit section, §26-2C-40 (Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, §73, eff. 31 Dec 2025), was itself repealed by Laws 2024, ch. 38, §19, so §26-2C-40 REMAINS IN FORCE and 16.8.8 NMAC stands under a live statute — the post-repeal framing is deleted [AUDIT CORRECTION 31 Oct 2026; the 11.5-11.10 checker's contrary repeal-effective claim was overruled on the Justia 2025 annotation] — that Verify item is now closed: no re-promulgation is needed because §26-2C-40 was never repealed.

Licence / categoryMature-plant limitSource / note

Producer, Level 22,001–6,00016.8.8.9(B)(2)
Producer, Level 36,001–12,000Run 1 anchor; 16.8.8.9(B)(3) — tier table not fully reproduced in this part, Verify against current 16.8.8.9

  • "Mature" defined (16.8.8.8(B)). A mature cannabis plant is a female cannabis plant in the flowering stage. The plant growth cycle in 16.8.8.8(A) has four stages (the stage names were not fully reproduced in this part — Verify if stage definitions matter to a counting dispute).
  • Tier placement (16.8.8.9(A)). For licences issued on or after 15 August 2021, CCD designates Level 1–4 based on: (1) the applicant's requested level; (2) demonstration of a legal right to use the quantity of water needed for that level under the applicant's cultivation plan; (3) if applicable, whether the applicant's reported mature plants harvested in the preceding six months were at least 80% of its authorised count; (4) if applicable, whether total sales were at least 75% of reported production in the preceding six months; and (5) the applicant's social-equity plan (race, ethnicity, gender, age, residential status of licensee/controlling persons/employees, and whether the applicant, controlling persons, employees or production locations are in an underserved rural community, including tribal, acequia, land grant-merced, federally designated opportunity zone, or other rural historic communities).
  • Plant-count increases (16.8.8.10). A licensee may request an increase in mature plants at renewal, supported by current inventory of mature plants and harvested cannabis, plants harvested in the preceding three months, and medical/commercial sales in the preceding three months, among other factors. CCD may deny for incomplete information, for violating the Act / Compassionate Use Act / CCD rules, including exceeding the authorised count in the prior three-month period, for pending/final enforcement action, for a medical shortage in the most recent six months (statewide or in underserved regions), or if the cultivation plan (including water access/usage) does not meet licensure requirements. An increase is also an amended-licence event for a producer (16.8.2.23(A)(3)–(4): any increase or decrease in plant count requires prior amended-licence approval).
  • No canopy limit stated. No square-footage canopy cap for producers was found in 16.8.8 NMAC or §26-2C-40 as summarised for this part. If a local ordinance imposes a canopy or premises-size limit, that is a local rule, not a CCD plant-limit rule — Verify locally.
  • Per-plant fees (Run 1 anchor, for context only). Producer fees include a per-plant element (secondary summaries cite $5 per adult-use plant / $2.50 per medical plant up to 8,000 plants in older fee summaries); the current 16.8.11 NMAC per-plant fee schedule was not re-verified for this part and no per-plant figure is relied on here. See Verify register.
  • Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0008.html and https://nmsrca-cf.rtscustomer.com/nmac/nmregister/xxxiii/16.8.8amend.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.3.2 Indoor / outdoor / greenhouse — what the rules actually regulate

New Mexico does not prohibit any of indoor, outdoor or greenhouse cultivation, and does not assign different plant counts to indoor vs. outdoor. What differs is the water right and the security / visibility treatment:

  • Water right by setting (16.8.2.22(A)(5)(b)). OSE documentation must show a valid and existing water right, or a permit to develop one, "for irrigation purposes for outdoor cultivation, or a commercial purpose for indoor cultivation at the proposed place of use". Greenhouse cultivation is treated in security rules as an outdoor-area analogue (see below); its water-purpose classification (irrigation vs. commercial) at a given premises is an OSE determination — Verify for a specific greenhouse, do not assume.
  • Security / visibility (16.8.2.10, full text in §11.4). All cultivation phases must occur in a designated limited-access area where cannabis is not visible from a public place without binoculars, aircraft or other optical aids (reasonably identifiable = visible). Outdoor areas and greenhouses must additionally have a perimeter security fence preventing unauthorised entry, 12"×12" limited-access signs, and a cover that obscures cultivation areas from ready view outside the fenced area (16.8.2.10(N); the 2021 rule text also describes fencing/gates at least 6 feet high and obscure, or with a cover obscuring all limited-access areas — the current (N) wording controls; the 6-foot figure is retained here only as the earlier formulation, Verify against current (N) if fence height is disputed).
  • Cultivation plan. A producer applicant must certify it will adhere to production requirements including creating and maintaining a cultivation plan and cannabis waste procedures (16.8.2.22(A)(12)), and must state the initial number of mature and immature plants proposed and the amount of water planned monthly for a 12-month period (16.8.2.22(A)(11)). A manufacturer applicant has parallel manufacturing-plan requirements.
  • Pesticide, waste, energy and water rules for cultivation are in §11.5 and §11.6, not repeated here.
  • No CCD rule found in this part prescribing indoor lighting hours, outdoor seasonality, greenhouse glazing, odour control, or setbacks beyond the §26-2C-12 local buffer ceiling (Run 1) and local zoning/building/fire compliance (16.8.2.8(A)). Odour, lighting and noise controls, if any, are local — Verify locally.
