Secondary corroboration: https://trianglehemp.com/new-mexico-home-grow-laws/ and https://www.howweedgrow.com/nm-legal-weed-grow/ — accessed 31 October 2026 (secondary; publication dates March 2026 and 29 October 2026 respectively).
  • PPL / non-profit sources (secondary reproduction of 7.34.4.8): https://www.casemine.com/regulation/us/64e49ca2e213e0035c66988d and https://newmexicostatecannabis.org/licensing/producer — accessed 31 October 2026. Both are secondary for the PPL figures.
  • Personal production is not a CCD commercial licence. A home grower needs no CCD producer licence; a medical patient who wants to grow beyond the adult-use limits, or to rely on a PPL, needs a DOH determination, not a CCD producer tier. Conversely, a CCD producer licence does not authorise growing at a private residence outside the licensed premises.

11.4 Security: cameras, alarms, storage, transport, courier vehicles

11.4.1 Limited-access areas — the umbrella rule (16.8.2.10, introductory text)

"All phases where cannabis or cannabis products are cultivated, stored or held, weighed, packaged, manufactured, disposed or wasted, all point-of-sale areas, and any room or area storing a digital video surveillance system storage device shall take place in a designated limited-access area where cannabis and cannabis products are not visible from a public place without the use of binoculars, aircraft, or other optical aids. For purposes of this rule, cannabis or cannabis products are not visible if it cannot be reasonably identified."

11.4.2 Alarms (16.8.2.10(A)–(C))

  • Operational security alarm system at each premises, continuously monitored (electronically, by a monitoring company, or other CCD-adequate means), alerting designated employees and, if necessary, law enforcement within 5 minutes of an alarm or system failure, by telephone, email or text message. Monitored sensors on all perimeter entry points and perimeter windows, if applicable. Audible alarm capable of being disarmed remotely by the designated employee or the security company.
  • Licensee must maintain and make available to CCD on request a description of the security system location and operation, including central-control location, a schematic of security zones, and the name of the alarm/monitoring company, if applicable.
  • Monthly maintenance inspection; all necessary repairs. If a failure due to loss of electrical power or mechanical malfunction is expected to exceed 8 hours, the licensee must immediately notify CCD within 48 hours of discovering the failure and provide alternative security, which may include closure. All security equipment must be maintained in a secure location to prevent theft, loss, destruction and alteration.
  • Documentation of all maintenance inspections, servicing, alterations and upgrades retained at least 12 months and available during a CCD inspection.

11.4.3 Cameras / digital video surveillance (16.8.2.10(D)–(G))

  • System at each premises, minimum camera resolution 1,280 × 720 pixels; at all times able to effectively and clearly record the area under surveillance; each camera permanently mounted in a fixed location, placed to clearly record activity in required areas and to provide clear and certain identification of any person and activities in those areas.
  • Areas that must be recorded (E): (1) areas where cannabis/products are cultivated, produced, manufactured, weighed, packed, stored, loaded and unloaded for transportation, prepared, or moved within the premises; (2) limited-access areas; (3) areas storing a digital video surveillance-system storage device; (4) entrances and exits; (5) all point-of-sale locations, to capture sale transactions.
  • Recording (F): cameras record continuously 24 hours per day, or may be motion-activated, at a minimum of 15 frames per second. Storage media/devices secured against tampering or theft. Recordings kept minimum 30 days; recordings of theft or security incidents (16.8.2.8, subsection on incident reporting — cited as Subsection N in the rule text as opened; the incident-reporting subsection in the current 16.8.2.8 text is the "Reporting of theft or security incident" paragraph — confirmed by this audit as 16.8.2.8(M); (N) is non-transferability ) kept minimum 12 months. Recordings subject to CCD inspection, kept so CCD can view and obtain copies at the premises immediately on request; on request, copies sent/provided to CCD within 48 hours. Recorded images must clearly and accurately display time and date; time measured per U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology standards.
  • Failure (G). The system must have a failure-notification system notifying the licensee of any interruption/failure of the system or storage device. A failure must be reported to CCD immediately and operations must cease as soon as safely possible until the system is again operational.
  • Multiple licensees, one premises (H). A single security / surveillance system covering the entire premises may be shared if: each licensee's premises diagram shows alarm and camera locations and recording storage; each application certifies all licensees are individually responsible for operation, maintenance and record-keeping and all have live-monitoring access; each application explains sharing with CCD/authorities, who maintains the systems, who may monitor footage, and who stores recordings; each licensee has immediate access to recordings to produce them under (F); and each licensee is held responsible for any violation of the security/surveillance requirements.

11.4.4 Locks, access, badges, lighting, doors/windows, fencing, guards, vault (16.8.2.10(I)–(P))

  • Locks (I). Limited-access areas must be securely lockable with commercial-grade locks meeting applicable building and fire codes; commercial-grade locks meeting building/fire codes also on all points of entry/exit to the premises and access points to storage areas.
  • Limited-access access (J). Only the licensee and its authorised employees, authorised vendors, contractors or other individuals conducting business requiring access, CCD staff/designees, state/local law enforcement within lawful jurisdiction, fire departments and emergency medical services in official capacity, or volunteers specifically permitted by the establishment. Licensee must ensure: only authorised employees/individuals have access; a daily record log (which may be a sign-in/sign-out sheet at the entrance) of all authorised employees and non-employee authorised individuals entering limited-access areas is maintained; logs kept minimum 90 days, or 12 months if a theft/security incident occurs, and made available to CCD within 48 hours on request; entrances to limited-access areas have a solid door (or adequate gate), a lock meeting (I), and — unless prohibited by building/fire codes — remain locked when not in use during regular business hours; every limited-access area identified by a sign minimum 12" × 12" stating "Do Not Enter - Limited Access Area - Access Limited to Authorized Personnel Only" in lettering no smaller than 1 inch in height; authorised employees visibly display an employee identification badge at all times in a limited-access area; other authorised individuals obtain and visibly display a visitor badge at all times in a limited-access area and return it on exit.
  • Employee badge (K). Licensee must issue a laminated or plastic-coated identification badge to all agents, officers or other persons acting for or employed by the licensee, including at minimum: the licensee's "doing business as" name and licence number, the individual's first name, an employee number exclusively assigned to that employee, and a colour photograph clearly showing the full front of the employee's face, at least 1 inch wide and 1.5 inches high.
  • Lighting (L). Any perimeter entry point must have lighting sufficient for observers to see, and cameras to record, any activity within 20 feet of the gate or entry; motion-detection lighting may be used in low-light conditions.
  • Doors/windows (M). All external entrances to indoor facilities must be lockable; all perimeter doors and windows of indoor facilities must be in good condition and lockable.
  • Outdoor / greenhouse fencing (N). See §11.3.2: perimeter security fence preventing unauthorised entry to cultivation areas, 12"×12" limited-access signs as above, and a cover obscuring cultivation areas from ready view outside the fenced area.
  • Guards (O). Security guards are permitted but not required. Contract guards must be licensed under the Private Investigations Act, §§61-27B-1 et seq. NMSA 1978. Guards must not consume cannabis/products or be intoxicated while performing duties for a licensee, and must comply with all firearms/weapons laws.
  • Vault (P). Licensees may (not must) store all non-growing cannabis, cannabis products or cash not being actively handled for cultivating, packaging, processing, transporting or selling within an adequately sized vault. No vault size, rating or mandatory-vault rule is stated in (P) as opened — Verify before treating a vault as mandatory for any licence type.
  • Theft / security incident reporting (16.8.2.8, incident paragraph). Licensees must submit written notification to CCD of any attempted theft, theft, assault of employees/patrons, robbery or attempted robbery, break-in, or security breach on the premises, no later than 24 hours after first becoming aware, including a description of property stolen/destroyed and quantity of plants/products stolen, with a copy of the police report, video footage and any other supporting evidence CCD requests. The premises must be secured before continuing operations, including replacement of locks, doors, windows and repair of damaged structures/access points with comparable or more secure material.
  • Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-10-NMAC and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-8-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.4.5 Storage (general)

Beyond the vault permission and limited-access storage, 16.8.2.8 and 16.8.7 impose: storage/transport conditions that maintain and protect cannabis/products against physical, chemical and microbial contamination and deterioration of product and container (16.8.2.13(A)(16)); segregation of batches awaiting test results (§11.1.3); secured designated holding area for product intended for wasting, minimum 72 hours (§11.5); and, for failed product, proper labelling and storage so it cannot be transferred for sale (§11.1.4). No general temperature, humidity or shelf-life storage rule for finished product was found in 16.8.2/16.8.7 for this part — Verify against 16.8.3 (packaging) and any food-safety rules for edibles/topicals (Run 1 §1.6 cross-reference).

11.4.6 Transport between licensees (16.8.2.13)

  • Who: only persons holding a cannabis establishment licence, or designated employees or contractors of a licensee.
  • Paperwork before movement: completed transfer/sales invoice or receipt and chain-of-custody form; only product listed on them may be transported; neither may be altered/changed once transport begins. A shipping manifest must be generated through the track-and-trace system (now NMS2S; BioTrack in the 2021 rule text) before transporting for (1) testing/sampling, (2) sale to a licensee, (3) destruction/wastage/disposal, or (4) any other activity required by CCD or another government authority; transmitted to CCD and (if applicable) the receiving licensee via the online track-and-trace portal before transport. If the transporting licensee cannot access the system, it completes the manifest outside the system and promptly transmits it by email to CCD and the receiving licensee; if the receiver lacks access, the transporter completes it in the system, transmits to CCD, and emails a copy to the receiver. A manifest and chain-of-custody form must accompany every transport. A manifest must not be voided or changed after departing the originating premises. The transporting licensee is responsible for any discrepancy between manifest and product in its possession during transport.
  • Vehicle and load: only inside a motor vehicle or trailer in reasonable operating condition; product must not be visible or identifiable from outside; locked in a box, container or cage secured inside the vehicle/trailer (including inside the trunk); vehicles/trailers locked and secured while unattended; must not be left unattended in a residential area; vehicle alarm system required; packages/containers must not be tampered with or opened during transport; no alcoholic beverages may be transported with cannabis/products under any circumstances; vehicle properly registered with the New Mexico Motor Vehicle Division; driver prepared to show employee badge, driver's licence, vehicle registration, proof of insurance, shipping manifest and chain-of-custody form to law enforcement and CCD on request. Vehicles/trailers are subject to CCD inspection at any licensed premises or during transport at any time.
  • Route discipline: when transporting, the licensee must only travel between licensees shipping/receiving product and its own licensed premises; multiple shipments may be transported at one time in accordance with applicable laws; no deviation except necessary rest, fuel or vehicle-repair stops. Human-powered or unmanned-vehicle transport is prohibited. Exception: transport by foot, hand truck, forklift or similar means is permitted if it is not operationally feasible to use a vehicle/trailer because the sending and receiving premises are in the same building or on the same premises.
  • Rejection: a licensee must not take into possession or transport product not on the manifest, or in a lesser/greater amount than the manifest (except marginal weight difference due to curing during transport).
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-13-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.4.7 Courier vehicles and delivery (16.8.2.41; cross-reference to Run 1 §1.6 for delivery limits)

Courier rules sit on top of §11.4.6, with delivery-specific additions:

  • Licence required. Unless licensed under the Cannabis Regulation Act and CCD rules, a person must not transport cannabis products directly to qualified patients, primary caregivers, reciprocal participants, or directly to consumers — 16.8.2.41(B).
  • Who may receive delivery: a qualified patient at least 18, a primary caregiver, a reciprocal participant, or a consumer at least 21 — 16.8.2.41(C)(1). Delivery only to the person identified by the retail licensee as the intended, authorised recipient (C)(2), and only of cannabis/products (and non-THC products for sale at that retail establishment) from the retail establishment from which the sale/delivery is initiated (C)(3).
  • Operational requirements (D), in outline: all delivered product must be obtained from a retail licensee with which the courier is employed or has a delivery agreement; all delivery agreements must be disclosed to CCD, with written notice of a new or modified agreement before delivery under it; a courier must not possess a delivery package for more than 24 hours and must return undelivered product to the originating retailer within that period; a delivery vehicle must not advertise or display signage, logos or symbols indicating it is used for cannabis transport (D)(8) — the opposite of branding: courier vehicles are unmarked as a matter of rule; only shelf-stable products (and non-THC retail products) may be delivered — perishable or time/temperature-controlled products may not be delivered (D)(9).
  • Maximum retail value in a courier vehicle: $10,000 at any one time in the rule text as opened, each product associated with a specific delivery order. Conflict/Verify: a CCD notice of proposed rulemaking (hearing 3 September 2025) proposed reducing that maximum to $5,000, clarifying that delivery is only by licensed couriers exclusively to residential addresses, and identifying approved payment sources as any legal method including gift-card pre-payments but excluding Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards. Whether the $5,000 reduction or the residential-address clarification was adopted is Verify — the $10,000 figure is the rule text as opened, the $5,000 figure is a proposal, and neither may be presented as the other.
  • Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.41 — accessed 31 October 2026; proposal notice: https://www.rld.nm.gov/2025/07/29/ccd-notice-of-proposed-rulemaking-september-3-2025/ — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Prepayment / payment at delivery. Secondary summaries state orders fulfilled through a courier must be prepaid and couriers may not collect payment at delivery. That prepayment rule was not verified in the 16.8.2.41 text opened for this part — Verify before relying on it. The 2025 proposal's payment-source clarification (above) is likewise a proposal, not adopted law as stated here.
  • Courier fee anchor (Run 1). Courier licence $250 per year (16.8.11 NMAC; §26-2C-9(A)(1) caps the courier fee at $1,500 per year plus up to $1,000 per additional premises — the rule fee and the statutory cap differ; the Run 1 $250 figure is the fee in 16.8.11 NMAC as amended 7 May 2024).

11.5 Waste disposal (16.8.2.15)

"Licensees that waste cannabis or cannabis products shall do so by rendering the cannabis or cannabis products unusable and unrecognizable prior to removal from licensed premises. The wastage of cannabis or cannabis products shall be documented, tracked by batch, and recorded in an electronic track and trace system specified by the division. Wastage of cannabis or cannabis products shall occur only within the licensee's ordinary business hours. Licensees shall dispose of wasted cannabis or cannabis products and shall not attempt to incorporate wasted cannabis or cannabis plants into any product intended for human consumption." — 16.8.2.15, introductory text (adopted 24 August 2021).

  • Permitted method (A). Wastage must be accomplished by grinding and incorporating the cannabis into other ground material, such as soil, compost material, or leaf and yard waste, so that the resulting mixture is at least 50% non-cannabis material by volume.
  • Disposal law (B). Disposal of wasted cannabis/plants must be conducted in accordance with all applicable waste-disposal laws, including hazardous-waste disposal laws. Wasted cannabis constitutes "solid waste" for disposal purposes (as carried in local codifications of the rule).
  • Holding time (C). Cannabis/products a licensee intends to waste must be held in a secured designated holding area for a minimum of 72 hours before being wasted, and must not be handled, moved or wasted during that 72-hour period unless by specific instruction of CCD (enforcement summary of the same rule).
  • Documentation and retention (D). The licensee must record wastage including batch number, weight, plant number, name of the receiving solid-waste facility, dates of wastage and disposal, and any test results associated with a wasted batch, using an electronic system specified by CCD, and must deduct wasted usable cannabis/plants from inventory. The electronic record must be retained for no less than two years following disposal. The licensee must additionally document wastage using a video recording and retain the video recording of destruction for no less than 120 days, making it available for CCD inspection and copying on request.
  • Notice (E). The licensee must notify CCD of wastage within five business days of the wastage. (Contrast the 24-hour failed-product notice formulation in §11.1.4 — both figures are stated in this dossier with their sources; the relationship between them is Verify.)
  • Waste transport. Transport for destruction/wastage/disposal requires a track-and-trace shipping manifest (16.8.2.13(B)(3)) and follows the §11.4.6 vehicle/paperwork rules.
  • Hemp waste. Hemp waste under NMED's 20.10.2 NMAC and NMDA's hemp programme is a separate regime (Run 1 hemp sections; NMED hemp rule effective 28 January 2026). No hemp-specific wastage method is stated in this Part 11 cannabis section — Verify against 20.10.2 NMAC before applying the 50% / 72-hour cannabis rules to hemp.
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.15 — accessed 31 October 2026; SRCA text: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.6 Environmental: water rights + proof-of-water (with OSE enforcement), pesticide limits, energy

11.6.1 Water — the proof-of-water rule (statute + rule, verbatim in substance)

Statute (§26-2C-7(A)(3), as amended 2024, effective 1 July 2024):

"if a cannabis producer or cannabis producer microbusiness, require as a condition of licensing that the applicant demonstrate that the applicant has a legal right to a commercial water supply, water rights or other source of water sufficient to meet the water needs as determined by the division related to the license as evidenced by documentation from the office of the state engineer of a valid water right or from a water provider that the use of water for cannabis production is compliant with that water provider's rules"

The 2024 amendment clarified that this condition applies only to cannabis producers and cannabis producer microbusinesses (the pre-2024 text had extended the energy/water plan to manufacturers; the water-proof condition itself is producer/microbusiness-only in the current statute). The rule (16.8.2.22(A)(5)) implements it for initial and renewal producer applications:

"demonstration of a legal right to use the quantity of water that the division determines is needed for cannabis production, as evidenced by either: (a) documentation from a water provider that the applicant has the right to use water from the provider and that the use of water from cannabis production is compliant with provider's rules, or (b) documentation from the office of the state engineer showing that the applicant has a valid and existing water right, or a permit to develop a water right, for irrigation purposes for outdoor cultivation, or a commercial purpose for indoor cultivation at the proposed place of use of the cannabis establishment."

OSE-acceptable documentation under (b) includes: (i) an OSE permit or licence in good standing, not including a permit issued under §§72-12-1, -1.1, -1.2 or -1.3 NMSA 1978 (the domestic-well statutes — a domestic well permit alone does not prove a commercial cannabis water right); (ii) a subfile order or decree issued by a water-rights adjudication court; (iii) findings of an OSE hydrographic survey; or (iv) other documentation OSE has deemed in writing as acceptable to OSE under the rule.

  • Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-7/ and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.22 — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.6.2 OSE enforcement / validation — how it works in practice

OSE's Commercial Cannabis Growing Water Use FAQs (version valid as of 10 July 2025) state the operational split:

  • Municipal water (e.g. City of Albuquerque, Las Cruces, Santa Fe): the applicant does not go to OSE; RLD/CCD reviews and validates this source.
  • Privately owned water right: the applicant is instructed to go to OSE to validate the right and determine if it is configured correctly for the proposed use and place of use. The water right must be in the applicant's name, or the applicant must have a lease or user agreement in place and provide copies to OSE with the Water Rights Accession Form. Incomplete forms or missing documents delay review; appointments with the appropriate OSE District Office are highly recommended. A water-right permit or change of ownership must be accomplished before submitting the Accession Form for verification.
  • What does not count: irrigation rights are required for outdoor cultivation, commercial rights for indoor cultivation; a producer must acquire valid rights and, where needed, transfer them into an existing well with an OSE permit; all permit approvals require meter installation and reporting; rainwater captured via rooftop catchment, while allowed, is NOT a valid water right and will not suffice as proof.
  • Water hauling — 1-year bridge only (Run 1 anchor, confirmed by OSE). OSE states: "The 1 year time frame for water hauling is a 'bridge' year to give users time to find a valid water right or water source." A hauler arrangement requires documentation from the provider that it will serve the applicant, stating the source of water the hauler is using, and the hauler itself must have legal access to that water. Hauling is not a permanent proof-of-water.
  • Backlog (context, not a rule). OSE's FAQ notes over 500 non-cannabis water applications backlogged statewide with an average wait of eight to ten months (July 2025 version). That wait affects OSE validation timelines; it does not waive the proof requirement.
  • Change triggers. A change in water source, or in the water/energy conservation plan including reuse of water and disposal of effluent, is an amended-licence event for a producer (16.8.2.23(A)(2)); a change in access to the water source, or a 10%+ increase in water usage, is a material/substantial change (16.8.2.23(D)(3)).
  • General compliance overlay. 16.8.2.8(A) requires compliance with all applicable state/local laws governing water use and quality, water supply, wastewater discharge, environmental impacts and natural-resource protection, among others. Producer applicants must also certify adherence to laws governing protection of public health and the environment, including occupational health and safety, food safety, environmental impacts, natural-resource protections, air quality, solid/hazardous waste management and wastewater (producer application attestations).
  • Sources: https://www.ose.nm.gov/WR/cannabis.php and https://api.realfile.rtsclients.com/PublicFiles/5f809ddfc9864dad89f9d03375144a14/f9872ec4-f50d-46fd-adf0-6a34392be86a/OSE Cannabis FAQv10071025.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026; checklist: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/CCD-Producer-Application-Checklist1.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.6.3 Pesticide limits — NMDA registration is the gate, Table 5 is the test

  • Only NMDA-registered-for-cannabis pesticides may be used. The New Mexico Pesticide Control Act prohibits use of any pesticide product on Cannabis sp. (both high-THC cultivars, total THC > 0.3%, and low-THC cultivars, total THC ≤ 0.3%) that has not been reviewed and registered by NMDA. NMDA states pesticides not on its Cannabis sp. list are not legal for use in Cannabis sp. production in New Mexico. The list is organised by brand name (products, not active ingredients, are reviewed/registered), is updated quarterly, and includes 25(b) minimum-risk products — which, although exempt from federal registration, must still be NMDA-registered and approved before use on Cannabis sp. Producer use of listed pesticides is at the producer's total responsibility; the list is not an endorsement.
  • Sources: https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/media/pdf/NMDA-registered-pesticides.pdf (NMDA, July 2026) and https://nmdeptag.nmsu.edu/aes/hemp/cannabis-registered-pesticides-and-growth-regulators.html — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • CCD notice of the registry. CCD Industry Bulletin 25-16 (20 October 2025) notified licensees that NMDA had issued an updated Cannabis Registered Pesticides and Growth Regulators Registry effective 1 August 2025, including new products and products marked "In D1" / "In D2" (first / second year of discontinuance in New Mexico — still available for purchase and use but may not be in future). NMDA Pesticide Compliance contact is given in the bulletin for registry questions (official public contact; no individual phone/email is reproduced here).
  • Testing enforcement. Table 5 action levels (§11.1.2) are the residue limits; use of an unregistered pesticide is separately a Pesticide Control Act violation (see the March 2024 malathion recall, §11.1.4, where CCD cited §76-4-5, Prohibited Acts). CCD alone or with NMDA may investigate suspected use of a pesticide not registered with NMDA for cannabis (16.8.7.15(J)(2)).
  • No pesticide quantity / application-rate limit is stated in this part beyond registration + residue action levels + label directions. Application must follow the product label and NMDA licensing/use requirements, which producer applicants certify they will adhere to. Verify the current NMDA list at the time of use — the July 2026 list is the latest found for this part, and quarterly updates may have superseded it by 31 October 2026 (see register).

11.6.4 Energy — a plan, not a consumption cap

  • Statute (§26-2C-7(A)(4)). For any type of cannabis producer or manufacturer licence (wording varies between the statute summary and the 2024/2025 bill texts — see Verify note), CCD must require the applicant to submit a plan to use, or demonstrate that it cannot feasibly use, energy or water reduction opportunities, including: (a) for a cannabis producer, drip irrigation and water collection; (b) natural lighting and energy efficiency measures; and (c) renewable energy generation.
  • Rule (16.8.2.22(A)(6)). A producer initial/renewal application must include "a plan to use, or certification that the applicant cannot feasibly use, energy and water reduction opportunities, including: (a) drip irrigation and water collection; (b) natural lighting and energy efficiency measures; (c) renewable energy generation; and (d) estimated water and energy use related to the applicant's cultivation plan". The applicant must also state monthly water use planned for a 12-month period (16.8.2.22(A)(11)).
  • No CCD energy-consumption cap, renewable-energy percentage mandate, or carbon rule was found in 16.8.2 or §26-2C-7 for this part. The requirement is to plan or certify infeasibility and to estimate use — not to meet a numeric energy target. Verify: whether the (A)(4) plan duty currently extends to manufacturers as well as producers (the 2024 amendment narrowed the water-proof duty to producers/microbusinesses; the energy-plan scope in the current statute text as summarised in 2025 bill text reads "for [any type of] a cannabis producer [or manufacturer license]" with bracketed deletions suggesting narrowing — the current §26-2C-7(A)(4) text must be checked on NMOneSource before advising a manufacturer).
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/N-M-Admin-Code-SS-16.8.2.22 — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.6.5 Other environmental overlays (brief, cross-reference only)

Wastewater discharge, hazardous materials, air quality, solid/hazardous waste management and food safety are compliance overlays under 16.8.2.8(A) and producer attestations, enforced by the relevant agency (NMED, NMDA, local jurisdiction) rather than by a cannabis-specific numeric standard in Part 11. No cannabis-specific wastewater discharge limit, odour limit or energy-benchmark figure is stated in this part. Hemp environmental rules are under NMED 20.10.2 NMAC (Run 1 hemp sections), not under 16.8.2.

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts, promotions

This is the thinnest area of Part 11 on official sources, and the dossier states that plainly rather than filling it with business practice.

11.7.1 What the rules do say

  • Testing samples are not retail samples. Sampling for testing is governed by §11.1.3 (laboratory collection, chain of custody, manifest). A testing sample is not a consumer giveaway, and a laboratory sample must not be diverted to sale or gift.
  • Advertising / marketing / commercial display (Run 1 §1.6 cross-reference). Packaging, labelling, advertising, marketing and commercial-display requirements are in 16.8.3 NMAC. Any promotion, discount advertisement or "free" claim must comply with 16.8.3 and with the Cannabis Regulation Act's advertising restrictions (including not targeting persons under 21). Part 11 does not reproduce 16.8.3; Run 1 §1.6 is the place to check the advertising rules before running a promotion. A promotion that advertises a product must still be for product that has passed all required testing (§11.1.1).
  • Delivery promotions are subject to the courier rules in §11.4.7 (residential-address / value-cap Verify items) and to Run 1 §1.6 delivery rules.
  • No "free cannabis" rule found in 16.8.2 or 16.8.3 in the searches for this part. In particular, no rule text was found stating a $0.01 minimum sale price, a ban on giveaways, or a ban on employee samples.

11.7.2 What is NOT law (secondary practice, flagged)

  • A licensee's internal employee policy (Elevated Labs, "Free Cannabis & Employee Samples", last updated 2024, citing NMAC 16.8.2.15 — which is the wastage rule, not a sampling rule) states: "Free cannabis or cannabis samples shall not be provided to any individuals, patients or otherwise, including vendors or employees… No cannabis may be given away, for any reason and must at minimum be sold for one (1) cent" and "Display products may not be given away… or otherwise sold, even at a discount. These products are considered no longer safe for consumption." That is one business's policy document, not a CCD rule, and its NMAC citation does not support the $0.01 proposition. It is recorded here only so it is not mistaken for law.
  • Source (secondary, business policy — not official): https://elevated-labs.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/1.11-Free-Cannabis-and-Employee-Samples-copy.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Discounts. No CCD discount cap, discount frequency limit, loyalty-programme rule, or "buy-one-get-one" rule was found for this part. Discounting is therefore Unavailable as a CCD operations rule in this dossier: a retailer discount is constrained, if at all, by tax (excise tax is on price — see Run 1 tax sections), by 16.8.3 advertising truthfulness, and by the possession/purchase limits in Run 1 §1.6, not by a discount rule stated here. Verify against current 16.8.3 before running a discount promotion.
  • Sampling at retail / consumption areas. No rule authorising or prohibiting in-store sampling, "tasting" or promotional distribution at a consumption area was found in 16.8.2 or 16.8.10 for this part. Consumption on licensed premises is prohibited unless a consumption area has been approved (16.8.2.8(D)); server-permit rules (§11.8.3) govern who may serve in an approved consumption area, not whether a sample may be free. Verify against 16.8.3 and the consumption-area licence sections before offering any sample.
  • Vendor samples. No vendor-sample rule (quantity, tracking, tax) was found. Any product moving to a vendor/employee/consumer must move through licensed channels, track-and-trace, and testing — a "sample" outside those channels is an unlicensed transfer, not a sampling exception.

Bottom line for §11.7: on official sources, Part 11 can confirm only that testing samples are laboratory-controlled, that promotions must comply with 16.8.3 advertising rules (Run 1 §1.6), and that no giveaway/discount/sampling rule was found. Everything else in this section is Verify/Unavailable, not a permission.

11.8 Drug testing, background checks, worker permit rules for licence holders and staff

11.8.1 Age — the universal worker rule

  • All applicants for licensure, including controlling persons, must be at least 21. All employees of a commercial cannabis establishment must be at least 21 — 16.8.2.8(C). There is no separate lower age for non-serving staff in the rule as opened. (Medical patients may be 18+ for purchase; that is a patient rule, not a worker rule — see §11.4.7 for the courier-delivery age split: patient 18+ / consumer 21+.)
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-8-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.8.2 Background checks — controlling persons only (not every employee), fingerprint-based, prior approval on change

Rule (16.8.2.9).

  • Initial licensure (A). Applicants for initial licensure must consent to and undergo a national criminal-history background check and a DPS statewide criminal-history screening background check. Checks are required for: (1) each partner of a limited partnership; (2) each member of a limited liability company; (3) each director, officer or trustee of a corporation or trust; and (4) any controlling person of the applicant.
  • Procedure (C, in outline). The applicant submits a background-screening request, fingerprints, and supporting documentation including an authorisation for release of information to CCD in accordance with DPS or its designated vendor's procedures; DPS (or its vendor) reviews state records and transmits fingerprints to the Federal Bureau of Investigation for a national screening; results are made available to CCD for review.
  • Fees (D). All applicable fees for the national and DPS checks are borne as provided in 16.8.2.9(D) (fee bearer/amount not reproduced in this part — Verify the current DPS fee schedule; do not state a dollar figure here).
  • Authorised change (B). See §11.2.2: amended application + background-check documentation, and each new member must be CCD-approved before assuming duties.
  • What background checks are NOT. No rule was found requiring fingerprint background checks for every employee (budtenders, trimmers, drivers, etc.). The check attaches to partners/members/directors/officers/trustees/controlling persons. Employer hiring checks for other staff are a matter of employer policy and general employment law, not a CCD worker-permit rule. Secondary summaries that state "all cannabis farm employees… must undergo a criminal history background check" overstate 16.8.2.9 as opened and are not adopted here.
  • Legislative history — do not present as law. House Bill 112 (57th Legislature, 1st Session, 2025), House Bill 226 and House Bill 128 (56th Legislature, 2nd Session, 2024) all proposed to codify state + federal criminal-history checks for controlling persons (fingerprints to DPS, forwarded to the FBI; name-based check if fingerprints twice unclassifiable; DPS compilation to CCD; CCD consideration of rehabilitation evidence, character references and educational achievements). Those bills are proposals; the rule that is current law for this dossier is 16.8.2.9 as above. Whether any 2025 bill was enacted is Verify — no enactment was confirmed for this part.
  • Sources: https://www.nmlegis.gov/sessions/25%20Regular/bills/house/HB0112CES.HTML — accessed 31 October 2026 (proposal); rule summary via the 16.8.2 text: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0002.html — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Criminal-history consequences / rehabilitation. Producer (and parallel) applications require a detailed description of any criminal convictions of the applicant and any controlling person (date, incarceration/probation/parole dates if applicable, offence description, statement of rehabilitation) and of any denial/suspension/revocation/surrender/discipline by another jurisdiction's cannabis licensing agency — 16.8.2.22(A)(8)–(10). No automatic disqualifying-offence list is stated in this part — Verify against current §26-2C-7 denial grounds and CCD practice before advising an applicant with a conviction history. Expungement is in Run 1 §1.2 (cross-reference only).

11.8.3 Cannabis server permits — consumption areas only (16.8.10 NMAC; §26-2C-11)

This is the only CCD worker permit in Part 11. It is not a general "cannabis worker card". New Mexico has no general state badge/card for regular dispensary or grow staff; staff identification is the employer-issued badge in §11.4.4(K).

  • Who needs one. A licensee approved to operate a cannabis consumption area, and all servers in it, must satisfactorily complete a programme every three years to obtain a server permit. No person may be employed as a server on a licensed consumption area unless that person obtains a server permit, except that a person not previously certified must obtain a server permit within 30 days of employment — 16.8.10.8(A); §26-2C-11(B) (same 30-day rule). A research laboratory or its employee is not required to obtain or possess a server permit while performing activities authorised under a research-laboratory licence — §26-2C-11(A).
  • Age. CCD issues server permits to persons 21 years of age or older who satisfy §26-2C-11 and CCD rules, on proof of satisfactory completion of a programme by a CCD-approved server-permit education provider — §26-2C-11(B).
  • Test pass mark. Satisfactory completion is determined by a score of 80% or higher on an approved test administered at the end of a classroom programme, or at the end of / after completion of a module for online programmes — 16.8.10.8(B).
  • Programme length / curriculum. The education programme curriculum is prescribed in §26-2C-11(C) (subjects include, in outline, cannabis law, responsible service, and related topics — full curriculum list not reproduced here, Verify against current §26-2C-11(C)). Secondary summaries describe the course as at least 4.5 hours; renewal requires proof of successful completion of up to 4.5 hours of continuing education and an examination as determined by CCD — §26-2C-11(E). The 4.5-hour figure for the initial programme is Verify against 16.8.10 (programme-approval sections), not stated as rule text here.
  • Validity and renewal. Server permits are valid for three years from issuance and may be renewed on proof of continuing education + examination as above — §26-2C-11(E); 16.8.10.8(A) (programme every three years).
  • Temporary permit. Temporary server permits are valid for 90 days from the date the exam is successfully completed — 16.8.10.8 (temporary-permit paragraph). CCD prepares and distributes server permits to the student within 90 days of satisfactory completion of a certified programme. The provider must submit a server-permit application for each passing student to CCD within 10 business days of satisfactory completion (name, personal identifier, address, date of birth, and other CCD-required information, on CCD forms, including electronically); an application received more than 10 business days after course completion subjects the provider to a $5 late fee per application. Permits are numbered sequentially.
  • Fee cap vs. actual fee (Run 1 anchor, retained). "The fee for the issuance of a cannabis server permit shall not exceed thirty-five dollars ($35.00)." — §26-2C-9(G). The actual fee charged is Verify per Run 1 — the $35 figure is a statutory cap, not a confirmed current fee. Course fees are set by providers (secondary), not by CCD, and are not stated here.
  • Replacement. Requests for replacement permits must be submitted in writing to CCD, by the server, on CCD forms, accompanied by a $10.00 replacement fee in a CCD-approved form — 16.8.10.8(F).
  • Child-support hold. If a student has a child-support hold placed by the Human Services Department, CCD must not issue a server permit until the hold is lifted — 16.8.10.8(B).
  • Property of the state; return. A server permit is the property of the state and must be immediately returned to CCD on suspension, revocation or denial of renewal — §26-2C-11(D).
  • Penalties for underage service (§26-2C-11(F)). In addition to other penalties: first offence of selling/serving/dispensing to a person under 21 — CCD may suspend the server permit for 30 days if the director finds the server guilty; further offences carry longer suspensions/revocation as provided in §26-2C-11(F) (full ladder not reproduced here — Verify against current §26-2C-11(F) before advising on a second offence). No person whose permit is suspended under §26-2C-11 may offer/sell/serve/dispense cannabis during suspension.
  • Provider approval. Education providers must be CCD-approved under 16.8.10 (provider application, curriculum approval, and related sections — provider requirements not detailed here, Verify against current 16.8.10 provider sections).
  • Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-10-8-NMAC; https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-11/; https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-9/; rule PDF: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title16/16.008.0010.pdf (16.8.10 NMAC, effective 12 July 2022) — all accessed 31 October 2026.

11.8.4 Training (all licence types) — 30 days, and food-handler training where applicable

  • Every licence type's policies-and-procedures section requires a CCD-approved training programme ensuring all personnel present at the premises receive information/training covering, at minimum, specified topics within 30 days of start of employment (testing laboratories: 16.8.2.47(B)(1); research laboratories: 16.8.2.61(B) — same 30-day formulation; producer/manufacturer/retailer/courier/consumption sections carry parallel training duties — section numbers vary by licence type, Verify the section for a specific licence type).
  • Food-handler course. A research-laboratory licensee or employee involved in handling, transportation, manufacture, extraction, testing or packaging of cannabis products must successfully complete a food-handler course accredited by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) before conducting any related activities, and maintain that training while employed under a research licensee — 16.8.2.61(C). Parallel food-handler duties apply in other licence types where food handling occurs (e.g. edibles manufacturing) — Verify the section for the specific licence type; the ANSI food-handler rule is confirmed here only for research laboratories.
  • Training documentation retention. Testing and research laboratories must maintain employee training documentation for two years (research: two years for current employees and at least six months after termination — 16.8.2.61; testing: two-year formulation in 16.8.2.47(B) as summarised — Verify the testing retention sentence against current 16.8.2.47).

11.8.5 Drug testing of workers — no CCD mandate found; general employment law applies

  • No CCD rule was found in 16.8.2, 16.8.10 or the Cannabis Regulation Act requiring licence holders or staff to undergo drug testing (pre-employment, random, post-accident or reasonable-suspicion) as a condition of a CCD licence or server permit. The server-permit test in §11.8.3 is a knowledge examination (80% pass), not a drug test.
  • General New Mexico employment position (secondary, for context only — not a CCD rule). New Mexico has no general drug-testing statute regulating private-employer drug testing (Baker Donelson New Mexico labour guide, summarising NMSA law); private employers may implement written, consistently applied testing policies (pre-employment after conditional offer, random for safety-sensitive roles, post-accident, reasonable suspicion), subject to federal DOT rules for regulated drivers and to medical-cannabis protections/limits in the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act and the Human Rights Act as interpreted by the courts (notably Garcia v. Tractor Supply Co., 154 F. Supp. 3d 1225 (D.N.M. 2016), holding an employer is not required to accommodate medical cannabis use — case law that subsequent commentary describes as creating inconsistencies, not a settled accommodation rule). Employment protections are in Run 1 §1.8 (cross-reference only).
  • Proposed, not law. House Bill 230 (2025) would have provided that an employee who is a qualified patient is not considered impaired solely because of cannabis metabolites, prohibited random cannabis drug testing for such employees, and permitted cannabis drug testing only on reasonable suspicion of impairment at work, after an accident involving another person, or after significant property damage, with medical-review-officer review. HB 230 was not confirmed as enacted for this part and must not be presented as current law.
  • Sources (secondary for general employment law; proposal for HB 230): https://www.bakerdonelson.com/webfiles/EZGuide/NewMexicoLEEasyGuide.pdf and https://legiscan.com/NM/supplement/HB230/id/512492/NewMexico-2025-HB230-FiscalNote.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Workplace conduct rules that are CCD rules (not drug tests). Licensees must prohibit consumption on licensed premises except in an approved consumption area (16.8.2.8(D)); security guards must not consume cannabis or be intoxicated while on duty (16.8.2.10(O)); and licence-type policies must address employee health and safety and drug/alcohol policies as part of the 30-day training programme (§11.8.4). Those are conduct rules, not testing mandates.

11.8.6 Hemp worker rules (brief)

Hemp production workers are under NMDA's hemp programme and NMED's 20.10.2 NMAC (manufacturing), not CCD server permits or CCD background checks. No hemp-specific worker permit, background-check or drug-testing rule is stated in this part — Verify against NMDA/NMED hemp rules before advising a hemp employer. The NMSU hemp-research rule (§11.9.3) requires a NMDA licence in the principal investigator's control before possession of viable seed/plants/cuttings, which is a research-licence rule, not a worker-permit rule.

11.9 Research / university licences (NMSU, UNM)

11.9.1 CCD cannabis research laboratory licences — Tiers I–III (16.8.2.56–16.8.2.63)

  • Definition (§26-2C-2(K)). "Cannabis research laboratory" means a facility that produces or possesses cannabis products and all parts of the plant genus Cannabis for the purpose of studying cannabis cultivation, characteristics or uses.
  • Tiers (16.8.2.56(A), effective 12 July 2022):
  • Tier I: may produce cannabis to be ingested by human or animal subjects, or produce cannabis not meant for ingestion, for division-approved clinical, agricultural or market research studies; produce federally legal cannabis products; and conduct division-approved clinical, agricultural or market research studies.
  • Tier II: may produce cannabis not meant for ingestion, or purchase cannabis to be ingested by human or animal subjects, for division-approved clinical, agricultural or market research studies; and conduct division-approved studies. (Tier II does not produce federally legal cannabis products as Tier I does, and does not produce ingestible cannabis — it purchases ingestible cannabis.)
  • Tier III: may not produce cannabis and may only purchase cannabis or cannabis products from licensed research laboratories Tier I and Tier II, as appropriate for approved clinical, agricultural or market research studies; and conduct division-approved studies.
  • Fee (Run 1 anchor, confirmed in statute). Research-laboratory licence $2,500 per year plus $1,000 per year for each additional licensed premises — §26-2C-9(A)(6); research application form states "Annual Licensing Fee: $2,500.00".
  • What a research laboratory is not. A research laboratory does not test cannabis for wholesale or retail use — that function belongs exclusively to a testing laboratory (§11.1.5). Conversely, a testing laboratory does not produce/possess cannabis for study. A research laboratory (unlike any other establishment) may hold an interest in a testing laboratory (§11.1.5 independence exception).
  • Server-permit exemption. A research laboratory or its employee need not obtain/possess a server permit while performing authorised research-laboratory activities (§26-2C-11(A)).
  • Policies and training (16.8.2.61). Minimum policies must include research criteria and procedures consistent with the Act, Compassionate Use Act and CCD rules, including protocols for research, recordkeeping and chain-of-custody protocols for transportation, and procedures for testing and destruction of cannabis/products. Training programme (CCD-approved) within 30 days of start of employment (employee health and safety and related topics); ANSI food-handler course before handling/transport/manufacture/extraction/testing/packaging activities (§11.8.4); training documentation retained two years (current employees) and at least six months after termination.
  • Premises diagram (16.8.2.60). All research licensees must have a detailed premises diagram on hand at all times, available for in-person CCD inspection on request, conforming to 16.8.2 requirements.
  • Expedited approval for DEA registrants (16.8.2.59). CCD must create an early-approval process for entities registered or conditionally approved by the FDA/DEA to manufacture bulk cannabis for research or to research cannabis: an entity registered/conditionally approved by DEA to manufacture bulk cannabis for research may seek early approval for a Tier I licence; an entity registered/conditionally approved by DEA to research cannabis may seek early approval for a Tier III licence. If the applicant meets all requirements, CCD must issue the research licence within 30 days of receiving a completed application. The 60-day application window in 16.8.2.59(A) ran from the rule's effective date (12 July 2022) and is spent as an application window; the 30-day issuance duty for qualifying DEA applicants is the surviving operational point — Verify whether CCD still operates an expedited track on that basis at 31 October 2026.
  • Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/nmac/nmregister/xxxiii/16.8.2amend_xxxiii13.html (16.8.2 amendment, Vol. XXXIII, Issue 13, 12 July 2022, replacing §56 and adding §§57–63); https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Research-Lab-Application.pdf; https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-61-NMAC — all accessed 31 October 2026.

11.9.2 How many research laboratories are licensed? — the zero that matters

  • June 2025 (official CCD presentation): Research Laboratory — 0 premises. The same presentation that gives 7 testing premises gives 0 research premises.
  • December 2024 (Run 1 count): 0 research laboratories approved (out of 3,071 approvals to 4 December 2024, which included 6 testing laboratories).
  • April 2023 (official CCD presentation): 1 research laboratory approved (with 4 testing laboratories, out of 1,518 approved applications / 2,533 premises approved as of 12 April 2023), and 0 research laboratories in the pending-applications table as of the same date (the pending table shows 0 research; the approved table shows 1 — the difference is approved vs. pending, not a conflict).
  • Conclusion for this part: no currently licensed CCD research laboratory was confirmed, and no university was confirmed as holding a CCD research licence, at 31 October 2026. The June 2025 zero-premises figure is the latest official count found. Any claim that NMSU or UNM "holds" a CCD research licence must be verified against CCD licensing records (IPRA / NM-PLUS) before it is stated.
  • Sources: June 2025: https://www.nmlegis.gov/(X(1)S(lwlkmr0y3i3lcdrg02ubogvl))/handouts/CCJ%20063025%20Item%201%20Cannabis%20Enforcement.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026; April 2023: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/CRAC-Presentation-4.14.23.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.

11.9.3 NMSU — hemp research (confirmed university rule) vs. CCD cannabis research (not confirmed)

  • NMSU Administrative Rules and Procedures 11.50 — Hemp Research, Extension, and Outreach Activities (official university source). Purpose: to further the state's interest in implementing the Hemp Manufacturing Act and to guide NMSU employees on permissible hemp research, extension and outreach consistent with state and federal law. Hemp is defined as in the 2018 Farm Bill: Cannabis sativa L. and any part, growing or not, with delta-9 THC concentration not more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis. Faculty may perform hemp research only if it complies with federal guidelines and state law, via either (1) the Controlled Substances Act route — DEA Schedule I registration for possession/use/distribution of industrial hemp, then registration with the New Mexico Board of Pharmacy, with research-grade hemp from a DEA-approved distributor; or (2) the 2014/2018 Farm Bill route — agricultural/academic research within New Mexico, for which the principal investigator is responsible for obtaining a licence from NMDA before possession of viable seed, plants, cuttings, etc., and for transportation of samples to laboratories; NMSU must not transport hemp outside New Mexico; NMSU employees must have a copy of a valid NMDA cultivation licence in their possession at all times when transporting raw hemp (seeds, plants, flower/bud, etc.).
  • Source: http://arp.nmsu.edu/chapter-11/11-50.html — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • NMSU hemp cultivation research in practice (secondary, dated). A 2021 High Plains Journal report describes NMSU students growing hemp cultivars ("Cherry Blossom", "Sweetened") in a supervised greenhouse-management class (fall 2020), after approvals from NMDA, DPS and university administration, to evaluate salt tolerance and nitrogen rates (100 ppm vs. 200 ppm). That is a teaching/research project under the hemp route, not evidence of a CCD cannabis research licence.
  • Source (secondary): https://hpj.com/2021/05/18/nmsu-students-grow-study-hemp-cultivars-on-campus/ — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • No NMSU CCD cannabis research licence (Tier I/II/III) was confirmed for this part. NMSU's Agricultural Science Center industrial-hemp work since 2019 (optimal growing conditions, pest management, economic viability — secondary summary) and Institute for Applied Biosciences cannabinoid work (secondary) are hemp / analytical work, not a confirmed CCD Tier I–III licence.

11.9.4 UNM — medical-cannabis research (secondary only, not a confirmed CCD licence)

  • Secondary summaries describe: UNM School of Medicine Medical Cannabis Research Fund providing grants for medical-cannabis research; UNM Department of Biology courses on medicinal plants/phytochemistry including cannabinoids; and a UNM-led Cannabis Environmental Best Management Practices research initiative for sustainable cultivation. None of these was confirmed on an official UNM or CCD source opened for this part, and none is stated here as a CCD licence, a funded programme with a current budget, or an operating research laboratory. They are recorded as Verify leads for Part 12 / follow-up, not as findings.
  • Source (secondary only): https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/research-and-development-in-new-mexico — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • No UNM CCD cannabis research licence (Tier I/II/III) was confirmed for this part, for the same reason as NMSU: the latest official CCD count is 0 research premises (June 2025).

11.9.5 Federal overlay for university cannabis research (brief)

University research involving high-THC cannabis (as opposed to hemp ≤ 0.3% THC) still engages federal controlled-substance law: DEA registration for Schedule I research (now, for state-licensed medical activity, Schedule III as of 28 April 2026 under the federal baseline — the effect of rescheduling on DEA research registration requirements for universities is Verify against current DEA rules and is not decided here), FDA approval for clinical studies involving ingestion by human subjects, and the CCD Tier I/II/III division-approval requirement. A CCD Tier I licence does not substitute for DEA/FDA authorisation, and DEA/FDA authorisation does not substitute for a CCD licence — both tracks are required for a New Mexico university to produce/possess high-THC cannabis for research in-state. The expedited CCD track for DEA registrants (§11.9.1) is the bridge between the two systems.

0. Consistency anchors carried from Run 1 (do not contradict)

The following Run 1 anchors are assumed, not re-litigated, in Part 12. Any Part 12 statement that appeared to conflict with them would have been flagged, not silently changed; no such conflict was found in the Part 12 sources, except for the two citation discrepancies flagged in §12.4 and §12.5.

  • Adult-use public possession/purchase limits: 2 oz cannabis / 16 g cannabis extract / 800 mg edible cannabis; excess at a private residence, not visible from a public place, is treated differently (§ 26-2C-25(A)(2)).
  • Home grow: 6 mature + 6 immature plants per adult, maximum 12 mature plants per household.
  • Medical purchase limit: 425 units per rolling 90 days (in-state patients and reciprocal participants alike — see §12.5).
  • Local buffer ceiling: local jurisdictions may not impose a buffer greater than 300 ft from a school or daycare (§ 26-2C-12) — relevant to consumption-area siting in §12.4, but local time/place/manner rules beyond that ceiling are a local-law question, not a state rule stated here.
  • Packaging, labelling, advertising and delivery rules: Run 1 §1.6. Employment protections: Run 1 §1.8. Expungement provisions in outline: Run 1 §1.2 (this Part gives the operative procedure and the numbers question in full).
  • Licence types and fees, water-proof rule, BioTrack → NMS2S tracking, and the NMED hemp rule (20.10.2 NMAC, eff. 28 January 2026; 0.30% total THC, 2 mg/serving, 20 mg/package for hemp products) are Run 1 matters and are not restated except where a Part 12 rule turns on them.

0.1 Federal baseline (fixed for this run — not re-researched; contradictions flagged only)

  • State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products: Schedule III, effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714).
  • Adult-use remains Schedule I.
  • 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg/container cap apply.
  • USDA DEA-lab hemp testing enforcement delayed to 31 December 2026; federal medical rider through 11 December 2026; no federal banking law.
  • No contradiction with that baseline was found in the Part 12 sources. Two secondary sources that still describe marijuana as simply "Schedule I" for all purposes (notably a law-firm page on guns, and a housing page that repeats the pre-rescheduling HUD position) are stale on that point and are not relied on for the federal schedule. Where a pre-rescheduling federal guidance document is discussed (§12.6, §12.7), its post-rescheduling status is flagged Verify rather than assumed to have been withdrawn or to remain in force.

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke-shop rules

12.1.1 What is lawful for an adult

§ 26-2C-25(A), Cannabis Regulation Act, Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, § 25, effective 29 June 2021 (history note on the opened page). The operative adult-use list, quoted verbatim from the page opened in this session, includes:

"(6) manufacturing, transporting or giving away to a person twenty-one years of age or older cannabis paraphernalia;"

and:

"B. Paragraph (6) of Subsection A of this section is intended to meet the requirements of 21 U.S.C. Section 863(f) by authorizing under state law any person in compliance with this section to manufacture, possess or distribute cannabis paraphernalia."

Source: § 26-2C-25, opened — https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-25/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

The same section makes the wider adult-use conduct lawful and not grounds for detention, search or arrest, and not contraband/forfeiture under the Controlled Substances Act or the Forfeiture Act, where it is within CRA / medical-program authorisation — § 26-2C-25(A)(1)–(5), (7)–(10) (opened, same page). Note in particular (A)(8): smoking cannabis "in an area authorized pursuant to the Cannabis Regulation Act or a local jurisdiction" — the consumption-area rule, not a general public-smoking right (see §12.4).

12.1.2 The Controlled Substances Act carve-out

§ 30-31-2(T) NMSA 1978 defines "drug paraphernalia" as, "except as to use in accordance with the Cannabis Regulation Act [Chapter 26, Article 2C NMSA 1978] or the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act [Chapter 26, Article 2B NMSA 1978]", equipment, products and materials used, intended or designed for use in planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analyzing, packaging, repackaging, storing, containing, concealing, injecting, ingesting, inhaling or otherwise introducing a controlled substance into the human body in violation of the Controlled Substances Act. The listed examples include metal, wooden, acrylic, glass, stone, plastic or ceramic pipes, water pipes, carburetion tubes and devices, smoking and carburetion masks, chamber pipes, carburetor pipes, electric pipes, air-driven pipes, chilams, bongs, and ice pipes or chillers.

Source (search-verified, 2025 text): https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-30/article-31/section-30-31-2/ — accessed 31 October 2026. Verify: re-check this definition on NMOneSource for the current (post-2025-amendment) text before republication; the 2021 (1st S.S.) amendment history on that page records the CRA / Compassionate Use Act carve-out being added, effective 29 June 2021.

Practical consequence, stated carefully: paraphernalia used in accordance with the CRA or the Compassionate Use Act is outside the § 30-31-2(T) "drug paraphernalia" definition. Paraphernalia used in violation of the Controlled Substances Act is not. The line is therefore use-compliance, not the object itself.

12.1.3 Retailers, and the "smoke shop" gap

  • A CCD-licensed cannabis retailer may sell cannabis paraphernalia alongside cannabis products; retailer sale of paraphernalia is part of the licensed-retail model described in Run 1 §1.6 and in secondary retailer guidance. No separate CRA licence type called a "smoke shop licence" appears in the CRA licence list carried from Run 1 (producer tiers, microbusiness, manufacturer Classes I–IV, retailer, courier, testing, consumption Type I/II, research Tiers I–III, VICE).
  • Verify — standalone paraphernalia-only shops: § 26-2C-25(A)(6) as opened authorises, for a person 21 or older, manufacturing, transporting or giving away cannabis paraphernalia. It does not, in the text opened, use the word "selling" for a non-licensee. Whether an unlicensed shop that sells only paraphernalia (no cannabis, no cannabis product) needs any CCD licence, and what age-gate (if any) applies to a retail sale of paraphernalia as opposed to giving it away, was not settled by any official source retrieved in this session. Do not assume either that such a shop is unregulated or that it is CCD-licensed. A local business licence, local zoning / time-place-manner rules, and any local paraphernalia ordinance still apply in any event (see local example below).
  • Verify — sale to minors: No current official text retrieved in this session states a standalone paraphernalia-sale-to-minors offence or age threshold distinct from the CRA's general protection of underage persons (§ 26-2C-14, Run 1 cross-reference) and the ban on providing cannabis products to minors. Do not state a paraphernalia-specific minor-sale penalty without a NMOneSource check.
  • Local conforming amendment (secondary/local record, not a state rule): the City of Albuquerque amended its criminal code § 12-4-10 (Council Bill O-21-82) to remove cannabis references and to provide that nothing in that section establishes a criminal penalty for possession of paraphernalia for the exclusive purpose of cannabis use, or for activities associated with cannabis use or commerce, in accordance with the CRA or the Compassionate Use Act. Source: https://cabq.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=5215167&GUID=500C25C7-05BA-4BF4-8E5B-52902E133A58&Options=&Search=&FullText=1 — accessed 31 October 2026. This is an Albuquerque example only; other local paraphernalia ordinances were not surveyed.

12.1.4 Storage and child-access (cross-reference)

Run 1 §1.6 covers packaging/labelling. For paraphernalia in the home, the only Part 12-specific official guidance retrieved is the CCD's general safe-storage advice (locked cabinet / locked storage, away from children and pets — see §12.8). No statewide statute retrieved in this session imposes a specific paraphernalia-storage offence distinct from child-endangerment / general criminal law. Verify if a storage offence is to be asserted.
