12.2 THC driving limits and impairment testing

12.2.1 The offence: no per se THC limit

§ 66-8-102(B) NMSA 1978 (search-verified; the subsection is consistently quoted across the 2025 bill text and secondary analyses retrieved):

"It is unlawful for a person who is under the influence of any drug to a degree that renders the person incapable of safely driving a vehicle to drive a vehicle within this state."

New Mexico has no per se THC blood-concentration limit (no equivalent of the 0.08 alcohol standard in § 66-8-102(C)). That is the unanimous position of the secondary analyses retrieved, and no statute or rule retrieved in this session sets a nanogram-per-millilitre THC threshold. A blood result showing THC therefore does not, by itself, prove the § 66-8-102(B) standard; the State must prove impairment to the "incapable of safely driving" degree beyond a reasonable doubt. The jury-instruction distinction is material and is routinely misstated: alcohol DWI is framed as "impaired to the slightest degree" (UJI 14-4501), drug DWI — including cannabis — as "incapable of safely driving" (UJI 14-4502). Secondary source for the instruction contrast: https://www.collinsattorneys.com/driving-influence-marijuana-new-mexico/ — accessed 31 October 2026. Verify the current UJI text on NMOneSource / nmcourts before quoting the instructions verbatim in a republication; the instructions themselves were not opened in this session.

Penalties for a drug-DWI conviction are the § 66-8-102 penalty scheme (first and subsequent convictions, aggravated forms, community service, DWI school, screening, ignition-interlock conditions as applicable to the conviction class). Verify the current penalty table against the current § 66-8-102 text before publishing a penalty figure: the secondary summaries retrieved give differing first-offence figures, and this Part does not adopt any of them as settled. Do not import the alcohol per se penalties into a cannabis case.

12.2.2 Odour, suspicion, and the DWI-investigation exception — opened text

§ 26-2C-25(C) (opened) provides that none of the following, individually or in combination, constitutes reasonable articulable suspicion of a crime or a basis to stop, detain or search a person: (1) the odour of cannabis or cannabis extract or of burnt cannabis or cannabis extract; (2) possession, or suspicion of possession, of cannabis without evidence of quantity in excess of 2 oz / 16 g / 800 mg; or (3) possession of multiple containers without evidence of quantity in excess of those limits.

§ 26-2C-25(D) (opened) then carves that protection back out:

"Paragraph (1) of Subsection A and Subsection C of this section shall not apply when a law enforcement officer is investigating whether a person is operating a vehicle or watercraft while intoxicated or under the influence of or impaired by alcohol or a drug or any combination thereof in violation of Section 66-8-102 or 66-13-3 NMSA 1978."

In plain terms: cannabis odour alone is not a stop/search basis in general, but that shield does not apply inside a § 66-8-102 / § 66-13-3 driving investigation. The opened page also carries an annotation on State v. Perry, 2025-NMSC-043, concerning odour and probable cause for a vehicle search in a post-decriminalisation, pre-legalisation setting — that case is not a statement of the current CRA-era rule and must not be cited as if it were.

Source: § 26-2C-25(C)–(D), opened — https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-26/article-2c/section-26-2c-25/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

12.2.3 How impairment is actually tested today

On the sources retrieved, the working method is:

  1. Observation — driving behaviour, field sobriety observations.
  2. Drug Recognition Evaluator (DRE) evaluation where available — the agency analyses retrieved treat DRE testimony as still potentially required to establish a drug-DWI, because a drug test alone does not prove impairment (see §12.2.4).
  3. Chemical testing of breath or blood under the Implied Consent Act (§§ 66-8-107 to 66-8-112 NMSA 1978, as amended). Breath testing addresses alcohol; for drugs, the confirmatory matrix in use is blood. Toxicology testing is conducted by the New Mexico Department of Health Scientific Laboratory Division (SLD), not by the DPS Forensic Laboratory (which focuses on DNA, firearms/toolmarks, chemistry and latent prints) — DPS agency analysis, 2025 Regular Session, HB 567 file: https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/25 Regular/AgencyAnalysis/HB0567_790.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  4. Refusal consequences under § 66-8-111 (licence/privilege revocation grounds) apply to refusal to submit to a chemical test on request after arrest for a Motor Vehicle Code offence, subject to the affidavit / probable-cause procedure in that section. The full current text was not opened in this session — Verify before stating a refusal procedure step-by-step.

There is no roadside THC breathalyser in lawful use as a determinative impairment test in New Mexico on the sources retrieved. Commercial "THC breathalyser" claims (detection of recent use within hours) are, even on their own terms, detection of recent use, not proof of impairment to the § 66-8-102(B) standard. No New Mexico adoption of such a device as a chemical test was located. Verify if a device adoption is to be asserted.

12.2.4 Oral-fluid / saliva testing: proposed, not current law

Two proposals were retrieved and must not be presented as current law:

  • HB 55 (2024 Regular Session), "Oral Fluid Drug Detection Pilot Project" — would have created a DPS roadside oral-fluid pilot, with rulemaking, device purchase, officer training and an expert panel. Agency analysis (Department of Justice staff analysis, 17 January 2024): https://nmlegis.gov/Sessions/24%20Regular/AgencyAnalysis/HB0055_305.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026. A later (2025) analysis records that the 2023 predecessor (HB 275) was tabled in House Judiciary and, to that analyst's knowledge, the pilot was never funded or created, and SLD had not approved any form of oral-fluid testing.
  • HB 567 (2025 Regular Session), "DWI Saliva Testing" — would have added oral-fluid testing to the Implied Consent Act (§ 66-8-107), added a presumption that a person is under the influence of drugs if blood or oral fluid contains a controlled substance, and extended that presumption to administrative Motor Vehicle Division proceedings. Agency analyses: DPS (21 February 2025), https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/25 Regular/AgencyAnalysis/HB0567790.pdf ; DOH (24 February 2025), https://www.nmlegis.gov/sessions/25 Regular/AgencyAnalysis/HB0567665.pdf ; AOC / Law Offices of the Public Defender analyses in the same HB 567 file set — all accessed 31 October 2026. The DOH analysis is explicit that SLD's existing DUI methodologies apply only to blood, that entirely new methodologies and new screening + confirmatory instruments would be needed, and that a statewide programme would align "more closely with a five-year timeframe." The DPS analysis adds that SLD "does not have a way to test it at this time."

Verify — HB 567 outcome: whether HB 567 was enacted, vetoed, or died in the 2025 session was not confirmed by any source retrieved in this session, and the related 2025 bill HB 106 (blood-withdrawal personnel) is likewise not confirmed as enacted here. Until that is checked on nmlegis.gov, HB 567 must be described only as a 2025 proposal. The scientific objection recorded in the agency analyses should also be carried forward if the proposal is discussed: presence of a controlled substance in blood or oral fluid does not, without more, establish impairment, because no established concentration–impairment relationship exists for cannabis comparable to alcohol.

12.2.5 Vehicles, passengers, and "open container" — a gap, not a rule

  • Driving while impaired by cannabis is unlawful (§ 66-8-102(B)); being a passenger, or merely having lawfully possessed cannabis in a vehicle, is not the same offence.
  • Verify — cannabis "open container" in a vehicle: No New Mexico cannabis open-container statute (equivalent to the alcohol open-container rule, or to California's cannabis open-container rule) was located in the official sources retrieved in this session. Secondary summaries assert that smoking in a vehicle is caught by the public-place rule in § 26-2C-26 (see §12.4), but the CRA definition of "public place" for that section was not opened, and a parked private vehicle is not obviously a "public place" on the text retrieved. Do not state a freestanding New Mexico cannabis open-container offence, or a passenger-smoking offence, without a NMOneSource check of §§ 26-2C-26, 66-8-102 and any vehicle-specific provision.
  • Medical patients are expressly not relieved from liability for operating a vehicle while under the influence of cannabis — § 26-2B-5(A)(2) (search-verified current text; see §12.9 sources). The same applies, a fortiori, to adult-use consumers.
  • CCD consumer guidance, opened: "you should never drive high. Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal and puts the public at risk." Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/yes-and-knows/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

12.3 Automatic expungement under the Cannabis Regulation Act

12.3.1 The law (opened text)

§ 29-3A-8 NMSA 1978, Criminal Record Expungement Act — "Expungement of arrest and conviction records; procedure." History: Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 3, § 5 (the companion bill to the CRA, SB 2 in the 2021 first special session); amended by Laws 2023, ch. 74, § 1, effective 16 June 2023. Current text, quoted verbatim from the page opened in this session:

"A. If a person was charged with an offense involving cannabis that is no longer a crime on June 29, 2021 or that would have resulted in a lesser offense if the Cannabis Regulation Act [Chapter 26, Article 2C NMSA 1978] had been in effect at the time of the offense, whether or not the person is convicted, all public records held by a court or an agency of the state or a local jurisdiction that relate to the person's arrest or conviction shall be automatically expunged two years after the date of the person's conviction or the date of the person's arrest if there was no conviction. If the person is or was under eighteen years of age at the time of the arrest or conviction, the public records under this section shall be retained for two years or until the person is eighteen years of age, whichever comes first, and shall then be automatically expunged. Automatic expungement under this section applies to public records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges and requires destruction of the records."

"B. The administrative office of the courts shall implement a procedure allowing persons charged with offenses eligible for automatic expungement under this section to verify whether automatic expungement has occurred and request expedited automatic expungement if eligible charges have not yet been expunged."

"C. If an arrest or conviction involved cannabis and non-cannabis charges, a person may request expungement of eligible cannabis charges as defined in Subsection A of this section by the administrative office of the courts through the procedure implemented in Subsection B of this section."

"D. Requests for expungement to the administrative office of the courts from persons charged with offenses eligible for automatic expungement shall remain confidential and are not subject to disclosure."

Source: § 29-3A-8, opened — https://law.justia.com/codes/new-mexico/chapter-29/article-3a/section-29-3a-8/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

The 2023 amendment's effect, per the annotation on the same opened page, was to (i) limit automatic expungement to records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges, (ii) require destruction of the records (replacing the 2021 formulation of removal from all statewide criminal databases), (iii) add the AOC verify / expedited-request procedure, (iv) add the mixed-charge request route, and (v) make AOC requests confidential. The pre-2023 formulation — under which only the cannabis portions of a mixed-charge record were expunged — is superseded and must not be quoted as current law.

Key mechanics, in plain terms:

ElementRule (§ 29-3A-8, as amended 2023)
Eligibility triggerCharged with a cannabis offence that is no longer a crime on 29 June 2021, or would have resulted in a lesser offence had the CRA been in effect at the time — whether or not convicted
Automatic timing2 years after conviction, or 2 years after arrest if no conviction
Under-18 at arrest/convictionRetain 2 years or until age 18, whichever comes first, then automatically expunge
Scope of automatic routePublic records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges; requires destruction of the records
Mixed cannabis + non-cannabis chargesNot automatic; the person may request expungement of the eligible cannabis charges through the AOC procedure (§ 29-3A-8(C))
If automatic expungement has not happenedVerify status and request expedited automatic expungement through the AOC (§ 29-3A-8(B))
ConfidentialityAOC requests are confidential, not subject to disclosure (§ 29-3A-8(D))
What "expungement" means hereDestruction of the public records (2023 formulation) — distinct from the general CREA "removal from public access" concept; do not conflate the two

Related routes (not automatic, and not a substitute for § 29-3A-8):

  • The general petition route under §§ 29-3A-4 / 29-3A-5 (petition to the district court, with waiting periods measured from completion of sentence and with ineligible categories). New Mexico Courts general information (search-verified) lists, among the convictions not eligible under the general petition route, offences causing death, sex offences (§ 29-11A-3), embezzlement (§ 30-16-8), and DWI offences — a cannabis-DWI conviction is therefore not to be assumed expungeable under the general route merely because it involves cannabis. Source: https://supremecourt.nmcourts.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/21/2023/11/General-Information-Sheet.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026 (search-verified; direct open rate-limited, see header note).
  • The New Mexico Courts cannabis-expungement application (search-verified): "This form allows you to apply for your cannabis (marijuana) criminal records to be expunged according to the Criminal Records Expungement Act. NMSA 1978 29-3A-1 et seq. If you have a case record involving cannabis, you may request that this charge be cleared. If your case record involves charges other than cannabis related charges, you may petition the court to expunge all charges." Source: https://nmcourts.gov/court-administration/office-of-general-counsel/expungement/ — accessed 31 October 2026 (search-verified; direct open rate-limited). The older (January 2022, rev. 7/12/22) "Steps to Filing Your Petition for Expungement (Automatic Expungement)" still states the pre-2023 mixed-charge rule ("only the portion … related to the cannabis charges will be expunged") and must not be relied on over the 2023 amended statute: https://nmcourts.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/21/2023/11/STEPS-TO-FILING-YOUR-PETITION-FOR-EXPUNGEMENTAutomatic-ExpungementJan-2022.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.
  • Post-conviction relief / sentence reduction for conduct legalised or downgraded is described in secondary summaries of the 2021 companion law (prosecutors reviewing cases, with an objection window in the original process). No current official sentence-reduction figure or procedure was retrieved in this session — Verify before stating a resentencing route or deadline; the original July 2022-era objection deadline in press reporting is historical, not current.

12.3.2 Numbers processed — OFFICIAL TOTAL: UNAVAILABLE (with the historical figures that do exist, labelled)

Answer to the task question, plainly: no official, current (as of 31 October 2026) total number of cannabis records automatically expunged in New Mexico was found. The routes tried were: the New Mexico Courts expungement page and general information sheet; the Administrative Office of the Courts (AOC) as the § 29-3A-8(B) procedure owner; the Department of Public Safety (DPS) as the source of the original eligibility list; and secondary compilations (Marijuana Policy Project, Collateral Consequences Resource Center state profile, updated 13 April 2026). None of those sources, as retrieved on 31 October 2026, publishes a current cumulative "records expunged to date" total. That gap is recorded as Unavailable, not filled with an estimate.

Do not publish any of the following as a 2026 total: "14,000 expunged" without the April 2023 date; "151,640 expunged" (that was the review pool, not completions); or any figure derived by adding district filings. The correct current statement is: official cumulative total as of 31 October 2026: Unavailable; last dated count located: ~14,000 cases as of April 2023 (AOC, via press reporting); original DPS review pool: ~151,640–155,000 cases (2022 reporting).

Recommended follow-up for a future run (not done here, because it requires a direct AOC/DPS request, not a web search): ask the AOC for the § 29-3A-8(B) procedure's cumulative verification/expedited-request and destruction counts, and ask DPS for the disposition of the original eligibility list. Until then the register entry stands.

12.4 Consumption areas and events

12.4.1 The default rule: no public consumption, except a licensed consumption area (or a private residence)

CCD consumer guidance, opened:

"Know that cannabis may only be consumed at a licensed consumption lounge or at an individual's residence. It is illegal to consume cannabis in public spaces like festivals, expos, and even at a licensed dispensary."

Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/yes-and-knows/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

The statutory smoking ban, § 26-2C-26(A)–(B) (search-verified; Laws 2021 (1st S.S.), ch. 4, § 26, effective 29 June 2021):

"A. Nothing in Section 25 [26-2C-25 NMSA 1978] of the Cannabis Regulation Act shall be construed to: (1) allow a person to smoke cannabis products in a public place, except in a cannabis consumption area; or (2) restrict the ability of a person to prohibit conduct otherwise allowed in the Cannabis Regulation Act on the person's privately owned property."

"B. A person who violates Paragraph (1) of Subsection A of this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of fifty dollars ($50.00)."

"C. As used in this section, 'smoke' means to inhale, exhale, burn or carry any lighted or heated device or pipe or any other lighted or heated cannabis products intended for inhalation, whether natural or synthetic, in any manner or in any form."

Source: https://law.uslawyerdatabase.com/section-26-2c-26-limits-on-personal-use-penalties/ — accessed 31 October 2026. Verify: re-check § 26-2C-26 on NMOneSource before republication (the opened-text route was not completed for this section). Note the drafting point: § 26-2C-26 as retrieved addresses smoking; whether non-smoked consumption (edibles, tinctures) in a public place is caught by the same $50 provision, or by a different provision, is not stated in the text retrieved — Verify. The CCD's consumer phrasing ("consume … in public spaces") is broader than the smoking text, but CCD guidance is not the statute. Also note § 26-2C-26(D) (search-verified): a person under 18, their family, or a person legally obligated to care for and support them, is not required to pay fees or fines under the CRA — do not apply the $50 penalty to a minor on the basis of this Part.

Medical patients are subject to a parallel restriction: § 26-2B-5(A)(3) (search-verified current text, via the RLD's published Article 2B) provides that participation in the medical programme does not relieve a patient, primary caregiver or reciprocal participant from criminal prosecution or civil penalty for possession or use of cannabis "(a) in the workplace of the qualified patient's, primary caregiver's or reciprocal participant's employment; or (b) at a public park, recreation center, youth center or other public place." The pre-2019 school-bus / school-grounds limbs were deleted by Laws 2019, ch. 247 and ch. 261, effective 14 June 2019 — the school position is now governed by § 22-33-5 (see §12.9), not by § 26-2B-5(A)(3). Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/ARTICLE-2B-Lynn-and-Erin-Compassionate-Use-Act-_-Chapter-26-Drugs-and-Cosmetics.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.

12.4.2 Licensed consumption areas: Type I and Type II

16.8.2.49 NMAC, "Cannabis Consumption Area Licensure; General Provisions" (adopted NM Register Vol. XXXII, Issue 01, 11 January 2022, eff. 11 January 2022; amended NM Register Vol. 11, Issue 11, 7 June 2022, eff. 7 June 2022), opened:

"A. License types: The division may license two classes of cannabis consumption areas: (1) Type I permit: A licensed cannabis consumption area where cannabis products may be consumed on the licensed premises, except for products consumed through the respiratory system. (2) Type II permit: A licensed cannabis consumption area where cannabis products may be consumed, including products that are consumed through the respiratory system."

"D. Other activities allowed: A licensee may conduct any lawful activity or any combination of lawful activities at a licensed premises; provided that the licensee is not a licensee pursuant to the Liquor Control Act."

"E. Cannabis consumption area license: Applicants for a cannabis consumption area must meet all qualifications for a cannabis retailer to be approved for, and authorized to conduct, a cannabis consumption area."

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-49-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

In plain terms: Type I = edibles / non-inhaled products only; Type II = including smoking/vaping. A consumption area is not a standalone licence divorced from retail — the applicant must meet retailer qualifications. The Run 1 licence list (consumption Type I/II) is consistent with this rule; no consumption-area fee distinct from the retailer fee was retrieved in this Part — Verify the current fee schedule in 16.8.11 NMAC before stating a consumption-area fee.

12.4.3 Minimum standards (16.8.2.54 NMAC, opened)

16.8.2.54 NMAC (adopted 7 June 2022, eff. 7 June 2022), opened in full:

  • Access: premises access is limited to (1) individuals at least 21 with valid identification, and (2) individuals at least 18 with a valid qualified-patient, primary-caregiver or reciprocal-participant registry identification card from the DOH medical cannabis programme (§ 16.8.2.54(A)–(B)).
  • Age/identity check before access: individuals are granted access to consume or purchase only after the consumption area or its employee has confirmed age and identity, and if applicable patient/caregiver/reciprocal status (§ 16.8.2.54(C)(1)).
  • Staffing: the consumption area or at least one employee must be physically present in the consumption area at all times when non-employees are in the retail area (§ 16.8.2.54(C)(2)).
  • Sales location: all sales of cannabis goods, except delivery sales, must take place within the retail area of the licensed premises (§ 16.8.2.54(C)(3)).
  • Hours: consumption only between the hours reported to the Division as regular business hours (§ 16.8.2.54(C)(4)).
  • Bring-back for patients: a consumption area may allow qualified patients to bring previously purchased goods from that consumption area for consumption, provided the product is properly stored in the requisite resealable packaging and the patient provides proof of purchase from that licensee (§ 16.8.2.54(C)(5)). This is a patient bring-back rule, not a general BYO rule — do not extend it to adult-use consumers or to products bought elsewhere.
  • Closed-hours security: when not open for consumption, the premises must be securely locked with commercial-grade, non-residential door locks, with an active alarm system per § 16.8.2.10, and access limited to employees and authorised individuals (§ 16.8.2.54(D)).
  • Who may be sold to / allowed to consume: commercial cannabis only to individuals at least 21 after ID inspection; medical cannabis only to individuals at least 18 with a valid registry card after confirming age, identity and registry status (§ 16.8.2.54(E)). Acceptable ID: a federal/state/county/municipal government document with name, date of birth and photo (including a motor-vehicle operator's licence); an armed-forces ID with name, date of birth and photo; or a US or foreign passport.
  • Display: products for inspection/sale only in the retail area; products removed from packaging for display must be in containers not readily accessible to customers without staff assistance, staff must remain with the customer during inspection, and display products must not be sold or consumed and must be destroyed under § 16.8.2.15 when no longer used for display (§ 16.8.2.54(F) — first (F)).
  • Server permits: "all employees of the licensed cannabis consumption area who directly offer, sell or serve cannabis must hold a current and valid cannabis server permit according to 16.8.10 NMAC [AUDIT CORRECTION: '18.8.10' was a Cornell rendering error]" (§ 16.8.2.54, second (F), as rendered on the opened Cornell page). Verify — citation discrepancy: the opened page renders this as "16.8.10 NMAC [AUDIT CORRECTION: '18.8.10' was a Cornell rendering error]"; the expected Title 16, Chapter 8 server-permit part is 16.8.10 NMAC, and the duplication of subsection (F) on the same page suggests a rendering error. Do not cite the server-permit part as settled without an SRCA check. [Note: the original “18.8.10 NMAC” was a Cornell rendering error; the correct part is 16.8.10 NMAC.]
  • Visibility: display and consumption must not be visible from outside the licensed premises. An outdoor consumption area is permitted only if all product is kept out of plain sight and not visible from a public place without optical aids (telescopes, binoculars) or aircraft, and the outdoor area is surrounded by a sight-obscuring wall, fence, hedge or other opaque or translucent barrier (§ 16.8.2.54(G)).
  • Mandatory signage (verbatim, minimum 12 inches × 12 inches, prominent place inside the consumption area):

"Cannabis may only be consumed in designated areas out of public view

No consumption of alcohol products on site

We reserve the right to refuse entry or service for reasons including visible intoxication

It is against the law to drive while impaired by cannabis"

(§ 16.8.2.54(H), opened.) Source for all of §12.4.3: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-mexico/16-8-2-54-NMAC — accessed 31 October 2026.

Related premises rule (search-verified, 16.8.2.8(D)): licensees must prohibit consumption of cannabis or cannabis products on or within the licensed premises unless a cannabis consumption area has been approved by the Division. That is why CCD guidance says consumption is illegal "even at a licensed dispensary" unless that dispensary holds an approved consumption area.

Clean Indoor Air Act interface: smoking in a consumption area is allowed only if the area is in a designated smoking area or in a standalone building from which smoke does not infiltrate other indoor workplaces or other indoor public places where smoking is otherwise prohibited under the Dee Johnson Clean Indoor Air Act (Chapter 24, Article 16 NMSA 1978) — CCD Industry Bulletin 25-09 (see §12.4.4) and 16.8.2.50 application-diagram requirement (search-verified: for a Type II area, the diagram must show the designated smoking area / area immediately surrounding the building to ensure smoke will not infiltrate other indoor workplaces or public places where smoking is prohibited).

12.4.4 Events, festivals, expos and competitions: no temporary event licence

There is no temporary / special-event cannabis licence in the CRA licence list carried from Run 1, and no such licence was located in 16.8.2 NMAC in this session. The CCD position, repeated in Industry Bulletins 25-04 (18 March 2025) and 25-09 (16 July 2025, opened), is:

  • All commercial cannabis business activities must occur on licensed premises approved by the CCD for the activity in question.
  • Licensees are obligated to monitor and appropriately respond to illegal consumption on their premises, including at cannabis conventions and other special events.
  • Advertising or hosting any event targeted as family-friendly, kid-friendly, or open to minors on any licensed premises is absolutely prohibited (citing 16.8.3.8(B) NMAC and 16.8.2.40(B) NMAC). The bulletins list bouncy houses, face painting, arts and crafts, games and contests, and interactive activities as examples of events meant to bring families, children or minors to a licensed premises. Breach exposes the licensee to immediate discipline; Bulletin 25-09 states the disciplinary range as a monetary penalty of $1,000–$10,000 per violation and suspension or revocation.
  • "Further, cannabis may not be sold nor be on display at special events such as festivals, expos, or competitions, unless they are taking place at a properly licensed cannabis establishment." (Bulletin 25-09, opened.)
  • CCD consumer guidance, opened, is to the same effect: cannabis "may only be purchased at a licensed dispensary and not at special events such as festivals, expos, or competitions."

Sources: Bulletin 25-09, opened — https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/25-09-Summertime-Events-and-Compliance-Reminders.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026; Bulletin 25-04 — https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/3.18.25.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026; CCD consumer guidance — https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/yes-and-knows/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

Consequences for event organisers, stated carefully:

  • A festival, expo or competition that is not itself a CCD-licensed premises for the relevant activity cannot lawfully host cannabis sales or display, even if licensed retailers are present as exhibitors. What it can host (e.g. education, non-cannabis merchandise, paraphernalia-only display) is a separate question on which no CCD bulletin retrieved here rules — Verify before advising an organiser.
  • A licensed consumption area may host an adult-only event on its own licensed premises, subject to §§ 16.8.2.49–54, the Clean Indoor Air Act interface, local time/place/manner rules, and the absolute ban on family/kid/minor-targeted events on licensed premises.
  • Local ordinances may be stricter within the § 26-2C-12 framework (e.g. a city may prohibit consumption areas in particular districts, or impose its own event rules). Two local examples retrieved illustrate the range, not a statewide rule: the City of Española's use regulations prohibit commercial cannabis activities and consumption areas in the respects stated in that code and prohibit smoking/consuming cannabis on city-occupied/controlled property and in public places in the city; the City of Roswell's Chapter 27 regulates on-site consumption and specialised events as a local land-use matter. Neither example is a substitute for checking the host jurisdiction's current ordinance. Verify the host jurisdiction for any specific event.

Verify — count of operating consumption areas: No official CCD count of currently operating Type I / Type II consumption areas as of 31 October 2026 was retrieved in this session. Secondary coverage describes the market as small relative to retail and notes that several communities have considered or approved consumption areas, but no number is adopted here. Unavailable as an official count.

12.5 Cannabis tourism and visitor purchase rules

12.5.1 Adult-use visitors: no residency requirement, same limits, no export

  • No residency requirement for adult-use purchase is the position of the secondary analyses retrieved, and it is consistent with the text of § 26-2C-25(A) as opened, which frames lawful adult-use conduct by age (21 or older) and by CRA / medical-program authorisation, without a residency qualifier. Verify the purchase provision itself (§ 26-2C-7 / retailer sale rules and Run 1 §1.6) on NMOneSource before stating "no residency requirement" as a direct statutory quote — the opened § 26-2C-25 text supports it by omission, but omission is not a quotation.
  • Limits are the same for visitors as for residents: 2 oz / 16 g / 800 mg (public possession / per-transaction framing in Run 1). There is no visitor-specific adult-use limit in the sources retrieved, and no limit on the number of transactions per day is stated in the CRA text opened — do not invent a daily cap. (Run 1 §1.6 governs the transaction-level rules; this Part does not re-state them.)
  • ID: a valid government-issued ID proving age 21+ is required at a licensed retailer (see §12.4.3 for the acceptable-ID list in the consumption-area context; retailer ID rules are Run 1 §1.6).
  • Stay in New Mexico: CCD consumer guidance, opened: "Know that cannabis bought in New Mexico should stay in New Mexico. It is federally illegal to travel across state lines with cannabis." Source: https://www.rld.nm.gov/cannabis/cannabis-in-new-mexico/yes-and-knows/ — accessed 31 October 2026. This applies with full force to visitors driving to a neighbouring state (including Texas, where no adult-use programme exists, and Arizona / Colorado, where the visitor's home-state limits do not authorise importation). Transport across a state line is a federal offence irrespective of both states' laws.
  • Where a visitor may consume: only at a private residence (with the property owner's permission — see §12.6) or at a licensed consumption area (§12.4). A hotel room, short-term rental, or parked vehicle is not automatically a lawful consumption place: a hotel/rental may prohibit cannabis under § 26-2C-26(A)(2) (private-property prohibition, §12.6), and a vehicle is not a residence. Verify any claim that a specific hotel room counts as a "private residence" for § 26-2C-25 purposes — no authority retrieved here decides it.
  • Federal and tribal land: possession/consumption on federal land (national parks, federal buildings, military installations) remains a federal offence; tribal land is governed by tribal law and any tribal compact / CCD licensure boundary (Run 1 cross-reference). No visitor guidance retrieved here states a federal-land penalty figure as settled — secondary summaries citing "up to one year / $1,000 minimum" for a first federal simple-possession offence are not adopted here. Verify against 21 U.S.C. § 844 before publishing a federal penalty.
  • Flying: no New Mexico rule authorises carrying cannabis onto a flight; TSA operates under federal law. Do not advise a visitor to fly with cannabis.

12.5.2 Medical visitors: reciprocal participants

The medical visitor route is the reciprocal participant programme under 7.34.3.22 NMAC (DOH Medical Cannabis Program rules; the DOH dispensary page renders the citation as "7.34.3.22 [AUDIT CORRECTION: DOH page's '7.34.2.22' is an error; correct citation is 7.34.3.22, eff. 22 Feb 2022]" — see citation flag below) and § 26-2B-3 / § 26-2B-7 framework.

DOH Medical Cannabis Program, "Licensees (Dispensaries)" page, opened:

"Patients who hold proof of authorization to participate in the medical cannabis program of another state of the United States, the District of Columbia, a territory or commonwealth of the United States or a New Mexico Indian nation, tribe or pueblo may lawfully purchase a quantity of cannabis in accordance with NMAC 7.34.3.22 [AUDIT CORRECTION: DOH page's '7.34.2.22' is an error; correct citation is 7.34.3.22, eff. 22 Feb 2022]."

"Eligible individuals can register at a participating dispensary by bringing: Government issued proof of enrollment in another medical cannabis program; and Government issued picture ID. Please Note: both the proof of enrollment and the picture ID must be government issued and from the same location: For example, if you are enrolled in the medical cannabis program in Colorado, the government issued ID must also demonstrate your residency in Colorado."

"Reciprocal Participants can purchase up to 425 units of medical cannabis tax-free in every 'rolling' 90-day period."

"Residents of New Mexico cannot be Reciprocal Participants but can enroll in The New Mexico Department of Health Medical Cannabis Program Online Portal."

Source: https://prod.nmhealth.org/about/mcp/svcs/pdb/ — accessed 31 October 2026.

Further mechanics (search-verified, 7.34.3.22 NMAC as amended 22 February 2022, NM Register Vol. XXXIII, Issue 4):

  • Reciprocity has applied since 1 July 2020.
  • A reciprocal participant is not required to comply with the registry identification card application and renewal requirements that apply to in-state patients, but must at all times possess proof of authorisation from the other jurisdiction's programme.
  • A practitioner's recommendation alone is not sufficient: the proof must be government-issued authorisation (card/document) from the other programme.
  • Registration is in person at a participating dispensary; not all dispensaries are reciprocal licensees, and a visitor must confirm before visiting. There is no online visitor-registration route on the sources retrieved.
  • The purchase limit is the same 425 units / rolling 90 days, tax-free, as for in-state patients (consistent with Run 1).

Sources: https://www.srca.nm.gov/nmac/nmregister/xxxiii/7.34.3amend.html — accessed 31 October 2026; https://prod.nmhealth.org/publication/view/rules/7021/ — accessed 31 October 2026 (7.34.3 NMAC amendment text, search-verified).

Citation discrepancy flagged: the DOH dispensary page cites "NMAC 7.34.3.22 [AUDIT CORRECTION: DOH page's '7.34.2.22' is an error; correct citation is 7.34.3.22, eff. 22 Feb 2022]" while the rule compilation and the 2022 amendment cite "7.34.3.22 RECIPROCITY." The substance is the same programme; the DOH page's "7.34.3.22 [AUDIT CORRECTION: DOH page's '7.34.2.22' is an error; correct citation is 7.34.3.22, eff. 22 Feb 2022]" is treated here as a typographical error on that page, to be confirmed against the current SRCA compilation. Verify the correct part number before republication.

Verify — other visitor-medical points (secondary only, not adopted as settled):

  • Whether a reciprocal participant whose home-state authorisation expires mid-visit must then enrol as a New Mexico patient (secondary Leafwell summary asserts this; no DOH text retrieved here states the expiry rule).
  • The tribal-programme exception to the "New Mexico residents cannot be reciprocal participants" rule (secondary Americans for Safe Access summary asserts an exception for members of a New Mexico Indian Nation, Tribe or Pueblo holding that nation's own programme authorisation; the DOH page as opened states the residency bar without an exception). Do not publish the exception without a DOH / 7.34.3.22 text check.
  • Any "90-day reciprocity period" framing (secondary Veriheal summary) — the DOH text retrieved states a rolling 90-day purchase period (425 units), not a 90-day visitor registration validity period. Do not conflate the two.
  • Whether other states recognise a New Mexico card (outbound reciprocity) is outside this Part's scope (it is the other state's law) and no outbound list is adopted here; secondary lists retrieved differ from each other and are stale-prone.

12.6 Landlord and tenant rules

12.6.1 The state-law starting point: a private owner may prohibit it

§ 26-2C-26(A)(2) (search-verified, see §12.4.1) is the landlord/tenant anchor for adult-use:

"Nothing in Section 25 [26-2C-25 NMSA 1978] of the Cannabis Regulation Act shall be construed to … (2) restrict the ability of a person to prohibit conduct otherwise allowed in the Cannabis Regulation Act on the person's privately owned property."

In other words, legalisation does not create a right to use cannabis on someone else's property against the owner's prohibition. A landlord may prohibit cannabis use — and, in practice, smoking — on the property by lease term, and a tenant who breaches a lease term faces the ordinary lease-enforcement route (see §12.6.3). Conversely, a landlord's silence is not a prohibition: if the lease does not prohibit cannabis use or smoking, the tenant's CRA-lawful use at home is not, by itself, a lease breach on the sources retrieved — but no case retrieved here decides a "silent lease" dispute, so that inference is flagged Verify for any specific lease.

For medical patients, the same private-property principle is applied in practice through lease terms and "reasonable restrictions" (see §12.6.2), but there is no CRA or Compassionate Use Act provision retrieved here that requires a private landlord to permit medical cannabis use in a rental unit.

12.6.2 Medical patients, disability, and the undecided discrimination question

The 2026 New Mexico Association of Realtors information sheet "Medical Marijuana and Rental Property" (secondary, association guidance — not law, and expressly "NOT a disclosure" and "not an exhaustive analysis") records the position as of 2026 as follows, and this Part adopts it only as a statement of what is undecided, not as law:

  • Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act, it is unlawful to refuse to sell, rent, assign, lease or sublease housing because of (among other characteristics) physical or mental handicap, provided the handicap is unrelated to the person's ability to acquire or rent and maintain the property. Whether refusal to rent to a medical-cannabis cardholder amounts to handicap discrimination is, per that sheet, silent in the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act as to penalties for refusal, and undecided by a New Mexico court of record — landlords therefore have, in that sheet's words, "no guidance in this area."
  • Before allowing a tenant to use medical cannabis on the property, a landlord may request a copy of the tenant's registry identification card (per that sheet's practice guidance).
  • A landlord may place reasonable restrictions on medical use; the "reasonableness" of such restrictions has not been determined by a New Mexico court of record, but the sheet gives as an arguable example: if the landlord has a non-smoking policy, the landlord may prohibit smoking of marijuana but allow it in other forms; or, if smoking is allowed, the landlord may reasonably restrict where it may be smoked (e.g. not in common areas).

Source: https://documents.sparkplatform.com/documents/abq/20260403190655950005000000.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026 (2026 NMAR information sheet; secondary).

Do not present the "ban smoking, allow other forms" example as a decided rule. It is an argument about reasonableness, explicitly flagged as undecided in its own source. Likewise, do not present medical-patient status as a protected housing class in New Mexico — no statute or decided case retrieved here so holds.

Employment-related protections (Run 1 §1.8; § 26-2B-9 and § 26-2C-34) do not transfer into housing law. The fact that an employer may not take adverse action for off-duty medical use (subject to safety-sensitive and federal-benefit carve-outs) says nothing about a landlord's position, and the two regimes must not be conflated.

12.6.3 Lease enforcement in general (Owner-Resident Relations Act)

Residential tenancies are governed by the Owner-Resident Relations Act, Chapter 47, Article 8 NMSA 1978. The general enforcement pattern retrieved (secondary form/notice summaries, not a cannabis-specific rule) is: a lease violation (including a smoking or drug-use prohibition in the lease, or a violation of health/building/safety/housing codes) is addressed by a notice to comply / notice of termination under § 47-8-33 and related provisions, with court process required for removal — a landlord may not self-help evict, and only a law-enforcement officer with a court order may remove a tenant. Verify the current §§ 47-8-33, 47-8-36 and 47-8-37 text and notice periods before stating a notice period for a cannabis-specific breach: the secondary summaries retrieved give inconsistent notice figures (7-day vs 30-day vs lease-stated 60-day change notice), and this Part does not adopt any of them for cannabis. In particular, a mid-tenancy change to impose a smoking/cannabis ban is a lease-change question governed by the lease's own change clause and by the Owner-Resident Relations Act's change-notice rules — it is not a right the CRA creates or removes. No New Mexico case retrieved here decides a mid-tenancy cannabis-ban change dispute.

12.6.4 Federally assisted housing: the federal overlay that state law cannot remove

Federally assisted housing (public housing, Housing Choice Voucher / Section 8, other HUD-assisted multifamily) is governed by federal law, not by the CRA:

  • HUD's 2014 guidance, "Use of Marijuana in Multifamily Assisted Properties," states that owners of federally assisted housing must deny admission to applicants determined to be illegally using a controlled substance, including marijuana, and may not establish lease provisions or policies that affirmatively permit occupancy by a household member who uses marijuana. The same guidance framework treats termination of an existing tenancy for drug use as discretionary for the owner/PHA in many circumstances, not mandatory — the ACLU of New Mexico's contemporary analysis of the Monarch Properties episode (a private operator of federally subsidised units in New Mexico that initially required lease addenda barring medical use/growing, then rescinded the notice for non-federally-assisted tenants and moved to case-by-case consideration for federally assisted tenants) makes exactly that discretion point, citing ACLU of Michigan counsel: "termination of a lease due to drug use is entirely discretionary under federal law."
  • HUD's reasonable-accommodation guidance has stated that a public housing agency may not make a reasonable accommodation for medical marijuana use.
  • Post-rescheduling status — Verify: HUD's 2014 guidance and reasonable-accommodation FAQ were written under the former Schedule I framework. A May 2026 Americans for Safe Access memorandum (AG Order No. 6754-2026 rationale, 11 May 2026) calls for HUD to withdraw and replace that guidance in light of the 28 April 2026 Schedule III rescheduling of state-licensed medical marijuana, and argues that state-authorised medical use should not, standing alone, support denial, eviction, termination or refusal of accommodation. That memorandum is advocacy for a policy change, not a HUD withdrawal. Whether HUD has in fact withdrawn, replaced, or left in place its marijuana housing guidance as of 31 October 2026 was not confirmed by any HUD source retrieved in this session. Do not state that HUD's position has changed, and do not state that it is unchanged, without a HUD-source check. The safe current statement is: HUD's 2014 guidance has not been shown, in sources retrieved here, to have been withdrawn as of 31 October 2026; its application to state-licensed medical use after the Schedule III rescheduling is Verify.

Sources: https://www.aclu-nm.org/news/medical-marijuana-mess/ — accessed 31 October 2026 (historical, pre-legalisation episode; used only for the discretion point); https://www.safeaccessnow.org/guidancerationaleag_order — accessed 31 October 2026 (May 2026 advocacy memorandum; not HUD guidance).

Practical summary for tenants (state law + federal overlay, not legal advice):

  • Private, non-subsidised rental: the lease governs; the landlord may prohibit cannabis/smoking; medical status has no decided housing-discrimination protection in New Mexico.
  • Federally assisted rental: federal admission/termination rules apply on top of the lease; a medical card does not override them on any HUD source retrieved here; post-rescheduling HUD treatment is Verify.
  • Growing cannabis in a rental: the same lease analysis applies, plus the home-grow limits (6+6 per adult, 12 mature per household), the water-proof / premises rules in Run 1, and any lease prohibition on cultivation, alterations, or increased utility/fire risk. No separate "tenant's right to grow" was located.

12.6.5 Commercial landlords and licensed premises

A commercial landlord's position is governed by the commercial lease and by the licence's premises-specific, non-transferable character (Run 1 consistency anchor: licences are 12 months, non-transferable). A retailer/producer/manufacturer cannot move its licence to a new landlord's building by assignment; a new premises requires the CCD application for that premises (16.8.2.8(X) concept, search-verified). Landlord consent, zoning compliance, and the § 26-2C-12 local buffer ceiling are premises-approval matters for the CCD application, not tenant rights against the landlord. No commercial-tenant protection specific to cannabis licensees was located. Verify the current additional-premises rule text before advising a licensee on relocation.

12.7 Gun-ownership conflicts

12.7.1 The federal statute has not changed

18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) makes it unlawful for any person "who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance (as defined in section 102 of the Controlled Substances Act)" to ship, transport, possess, or receive any firearm or ammunition. Congress has not amended § 922(g)(3). That is the fixed starting point for this section; everything below is about how the 2026 rescheduling interacts with the word "unlawful" in that statute, not about a repeal.

ATF Form 4473 (Firearms Transaction Record), completed for every purchase from a federally licensed dealer, has historically asked (Question 21(f) / 21(e) in successive form versions) whether the buyer is an unlawful user of, or addicted to, marijuana or any other controlled substance, with a warning that marijuana use remains unlawful under federal law regardless of state legalisation or decriminalisation for medicinal or recreational purposes. Answering that question untruthfully is a separate federal felony exposure; this Part states that risk without quantifying a penalty from a secondary source.

12.7.2 What the 28 April 2026 Schedule III rescheduling does — and does not — do

Applying the fixed federal baseline for this run:

  • Adult-use users: adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. An adult-use user is therefore still an "unlawful user" of a controlled substance for § 922(g)(3) purposes, regardless of compliance with New Mexico adult-use law. State-law legality does not cure the federal prohibition. This is the unanimous position of the post-rescheduling secondary analyses retrieved, and no source retrieved here suggests otherwise.
  • State-licensed medical users: state-licensed medical marijuana is now Schedule III (effective 28 April 2026). A patient using cannabis in compliance with the New Mexico medical programme (qualified patient / primary caregiver / reciprocal participant, within programme limits) is therefore arguably no longer an "unlawful user" of a controlled substance, because the use is of a Schedule III substance under a state-licensed programme rather than unlawful use of a Schedule I substance. The word "arguably" is deliberate: § 922(g)(3) itself was not amended, the rescheduling order's firearms consequences have not been decided by a binding nationwide court ruling retrieved here, and the Supreme Court litigation over § 922(g)(3) (United States v. Hemani, heard in the period covered by the secondary analyses) was decided 18 June 2026: United States v. Hemani, 608 U.S. 772 (2026), 9-0 in judgment, as-applied only — 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) was NOT struck down facially, and addiction, present intoxication and individualised-danger cases were reserved . Verify the Hemani disposition and any ATF final rule before advising a patient that the prohibition no longer applies to them.
  • Hemp-derived CBD: hemp-derived CBD (within the federal hemp definition, and, after 11 December 2026, within the tightened total-THC / container-cap framework in the fixed baseline) is not marijuana use for § 922(g)(3) purposes on the sources retrieved. No New Mexico-specific CBD-and-guns rule was located. Do not extend this to marijuana-derived CBD for a non-patient, or to any THC product used outside a programme.
  • ATF draft Form 4473 (May 2026): ATF published a draft revision of Form 4473 that recasts the marijuana question to remove the medical-marijuana reference and to warn that "Federal law does not permit the use or possession of marijuana for recreational purposes." Secondary analyses retrieved agree on three points: (i) the draft is a form revision, not a statutory change; (ii) it was in a public comment period running to August 2026 (one analysis) / July 2026 (another — the discrepancy itself is flagged); and (iii) until a final revised form is in use, the existing form governs. Verify — final-form status as of 31 October 2026: whether ATF has published a final revised Form 4473, and what its marijuana question now says, was not confirmed by any ATF source retrieved in this session. Do not tell a buyer which form question they will face at a New Mexico gun counter on the basis of the draft.
  • ATF "unlawful user" definition (January 2026 interim final rule): one secondary analysis reports a January 2026 ATF interim final rule rewriting "unlawful user" as regular use over an extended period continuing into the present, without a lawful prescription or substantially different from a prescription, dropping single-incident triggers (one failed test / arrest / conviction in the past year). That analysis is not adopted here as settled: no Federal Register text was opened in this session. Verify on the Federal Register / ATF site before relying on the redefinition.

12.7.3 New Mexico state law: no state firearms disqualification located

No New Mexico statute retrieved in this session imposes a state-law firearms disqualification on medical-cannabis patients, adult-use consumers, or cardholders as such, and no New Mexico statute retrieved here creates a state-law firearms permission that overrides § 922(g)(3). Secondary summaries agree that New Mexico "has not enacted a law relating to the possession of firearms for medical marijuana patients" and that the operative restriction is federal. Those same secondary pages are, however, stale in other respects (one still states that New Mexico has not authorised recreational use, and gives superseded medical possession figures) and must not be cited for current New Mexico cannabis limits or for the federal schedule. The only proposition taken from them here is the narrow one that no NM-specific patient firearms statute was located — and that proposition is itself flagged Verify by a NMOneSource search of Title 30, Article 7 (Weapons and Explosives) and § 29-19-1 et seq. (concealed handgun licensing) before republication.

Related state points, each flagged rather than asserted:

  • New Mexico concealed-handgun licensing (§ 29-19-1 et seq.) is a state licensing regime; whether a concealed-carry licence application or renewal asks about, or is affected by, cannabis use, and whether a licence protects a carrier against the federal § 922(g)(3) prohibition, was not established by any source retrieved here. Verify. A state carry licence does not, as a matter of federal law, authorise possession by a person prohibited under § 922(g)(3) — that federal point is settled by the statute's text, but the state application-form question is not stated here.
  • Background checks (NICS) do not, on the secondary sources retrieved, reveal a New Mexico medical-card registration (which is confidential under the Compassionate Use Act framework), but a buyer who answers the Form 4473 drug question untruthfully creates independent felony exposure regardless of what NICS can see. The confidentiality point is programme-confidentiality, not a safe harbour for a false answer.
  • Spouses / household members: no New Mexico rule retrieved here addresses a non-using spouse's firearms possession in a household where another member uses cannabis. Federal "constructive possession" / household-access questions are fact-specific and are not answered here. Verify / legal advice, not a dossier answer.

12.8 Pet and veterinary products

12.8.1 No New Mexico medical-cannabis programme for animals

Animals are not qualified patients under the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act, and no New Mexico rule retrieved here admits animals to the medical programme:

  • In 2019 a petition was submitted to the Medical Cannabis Advisory Board to open the programme to pets (the petition as reported concerned epileptic dogs). The Board tabled it while seeking input from the veterinary board.
  • On 9 December 2020 the Board voted unanimously to deny the petition. Board Chair Stephanie Richmond reported that the veterinary board had declined to offer an opinion but pointed to national veterinary guidelines noting a lack of research on efficacy for animals; Board Member Davin Quinn said providing cannabis to animals "falls outside of our scope," noting the state had created separate boards for human and animal medical programmes.

Source (secondary reporting of the Board meeting): http://abq.news/2020/12/new-mexico-panel-votes-down-pot-for-pets-plan/ — accessed 31 October 2026 (published 17 December 2020). The denial is historical; no later reversal, and no 2021–2026 Board decision admitting animals, was located. Verify the current Advisory Board position if a post-2020 reversal is to be ruled out definitively — the search found no reversal, which is not the same as a Board statement that none occurred.

Consequence: there is no lawful route in New Mexico by which a veterinarian certifies, or an owner enrols, a dog, cat or other animal as a medical-cannabis patient, and no animal purchase limit, animal registry card, or animal-specific product authorisation exists in the programme rules retrieved.

12.8.2 What veterinarians may do: no NM veterinary-cannabis rule located

  • Under current federal and state law as summarised by the American Veterinary Medical Association (via the American Kennel Club's veterinary guidance, secondary), "veterinarians may not administer, dispense, prescribe or recommend cannabis or its products for animals." That AVMA summary is a national statement, not a New Mexico Board of Veterinary Medicine rule.
  • Verify — New Mexico Board of Veterinary Medicine: No guidance, rule, or disciplinary statement from the New Mexico Board of Veterinary Medicine (or the Regulation and Licensing Department's veterinary board) on cannabis/CBD discussion, recommendation, or dispensing was located in this session. Whether a New Mexico veterinarian may discuss hemp-derived CBD with a client without recommending it, and whether discussion alone risks licensure or DEA-registration consequences, is therefore not answered here. Do not import another state's veterinary-cannabis law (e.g. California's discussion-protection law) into New Mexico.
  • DEA-registration risk is noted in the secondary reporting as the reason THC dispensing for animals is "more complicated": a veterinarian holding a DEA licence places that licence in jeopardy when dispensing a federally illegal substance without explicit state authorisation. After the 2026 Schedule III rescheduling, that analysis is different for state-licensed medical (human) products and unchanged for adult-use / non-programme animal THC, because there is no state-licensed animal programme to bring animal THC within Schedule III. That distinction is the dossier's application of the fixed baseline, flagged Verify for a DEA-source check before advising a veterinarian.

12.8.3 Hemp-derived pet products (CBD treats, oils): the regulatory gap

  • No New Mexico pet-specific hemp/CBD rule was located. The NMED hemp rule (20.10.2 NMAC, eff. 28 January 2026 — Run 1 anchor) addresses hemp products generally (0.30% total THC, 2 mg/serving, 20 mg/package in the Run 1 summary); whether that rule, or any NMDA animal-feed / pet-food rule, covers products marketed for animals, with animal-specific labelling, dosage, or species warnings, was not established by any source retrieved here. Verify against 20.10.2 NMAC text and NMDA feed rules before stating that a hemp CBD pet treat is, or is not, a compliant New Mexico hemp product.
  • At the federal level, no CBD product (human or animal) other than the FDA-approved drug Epidiolex (human epilepsy) is FDA-approved, and the FDA has not approved CBD for use in animals. The CCD's pet guidance (opened, see §12.8.4) states the same point in consumer terms: health-benefit claims for pets "have not been tested or verified by the Federal Drug Administration."
  • Marketing a hemp pet product with a disease-treatment claim (e.g. "treats seizures," "treats arthritis") would raise FDA drug-claim and FTC advertising issues that are outside this Part's New Mexico scope and are not analysed here. The absence of a New Mexico pet-CBD rule does not make a therapeutic claim lawful.
  • Verify — animal cruelty / administering THC to a pet: No New Mexico statute retrieved here creates a specific offence of administering cannabis to an animal, or states the penalty for doing so. General animal-cruelty law (§ 30-18-1 NMSA 1978) was not examined in this session and must not be assumed to cover, or not to cover, a given administration. Verify before asserting an offence.

12.8.4 Accidental exposure, toxicity, and safe storage (CCD guidance, opened)

CCD, "Cannabis & Pets" FAQ, opened in full — https://www.rld.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/CannabisandPets.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026:

  • Dogs and cats can be more sensitive to cannabis than people; dogs have more cannabinoid receptors in their brains, which can dramatically increase effects and make products more toxic for dogs compared with humans. Even small amounts of cannabis or a cannabis product may be enough to develop life-threatening toxicity in a pet.
  • Exposure routes: plant / plant products (leaves, pre-rolls, buds), edibles (food or drinks containing cannabis), oils and butters, and smoke (secondhand smoke can be harmful; "Do not blow smoke in a pet's face").
  • Common signs of cannabis toxicity in pets listed by CCD: lack of balance and coordination; disorientation; dilated pupils; sensitivity to light and sound; dribbling urine; seizures; vomiting; tiredness.
  • Storage advice: keep all forms of cannabis, medical or recreational, out of reach of a pet; pets are attracted by smell (candies, chips, chocolates, baked items, flower); consider sealed containers (to reduce smell) and locked upper cabinets (closer to the ceiling) when not in use; if smoking, keep pets in a separate, well-ventilated room (or outside), away from smoke.
  • If exposure is suspected: contact an emergency veterinary service by phone and take the pet to a veterinary hospital immediately; bring any remaining product and its label (or a clear picture of the label) if possible, safely and securely stored during transit. CCD adds: do not cross state lines with cannabis, as it is currently illegal federally.

This CCD FAQ is consumer safety guidance, not a product-authorisation or veterinary-practice rule. It does not authorise giving a pet any cannabis product, and it does not state a safe THC or CBD dose for any species — no safe dose is stated in this Part, because none was located in an official source.

12.9 Medical cannabis in schools

12.9.1 The statute: § 22-33-5 NMSA 1978 (SB 204, 2019)

Enactment: Senate Bill 204, 54th Legislature, First Session (2019), "Medical Cannabis — Possession — Storage — Administration — Restriction — Exemptions," enacted a new section of the Public School Code (§ 22-33-5) and amended § 26-2B-5. Introduced by Senators Candace Gould and Gail Armstrong and Representative Jacob R. Candelaria (Legislative Health and Human Services Committee). Senate passed 18 February 2019; House passed 11 March 2019; signed by the Governor 4 April 2019 (secondary Vote Smart record); Laws 2019, ch. 261. The PED rule implementing it (6.12.10 NMAC) is effective 27 August 2019 (see §12.9.2). The 14 June 2019 effective date for SB 204 is stated in a local school policy summary (La Academia Dolores Huerta) and is flagged Verify against the session law, because the bill text retrieved does not itself state an emergency clause.

Source for the bill text (search-verified): https://www.NMLegis.gov/sessions/19%20Regular/final/SB0204.PDF — accessed 31 October 2026; https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/19%20Regular/bills/senate/SB0204.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026.

Operative duties (SB 204 § 1, search-verified text):

"Except as provided pursuant to Subsection C of this section, local school boards and the governing bodies of charter schools shall adopt policies and procedures to authorize the possession, storage and administration of medical cannabis by parents and legal guardians, or by designated school personnel, to qualified students for use in school settings; provided that: (1) a student shall not possess, store or self-administer medical cannabis in a school setting; (2) a parent, legal guardian or designated school personnel shall not administer medical cannabis in a manner that creates disruption to the educational environment or causes other students to be exposed to medical cannabis; (3) a written treatment plan for the administration of the medical cannabis is agreed to and signed by the principal or the principal's designee of the qualified student's school and the qualified student's parent or legal guardian; and (4) before the first administration of medical cannabis in a school setting, the qualified student's parent or legal guardian completes and submits documentation as required by local school board or charter school rules that includes a copy of [the] written certification for [use of] medical cannabis pursuant to the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act [and] a written statement [from the parent or legal guardian] releasing the school and school personnel from liability, except in cases of willful or wanton misconduct [text truncated in the retrieved rendering — Verify the full liability-release proviso on NMOneSource]."

A school board / charter governing body may adopt policies that: (1) restrict the types of designated school personnel who may administer medical cannabis; (2) establish reasonable parameters regarding administration and use and the school settings in which administration and use are authorised; and (3) ban student possession, use, distribution, sale or being under the influence of a cannabis product in a manner inconsistent with § 22-33-5.

Federal-funding exemption (SB 204 § 1(C), search-verified in substance): § 22-33-5(A) does not apply to a charter school or school district if that school/district reasonably demonstrates that it would lose, or has lost, federal funding (by reason of the medical-cannabis-in-schools provisions). The full demonstration standard and the consequence (suspension of the policy) are stated in local policies as immediate suspension if the federal government indicates federal funds are jeopardised — that local-policy formulation is not the statute's text and is flagged Verify against § 22-33-5(C) itself.

Anti-discipline / anti-exclusion protections (SB 204 § 1(D), search-verified in substance): a public school, charter school or school district shall not: (1) discipline a qualified student on the basis that the student requires medical cannabis as a reasonable accommodation necessary to attend school; (2) deny eligibility to attend school (or a school-sponsored activity) to a qualified student on that basis; or (3) discipline a school employee who refuses to administer medical cannabis [full text of the employee-refusal limb was truncated in the retrieved rendering — Verify]. These protections are tied to the student being a qualified student (see §12.9.2) and to the § 22-33-5 procedure being followed; they are not a general permission for a student to possess or use cannabis at school outside that procedure.

12.9.2 The rule: 6.12.10 NMAC, "Medical Cannabis in Schools" (PED)

Title 6, Chapter 12, Part 10 NMAC. Issuing agency: Public Education Department. Statutory authority: §§ 9-24-8, 22-2-1, 22-2-2 and 22-33-5 NMSA 1978. Duration: permanent. Effective date: 27 August 2019 (unless a later date is cited at the end of a section). Objective: to provide parameters for the possession, storage, and administration of medical cannabis to qualified students for use in school settings.

Source (search-verified, SRCA compilation): https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title06/06.012.0010.pdf — accessed 31 October 2026. Note: the direct open of this PDF was rate-limited (see header); the provisions below rest on the search-returned text of that compilation and on local policies that implement it, and are therefore labelled Search-verified. A NMOneSource / SRCA re-open is required before quoting 6.12.10 verbatim in republication.

Key definitions and mechanics (search-verified):

  • "Qualified student" means a student who demonstrates evidence to the school that the student is authorised as a qualified patient under the Lynn and Erin Compassionate Use Act (written, signed certification by a certifying practitioner for a debilitating medical condition, and current DOH registry enrolment).
  • "Designated school personnel" means a school employee whom a public school, charter school, or school district authorises to possess, store and administer medical cannabis to a qualified student in accordance with § 22-33-5, 6.12.10 NMAC, the Compassionate Use Act, and DOH rules.
  • "Licensee" / "licensee representative": for 6.12.10 purposes, school districts / local school boards / charter schools and their governing bodies are deemed licensees, and designated school personnel are deemed licensee representatives, authorised within their scope of employment (and licensure, if applicable) to possess and store medical cannabis for this purpose. This is a deeming device for the school setting; it does not make a school a cannabis retailer or producer.
  • "School setting" (local-policy rendering, search-verified — Verify against 6.12.10.7): any of the following during a school day: a school building; a school bus or activity vehicle used within the state during, in transit to or in transit from a school-sponsored activity; a public vehicle used within the state during, in transit to or in transit from a school-sponsored activity in the state; or a public site in the state where a school-sponsored activity takes place.
  • "Self-administering" means ingestion by a qualified student without the presence of a primary caregiver or designated school personnel in a school setting — which § 22-33-5(A)(1) prohibits.
  • Written treatment plan: must include the certifying practitioner's diagnosis / affirmation of a qualifying debilitating condition, the recommended dosage allotment, the recommended frequency of administration in a school setting, and the signatures of the primary caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and the certifying practitioner; it is agreed to and signed by the principal / principal's designee and the parent/guardian. Local policies state the plan is valid for no more than one year from issuance and must be presented before the school year or when obtained — the one-year validity is a local-policy statement retrieved here, flagged Verify against 6.12.10.9/10 before stating it as a rule requirement.
  • Storage: policies must require a secure location with a locked storage container accessible only by designated school personnel; medical cannabis used in a school setting outside school premises must be immediately returned to a locked storage container; designated personnel responsible for storage must return any unused medical cannabis to the primary caregiver at the end of each school year or upon disenrollment, withdrawal, transfer, or graduation, whichever occurs first (6.12.10.9, search-verified).
  • Training: districts must provide appropriate / annual training to school personnel on medical-cannabis policies (6.12.10.9(6), search-verified; local policies frame it as at least annual training).
  • Student discipline for inconsistent use: each school district and charter school shall ban a student's possession, use, distribution, sale, or being under the influence of a cannabis product in a manner inconsistent with the Compassionate Use Act / § 22-33-5 / 6.12.10 (6.12.10.11, search-verified). No school shall discipline a qualified student on the basis that the student requires medical cannabis as a reasonable accommodation necessary to attend school (6.12.10.11(B), search-verified).

12.9.3 Local variation and limits — what schools actually do, and what is not covered

Local policies retrieved (Deming Cesar Chavez Charter High School, Policy JK; Public Academy for Performing Arts, Policy E.2.16.2; Mountain Mahogany Community School, Draft JL04; La Academia Dolores Huerta policy) all implement the same skeleton — parent/guardian or designated personnel only, no student possession/self-administration, written treatment plan, locked storage, HIPAA authorisation for DOH enrolment verification in at least one policy — but they differ in operational detail, and at least one (Deming) states that medical cannabis cannot be administered to a qualifying student while aboard a school bus or at a school-sponsored event, and that the policy conveys no right to demand access to any particular location on school property, a bus, or a school-sponsored event. That local restriction is narrower than the broad "school setting" definition above and illustrates why a parent must check the specific school's policy, not just the statute: a district/charter may, under § 22-33-5(B)(2), establish reasonable parameters on the settings in which administration is authorised.

Not covered / Verify:

  • Private schools: § 22-33-5 and 6.12.10 by their terms apply to school districts, local school boards, and state-chartered / locally chartered charter schools and their governing bodies. No provision retrieved here extends the possession/storage/administration authorisation to private schools. A private school's position is governed by its own policy and by general law — Verify before stating anything about private schools.
  • Post-secondary institutions (universities, colleges): no provision retrieved here addresses medical cannabis administration by or for a university student on campus, in dormitories, or at university events. University housing / drug-free-campus federal funding rules are a separate overlay and are not analysed here.
  • Form / route of administration at school: no source retrieved here states whether smoking/vaping is permitted as a school administration route, or whether administration is in practice limited to non-inhaled forms. The statute's "no disruption / no exposure to other students" condition would, in practice, rule out smoking in a shared school setting, but that inference is flagged Verify — do not state a route ban without a 6.12.10 / local-policy text.
  • Adult-use cannabis at school: § 22-33-5 is a medical-only regime for qualified students. Adult-use possession or use by a student, or possession/use on school grounds outside the qualified-student procedure, remains subject to school discipline and to § 26-2C-29 (cannabis within a restricted area, including school/daycare premises — Run 1 §1.2 cross-reference; the penalty for § 26-2C-29 was described in a 2024 agency analysis as a misdemeanour, search-verified only — Verify the current § 26-2C-29 text before publishing a penalty).
  • Counts: no official count of qualified students receiving medical cannabis in a school setting, or of schools with a § 22-33-5 policy in place, was retrieved. Unavailable.
